docs.title: Generative AI and Automated Tools for Circuit Diagram Creation
Introduction
docs.text: Creating clear circuit schematics from textual descriptions is a long-standing challenge. Unlike standard images, circuit diagrams demand precise control of symbols, connections, and labels. Recent advances combine generative AI with automation to translate either natural language or structured code into high-quality analog and digital circuit diagrams. This report surveys current tools and methods that accept descriptions of circuits (in plain English or in code) and output well-laid-out schematics. We focus on solutions that integrate with Markdown or browser-based workflows (e.g. via SVG or JavaScript), support Python/JavaScript environments, and offer productivity features like auto-layout and reusable components. Emphasis is on open-source or cost-effective tools suitable for instructors building English-language course materials.

docs.title: Circuit Description DSLs and Code Libraries
docs.text:
One approach is to use domain-specific languages or libraries to describe circuits as code, then automatically render the schematic. For example, Schemdraw is a Python library that allows step-by-step drawing of circuit elements via code. It produces publication-quality schematics by letting you add components one at a time "similar to how you might draw them by hand" using Python methods. Schemdraw supports many common circuit symbols (resistors, capacitors, sources, etc.) and outputs images (including SVG or PNG). In a Markdown or Jupyter notebook workflow, an instructor can programmatically generate a circuit diagram with just a few lines of Python and embed the resulting image.

Another code-driven toolset is SKiDL, a Python EDA library that represents circuits as Python objects (netlists). While SKiDL was originally for generating PCB netlists, it now supports schematic generation. SKiDL can export a schematic to an SVG image using NetlistSVG under the hood. In this pipeline, the instructor writes a SKiDL script defining components and connections (a "structured" input). By calling generate_svg() at the end, SKiDL invokes NetlistSVG to produce an SVG schematic automatically. The output uses standard KiCad-style symbols for each component, so the diagrams look professional. Notably, SKiDL/NetlistSVG handles placing the symbols and routing connections (using auto-layout algorithms, discussed below), sparing the user from manual drawing. This facilitates reusing circuit definitions: the same SKiDL code can generate a netlist for simulation or an SVG for documentation, which is very useful for instructors.

A more traditional DSL approach is CircuitTikZ (a LaTeX package). In CircuitTikZ, one writes textual commands in a LaTeX document to place circuit components and wires, and the LaTeX compiler renders a high-quality schematic. This method isn't AI-driven, but it's a proven open-source solution for text-to-diagram conversion. It can be integrated into markdown-based workflows by compiling the LaTeX to PDF/SVG and embedding the image. CircuitTikZ offers fine control over layout and is often used in academic materials. However, writing TikZ code manually has a steep learning curve. Some researchers have used generative AI to bridge this gap -- for instance, by training LLMs to produce CircuitTikZ code automatically. In summary, DSLs like CircuitTikZ or code libraries like Schemdraw/SKiDL provide a foundation for structured circuit description, which can then be automated into diagrams.

docs.title: Auto-Layout and Graph-Based Rendering
docs.text:
A key aspect of automated schematic drawing is automatic layout -- deciding where to place each symbol and how to route connections for clarity. General graph layout engines (like Graphviz or ELK) have been applied to circuit schematics with mixed success. An illustrative toolchain here is NetlistSVG, a Node.js/JavaScript tool that "draws an SVG schematic from a Yosys JSON netlist" (the output of a digital logic synthesis). NetlistSVG uses the ELK graph layout library to arrange gates and wires automatically. Originally designed for gate-level digital circuits, it now includes symbol "skins" for both logic gates and analog components. This means you can feed NetlistSVG a structured netlist (e.g. a JSON file describing gates or a list of components and nodes) and get back a neatly routed schematic in SVG format. In a teaching workflow, one could use an HDL (like Verilog or VHDL) to describe a logic circuit, synthesize it to a netlist (using an open tool like Yosys), then use NetlistSVG to automatically generate a gate-level diagram. The result can be embedded directly into course notes as an SVG image. NetlistSVG's algorithm tends to produce a layered, readable diagram (e.g. logic inputs on left, outputs on right, signals routed orthogonally), which addresses the major challenge that a human would otherwise face arranging a complex schematic.

Another open-source solution, closely related to NetlistSVG, is d3-hwschematic. This is a JavaScript library by Nic30 that also leverages ELK for layout and is designed for interactive schematics in documentation. It accepts an ELK-formatted JSON graph as input and renders an interactive diagram (using D3.js). The focus of d3-hwschematic is on digital hardware documentation (it's part of a tool ecosystem for HDL design). For instance, Nic30 provides a Sphinx plugin (sphinx-hwt) that can insert these auto-generated schematics into HTML docs automatically. This kind of integration is valuable for instructors writing course content in Sphinx or Markdown -- the circuit diagram can be generated on the fly from a JSON or Python description and embedded, rather than stored as a static image. The productivity boost comes from not having to manually draw or adjust the schematic; the layout engine handles it consistently.

It's worth noting that auto-layout for analog circuits (as opposed to logic gate networks) is inherently harder, since there isn't always a clear left-to-right signal flow. Tools like NetlistSVG do have an analog mode, and SKiDL's use of KiCad symbols plus ELK can handle moderate analog schematics (e.g. op-amp circuits, filters) with decent results. They place components in a logical graph structure (for example, power rails at top/bottom, signal path left-to-right). While the result might not rival a human-designed layout for very complex analog schematics, it is often acceptable for classroom examples, and far quicker than manual drawing. Minor adjustments (like labeling inputs/outputs or reordering parallel branches) can be done by tweaking the input netlist or using provided hints (such as SKiDL's netio attributes to mark input/output nodes for the layout).

docs.title: LLMs for Circuit Diagram Generation
docs.text:
The rise of large language models has opened up new possibilities for generating diagrams from natural language. In the realm of circuits, one cutting-edge example is Schemato, a specialized LLM developed to convert circuit netlists into human-readable schematics. Schemato treats netlist-to-schematic as a "language translation" problem, outputting either an LTspice schematic file or LaTeX CircuitTikZ code. Impressively, it achieves a 93% success rate on netlist-to-TikZ conversion (versus only 26% using a general GPT-4 approach). This indicates that with fine-tuning, LLMs can learn the structured task of formatting a correct circuit diagram. Schemato's output is intended to be compiled into actual schematics, bridging the gap between an ML-generated netlist (often the result of AI circuit synthesis) and a readable diagram for engineers. While Schemato itself may be a research project, it exemplifies how generative AI can aid automation: an instructor could potentially use a future LLM-based tool to write a plain description or provide a SPICE netlist and get back a schematic drawing without manual coding. Such an AI assistant would greatly accelerate creating examples and homework solutions in educational settings.

Another forward-looking system is DiagrammerGPT (2024), which, though not circuit-specific, is designed for text-to-diagram generation using a hybrid of LLM planning and image generation. DiagrammerGPT uses GPT-4 to first produce a detailed "diagram plan" (listing all objects, connections, and their layout coordinates) and then renders the image with a graphics engine. While its authors focused on diagrams like flowcharts or biological processes, the approach is general-purpose. In principle, a similar two-stage method could be applied to circuit diagrams: the LLM would output a list of components (with positions and connection lines), and a renderer would draw the schematic symbols accordingly. DiagrammerGPT even demonstrates generating vector-graphic outputs for editing in tools like Inkscape. For circuits, an "open-platform" vector output is ideal (since instructors might want to tweak the final diagram). We might envision an experimental system where an instructor types: "Draw a logic diagram of a 2-to-4 decoder using AND and NOT gates", and an LLM-guided tool produces an SVG schematic of the decoder, correctly laid out. While this level of natural language schematic synthesis is still emerging, DiagrammerGPT's success with other diagram types suggests it's on the horizon.

docs.title: ChatGPT and Code Generation Hacks
docs.text:
Even without specialized models, inventive users have leveraged general LLMs (like ChatGPT) for circuit diagrams. One practical tip from the electronics community is to have the LLM produce a structured description (code or netlist) rather than an ASCII art drawing. For example, if you ask ChatGPT to "draw a monostable 555 timer circuit," it might attempt a crude text art schematic which is hard to read. However, if you instead prompt it to "generate a SPICE netlist for a 555 monostable" or "write TikZ code for the circuit," the LLM is more likely to output a machine-readable description. A Reddit user reported success with this approach -- "Ask it to generate a netlist instead." -- and then feeding that netlist into a schematic tool. This two-step workflow (LLM → intermediate code → diagram via another tool) plays to the strengths of each: the LLM uses its knowledge to create the connection list, and a deterministic renderer ensures the layout is correct. For instance, ChatGPT could generate a list of components and nodes, which you then pass to SKiDL or NetlistSVG to visualize. Similarly, one could ask for Python code targeting the Schemdraw API (ChatGPT can often produce plausible code for known libraries), and then run that code to get an image. This "AI-assisted coding" method is essentially using the LLM as a helper to write the input for the actual diagram generator. It's a cost-effective way to introduce natural language convenience: the instructor describes the circuit in English to ChatGPT, and with a bit of iteration obtains scriptable output that yields the diagram.

It should be noted that pure end-to-end text-to-diagram with a general AI (without human in the loop) is still imperfect in 2025. One must verify the AI's output (it might draw an incorrect connection or choose a non-ideal layout without guidance). However, the landscape is rapidly improving. As we've seen, specialized models like Schemato and DiagrammerGPT are pushing the boundary, and they might soon be integrated into user-friendly tools. For now, instructors can experiment with LLMs to generate diagram source code, or use open platforms like Eraser's DiagramGPT (a web tool for generating diagrams from English) to see if they support basic circuit symbols. The convergence of LLMs with established libraries (e.g., an AI that internally uses CircuitTikZ or SchemDraw) is a promising area for research-grade tools that may become classroom-ready in the near future.

docs.title: Browser-Based and Interactive Diagram Tools
docs.text: Some instructors may want interactive circuit visuals or the ability to embed diagrams directly in a web page (for online textbooks or slides). A number of JavaScript libraries can fulfill this need:

docs.title: DigitalJS
docs.text: This is a teaching-focused digital logic simulator that runs entirely in the browser. Developed by Marek Materzok, DigitalJS takes a circuit (defined in a JSON format or even via a converted Verilog file) and produces a live circuit diagram with simulation capabilities. It was created to help students learn digital design, and it can display logic gate diagrams complete with toggle-able inputs and outputs. The layout in DigitalJS is automated to some degree and optimized for simulation (it will arrange gates and draw wires, then allow the user to simulate signal changes). To use it in materials, one can either embed the DigitalJS applet for an interactive experience or export a static image of the circuit. Because DigitalJS is open-source, it's freely available for integration. It shines for digital circuits where being able to simulate within the diagram is a bonus (e.g., demonstrating a flip-flop's behavior). For pure schematic generation, its visuals are serviceable though perhaps less polished than NetlistSVG's (since simulation imposes some layout constraints).

docs.title: Logisim and Forks
docs.text: (e.g. Digital by hneemann) Logisim is a classic open-source logic circuit drawing tool. Modern forks like hneemann's Digital have added features like VHDL/Verilog import. These are GUI programs rather than code-driven engines, but some can be scripted or used headlessly to render circuits. For example, Digital can load a circuit file and export an image via command-line. This could be used in an automated workflow, but it's somewhat heavyweight and not as web-friendly as the JS libraries.

docs.title: Circuit Diagram Web Editor
docs.text: (circuit-diagram.org) This is a browser-based schematic editor for analog circuits. It's not text-driven or AI-driven -- it requires manual assembly of the circuit on-screen -- but because it's web-based and free, an instructor could use it to quickly draw a circuit and then export an SVG. It doesn't integrate with Markdown automatically, but the exported SVG can be pasted into markdown. The tool does have an open JSON format for saved circuits, though no auto-layout from that format (the user still positions the parts). Thus, while useful for quick manual drawing, it doesn't meet the "generate from code or language" criterion directly.

docs.title: p5.js or D3 custom scripts
docs.text: For maximum flexibility, one can always write a custom JavaScript (or p5.js) script to draw a circuit diagram on an HTML5 canvas or SVG. This is essentially creating your own mini library -- for instance, defining functions to draw a gate or resistor at coordinates, and writing an algorithm to position them. As an example, one Stack Overflow user described a JSON structure for series/parallel circuits and sought to draw it with p5.js automatically. Achieving high-quality layout with a custom script is difficult, so most people prefer to leverage existing layout engines. Nonetheless, if a very specific visualization or animation is needed (say, animating current flow in a circuit for a demo), a p5.js sketch with hard-coded placement can be integrated into Markdown via embedded iframes or <script> tags. The trade-off is development time versus using an existing tool. For most educational content, the dedicated libraries (Schemdraw, NetlistSVG, etc.) are preferable because they already implement standard schematic conventions (so you don't have to reinvent symbol drawing or layout algorithms).

docs.title: Integration into Markdown Workflows
docs.text:
A major consideration is how these tools fit into an instructor's content creation workflow, especially if using Markdown or Jupyter notebooks. Here we compare capabilities and integration options:

Tool / Method Input Format Output Integration Use Cases & Limits Schemdraw (Python) Python API calls (one per part) SVG, PNG, etc. image Use in Jupyter or script; embed image Great for small analog circuits; manual sequence of element placement (no global auto-place). Open-source. No natural language input. --- --- --- --- --- SKiDL + NetlistSVG Python circuit code (SKiDL) → JSON netlist SVG image Automate in Python, output SVG to file or inline Good for analog or digital. Auto-layout via ELK yields neat schematics. Requires Node (for NetlistSVG) setup. Open-source. CircuitTikZ (LaTeX) LaTeX code (TikZ DSL) PDF or SVG (compiled) Compile as part of LaTeX docs or via command-line, then embed Professional-quality output for any circuit. Fully manual coding (unless assisted by AI). Open-source. Steeper learning curve. NetlistSVG (CLI/JS) Yosys JSON netlist (digital), or custom JSON (analog) SVG image (static) Node.js CLI (generate file); or embed via <script> in browser for dynamic use Excellent for logic gate diagrams from HDL. Analog support basic but available. No interactive features (static render). d3-hwschematic (JS) JSON (ELK graph format) SVG/HTML (interactive) Include library in web page; or use Sphinx plugin for docs Useful for documentation with interactive highlighting. Requires more setup (web dev skills). Open-source. Primarily digital (HDL) focused. DigitalJS (JS) JSON circuit or Verilog (via converter) Canvas/SVG (interactive) Embed the DigitalJS viewer in HTML (requires hosting its scripts) Great for live simulation of logic circuits in-browser. Layout is auto but oriented to simulation. Open-source. Not aimed at printed/static schematic aesthetics. LLM-based (experimental) English description or netlist Varies (ASCII art, code, or image via tool) Currently via external services or research code Emerging tech -- e.g., Schemato generates TikZ code from netlist. ChatGPT can produce partial diagrams or code. Not yet plug-and-play; results may require verification.

docs.title: Integration tips
docs.text:
In a Markdown environment (such as Jupyter Notebook, MkDocs, or GitHub Pages), the simplest integration is to generate an SVG or PNG file of the schematic and then reference it in the Markdown. Tools like Schemdraw or SKiDL (with NetlistSVG) can be scripted to save their output image as part of a build process. The SVG format is ideal because it scales and can be inlined. For example, an instructor using Jupyter could write a SKiDL circuit in a cell, call generate_svg(), and display the SVG output directly in the notebook. Similarly, in a static Markdown site, one could use a preprocessor or plugin to run a Schemdraw script and inject the resulting image. Some static site generators allow custom diagram plugins (for instance, there are Markdown extensions for Graphviz or Mermaid diagrams; a similar extension could be made for circuit diagrams using these tools).

For the JavaScript approaches, integration might involve embedding a <script> that draws the diagram when the page loads. This is feasible but requires that the Markdown pipeline supports raw HTML/JS (which many do). The advantage is true interactivity (e.g., a DigitalJS embed where students can flip a switch in the circuit within the web page). The disadvantage is complexity and potential loading time or browser compatibility issues. In many cases, a static image is sufficient for course notes, while an interactive widget might be used sparingly for demonstrations.

docs.title: Productivity features for instructors
docs.text: Many users are well-served by the above tools: auto-layout greatly reduces fiddling with positions, auto-labeling of nets or pins keeps the diagram clear (most tools label node names or allow you to specify labels, and will place them near wires automatically). Reuse is enabled by code-based definitions -- you can define a subcircuit once in SKiDL or Schemdraw (or as a TikZ style) and use it in multiple diagrams. Open-source availability means these solutions are either free or have negligible cost, especially compared to proprietary EDA software. They also avoid the licensing and installation hurdles of heavy desktop tools; many run in the browser or via simple Python packages.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
In summary, the ecosystem for generating circuit diagrams from descriptions is rapidly evolving. Mature code-centric tools (like Schemdraw, SKiDL, CircuitTikZ) let you script high-quality schematics with fine control and integrate those into markdown-based workflows. Meanwhile, automation and AI-driven methods (like NetlistSVG's auto-layout or LLM-powered schematic generation) are reducing the manual effort needed to produce clear circuit visuals. For digital logic and classroom logic gate diagrams, tools leveraging graph layout (NetlistSVG, d3-hwschematic) excel at producing neat SVG renderings that can be embedded seamlessly. For analog schematics, structured drawing libraries and some AI assistance can save time, though complex analog layouts may still need occasional manual adjustment. Crucially, many solutions are open-source and can be tied into Python or JavaScript, fitting modern teaching workflows that favor Jupyter notebooks and browser-based content.

As experimental projects like Schemato and DiagrammerGPT show, we're on the cusp of even more intuitive options -- where one might simply describe a circuit and let an AI figure out both the connections and an elegant drawing. Until then, instructors can mix and match the tools surveyed here to achieve a high level of productivity: for instance, using ChatGPT to draft a netlist, refining it, and then rendering it with an auto-layout tool. By leveraging these generative and automated approaches, educators can generate clear, accurate circuit diagrams with significantly less effort, ensuring that the visuals in their course materials keep pace with the content itself.

Sources: The information above was gathered from tool documentation, research papers, and user reports, including Schemdraw's official docs, the SKiDL project page, NetlistSVG's repository, and recent academic work on diagram generation, among others. Each cited source is referenced in the text to provide further details on the capabilities and context.

docs.title: Signal Processing MicroSims
docs.text: Interactive Micro Simulations to help students learn signal processing fundamentals. Every MicroSim runs in your browser, uses p5.js 2.x, and has a lesson plan with activities and assessment questions.

docs.title: Signal Processing MicroSims
docs.text:
• 2-D Convolution and Image Filtering

    Slide a 3×3 or 5×5 kernel over a small grayscale image and see every multiply-add: blur, sharpen, Sobel and Laplacian kernels, padding, flipping and noise.

  • A Convolutional Layer Is a Learned FIR Filter

    Train a tiny 1-D convolutional network in the browser and watch its kernels become band-pass FIR filters tuned to the tones it must tell apart.

  • Adaptive Algorithm Comparison Tool

    LMS, NLMS and RLS identify the same unknown FIR plant from the same noisy data. Compare convergence speed, steady-state error, stability and tracking.

  • Adaptive Noise and Echo Cancellation

    One NLMS adaptive filter, three jobs - noise cancellation with a reference input, acoustic echo cancellation with double-talk, and channel equalization.

  • Analog Modulation

    Compare amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM) of a sine carrier by a sine message, in time and as a line spectrum with its bandwidth.

  • Basic FFT MicroSim

    A sine-wave generator with its live FFT - the waveform in the time domain on top and its magnitude spectrum below, with frequency and amplitude sliders.

  • Bass and Treble Amplifier Controls

    Frequency response of an amplifier's bass and treble controls, drawn as gain in dB against log frequency, with two sliders and a mouse probe that reads the gain.

  • Bilinear Transform and Frequency Warping

    Compare the bilinear transform and impulse invariance - frequency warping, prewarping, aliasing near Nyquist and how s-plane poles map into the z-plane.

  • Citation Graph for FFT on Microcontrollers

    Explore a 15-paper citation graph of FFT research on microcontrollers. Filter by research area and citation count, then compare three layouts.

  • Complex Plane

    Interactive visualization of complex numbers in the complex plane, showing both rectangular (a + bi) and polar (r angle theta) forms with geometric representations.

  • Compressed Sensing

    Recover a sparse spectrum of k tones from m random time samples with orthogonal matching pursuit, and compare it with the minimum-energy solution and uniform sampling.

  • Convolution

    A blue square slides across a red triangle while a purple gauge shows the area of overlap, the introductory picture of convolution.

  • Convolution Theorem and Circular Convolution

    Compare linear convolution with L-point circular convolution computed as IDFT(DFT(x)·DFT(h)), and watch the tail wrap around when L < N + M − 1.

  • Convolution Visualizer

    Step through the flip-and-slide picture of convolution. The impulse response is time-reversed, shifted, multiplied by the input, and the area under the product builds the output y(t).

  • Correlation and Matched Filtering

    Find copies of a known template hidden in noise by cross-correlating the received signal with the template, and compare the matched filter with a simple moving average.

  • DCT Basis Explorer

    Explore the 8-point DCT-II basis functions and the 64 basis images of the 8x8 DCT, and see why energy compaction makes the DCT the core of JPEG.

  • DFT Explorer

    Build each DFT value X[k] by multiplying x[n] by a rotating phasor and adding the products head to tail, then rebuild x[n] from the bins you keep.

  • Euler's Formula Explorer

    Watch the point e^(iθ) travel around the unit circle while its real and imaginary parts trace the cosine and sine waves, with live numeric read-outs.

  • Even and Odd Signal Decomposition

    Decompose a preset or hand-drawn signal x(t) into its even part and odd part, read the worked calculation at a probe time, and verify that the two parts sum back to x(t).

  • FFT Butterfly

    Step through the input reordering of a radix-2 FFT, splitting every group into even and odd samples until they sit in bit-reversed order.

  • FFT Live Audio from Microphone

    A live spectrum analyzer for your microphone with adjustable smoothness and FFT size, showing bin width, window length and the strongest peak.

  • FFT of Sound File

    A music player with a track list that shows the waveform and the FFT frequency spectrum of the song you are listening to.

  • FFT Size MicroSim

    A sine wave analysed with FFT sizes from 512 to 8192 bins. Larger FFTs give narrower bins and peaks but need a longer analysis window.

  • FFT Spectrum Analyzer

    Analyze test signals or the microphone with a radix-2 FFT, choosing FFT size, window and a magnitude, dB or phase display, with peak markers and a spectrogram.

  • FFT Waveform Types

    Compare the harmonic spectra of sine, square, triangle and sawtooth waves - which harmonics each shape contains and how fast they decay.

  • FFT with Multiple Frequency Components

    Three sine-wave oscillators are added together - the combined waveform in the time domain and its FFT spectrum with one labelled peak per component.

  • FFT with Two Oscillators

    A sine and a cosine oscillator are added and played; see their sum in the time domain and one FFT peak per oscillator in the magnitude spectrum.

  • Filter Bank and Polyphase Explorer

    Split a signal into M subbands with a cosine-modulated filter bank, measure the reconstruction error, and see why polyphase decimation is M times cheaper.

  • FIR Filter Design Comparison Tool

    Compare two linear-phase FIR designs (window method, frequency sampling or Parks-McClellan) for the same specification, with measured ripple, attenuation and transition width.

  • FIR vs IIR Filters

    Compare an FIR windowed-sinc and an IIR Butterworth low-pass with the same cutoff - response, phase, delay, cost and stability under coefficient rounding.

  • Fourier Series Explorer

    Build square, triangle, sawtooth, pulse and hand-drawn waveforms from their first N harmonics; read each harmonic's amplitude, phase and the Gibbs overshoot.

  • Fourier Transform Pairs

    Explore five classic Fourier transform pairs and the time-scaling and time-shift properties, with each analytic X(f) checked against an FFT estimate.

  • Frequency Detection

    A winding machine wraps a sine wave around a spinning circle; the center of mass of the wound curve reveals the signal frequency, as the Fourier transform does.

  • Huffman Coding

    Build a Huffman tree one merge at a time, read off the prefix-free code, and compare the average code length L with the entropy H and a fixed-length code.

  • IIR Prototype Comparison

    Compare Butterworth, Chebyshev I and II, elliptic and Bessel low-pass prototypes at the same order - magnitude, phase, group delay, step response and poles.

  • Impulse and Frequency Response Analyzer

    See the impulse response, step response, magnitude response and phase response of five LTI systems side by side, with linked cursors and sliders for cutoff frequency, filter order and damping ratio.

  • Interactive Filter Design and Analysis Tool

    Design low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop, notch, comb and all-pass filters as IIR or FIR and see their responses, poles, stability and effect on three tones.

  • Interactive Pole-Zero Analysis Tool

    Place poles and zeros on the z-plane and watch the magnitude response, phase response, impulse response, step response and stability verdict of the discrete-time system update.

  • Interactive Spectrogram Parameter Explorer

    Compare two spectrograms of one signal or your microphone, each with its own window length, overlap, window, zero padding, dB floor and color map.

  • Interactive STFT Spectrogram Analyzer

    Compare short- and long-window STFT spectrograms of one test signal and use cursors to see what each window can and cannot separate in time and frequency.

  • Microphone Frequency Visualization with FFT

    A real-time spectrum analyzer for your microphone. An FFT turns live sound into colored frequency bars with a decibel scale and a peak-frequency read-out.

  • Multirate Sample Rate Converter

    Change a signal's sample rate by L/M and watch zero insertion create images, downsampling fold aliases, and the low-pass filter remove both.

  • Möbius Transform

    Drag the coefficients of w = (Az + B)/(Cz + D), draw in the z-plane and watch lines and circles map, including the bilinear transform used for IIR filters.

  • Noise Analysis and Reduction Tool

    Generate white, pink, brown, band-limited and impulsive noise, measure its histogram, autocorrelation and Welch PSD, and see SNR improve with averaging and filtering.

  • Nyquist-Shannon Sampling

    Sample a 5 Hz sine wave at 1 to 50 Hz and compare ideal sinc and straight-line reconstructions to see the Nyquist rate and aliasing at work.

  • Phase Spectrum - What the Magnitude Hides

    Same magnitude spectrum, different phases, different waveforms. Explore harmonic phases, the linear phase of a time shift, and the magnitude/phase swap experiment.

  • Phasor Addition

    Add up to three sinusoids by adding their rotating phasors head to tail, read the resultant amplitude and phase, and see beats when one frequency differs.

  • Power Spectral Density and the Wiener-Khinchin Theorem

    Estimate a PSD two ways, by averaged periodograms and by the Fourier transform of the sample autocorrelation, and compare both with the exact S(ω).

  • Probability Distribution Explorer

    Sample uniform, Gaussian, exponential, binomial and Poisson distributions, compare sample and true mean and variance, and watch the central limit theorem.

  • Quantization and Noise Shaping

    Quantize a full-scale waveform with 1 to 16 bits, see the quantization error and its spectrum, and measure how oversampling and noise shaping raise the SQNR in the signal band.

  • RC Low-Pass Filter Bode Plot

    Set R and C of an RC low-pass filter and watch its Bode plot, with the corner frequency fc = 1/(2πRC), the -3 dB and -45° points, and the -20 dB/decade roll-off.

  • Real-Time Processing Simulator

    Explore block size, latency, processor load and deadlines in a double-buffered real-time FIR filter running on an MCU, Cortex-M4, DSP or FPGA.

  • s-Plane Explorer

    Drag poles and zeros in the s-plane and watch the frequency response along the jω axis, the step response, the ROC, stability, and the z = e^(sT) map.

  • Sampling Theorem Explorer

    Sample a sine wave at an adjustable rate, rebuild it from its samples, and see why a tone above the Nyquist frequency folds to a lower alias frequency.

  • Signal Operations - Shift, Scale and Reverse

    Transform elementary signals by time shifting, time scaling and time reversal, and track which points of x(t) map to which points of y(t).

  • Signal Processing Timeline

    Pan and zoom a timeline of 50 milestones in the history of electronic signal processing, from the telegraph in 1837 to cloud-based processing in 2022.

  • Signal Type Explorer

    Compare continuous-time and discrete-time views of four basic signals and see how amplitude, frequency, phase, shift and scale affect energy, power and RMS.

  • Sine Wave

    Plot y(t) = A sin(2πt/T + φ) and use three sliders to see how amplitude, period and phase change a sine wave, with frequency and time-shift read-outs.

  • Sound Reverb Effect

    Play a music clip through a convolution reverb, set the decay time and the dry/wet mix, and watch the reverb tail fade after the source stops.

  • Spectral Leakage and Windowing

    Move a tone between DFT bin centres to see spectral leakage, then compare how rectangular, Hamming, Hanning, Blackman and Kaiser windows trade main-lobe width against side-lobe level.

  • Synth Timeline

    A scrollable timeline of ten landmark synthesizers, from the 1920 Theremin to the 1987 Roland D-50, in three color-coded categories.

  • System Interconnections - Series, Parallel, Feedback

    Connect gain, low-pass and delay blocks in series, parallel, negative feedback or feedforward and see the overall H(z), its poles, stability and responses.

  • System Property Explorer

    Run linearity, time-invariance, causality and BIBO stability tests on eight example systems and see which properties each system has, and why.

  • Time-Frequency Analysis Explorer

    Compute spectrograms of a chirp, an FSK signal and a note sequence, and vary the STFT window length, overlap and type to see the time-frequency trade-off.

  • Tone Generator MicroSim

    A sine-wave tone generator with a live FFT spectrum - hear the tone, set its frequency and amplitude, and watch its single spectral peak move.

  • Wavelet Explorer - CWT Scalogram and Haar DWT

    Compare a continuous wavelet transform scalogram (Morlet, Mexican hat, Haar) with a multilevel Haar DWT, and denoise a signal by hard thresholding.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim runs a system-identification experiment. An unknown FIR plant \(\mathbf{w}_o\) (scaled to unit energy) is driven by an input \(x[n]\) of power \(\sigma_x^2 = 1\), and white noise \(v[n]\) of power \(\sigma_v^2\) is added to its output: \(d[n] = \mathbf{w}_o^T\mathbf{x}[n] + v[n]\). Three \(M\)-tap adaptive filters learn \(\mathbf{w}_o\) from exactly the same data:

  • LMS (blue): \(\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \mu\, e[n]\,\mathbf{x}[n]\)
  • NLMS (green): \(\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \tilde{\mu}\, e[n]\,\mathbf{x}[n] / (\epsilon + \|\mathbf{x}[n]\|^2)\)
  • RLS (maroon): \(\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{x} / (\lambda + \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{P}\mathbf{x})\), \(\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{k}\,e[n]\), \(\mathbf{P} \leftarrow (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{k}\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{P})/\lambda\), starting from \(\mathbf{P}(0) = \mathbf{I}/\delta\)

The learning curves plot the error power \(e^2[n]\) in dB, averaged over 1-20 runs and over blocks of 5 iterations. The dashed line is the Wiener floor \(J_{min}\). The weight-error norm \(\|\mathbf{w}_o - \mathbf{w}[n]\|^2\) shows how close the coefficients are. The right panel shows run 1's weights, frequency response, or the trajectories of its two largest taps. The read-out table gives the final MSE (mean over \(n\) = 1000-1499) and the measured misadjustment beside the textbook approximations \(\mu M\sigma_x^2/2\), \(\tilde{\mu}/(2-\tilde{\mu})\) and \((1-\lambda)M/(1+\lambda)\). It also gives the iteration at which each curve first comes within 3 dB of its final value.

The MicroSim opens paused: press Run to start the experiment; Pause freezes it and Reset returns every control to its default and pauses. Change the plant at n = 500 flips the sign of every plant tap halfway through, to test tracking. Every setting reuses the same random data, so any difference comes from the control you changed. A red warning appears when \(\mu > 2/(M\sigma_x^2)\). With \(\lambda = 1\), RLS gives the same estimate as a Kalman filter whose state is the constant weight vector, so it stands in for the Kalman filter here.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 11: Adaptive Signal Processing.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Compare the convergence speed and final MSE of LMS, NLMS and RLS on the same system-identification problem, using the learning curves and the read-out table
  2. Analyze how input correlation, measured by the eigenvalue spread \(\chi(\mathbf{R})\), slows LMS and NLMS but not RLS
  3. Evaluate the LMS step-size trade-off by predicting the misadjustment \(\mu M\sigma_x^2/2\) and the stability limit, then judging how well each approximation matches the measured values
  4. Evaluate a choice of RLS forgetting factor \(\lambda\) for tracking, explaining why \(\lambda = 1\) fails after the plant changes
  5. Explain why a filter shorter than the plant settles at a floor above the noise power (\(J_{min} > \sigma_v^2\))

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate juniors and seniors in a digital signal processing or adaptive filtering course. The four activities take about 45 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• FIR filters and convolution
  • Mean-squared error, the Wiener solution \(\mathbf{w}^* = \mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{p}\), and eigenvalues of the autocorrelation matrix \(\mathbf{R}\)
  • The LMS, NLMS and RLS update equations from Chapter 11

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Press Reset before each activity. The defaults are plant B (8-tap lowpass), white input, noise \(-30\) dB, 10 runs, \(M = 8\), \(\mu = 0.010\), \(\tilde{\mu} = 0.50\), \(\lambda = 0.990\) and \(\delta = 0.01\). Each experiment takes about 1.5 s.

Activity 1: The baseline race (10 min).

  1. Press Run and watch the default run. RLS comes within 3 dB of its final MSE at \(n = 20\) (about \(2M\)), NLMS at \(n = 50\) and LMS at \(n = 305\). The final MSEs are \(-29.8\), \(-28.5\) and \(-29.8\) dB, against \(J_{min} = -30.0\) dB.
  2. Read the misadjustment column: LMS 4.1% (approximation 4.0%), RLS 4.0% (4.0%), NLMS 41% (33%). NLMS converges fast but pays for it with a higher floor.
  3. Set \(\tilde{\mu} = 0.08\). NLMS now reads 5.4% / 4.2% and converges at \(n = 350\), about as slowly as LMS. For white input NLMS behaves like LMS with \(\mu = \tilde{\mu}/(M\sigma_x^2) = 0.01\).
  4. Evaluate the NLMS approximation. \(\tilde{\mu}/(2-\tilde{\mu})\) assumes a long filter. For Gaussian white input, multiplying by \(M/(M-2)\) gives 44% at \(\tilde{\mu} = 0.5\) and 5.6% at \(\tilde{\mu} = 0.08\), much closer to the measured 41% and 5.4%.

Activity 2: Colored input and eigenvalue spread (10 min).

  1. Set Input to AR(1) a = 0.5. The footer shows \(\chi(\mathbf{R}) = 7.47\), and LMS still converges at \(n = 285\).
  2. Set Input to AR(1) a = 0.9, so \(\chi(\mathbf{R}) = 113\). RLS does not change (within 3 dB at \(n = 20\), 3.9% / 4.0%). LMS needs 690 iterations and its misadjustment reads 41% against 4.0%, because it has not finished converging.
  3. Compare the weight-error plot. The LMS curve is still falling at \(n = 1500\) (about \(-27\) dB), whereas with white input it reached about \(-45\) dB.
  4. Switch Panel to Freq. response. All three estimates match the plant at low frequencies, where the input has power. Above about \(0.6\pi\), LMS and NLMS miss the stopband while RLS follows it.

Activity 3: Step size, misadjustment and stability (10 min).

  1. With white input, set \(\mu\) = 0.005, 0.02 and 0.04. The read-outs are 2.9% / 2.0% (converged at \(n = 645\)), 8.7% / 8.0% (\(n = 170\)) and 20% / 16% (\(n = 90\)). Faster convergence costs a higher floor.
  2. The textbook value \(\mu M\sigma_x^2/2\) falls short at large \(\mu\). Mean-square analysis for white Gaussian input gives \(\mu M\sigma_x^2 / (2 - \mu(M+2)\sigma_x^2)\), which predicts 8.9% at \(\mu = 0.02\) and 20.0% at \(\mu = 0.04\). At \(\mu = 0.005\) the measured 2.9% is still above the predicted 2.1%, because LMS is still settling after \(n = 1000\).
  3. Raise \(\mu\) toward the warning. At \(\mu = 0.13\) the learning curve shows spikes and the final MSE is \(-25.8\) dB. At 0.18 it is \(-6.9\) dB, and at 0.20 it is \(+23.9\) dB. At 0.22 the table reports diverged in 5 of 10 runs, and at 0.23 10 of 10. The red warning appears only above 0.250.

Activity 4: Tracking and the RLS memory (12 min).

  1. Click Change the plant at n = 500. LMS and RLS jump to about \(+6\) dB: the error becomes twice the plant output, so its power is 4 times \(\sigma_x^2\|\mathbf{w}_o\|^2 = 1\). NLMS starts re-adapting so quickly that its curve peaks near \(+4\) dB. The Recovered after n = 500 column reads LMS 340, NLMS 75 and RLS 405.
  2. Set \(\lambda = 0.980\) (memory \(1/(1-\lambda) = 50\) samples). RLS now recovers in 215 iterations, with misadjustment 8.3% / 8.1%. At \(\lambda = 0.950\) it recovers in 90 iterations but reads 22% / 21%.
  3. Set \(\lambda = 1.000\). RLS never recovers (> 1000): its final MSE is \(-1.8\) dB, because it weights the old plant as heavily as the new one.
  4. Click Keep the plant fixed and set \(\lambda = 0.990\). Change RLS δ to 1, 10 and 100. RLS now converges at \(n\) = 50, 155 and 350 instead of 20. The fast start of RLS comes from a large initial \(\mathbf{P}(0) = \mathbf{I}/\delta\).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With white input, \(M = 16\) and \(\mu = 0.01\), predict the LMS misadjustment and the \(\mu\) at which the warning appears. (Answer: \(\mu M\sigma_x^2/2 = 8\%\) and the sim measures 8.3%. The warning threshold is \(2/(M\sigma_x^2) = 0.125\).)
  2. For RLS with \(\lambda = 0.98\) and \(M = 8\), estimate the misadjustment and the memory length. (Answer: \((1-\lambda)M/(1+\lambda) = 0.02 \times 8 / 1.98 = 8.1\%\) (measured 8.3%), and the memory is about \(1/(1-\lambda) = 50\) samples.)
  3. Why does the AR(1) input with \(a = 0.9\) slow LMS but not RLS? (Answer: \(\chi(\mathbf{R}) = 113\). Each LMS mode converges at a rate set by \(\mu\lambda_i\), so the slowest mode is about 113 times slower than the fastest. RLS scales its update by \(\mathbf{P} \approx \mathbf{R}^{-1}\), which equalizes the modes, so it still converges in about 20 iterations.)
  4. With plant C (12 taps) and \(M = 8\), LMS and RLS settle at \(-11.4\) dB (NLMS at \(-10.0\) dB) instead of near \(-30\) dB, and the approximation column shows a dash. Why, and what fixes it? (Answer: an 8-tap filter cannot represent taps 8-11 of the plant. Their output power sets the Wiener floor \(J_{min} = -11.5\) dB, so no step size can do better. Setting \(M = 12\) restores \(J_{min} = -30.0\) dB, and LMS then reaches \(-29.7\) dB.)
  5. LMS with \(\mu = 0.01\) and RLS with \(\lambda = 0.99\) have the same misadjustment (about 4%). Which recovers faster after the plant change, and why? (Answer: neither has an advantage; LMS needs 340 iterations and RLS 405. Once converged, \(\mathbf{P} \approx (1-\lambda)\mathbf{R}^{-1}\), so RLS acts like LMS with step \(1-\lambda = 0.01\) on whitened data. Its fast start came from \(\mathbf{P}(0)\), not from better tracking.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Any step size below \(2/(M\sigma_x^2)\) is safe." That bound guarantees convergence of the mean weight vector, because \(\lambda_{max} \le \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{R}) = M\sigma_x^2\). The MSE needs a smaller step: about \(2/((M+2)\sigma_x^2) = 0.20\) for white Gaussian input with \(M = 8\). In Activity 3, half the runs diverge at \(\mu = 0.22\) with no warning shown. With the AR(1) a = 0.9 input, one run in ten already diverges at \(\mu = 0.03\), because a burst of large input samples makes \(\mu\|\mathbf{x}\|^2\) exceed 2. NLMS divides by \(\|\mathbf{x}\|^2\), so it stays stable for any \(0 < \tilde{\mu} < 2\).

"RLS always tracks faster than LMS." RLS converges fast from its start-up. After the plant changes, its speed is set by \(\lambda\), and at equal misadjustment it recovers no faster than LMS (Activity 4, step 1).

"A flat learning curve means the weights are right." With AR(1) a = 0.9, the LMS MSE is within 1.6 dB of \(J_{min}\), yet its weight error is still about \(-27\) dB rather than \(-45\) dB. Errors along small-eigenvalue directions barely change the output, so the MSE hides them.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Least mean squares filter - Wikipedia - the LMS and normalized LMS updates, the step-size bound and misadjustment
  2. Recursive least squares filter - Wikipedia - the RLS recursion, the forgetting factor and the inverse correlation matrix \(\mathbf{P}\)
  3. Adaptive filter - Wikipedia - the adaptive filter structure and the system-identification configuration used here
  4. System identification - Wikipedia - estimating an unknown system from its input and noisy output
  5. Wiener filter - Wikipedia - the minimum-MSE solution and the floor \(J_{min}\) drawn on the learning curves
  6. Kalman filter - Wikipedia - the state-space estimator that RLS matches when the state is constant

docs.title: Adaptive Noise and Echo Cancellation
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/adaptive-noise-cancellation/main.html" width="100%" height="682px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim runs one normalized LMS (NLMS) adaptive filter on three classic problems, chosen from the drop-down list. In every case the filter output is \(y[n] = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}[n]\), the error is \(e[n] = d[n] - y[n]\), and the taps follow

\[\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \frac{\mu\, e[n]\, \mathbf{x}[n]}{\varepsilon + \|\mathbf{x}[n]\|^2}, \qquad \varepsilon = 0.05 .\]
  • Noise cancellation. The primary input is \(d = s + P * x\): a clean two-tone signal \(s\) plus white noise \(x\) that reached the sensor through an unknown 10-tap path \(P\). The reference input is \(x\) itself, so the error \(e\) becomes the cleaned signal. Signal leaks into reference adds \(0.3\,s\) to the reference.
  • Echo cancellation. A speech-like far-end signal \(x\) plays through a loudspeaker and returns to the microphone through an echo path \(H\) (a 4-sample delay and 20 decaying taps) scaled by the echo level \(g\). Near-end talker adds a local voice (double-talk); Freeze during double-talk stops adaptation while that voice is active, like an ideal double-talk detector.
  • Equalization. Random \(\pm 1\) training symbols \(a[n]\) pass through the dispersive channel \(C = [0.31, 0.69, 0.54, -0.31, 0.23]\) plus noise. The equalizer learns to output \(a[n - \Delta]\), where the delay \(\Delta\) minimizes the Wiener (optimum) MSE for the chosen length. Decision-directed replaces the training symbol by the sign of the output.

The sliders set the step size \(\mu\), the filter length \(M\), the noise level, echo level or channel noise, and the speed. The MicroSim opens paused; press Run to start the adaptation and Pause to freeze it. Changing \(M\) or pressing Reset restarts the same random run. The stem plot compares the learned taps with the true path (system identification), or shows the equalizer and the combined response \(C * w\). The convergence curve plots noise reduction, ERLE \(= 10\log_{10}(E[d^2]/E[e^2])\) (echo part only), or MSE.

This simulation is used in Chapter 11: Adaptive Signal Processing.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Apply the NLMS update to noise cancellation, echo cancellation and equalization, identifying the input \(x\), the desired signal \(d\) and the useful output in each configuration
  2. Analyze how the step size \(\mu\) trades convergence speed against steady-state noise reduction, using the misadjustment estimate \(\mu/(2-\mu)\)
  3. Explain why the filter length must cover the unknown path or channel, by comparing the learned taps with the true path
  4. Evaluate when an adaptive canceller fails: a reference that contains the signal, double-talk during echo cancellation, and decision-directed training from a closed eye
  5. Interpret ERLE, noise reduction, misalignment, mean-squared error, symbol error rate and eye opening as measures of performance

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a digital signal processing course (junior or senior engineering, physics or computer science). Plan 30 to 40 minutes for the four activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• FIR filters and convolution
  • Mean-squared error and the Wiener filter idea (Chapter 11)
  • The LMS and NLMS update equations (Chapter 11)
  • Decibels as a power ratio

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
The numbers below come from the sim's own engine. Each run uses the same random numbers, so Reset reproduces them. Read-outs are averages over the last few hundred samples, so in steady state they wander by a few dB.

Activity 1: Step size in noise cancellation (10 min). Start with the defaults (\(\mu = 0.05\), \(M = 16\), \(\sigma = 1.00\)). The input SNR is about −4 dB. Noise reduction passes 10 dB near \(n = 1{,}260\) and settles around 20 dB (between about 17 and 23 dB), so the output SNR is about 16 dB. The green output now follows the dashed clean signal. Set \(\mu = 0.01\) and press Reset: 10 dB now takes until \(n \approx 2{,}550\), but the reduction settles near 27 dB. With \(\mu = 0.50\) it reaches its final value within 200 samples, but that value is only about 9 dB. With \(\mu = 1.00\) it settles near 4 dB, and with \(\mu = 1.50\) near −2 dB, which is worse than no canceller at all.

Activity 2: Filter length, noise level and leakage (10 min). Return to \(\mu = 0.05\). Set \(M = 4\): the taps panel shows that taps 4 to 9 of \(P\) are outside the filter, and the noise reduction stops near 8.5 dB. Set \(M = 16\) again and change the noise level. With \(\sigma = 0.50\) the reduction settles near 14 dB and with \(\sigma = 2.00\) near 26 dB, yet the output SNR stays near 16 dB in both cases. Finally check Signal leaks into reference. The "Signal kept" read-out falls to about 57% and the noise reduction to 9 to 10 dB: the filter now also cancels part of \(s\), and the green output is visibly smaller than the dashed clean signal.

Activity 3: Echo cancellation and double-talk (10 min). Choose Echo cancellation (defaults \(\mu = 0.50\), \(M = 32\), \(g = 0.50\)). ERLE climbs in steps, because the filter only learns while the far end talks. It passes 10 dB near \(n = 1{,}390\) and 20 dB near \(n = 3{,}600\), and settles near 24 dB. The learned taps match \(H\), including its four zero taps of delay. Try \(M = 16\) (about 19 dB) and \(M = 8\) (about 5 dB). With \(M = 32\) again and the run converged (about \(n = 8{,}000\)), check Near-end talker. Within about 600 samples ERLE falls below −5 dB and then stays near −9 dB: the canceller now adds more echo than it removes, and the misalignment rises above 0 dB. Uncheck it and the filter recovers. Press Reset, check Freeze during double-talk, let it converge, then add the near-end talker: ERLE stays near 22 dB.

Activity 4: Equalization and the eye (10 min). Choose Equalization (defaults \(\mu = 0.10\), \(M = 11\), \(\sigma = 0.05\)). Before the equalizer the eye is closed (opening about −0.75) and about 25% of the symbols are wrong. With training, the eye opens after about 400 symbols. The MSE reaches −20 dB near \(n = 1{,}030\) and settles near −23.5 dB, close to the Wiener minimum of −23.7 dB at \(\Delta = 8\). The combined response \(C * w\) becomes a single spike at tap 8. Set \(M = 3\): the Wiener minimum is only −7.4 dB and the eye stays slightly closed (about −0.1). \(M = 5\) opens it (about +0.6). Back at \(M = 11\), check Decision-directed and press Reset: the MSE stays near +3 dB and about half the decisions are wrong. Uncheck it, train for 3,000 symbols, then check it again: the error rate stays at 0.0%.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. In Activity 1 the residual noise is roughly \(\frac{\mu}{2-\mu}P_s\), where \(P_s = 0.40\) is the signal power. Predict the steady-state noise reduction for \(\sigma = 1\) and \(\mu = 0.5\), and compare it with the sim. Answer: \(\frac{0.5}{1.5} \times 0.40 = 0.133\), so the noise reduction is \(10\log_{10}(1/0.133) \approx 8.8\) dB. The sim settles near 9 dB.
  2. Why does the output SNR stay near 16 dB when the noise level changes from 0.5 to 2, as long as \(\mu = 0.05\)? Answer: the residual is set by the misadjustment, \(\frac{\mu}{2-\mu}P_s\), which does not depend on the noise level. So the output SNR is about \(10\log_{10}\frac{2-\mu}{\mu} = 15.9\) dB.
  3. Taps 4 to 9 of the noise path hold 11.7% of its energy. What is the best noise reduction a 4-tap canceller can reach with a white reference? Answer: \(10\log_{10}(1/0.117) = 9.3\) dB. The sim shows about 8.5 dB because misadjustment adds a little residual.
  4. During double-talk without freezing, ERLE becomes negative. Explain how a canceller can make the echo worse. Answer: the near-end voice is part of \(e[n]\) but is not correlated with the far-end input. The NLMS update treats it as error and pushes the taps away from \(H\) (misalignment above 0 dB), so \(y[n]\) no longer matches the echo.
  5. Why does decision-directed adaptation fail from the start but work after training? Answer: with a closed eye about a quarter of the decisions are wrong, so the filter is trained toward wrong targets. After training the eye is open and the decisions equal the training symbols, so the update is unchanged.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A bigger step size is always better because the filter converges faster." Activity 1 shows the price. \(\mu = 0.5\) reaches its final value within 200 samples, but that value is only about 9 dB. \(\mu = 0.01\) needs about 2,550 samples just to reach 10 dB, but it ends near 27 dB. \(\mu = 1.5\) makes the output worse than the input.

"Once an echo canceller has converged, it stays converged." Turning on the near-end talker shows that adaptation itself is the danger. Without a double-talk detector the taps wander far from \(H\) and ERLE drops from about 24 dB to about −9 dB. Freezing adaptation during double-talk keeps it near 22 dB.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Adaptive filter - Wikipedia - structure of an adaptive filter and its noise-cancellation, echo-cancellation and equalization configurations
  2. Least mean squares filter - Wikipedia - the LMS and normalized LMS updates, step-size bounds and convergence
  3. Echo suppression and cancellation - Wikipedia - acoustic echo cancellation, ERLE and double-talk
  4. Adaptive equalizer - Wikipedia - training and decision-directed equalization of dispersive channels
  5. Eye pattern - Wikipedia - how intersymbol interference and noise open or close the eye
  6. System identification - Wikipedia - estimating an unknown system from its input and output, as the taps panel does
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook covering FIR filters and convolution

docs.text:

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim places 23 milestones in the history of artificial intelligence, from the 1956 Dartmouth Conference to 2025, on one time axis. Each milestone is a stem with a circle on top. The stem color shows the era, and the legend counts the events in each era: 5 before 2000, 5 in 2000-2014, 6 in 2015-2022 and 7 from 2023 on. Hover over a circle to read what happened.

The Time-axis scale slider changes how years are mapped to horizontal position. The position of a year along the axis is \(\left(\frac{\text{year} - 1956}{69}\right)^p\), where the exponent is \(p = 1 + 2.5 \times \text{slider}/100\). At the left end \(p = 1.00\) and the axis is linear. At the right end \(p = 3.50\), 1956 and 2025 stay at the ends, and every year in between moves left, so recent years get more room. Stem height is only a layout device that grows with time. It is not a measurement.

AI methods for signal processing are covered in Chapter 15: Signal Processing Applications and AI Integration.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Identify the era of a milestone from the color of its stem and the legend
  2. Compare how many milestones the plotted list contains in each era
  3. Predict how a larger exponent \(p\) moves each milestone along the time axis
  4. Evaluate whether a hand-picked event list is enough evidence that AI progress is accelerating

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in a signal processing or introductory AI course. Allow 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Reading a timeline
  • Powers and exponents, for example that \(0.5^2 = 0.25\)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Linear view (3 min). Leave the slider at 0 (\(p = 1.00\)). Read the legend: 5, 5, 6 and 7 events. The 7 red events share only three stem positions (2023, 2024 and 2025), all in the last 2 of the 69 years, about 3% of the axis.

Activity 2: Expand recent years (4 min). Drag the slider to 100 (\(p = 3.50\)). The 5 events before 2000 move into the left 16% of the axis, and the red events spread out: 2023 now sits at 90% of the axis instead of 97%.

Activity 3: Predict, then check (3 min). At \(p = 1.00\) AlexNet (2012) sits at 81% of the axis. Predict whether it moves left or right when you drag the slider to 100, then check. It moves left, to 48% of the axis.

Activity 4: Read the descriptions (3 min). Hover over Transformer Architecture (2017), BERT (2018), GPT-3 (2020) and ChatGPT (2022). Note the gaps between them are 1, 2 and 2 years. Read each description and find the wording that links BERT to Transformers.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. How many events does the legend count for 2023 and later, and how many separate stem positions do they use at \(p = 1.00\)? (7 events on three stem positions, one each for 2023, 2024 and 2025.)
  2. The five events before 2000 are 1956, 1966, 1980, 1990 and 1997. The six events in 2015-2022 are 2016, 2017, 2018, 2020, 2021 and 2022. Which group has the smaller average gap between neighbors? (2015-2022: the gaps are 1, 1, 2, 1 and 1 years, an average of 1.2 years, versus 10, 14, 10 and 7 years, an average of 10.25 years, before 2000.)
  3. At the right end of the slider, what is \(p\) and where does Deep Blue (1997) sit? (\(p = 3.50\) and \((41/69)^{3.5} \approx 0.16\), so Deep Blue is at about 16% of the axis.)
  4. Does this MicroSim show that AI progress is accelerating? (Not by itself. It plots a hand-picked list of 23 milestones, so it shows that the list is denser in recent years. Counting events does not measure capability.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A taller stem means a more important or more capable system." Stem height grows with the year and is nudged up so neighboring names do not collide. Only the year, the name and the description are data.

"The list shows how fast AI improved." The list is a selection, and recent products are easier to list than older research. Compare the slider at 0 and at 100: the clustering depends on the axis, and the count of events is not a measure of performance.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Timeline of artificial intelligence - Wikipedia - a longer, sourced list of AI milestones to compare with this one
  2. History of artificial intelligence - Wikipedia - narrative history of the field and its funding cycles
  3. Dartmouth workshop - Wikipedia - the 1956 event that starts the timeline
  4. Transformer (deep learning architecture) - Wikipedia - the 2017 architecture behind BERT and later language models
  5. Exponential growth - Wikipedia - what a measured exponential trend looks like, for contrast with a count of events

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text: Version 2.0.0 (2026-10-14). Ported to p5.js 2.3.2 and standardized. The slider's response was discontinuous in the earlier sketch: it jumped from a near-cubic axis back to a linear one at the middle of the slider, and its right end was labeled "Logarithmic" although the mapping is a power law that expands recent years. It is now one monotone mapping, \(p = 1 + 2.5 \times \text{slider}/100\), and the sketch starts at the linear end (the same first view as before). Name labels now avoid each other, hover detection matches where the circles are drawn (it was off by 10 px horizontally and 50 px vertically), and the years of DeepSeek R1 and the Y-Combinator coding survey were corrected to 2025.

docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/analog-mod/main.html" width="100%" height="652px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A sinusoidal message \(m(t) = A_m \sin(2\pi f_m t)\) is placed on a sinusoidal carrier of amplitude \(A_c\) and frequency \(f_c\) in one of two ways:

\[\text{AM:}\quad s(t) = \left[A_c + m(t)\right]\sin(2\pi f_c t)\] \[\text{FM:}\quad s(t) = A_c \sin\!\left(2\pi f_c t - \beta\cos(2\pi f_m t)\right), \qquad \beta = \frac{\Delta f}{f_m},\quad \Delta f = k_f A_m\]

so the FM signal's instantaneous frequency is \(f_i(t) = f_c + k_f\,m(t)\). The sensitivity is fixed at \(k_f = 0.05\) Hz per unit of message amplitude.

  • Modulation selects AM (red), FM (blue), or AM + FM to stack both signals on the same scale.
  • Carrier amplitude Ac (0–200) and Message amplitude Am (0–200) are in arbitrary amplitude units.
  • Carrier frequency fc and Message frequency fm (1–30 Hz) set the frequencies. The plots span 1 s, so a frequency in hertz equals the number of cycles you see.

In AM mode, the dashed envelope \(\pm[A_c + m(t)]\) follows the message. The read-outs give the modulation index \(\mu = A_m/A_c\), the bandwidth \(B = 2f_m\) and the share of power carried by the sidebands. In FM mode, the amplitude stays at \(A_c\). Instead, the cycles bunch together where the dashed message is high. The read-outs give \(\Delta f\), \(\beta\), the range of \(f_i\), and Carson's bandwidth \(B \approx 2(\Delta f + f_m)\). The lower plot is the amplitude spectrum. AM has a line at \(f_c\) and one at each of \(f_c \pm f_m\). FM has lines at \(f_c \pm n f_m\) with heights \(A_c|J_n(\beta)|\). The gold bar marks the bandwidth.

The frequencies are scaled down so that single carrier cycles are visible. Real broadcast stations use far higher carriers, near 1 MHz for AM and 88–108 MHz for FM. Analog modulation is not a separate learning-graph concept. It builds on Sinusoidal Signals, Signal Amplitude and Signal Frequency in Chapter 2: Introduction to Signals and Systems. It also applies the Frequency Domain view of Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals. There, multiplying by a carrier shifts a spectrum and creates sidebands.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the AM modulation index \(\mu = A_m/A_c\) and predict the envelope limits \(A_c \pm A_m\)
  2. Predict the frequencies and heights of the AM spectral lines (\(f_c\) with height \(A_c\), and \(f_c \pm f_m\) with height \(A_m/2\)) and the AM bandwidth \(2f_m\)
  3. Calculate the FM peak deviation \(\Delta f = k_f A_m\), the modulation index \(\beta = \Delta f/f_m\) and Carson's bandwidth \(2(\Delta f + f_m)\)
  4. Compare AM and FM in the time domain and the frequency domain: which property of the carrier carries the message, and how the bandwidth depends on \(A_m\) and \(f_m\)
  5. Explain over-modulation (\(\mu > 1\)) in AM and the vanishing FM carrier line at \(\beta \approx 2.405\)

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in a first signals and systems or communications course, after sinusoids and the Fourier transform have been introduced. Plan 25–35 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Amplitude, frequency and phase of a sinusoid
  • The product-to-sum identity \(\sin a \sin b = \tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(a-b) - \cos(a+b)]\)
  • Reading a one-sided amplitude spectrum (line height = amplitude of that sinusoid)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: AM lines (6 min). Select AM and set \(A_c\) = 100, \(A_m\) = 50, \(f_c\) = 20 Hz, \(f_m\) = 2 Hz. The envelope swings between 50 and 150, \(\mu\) = 0.50, and the spectrum shows 25.0 at 18 Hz, 100.0 at 20 Hz and 25.0 at 22 Hz, so \(B\) = 4.0 Hz. Change \(f_m\) to 4 Hz: the sidebands move to 16 and 24 Hz and \(B\) = 8.0 Hz. Then set \(A_m\) = 80: the sidebands grow to 40.0 and the sideband power rises to 24.2%, but the lines do not move and the carrier stays at 100.0.

Activity 2: Over-modulation (5 min). Keep AM, set \(f_m\) = 2 Hz and raise \(A_m\) to 100. Now \(\mu\) = 1.00, the envelope just touches zero, and the sidebands carry 33.3% of the power. Raise \(A_m\) to 150 (\(\mu\) = 1.50). \(A_c + m(t)\) now dips to \(-50\), the dashed envelope lines cross, and the waveform no longer has the shape of the message. The spectrum still has only three lines (75.0, 100.0, 75.0), so the spectrum alone does not reveal the problem.

Activity 3: FM lines and the carrier null (8 min). Select FM with \(A_c\) = 100, \(A_m\) = 50, \(f_c\) = 20 Hz, \(f_m\) = 2 Hz. Then \(\Delta f\) = 2.50 Hz, \(\beta\) = 1.25 and \(f_i\) runs from 17.50 to 22.50 Hz. The carrier line is 64.6. The pairs at 18/22, 16/24 and 14/26 Hz are 51.1, 17.1 and 3.7, and Carson's \(B\) = 9.0 Hz. Raise \(A_m\) slowly to 96 (\(\Delta f\) = 4.80 Hz, \(\beta\) = 2.40). The carrier line falls to about 0.3, while the time plot still peaks at 100. Then set \(A_m\) = 50 and \(f_m\) = 5 Hz. \(\Delta f\) stays 2.50 Hz, but \(\beta\) drops to 0.50, the carrier line rises to 93.9, and only the 15 and 25 Hz pair (24.2) stays large.

Activity 4: AM and FM side by side (6 min). Select AM + FM and set \(f_c\) = 10 Hz, \(f_m\) = 2 Hz, \(A_m\) = 100. The AM envelope swings from 0 to 200. The FM signal keeps a peak of 100, while its frequency swings from 5 to 15 Hz (\(\Delta f\) = 5.00 Hz). Find the moments where the message is highest. AM is tallest there, and FM has its shortest cycles.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. An AM signal has \(A_c\) = 100, \(A_m\) = 80, \(f_c\) = 20 Hz and \(f_m\) = 4 Hz. Give \(\mu\), the line frequencies and heights, and the bandwidth. (Answer: \(\mu\) = 0.8; lines at 16, 20 and 24 Hz with heights 40, 100 and 40; \(B = 2f_m\) = 8 Hz. Check it in the sim.)
  2. Show that the sidebands of a tone-modulated AM signal carry the fraction \(\mu^2/(2+\mu^2)\) of the total power, and evaluate it at \(\mu = 1\). (Answer: the carrier power is \(A_c^2/2\), and each sideband has amplitude \(\mu A_c/2\) and power \(\mu^2 A_c^2/8\). The ratio is \((\mu^2 A_c^2/4)/(A_c^2/2 + \mu^2 A_c^2/4) = \mu^2/(2+\mu^2)\), which is 1/3 (33.3%) at \(\mu\) = 1.)
  3. With \(k_f\) = 0.05 Hz per unit, \(A_m\) = 120 and \(f_m\) = 3 Hz, find \(\Delta f\), \(\beta\) and Carson's bandwidth. (Answer: \(\Delta f\) = 6 Hz, \(\beta\) = 2.0, \(B \approx 2(6 + 3)\) = 18 Hz. At \(f_c\) = 20 Hz the carrier line is \(100\,|J_0(2)|\) = 22.4.)
  4. Why does the FM signal's peak stay at \(A_c\) while its carrier line shrinks as \(A_m\) grows? (Answer: FM changes only the phase, so the envelope and the total power \(A_c^2/2\) stay constant. A larger \(\beta\) moves that fixed power from the carrier into more sideband pairs, \(A_c J_n(\beta)\).)
  5. With \(f_m\) = 1 Hz, which message amplitude makes the FM carrier line vanish? (Answer: the first zero of \(J_0\) is at \(\beta \approx 2.405\), so \(\Delta f = 2.405\) Hz and \(A_m = 2.405/0.05 \approx 48\). At \(A_m\) = 48 the sim gives \(\beta\) = 2.40 and a carrier line of about 0.3.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A louder message widens an AM signal." In AM the sidebands always sit at \(f_c \pm f_m\). Raising \(A_m\) from 50 to 150 (Activities 1 and 2) makes them taller but leaves \(B = 2f_m\) unchanged. In FM, the same change raises \(\Delta f\) from 2.50 to 7.50 Hz and Carson's bandwidth (at \(f_m\) = 2 Hz) from 9.0 to 19.0 Hz.

"The carrier is always the strongest line." In AM the carrier line is always \(A_c\). In FM its height is \(A_c|J_0(\beta)|\), which can be zero. Activity 3 makes the carrier vanish at \(\beta\) = 2.40 while the waveform keeps its full amplitude.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Amplitude modulation - Wikipedia - the AM equation, modulation index, sidebands and over-modulation
  2. Frequency modulation - Wikipedia - instantaneous frequency, peak deviation and the Bessel-function spectrum of tone FM
  3. Carson bandwidth rule - Wikipedia - the estimate \(B \approx 2(\Delta f + f_m)\) shown by the gold bar
  4. Bessel function - Wikipedia - \(J_n(\beta)\), which sets the heights of the FM lines, and the zeros of \(J_0\)
  5. Sideband - Wikipedia - why multiplying by a carrier creates lines at \(f_c \pm f_m\)
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free textbook on the Fourier transform and spectra used to read the lower plot
  7. Analogue Modulation - CDT design guide - the introduction cited by the original version of this page
