docs.title: Bilinear Transform and Frequency Warping
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/bilinear-transform/main.html" width="100%" height="742px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim turns an analog Butterworth low-pass filter into a digital one in two ways. The bilinear transform (blue) substitutes \(s = \frac{2}{T}\frac{z-1}{z+1}\), which maps the whole \(j\Omega\) axis exactly once onto the unit circle with the warping \(\omega = 2\arctan(\Omega T/2)\). Impulse invariance (purple) samples the impulse response, \(h[n] = T\,h_a(nT)\), so each pole moves to \(z_k = e^{s_k T}\) and \(\omega = \Omega T\) is linear, but the digital response is the aliased sum \(\sum_k H_a\big(j(\Omega - k\,2\pi f_s)\big)\).

  • Warping plot (top left): digital frequency \(\omega\) against analog frequency \(\Omega/2\pi\). Drag the gold marker; the read-out gives its image under both mappings, and turns red when impulse invariance aliases it.
  • s-plane and z-plane: drag the gold test pole \(p\) and watch its two images. The gold diamond is the marker on the \(j\Omega\) axis. The dashed purple lines are \(\Omega = \pm\pi/T\), the edges of the strip that impulse invariance wraps around the circle.
  • Magnitude plot and table: the analog target (gray dashed), both digital designs, the aliasing gap (red), and their DC gain, \(-3\) dB frequency and gain at \(f_s/2\). Hover over the plot to read all three gains.

The sliders set the sampling rate \(f_s\) (2 to 16 kHz), the desired cutoff \(f_c\) (up to \(0.45f_s\)) and the order \(N\) (1 to 4). Prewarp the cutoff designs the bilinear prototype at \(f_c' = \frac{f_s}{\pi}\tan(\pi f_c/f_s)\), that is \(\Omega_c = \frac{2}{T}\tan(\omega_c/2)\), so the digital \(-3\) dB point lands exactly on \(f_c\). For \(N = 1\) the analog impulse response jumps at \(t = 0\), so impulse invariance adds \(T\,h_a(0^+)/2\) to the aliased sum.

The bilinear map is a Möbius (linear fractional) transformation, the family explored in the Möbius Transform MicroSim: it sends lines to circles, which is why the \(j\Omega\) axis becomes the unit circle. This MicroSim is used in Chapter 10: Advanced Filter Design and Implementation.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the digital frequency \(\omega = 2\arctan(\Omega T/2)\) that the bilinear transform assigns to an analog frequency, and the prewarped analog cutoff \(\Omega_c = \frac{2}{T}\tan(\omega_c/2)\) that places a digital cutoff exactly
  2. Compare how the two methods map the \(j\Omega\) axis: a one-to-one compression onto the unit circle versus a linear map that wraps around the circle once every \(f_s\)
  3. Analyze the aliasing error of impulse invariance in the passband and at \(f_s/2\), and explain why the bilinear Butterworth response is exactly zero at \(f_s/2\)
  4. Predict where an s-plane pole lands in the z-plane under \(z = e^{sT}\) and \(z = (1 + sT/2)/(1 - sT/2)\), and verify that the left half-plane maps inside the unit circle
  5. Evaluate when prewarping matters by measuring the bilinear \(-3\) dB point at different ratios \(f_c/f_s\)

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a digital signal processing or digital filter design course (junior or senior engineering). Plan 25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Poles of a transfer function in the s-plane and the z-plane, and the unit circle as the frequency axis
  • The magnitude response of a Butterworth low-pass filter
  • Sampling and aliasing (the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\))

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Two maps of the frequency axis (6 min). Keep \(f_s = 8.0\) kHz and drag the gold marker. At 1 kHz the two mappings nearly agree: bilinear 0.95 kHz, impulse invariance 1.00 kHz. At 3 kHz they differ: bilinear \(\omega = 0.55\pi\) (2.21 kHz), impulse invariance \(0.75\pi\) (3.00 kHz). Move past \(f_s/2\) to 6 kHz: the bilinear transform still gives a frequency of its own, 2.98 kHz, but the impulse-invariance read-out turns red, "aliased to 2.00 kHz", the same place an analog 2 kHz tone lands. At 8 kHz (\(= f_s\)) impulse invariance returns to 0 Hz while bilinear gives 3.22 kHz. In the z-plane the blue diamond creeps toward \(z = -1\) but never reaches it; the purple diamond goes all the way around the circle.

Activity 2: Warping moves the cutoff, prewarping puts it back (7 min). Use the defaults: \(N = 2\), \(f_c = 2.00\) kHz, \(f_s = 8.0\) kHz, prewarp off. The table shows the bilinear \(-3\) dB point at 1.70 kHz instead of 2.00 kHz, and the blue dotted path on the warping plot shows why: \(f_c\) on the analog axis meets the curve at \(\frac{8}{\pi}\arctan(\pi/4) = 1.70\) kHz. Check Prewarp the cutoff: the prototype moves to \(f_c' = 2.55\) kHz and the bilinear \(-3\) dB point becomes exactly 2.00 kHz. Uncheck it and raise \(f_s\) to 16 kHz: the \(-3\) dB point is 1.91 kHz, so the error falls from 0.30 kHz to 0.09 kHz, and prewarping now needs only \(f_c' = 2.11\) kHz.

Activity 3: Aliasing in impulse invariance (7 min). Return to the defaults. The impulse-invariant design has a DC gain of \(-1.9\) dB and a gain of \(-6.6\) dB at \(f_s/2\), where the analog target is at \(-12.3\) dB: the red gap is the aliased copies of \(H_a\). The bilinear gain at \(f_s/2\) is \(-\infty\), because the \(N = 2\) zeros of \(H_a\) at \(s = \infty\) land at \(z = -1\) (the blue circle marked ×2). Now lower \(f_c\) to 0.50 kHz: the passband error shrinks to \(-0.1\) dB and the \(-3\) dB point is 0.50 kHz, yet the gain at \(f_s/2\) is still 7.7 dB above the analog value (\(-28.4\) versus \(-36.1\) dB), because at exactly \(f_s/2\) the mirror image at \(-f_s/2\) is as large as the response itself. Finally set \(f_c = 2.00\) kHz and \(N = 1\): the impulse-invariant DC gain is \(+5.9\) dB and the response never falls to \(-3\) dB (the table says "none").

Activity 4: Where does a pole go? (5 min). The default test pole is \(p/2\pi = -2 + j3\) kHz. Its bilinear image is \(z = 0.560\angle 113.1^\circ\) and its impulse-invariant image is \(0.208\angle 135.0^\circ\), where \(0.208 = e^{-\pi/2} = e^{\sigma T}\). Drag the pole onto the \(j\Omega\) axis at 3 kHz: both images move onto the unit circle (\(|z| = 1.000\), at \(99.3^\circ\) and \(135.0^\circ\)). Drag it to \(\sigma/2\pi = +1\) kHz: the images (\(|z| = 1.376\) and \(2.193\)) leave the circle, so an unstable analog pole stays unstable. Then drag it to \(-2 + j5\) kHz, above the dashed \(f_s/2\) line: the impulse-invariant image jumps to \(0.208\angle{-135.0^\circ}\), exactly where a pole at \(-2 - j3\) kHz would go, while the bilinear image, \(0.744\angle 131.5^\circ\), stays distinct.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With \(f_s = 8\) kHz and no prewarping, a bilinear design starts from an analog cutoff of 2 kHz. Where is the digital cutoff? Answer: \(\frac{f_s}{\pi}\arctan(\pi f_c/f_s) = \frac{8}{\pi}\arctan(\pi/4) = 1.70\) kHz, as the table shows.
  2. You need a digital \(-3\) dB point at 2 kHz with \(f_s = 8\) kHz. What cutoff must the analog prototype have? Answer: \(f_c' = \frac{8}{\pi}\tan(\pi/4) = 8/\pi = 2.55\) kHz.
  3. Why is the bilinear Butterworth response exactly zero at \(f_s/2\) while the impulse-invariant one is not? Answer: \(s = \infty\) maps to \(z = -1\), so the \(N\) zeros of \(H_a(s)\) at infinity become \(N\) zeros at \(\omega = \pi\). Impulse invariance creates no such zeros; its response at \(f_s/2\) is the analog response plus its aliased copies (\(-6.6\) dB instead of \(-12.3\) dB with the defaults).
  4. With \(f_s = 8\) kHz, which other analog frequencies does impulse invariance map to the same digital frequency as 3 kHz? Answer: 5, 11, 13, 19 kHz, ... (\(k \cdot 8 \pm 3\) kHz), because \(e^{j\Omega T}\) repeats every \(f_s\). The bilinear transform gives each analog frequency its own \(\omega\).
  5. An analog pole at \(p/2\pi = -2 + j3\) kHz is mapped by impulse invariance with \(f_s = 8\) kHz. Where does it land? Answer: \(z = e^{pT}\) has \(|z| = e^{2\pi(-2)/8} = e^{-\pi/2} = 0.208\) and \(\angle z = 360^\circ \cdot 3/8 = 135^\circ\).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Prewarping removes the warping." It matches one frequency only. With the defaults and prewarping on, the \(-3\) dB point is exactly 2.00 kHz, but hover at 3.00 kHz: the bilinear gain is \(-15.4\) dB against \(-7.8\) dB for the analog target, because the rest of the response is still squeezed toward \(f_s/2\).

"Impulse invariance is distortion-free because \(\omega = \Omega T\) is linear." The map is linear, but every digital frequency also collects the analog response from \(f_s - f\), \(f_s + f\), and so on. The red gap shows it: with the defaults the gain at \(f_s/2\) is \(-6.6\) dB instead of \(-12.3\) dB, and with \(N = 1\) even the DC gain is \(+5.9\) dB.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Bilinear transform - Wikipedia - the substitution \(s = \frac{2}{T}\frac{z-1}{z+1}\), frequency warping and prewarping
  2. Impulse invariance - Wikipedia - sampling the analog impulse response, pole mapping \(z = e^{sT}\) and the aliasing it causes
  3. Butterworth filter - Wikipedia - the maximally flat prototype, its pole positions and its magnitude response
  4. Möbius transformation - Wikipedia - the family of conformal maps the bilinear transform belongs to
  5. Chapter 33: The z-Transform - Steven W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - free chapter that designs Butterworth and Chebyshev filters with the bilinear transform

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/blooms-taxonomy/main.html" width="100%" height="642px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim draws Bloom's taxonomy of cognitive levels as a stepped pyramid of six blocks of equal height, each narrower than the one beneath it. From the base up the blocks are Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate and Create. The title, Bloom's Taxonomy: RUAAEC, spells the first letter of each level in that order. The blocks taper in a straight line and carry no data.

The MicroSim has no sliders or buttons. Move the pointer over a block, or tap it on a touch screen, and the block is outlined in black, a color key under the pyramid shows its swatch and name, and the text below gives a definition of the level and the cognitive processes it includes. For most levels it also notes how a feature of this textbook can support that level. Move the pointer away and the text returns to the instruction line.

The level names are those of the 2001 revision of Bloom's taxonomy. The course description uses the same six levels to organize this course's 18 learning objectives, three per level, and the Instructor's Guide explains how to use the levels when writing assignments and reading quiz questions.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Identify the six levels of the revised Bloom's taxonomy in order, from Remember at the base to Create at the apex.
  2. Explain how Understand, which constructs meaning by interpreting and summarizing, differs from Remember, which retrieves facts and terminology.
  3. Classify a learning objective into the level whose description fits its verb and task.
  4. Differentiate Analyze, which breaks material into parts, from Evaluate, which makes judgments against criteria and standards.
  5. Write a Create-level learning objective in which students build or modify their own MicroSim.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Instructors who write objectives, assignments and quiz questions for this course, and the college undergraduates who read those objectives. Plan 15 minutes for Activities 1 to 3 and 10 more for Activity 4.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Having read at least one learning objective, for example in the course description
  • No signal processing background: the activities use the course objectives only as sentences to classify

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Tour the pyramid (5 min). Hover over the six blocks from the base to the apex and write down the processes each description lists. Expected: Remember lists recognizing and recalling; Understand lists seven processes (interpreting, exemplifying, classifying, summarizing, inferring, comparing and explaining); Apply lists executing and implementing; Analyze lists differentiating, organizing and attributing; Evaluate lists checking and critiquing; Create describes putting elements together and reorganizing them into new patterns.

Activity 2: Read the mnemonic (3 min). Compare the title RUAAEC with the blocks from the base up. Expected: the letters are R, U, A, A, E, C. The two A's are Apply (third block) and Analyze (fourth block), so a first letter does not separate them; only the descriptions do.

Activity 3: Classify course objectives (10 min). Open the learning objectives in the course description. For objectives 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 and 16, hover over the levels and choose the description that fits the verb and the task. Expected: objective 1 (Define key signal processing terms...) is Remember, 4 (Explain the importance...) is Understand, 7 (Apply Fourier analysis...) is Apply, 10 (Differentiate between types of filters...) is Analyze, 13 (Assess the effectiveness...) is Evaluate and 16 (Design custom signal processing algorithms...) is Create. These agree with the group headings in the course description.

Activity 4: Write a Create objective (10 min). Hover over Create and read its last sentence. Write one objective about a MicroSim in this book, for example Design a MicroSim that plots the sum of two sine waves with adjustable amplitudes. Swap with a partner, who checks that the verb and task fit the Create description. Expected: an objective whose verb is list or describe fails the check even when the topic is a MicroSim.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Which level forms the base of the pyramid and which forms the apex? Remember is the base and Create is the apex.
  2. A student is asked to check two filter designs against a specification and justify which one to use. Which level is this? Evaluate: it makes a judgment based on criteria and standards, including checking and critiquing.
  3. Using the descriptions in the MicroSim, state the difference between Analyze and Evaluate. Analyze breaks material into constituent parts and determines how the parts relate to each other and to the whole; Evaluate judges material against criteria and standards.
  4. Classify each task: (a) state the definition of a filter from memory, (b) use a given procedure on a new pair of signals, (c) design a new MicroSim. (a) Remember, (b) Apply, (c) Create.
  5. Why can the first letter of a level in RUAAEC not identify the level? Apply and Analyze both begin with A; the descriptions (executing a procedure versus breaking material into parts) separate them.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
The verb in an objective decides its level. The Understand description lists comparing, yet objective 14 in the course description (Compare signal processing outcomes...) is grouped under Evaluating. The same verb can serve different levels, so read the task and the criteria as well as the verb: comparing two descriptions of a filter is different from comparing two designs against a specification.

Only the upper levels matter. The pyramid is widest at the base and stacks every level on Remember. The Apply description speaks of learned material, which must first be remembered and understood, so the higher levels build on the lower ones rather than replace them.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Bloom's taxonomy - Wikipedia - the original 1956 levels and the 2001 revision to Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate and Create
  2. Benjamin Bloom - Wikipedia - background on the educational psychologist whose name the taxonomy carries
  3. Educational aims and objectives - Wikipedia - what a learning objective is and how objectives are written
  4. Instructional design - Wikipedia - how learning objectives guide the design of instruction and assessment

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text:
Prompt history

The original page was created from the p5.js starter template and kept the template's sample prompt, which describes a green-circle sketch and not this MicroSim. It is preserved here unchanged.

Create a single file p5.js sketch.
Draw a green circle on a 600x400 canvas with a radius of 200.

Version 2.0.0 ports the sketch from p5.js 1.4.0 to p5.js 2.3.2, renames sketch.js to blooms-taxonomy.js, and adds touch support, a minimum 14 px text size and a 40 px taller canvas.

docs.title: Book Build Workflow
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/book-gen-workflow/main.html" width="100%" height="652px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a map of the workflow used to generate an intelligent textbook such as this one. It has 16 boxes and 16 arrows, and an arrow means "is an input to". The top row is the primary path: a Course Description passes through the 2001 Bloom Taxonomy, Concept Enumeration and Concept Dependencies to the Learning Graph. A side branch, Concept Taxonomy, also feeds the Learning Graph.

The Learning Graph then feeds five book-level outputs (light blue): Chapters & Sections, Glossary of Terms, Word Cloud, FAQ and Summaries. Chapters & Sections in turn feeds five chapter-level items (light green): Figures, Diagrams, Charts; Interactive Infographics; MicroSims; Graphic Novel Stories; and Assessments.

There are no sliders or buttons. Hover over a box (on a touch screen, tap it) to read what that step does in the panel at the bottom. The box gets a thick blue border, every box downstream of it gets a thinner blue border, the arrows that lead to them turn blue, and the panel reports how many components are downstream. Click the same box (tap it a second time) to open its documentation page in a new tab. Fifteen of the 16 boxes have a page; Summaries has none.

This diagram is embedded on the About page, which explains how this textbook was generated.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Trace the primary path in row one from the Course Description to the Learning Graph, naming the five boxes in order and the side branch through Concept Taxonomy
  2. Explain why the Learning Graph is the central step: it is the only box with arrows into all five book-level outputs, and ten components lie downstream of it
  3. Distinguish book-level outputs (row two, light blue) from chapter-level content (row three, light green) and name the box the chapter-level items depend on
  4. Predict how many components are downstream of a chosen box, then verify the count with the hover highlight
  5. Identify the boxes that have nothing downstream and say what they have in common

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates, and instructors, who will use generative AI to help build or review a textbook. No signal processing background is needed because the subject of this sim is the book-generation workflow, not a signal processing topic. Plan 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Reading a directed diagram: an arrow from A to B means A is needed before B
  • A general idea of what a course description and learning objectives are

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Trace the primary path (5 min). Hover over each box in row one from left to right and read the count in the panel. Hovering Course Description highlights all 15 other boxes. Bloom Taxonomy gives 14, Concept Enumeration gives 13, Concept Dependencies gives 11 and Learning Graph gives 10. Explain why the count falls by two between Concept Enumeration and Concept Dependencies (Concept Enumeration reaches both Concept Dependencies and Concept Taxonomy).

Activity 2: The side branch (5 min). Hover over Concept Taxonomy, then over Concept Dependencies. Both give 11, and both have an arrow directly into the Learning Graph. Which box do both of them depend on? (Concept Enumeration.)

Activity 3: Book level versus chapter level (5 min). Hover over Learning Graph (10 downstream), then Chapters & Sections (5 downstream), then Glossary of Terms (0 downstream). Observe that the five light green boxes are highlighted for Chapters & Sections but not for Glossary of Terms.

Activity 4: Predict the blast radius (10 min). Choose three boxes. For each one, write down how many components you expect to be downstream, and list them, before you hover. Then hover and compare. Finally, click a box such as Learning Graph to open its documentation page, and click Summaries to see that it has none.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. How many components are downstream of the Learning Graph, and what are they? (Answer: ten, the five book-level outputs and the five chapter-level items. The panel reads "Feeds 10 downstream components.")
  2. Which box do the five chapter-level items depend on directly? (Answer: Chapters & Sections.)
  3. Which two boxes have an arrow directly into the Learning Graph? (Answer: Concept Dependencies and Concept Taxonomy.)
  4. If the Course Description changes, which boxes lie downstream of it? (Answer: all 15 other boxes, so every later step depends on it.)
  5. Nine boxes have nothing downstream. Name the kind of box they are. (Answer: they are all outputs: four book-level outputs (Glossary of Terms, Word Cloud, FAQ, Summaries) and the five chapter-level items. No other box in the diagram uses them as an input.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The workflow is one straight line." Only row one is a chain, and even it branches at Concept Enumeration. Hover over Concept Enumeration: 13 boxes light up, because it leads into the Learning Graph by two routes and the Learning Graph fans out to ten outputs.

"Everything is generated directly from the Learning Graph." Only the five book-level boxes have arrows from the Learning Graph. The arrows into the chapter-level items start at Chapters & Sections, so hovering Glossary of Terms highlights none of them.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Bloom's taxonomy - Wikipedia - background on the cognitive levels that the 2001 Bloom Taxonomy box uses to categorize learning objectives
  2. Dependency graph - Wikipedia - the idea behind the concept-dependency arrows and the "downstream" count in this diagram
  3. ISO/IEC 11179 - Wikipedia - the metadata-registry standard behind the definition style named in the Glossary of Terms box
  4. Book Generation Workflow - Dan McCreary, Intelligent Textbooks - overview of the workflow steps that this diagram shows
  5. Learning Graph - Dan McCreary, Intelligent Textbooks - the page that the Learning Graph box opens

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text:
• The p5.js editor link points to the earlier p5.js 1.x version of this sketch. The sketch in this folder runs on p5.js 2.3.2.
  • Link targets were checked on 2026-10-14. Five boxes used addresses that no longer exist (Concept Dependencies, Word Cloud, MicroSims, Summaries, Assessments) and the Bloom Taxonomy box pointed at the Course Description page. They now point at the closest matching pages of the intelligent-textbooks site. Summaries has no page, and Interactive Infographics gained one.
  • The p5.js 2.3.2 upgrade added the downstream highlight, the legend, the panel heading and count, and the touch behavior (first tap selects, second tap opens the page). The colors, the boxes and the description texts are unchanged.

docs.title: Five Levels of Intelligent Textbooks
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/book-levels/main.html" width="100%" height="502px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This guide explains how to use the interactive "Five Levels of Intelligent Textbooks" MicroSim to understand the progression from traditional static textbooks to advanced AI-driven educational resources. The iframe above makes it easy to include on any website, and the same diagram is used in the Instructor's Guide to explain how this textbook is classified.

The MicroSim presents a stair-step diagram. From the bottom step to the top step the five levels are:

  1. Level 1: Static Textbooks (red)
  2. Level 2: Interactive Content Textbooks (blue)
  3. Level 3: Adaptive Textbooks (teal)
  4. Level 4: Textbooks with Chatbots (purple)
  5. Level 5: Autonomous AI Textbooks (gold)

A dashed red rectangle labelled Highly Regulated Textbooks encloses Levels 3, 4 and 5. Those are the levels whose descriptions depend on information about the individual student (user input and performance, student questions, knowledge of the student), so they raise the privacy questions discussed under Privacy Considerations Across Levels below.

docs.title: How to Interact with the MicroSim
docs.text:
There are no sliders or buttons. Selecting a level highlights its step with a blue border and shows its description below the staircase.

  1. Hover Interaction: Move your cursor over any of the five colored step levels to display detailed information about that level.
  2. Touch Interaction: On touch devices, tap a step to see its description.
  3. Keyboard Interaction: Press Tab to focus the diagram (or click it), then press the keys 1 to 5 to select a level, the Up and Down arrow keys to move between levels, and Escape to clear the selection.
  4. Responsive Design: The visualization automatically adjusts to your screen size, making it accessible on various devices. Below 500 px of width the step labels shorten to L1 - Static, L2 - Interactive, L3 - Adaptive, L4 - Chatbots and L5 - AI.

docs.title: Level 1: Static Textbooks
docs.text:
• Characteristics: Traditional printed or digital formats with no interactive elements
  • Usage: The MicroSim states that over 90% of textbooks used by college students remain at this level; it gives no source for the figure
  • Applications: Suitable for simple content delivery where interaction isn't necessary

docs.title: Level 2: Interactive Content Textbooks
docs.text:
• Characteristics: Digital elements that engage readers beyond passive consumption
  • Features: Keyword search, hyperlinks, embedded videos, simple quizzes, AI-generated MicroSims, a detailed glossary, social sharing compatibility and usage analytics
  • Benefits: Cost-effective enhancements that improve engagement with multimedia elements

docs.title: Level 3: Adaptive Textbooks
docs.text:
• Characteristics: Dynamic content adjustment based on user input and performance
  • Features: Personalized learning pathways, concept graph traversal, performance-based content selection
  • Implementation: Requires data management systems and graph algorithms
  • Privacy Caution: These systems collect and analyze student learning data to provide adaptivity, raising important privacy considerations that educators should address when implementing

docs.title: Level 4: Textbooks with Chatbots
docs.text:
• Characteristics: Integration of intelligent conversational interfaces
  • Features: LLM-powered tutoring assistants, GraphRAG architecture combining multiple AI technologies
  • Implementation: Balances powerful LLMs with cost-effective smaller models
  • Privacy Caution: Interactions with chatbots involve collecting potentially sensitive student questions and responses; institutions should implement proper data protection measures and transparency about how this interaction data is used

docs.title: Level 5: Autonomous AI Textbooks
docs.text:
• Characteristics: Future systems that fully understand individual learner needs
  • Features: Deep understanding of student knowledge, real-time generation of customized lessons
  • Current Status: Aspirational, requiring advanced hardware and more reliable LLMs
  • Privacy Caution: The most advanced system would require extensive student data collection, including detailed cognitive and behavioral patterns; the educational benefits must be balanced against stringent privacy protections and ethical considerations about AI autonomy in educational settings

docs.title: Privacy Considerations Across Levels
docs.text:
As textbooks advance from static (Level 1) to autonomous (Level 5), data collection and privacy concerns increase significantly:

  • Level 1-2: Minimal privacy concerns as little or no student-specific data is collected
  • Level 3: Begins collecting student performance and behavior data to enable adaptation
  • Level 4: Stores conversation histories and student queries that may contain personal information
  • Level 5: Would require comprehensive student profiling to deliver fully personalized experiences

Educational institutions implementing higher-level intelligent textbooks should:

  1. Develop clear data privacy policies
  2. Obtain informed consent from students
  3. Implement robust data security measures
  4. Consider data minimization principles
  5. Provide transparency about how AI systems use student data
  6. Offer opt-out options where feasible

docs.title: Technical Notes
docs.text:
The MicroSim is built using p5.js and adapts to different screen sizes by:

  • Adjusting step sizes and text formatting based on screen width (the layout changes at 400 px and 600 px)
  • Shortening labels on smaller screens for better readability
  • Shrinking the description text, down to a minimum size, so that it always fits below the staircase
  • Maintaining touch functionality for mobile devices

By exploring this MicroSim, users can gain a deeper understanding of how educational content is evolving with technology and the important considerations that come with these advancements.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Identify the five levels of intelligent textbooks in order from the stair-step diagram: Static, Interactive Content, Adaptive, Chatbot Integration and Autonomous AI
  2. Distinguish Level 2 interactive content such as search, hyperlinks and embedded MicroSims from Level 3 adaptivity, which adjusts content from learner input and performance
  3. Explain why Level 3 adaptive textbooks require concept graph traversal and data management systems that Level 2 textbooks do not
  4. Evaluate the student-privacy considerations that arise once a textbook records learner data, using the dashed Highly Regulated Textbooks rectangle around Levels 3 to 5
  5. Classify a given textbook or course website into one of the five levels from its interactive and personalization features

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text:
College students, instructors and academic administrators. No signal processing background is needed; plan 10 to 15 minutes for the activities. Typical uses are:

  • Comparative Analysis: Use the MicroSim to compare the features and capabilities of different textbook technologies
  • Educational Planning: Help administrators understand the progression of educational technology to make informed decisions about textbook adoption
  • Student Information: Introduce students to the different types of learning resources they might encounter in their educational journey

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Experience reading a digital textbook or course website
  • Basic awareness of what a chatbot is

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Climb the staircase (3-5 min). Move the pointer over Level 1, then Level 2, up to Level 5 (or press the keys 1 to 5). Each step gets a blue border and its description appears below the staircase. The Level 1 description says the content is fixed and doesn't adapt to the learner; the Level 5 description says the level remains aspirational.

Activity 2: Interactive versus adaptive (5 min). Select Level 2 and count the features it lists: keyword search, hyperlinks, embedded videos, simple quizzes, AI-generated MicroSims, a detailed glossary, social sharing compatibility and usage analytics, which is eight. None is described as changing the content for the individual learner. Now select Level 3: its description says the content adjusts to user input, performance and behavior, using personalized learning pathways and continuous recording of concept mastery.

Activity 3: Find the regulated levels (5 min). Find the dashed red rectangle and read its label. It encloses Levels 3, 4 and 5. Select each of those three levels and find the phrase that shows the system depends on information about the student: "user input, performance, and behavior" (Level 3), "real-time feedback on student questions" (Level 4) and "deep understanding of student knowledge" (Level 5). The Level 3 description also says the level "raises privacy considerations".

Activity 4: Classify a textbook (5-10 min). Choose a textbook or course website you have used and list its features. Place it on the staircase and justify the placement with phrases from the descriptions. Then check the Instructor's Guide statement that this textbook is a Level 2 Interactive Intelligent Textbook: hover over Level 2 and find which named features (for example MicroSims, quizzes and a glossary) this book has, and which Level 3 feature it lacks.

Extension (optional). Using the six practices listed under Privacy Considerations Across Levels, write one sentence of policy for each that an institution could adopt for a Level 3 textbook.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Which levels does the dashed red rectangle enclose, and what is its label? (Answer: Levels 3, 4 and 5; the label is "Highly Regulated Textbooks".)
  2. Name two features that the MicroSim lists for Level 2 textbooks. (Answer: any two of keyword search, hyperlinks, embedded videos, simple quizzes, AI-generated MicroSims, detailed glossary, social sharing compatibility and usage analytics.)
  3. In one sentence, how does a Level 3 textbook differ from a Level 2 textbook? (Answer: a Level 3 textbook adjusts its content to the individual learner's input, performance and behavior, using personalized pathways, concept graph traversal and recorded concept mastery; a Level 2 textbook adds interactive elements without that personalization.)
  4. Why does a Level 3 textbook raise privacy considerations that a Level 1 textbook does not? (Answer: it continuously records concept mastery and uses learner performance and behavior to adapt, so it holds student-specific data; a Level 1 textbook has fixed content that doesn't adapt to the learner and needs no such data.)
  5. Which level uses LLMs as tutoring assistants with a GraphRAG architecture, and what does the MicroSim say about the current status of Level 5? (Answer: Level 4, Textbooks with Chatbots; Level 5 remains aspirational, requiring advanced hardware and more reliable LLMs.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A higher level is simply a better textbook." Each step adds capability but also requirements. Select Level 1: the description says it is suitable for simple content delivery where interaction isn't necessary. Select Level 3: it requires data management systems and raises privacy considerations. Select Level 5: it remains aspirational.

"Adding videos, quizzes or MicroSims makes a textbook adaptive." Those features are listed under Level 2. A textbook becomes adaptive (Level 3) when it adjusts content to the individual learner's input and performance. Compare the Level 2 and Level 3 descriptions side by side (Activity 2).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Building Intelligent Textbooks - Book Levels MicroSim - Dan McCreary - the original version of this MicroSim in the book on building intelligent textbooks
  2. Adaptive learning - Wikipedia - background on systems that adjust content to the learner, the idea behind Level 3
  3. Intelligent tutoring system - Wikipedia - computer tutors that give feedback to individual learners, related to Levels 4 and 5
  4. Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia - the family of techniques that GraphRAG, named in the Level 4 description, belongs to
  5. Large language model - Wikipedia - the LLMs that the Level 4 description uses as tutoring assistants
  6. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act - Wikipedia - an example of a law that regulates student education records in the United States
  7. Data minimization - Wikipedia - the principle named in the privacy practices for higher-level textbooks

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text: Version 2.0.0 (2026-10-14). Ported from p5.js 1.11.1 to p5.js 2.3.2. The description text is now wrapped and shrunk to fit at any width, taps are handled with the unified mouse handlers, the selected step is drawn on top so its blue border is not covered, keys 1 to 5 select a level, and the step labels are black on every level for contrast. The p5.js editor link above opens the earlier p5.js 1.x version of the sketch.

docs.title: Citation Graph for FFT on Microcontrollers
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/citation-graph/main.html" width="100%" height="702px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A citation graph turns a reading list into a network. Each node is a paper, and each arrow points from the paper that cites to the paper being cited. This MicroSim shows 15 sample papers about running the fast Fourier transform (FFT) on microcontrollers and other embedded hardware, as described in Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals.

Node size grows with citation count in hand-chosen steps, so it ranks papers but is not proportional to the count. Node color shows the research area listed in the legend.

  • Filter by Group shows one research area only.
  • Min Citations hides papers cited fewer times than the slider value. A link is drawn only when both of its papers are visible, so filtering also removes links to hidden papers.
  • Layout switches between Physics (linked papers pull together), Hierarchical (cited papers sit below the papers that cite them) and Circular.
  • Reset View restores the defaults, and Export Data downloads the visible papers and links as JSON.

Click a paper to read its authors, year, venue, abstract, and the papers it cites or is cited by. Click empty space to close the panel. The statistics line under the legend updates with every change. The full data set is also available as fft-citations.json.

The data are illustrative: the citation counts and links were assembled for this demonstration and have not been checked against a citation database.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, a student can:

  1. Explain how a citation network encodes papers as nodes and directed citation relationships as edges
  2. Identify foundational FFT papers by their large node size, since node diameter is scaled to citation count
  3. Distinguish the color-coded research domains in the graph, including foundational, manycore, and FPGA approaches to FFT implementation
  4. Analyze how filtering by research area or minimum citation count changes which clusters remain visible
  5. Evaluate the coverage limits of a 15-paper demonstration dataset relative to a systematic search using the Scopus, OpenAlex, or Semantic Scholar APIs

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Upper-level undergraduates in electrical engineering, computer engineering or computer science who are taking a signal processing course. It is also useful for graduate students who are starting a literature review.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Know what the FFT computes and why it is faster than the direct DFT (Chapter 6)
  • Know that a directed graph consists of nodes and arrows
  • Know the difference between a microcontroller and a general-purpose computer

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Find the hub (5 minutes). Leave every control at its default (All Groups, Min Citations 0, Physics). Click the largest dot, labeled "Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm". The panel shows the 1965 paper "An Algorithm for the Machine Calculation of Complex Fourier Series" with 5000 citations and 12 entries that begin "cited by". It has no entries that begin "cites", because it cites no other paper in the sample. Count the papers that do not cite it: two, both in the Foundational group.
  2. Filter by area and by citation count (10 minutes). Set Filter by Group to FPGA. The statistics line reads 2 papers and 1 citation link. Both FPGA papers also cite Cooley-Tukey, but its links are hidden because Cooley-Tukey belongs to another group. Next choose Neural Networks, which gives 2 papers and 2 links, and then Foundational, which gives 3 papers and 0 links. Return the group to All Groups and drag Min Citations to 50: 4 papers, 2 links and 2 research areas remain. At 100 only the 3 foundational works remain, with 0 links.
  3. Compare layouts (5 minutes). Set Min Citations back to 0 and choose Hierarchical. Arrows now run downward, and "DSP processor architectures" and "Embedded Systems Design" sit on the bottom row, below the papers that cite them. Choose Circular to see the 15 papers spaced evenly around a circle. Press Reset View to return to the Physics layout, where the Cooley-Tukey paper sits near the middle and the papers that cite it surround it.
  4. Plan a real search (10 minutes, no controls). On paper, outline how you would replace the sample with a systematic search. Write the query (for example "fast fourier transform" AND (microcontroller OR "embedded system*")), the filters (peer-reviewed, 2000 to 2024), and the expansion step (for each of the top 50 papers, collect its references and the papers that cite it). Then decide which papers to drop, such as those cited only once, and which database you would use.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Which way does an arrow point, and what does a node with many incoming arrows tell you? The arrow points from the citing paper to the cited paper. Many incoming arrows mean that many papers in the sample cite it; the 1965 Cooley-Tukey paper has 12.
  2. With Filter by Group set to FPGA the statistics line reads 2 papers and 1 citation link, yet both FPGA papers cite Cooley-Tukey. Why is only one link drawn? A link is drawn only when both of its papers are visible. Cooley-Tukey belongs to the Foundational group, so it is hidden and its links are hidden with it.
  3. With All Groups selected and Min Citations at 100 the graph shows 3 papers and 0 links. Why are there no links? The three remaining papers are foundational works that cite none of one another, and every link in the sample starts at a paper with fewer than 100 citations, which the slider has hidden.
  4. In the Neural Networks group the two papers cite each other. Why is this unusual in a real citation graph, and how would you check it? A paper can only cite work that already exists, so two papers rarely cite each other. Look up the reference list of each paper in a database such as OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar to see whether the link is a data error.
  5. Why is a raw citation count a poor way to compare a 2022 paper with a 1965 paper? The older paper has had decades to accumulate citations. Counts should be normalized by the age of the paper or compared within the same publication year.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• A bigger node means a better paper. Node size reflects how often a paper is cited, not whether it is correct or well written. Click the 2022 CORDIC paper (15 citations) and the 1965 Cooley-Tukey paper (5000 citations): the size difference reflects 57 years of accumulated citations as much as quality.
  • Papers drawn close together are more similar. In the Physics layout, linked papers are pulled together, but the position of an unlinked paper is arbitrary. Switch to Circular: the same papers are now spaced evenly, and only the arrows and colors still carry information.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Citation graph - Wikipedia - defines a citation graph as a directed graph of papers and the citations between them
  2. Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm - Wikipedia - background on the 1965 paper that is the hub of this graph
  3. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - overview of FFT algorithms and their complexity
  4. The Fast Fourier Transform - S. W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - a free textbook chapter on how the FFT works
  5. OpenAlex documentation - OpenAlex - an open index of papers and citations that can be queried to build a full graph
  6. vis-network documentation - vis.js community - node, edge, group and physics options of the library this graph is built on

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text:
The graph is built with the legacy monolithic vis library, version 4.21.0, loaded from cdnjs and pinned to that version. The paper data are embedded in main.html and are identical to fft-citations.json. A single list of research groups drives the filter menu, the legend and the node colors, so the three cannot disagree.

Prompt history

The text below is the original AI-generated narrative that used to be the body of this page. It is kept for provenance.

I'll help you create a citation graph for papers on FFTs in modern microcontrollers. This is a complex research task that will require searching for academic papers and analyzing their citations. Let me start by finding relevant papers.I understand you want to create a comprehensive citation graph for FFT research in microcontrollers. This is an excellent research idea, but it's a very extensive task that would typically require access to academic databases like Scopus, Web of Science, or Google Scholar's advanced search APIs to systematically find the top 50 papers and trace all their citations.

However, I can demonstrate how this would work using the papers I've found so far. Let me create a working example with the academic papers I've discovered, showing you the structure and implementation approach.I've created a demonstration citation graph visualization based on the FFT microcontroller papers I was able to find through web search. This shows you exactly how the full research project would work and provides a working foundation you can build upon.

What Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.0 Created

1. Sample Dataset (JSON): Contains 15 academic papers with metadata including:

  • Paper titles, authors, years, venues
  • Citation counts and abstracts
  • Research group classifications
  • Citation relationships between papers

View FFT Microcontroller Citations

2. Interactive Visualization: A fully functional vis.js-based citation graph with:

  • Node-link network where papers are nodes and citations are directed edges
  • Interactive features: Click nodes for detailed information, hover effects
  • Filtering capabilities: By research area, minimum citations, layout type
  • Color coding by research domain (foundational, manycore, FPGA, etc.)
  • Node sizing based on citation count
  • Export functionality for the filtered data

To Scale This to Your Full Research Project

To implement your original vision of 50+ papers with comprehensive citation networks, you would need:

1. Systematic Literature Search

Use academic databases with API access:

  • Scopus API or Web of Science API for comprehensive paper searches
  • Google Scholar API (unofficial) for broader coverage
  • Microsoft Academic Graph (now replaced by OpenAlex)
  • Semantic Scholar API for citation data

2. Search Strategy

Primary search: "fast fourier transform" AND (microcontroller OR "embedded system*")
Filters: Peer-reviewed journals, 2000-2024, minimum citation threshold

3. Citation Expansion

For each of the top 50 papers:

  • Extract all references cited by the paper
  • Find papers that cite this paper (forward citations)
  • Build the complete citation network
  • Filter out papers cited only once

4. Data Processing Pipeline

# Pseudo-code for the full pipeline
papers = search_academic_databases(query, limit=50)
all_citations = []
for paper in papers:
    citations = get_citations(paper.id)
    all_citations.extend(citations)

# Remove papers cited only once
citation_counts = count_citations(all_citations)
filtered_papers = filter_by_min_citations(all_citations, min_count=2)

# Generate vis.js format
network_data = generate_network_format(filtered_papers)

Key Insights from the Demo

From the sample I created, you can see that FFT research in microcontrollers spans several important areas:

  1. Foundational algorithms (Cooley-Tukey, 1965)
  2. Hardware implementations (FPGA, ASIC designs)
  3. Embedded applications (biomedical, IoT, edge computing)
  4. Optimization techniques (memory, power, real-time constraints)
  5. Modern applications (neural networks, deep learning acceleration)

The visualization reveals citation patterns showing how foundational FFT work influences modern embedded implementations, and how different hardware approaches (FPGA vs. microcontroller vs. DSP) create distinct research clusters.

Next Steps

  1. Academic Database Access: Obtain API keys for Scopus or Web of Science
  2. Automated Data Collection: Build scripts to systematically gather papers and citations
  3. Data Validation: Clean and verify citation relationships
  4. Network Analysis: Add metrics like centrality, clustering coefficients
  5. Enhanced Visualization: Add temporal evolution, collaboration networks

The demo I've created gives you a solid foundation and working example of how the final system would function. You can use this as a template and expand the dataset as you gather more comprehensive citation data from academic databases.

docs.title: Complex Plane
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/complex-plane/main.html" width="100%" height="532px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows the geometric representation of a complex number in the complex plane (the Argand diagram). Drag the two sliders to set the real part \(a\) and the imaginary part \(b\) of \(z = a + bi\). The green vector, the right triangle beneath it, and the green arc update immediately, and the two panels show the same number in rectangular form and in polar form.

This simulation is used in Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations.

Visual components

  • Coordinate axes: the blue horizontal axis is the Real axis and the red vertical axis is the Imaginary axis
  • Complex number vector: a green arrow from the origin to the point \(z\)
  • Right triangle: shows how the real part, imaginary part, and magnitude are related
  • Angle arc: a green arc showing the phase angle \(\theta\) measured from the positive real axis
  • Dashed projections: lines showing how the point projects onto both axes

Information displays

  • Left panel: \(\mathrm{Re}(z)\), \(\mathrm{Im}(z)\), the magnitude \(|z|\), and the phase angle \(\theta\)
  • Right panel: the rectangular form \(a + bi\) and the polar form \(r\angle\theta\)

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
A complex number can be written in rectangular form

\[z = a + bi\]

where \(a = \mathrm{Re}(z)\), \(b = \mathrm{Im}(z)\), and \(i^2 = -1\). The same number in polar form is

\[z = r\angle\theta = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = re^{i\theta}\]

with magnitude \(r = |z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) and phase angle \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(b, a)\). The polar form connects directly to Euler's formula,

\[e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\]

which is why sinusoidal signals can be written as rotating phasors in signal processing.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Understand the geometric interpretation of complex numbers as points in a two-dimensional plane
  2. Convert between rectangular (\(a + bi\)) and polar (\(r\angle\theta\)) forms
  3. Calculate magnitude and phase from the real and imaginary components
  4. Explain how changing the real and imaginary parts affects the polar representation
  5. Connect the complex plane to the phasor representation of signals

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College-level introductory signal processing, or pre-calculus and calculus courses. Plan 15-20 minutes for exploration and 30-45 minutes with instruction.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Cartesian coordinate system
  • Basic trigonometry (sine, cosine, tangent)
  • The Pythagorean theorem

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Quadrant Exploration (5 min). Move the sliders so the number lies in each quadrant. How does the phase angle change from quadrant to quadrant? When is the phase positive and when is it negative?

Activity 2: Special Cases (5 min). Set the sliders to each of these and discuss what you see:

  • Real = 1, Imag = 0 (a pure real number)
  • Real = 0, Imag = 1 (a pure imaginary number)
  • Real = 1, Imag = 1 (the 45 degree case)
  • Real = 0, Imag = 0 (the origin)

Activity 3: Pythagorean Triples (5 min). Find slider settings where the magnitude is exactly 5 (for example \(3 + 4i\), \(4 + 3i\), and \(-3 + 4i\)).

Activity 4: The Unit Circle (5 min). Find real and imaginary values that give a magnitude of exactly 1. What shape do all of these points trace out?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. If \(z = 3 + 4i\), what is the magnitude \(|z|\)? (Answer: 5)
  2. What is the phase angle of \(z = -1 + i\) in degrees? (Answer: 135 degrees)
  3. Convert \(z = 2\angle 60^\circ\) to rectangular form. (Answer: \(1 + 1.73i\))
  4. Why is the complex plane useful for representing signals? (Answer: a sinusoid's amplitude and phase become the magnitude and angle of one number, so adding and scaling signals becomes simple vector arithmetic.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text: Students often compute the phase as \(\arctan(b/a)\) and stop. That formula cannot tell \(1 + i\) from \(-1 - i\). Move the point across the origin and watch the arc: the angle must be placed in the quadrant where the point lies.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Complex number - Wikipedia - overview of rectangular and polar forms, arithmetic, and the complex plane
  2. Complex plane - Wikipedia - the Argand diagram, modulus and argument
  3. Phasor - Wikipedia - how rotating complex numbers represent sinusoidal signals
  4. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with a chapter on complex numbers
  5. Euler's formula - Wikipedia - the link from the polar form to \(e^{i\theta}\)

docs.title: Compressed Sensing: Recovering a Sparse Spectrum
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/compressed-sensing/main.html" width="100%" height="708px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The signal is \(N = 128\) samples long (1 s at 128 Hz) and real: \(x[n] = \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i\cos(2\pi f_i n/N + \varphi_i)\), with \(k\) tones at whole-hertz frequencies from 1 to 63 Hz and amplitudes from 0.4 to 1. Because the signal is real, each tone occupies a conjugate pair of DFT bins, \(f\) and \(N - f\), so the spectrum \(\mathbf{x}_f\) is sparse. Only \(m\) samples are measured: \(\mathbf{y} = \Phi\mathbf{x}_f\) (plus noise), where \(\Phi\) holds the \(m\) rows of the inverse DFT matrix for the sample times \(t_i\).

Orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) recovers \(\mathbf{x}_f\) in \(k\) iterations. Each iteration picks the frequency whose DFT column is most correlated with the residual, \(c(f) = \lvert\sum_i r_i e^{-j2\pi f t_i/N}\rvert\), adds both bins of its pair (a cosine and a sine column) to the support, and solves least squares on the support. The minimum-energy (least-squares) solution \(\Phi^H(\Phi\Phi^H)^{-1}\mathbf{y}\) is shown for contrast: it keeps the measured samples and sets the others to zero, which spreads its spectrum over many frequencies.

The top plot shows \(x(t)\) (blue), the samples (orange) and the OMP estimate (green); below are the minimum-energy spectrum and the OMP spectrum, with the true tones as blue rings. The dashed line at \(m/2\) Hz is the Nyquist frequency of \(m\) evenly spaced samples per second. Sliders set \(k\) (1 to 10), \(m\) (8 to 128) and the noise standard deviation \(\sigma\) (0 to 0.30). The menu chooses random or evenly spaced sample times, and New signal moves to the next seed (new tones, sample times and noise). Read-outs give both recovery errors \(\lVert\hat{x} - x\rVert/\lVert x\rVert\), whether the support was recovered, the \(m \ge C\,k\ln(N/k)\) rule, and the success rate over seeds 1 to 100. Reloading the page returns to seed 1.

This simulation is used in Chapter 14: Time-Frequency Analysis and Advanced Topics. It builds on the Sampling Theorem Explorer.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain why \(m\) random samples can recover a \(k\)-tone spectrum whose tones lie far above \(m/2\) Hz, while \(m\) evenly spaced samples alias
  2. Analyze one run of OMP (correlate, select, least squares, update the residual) and relate its first pick to the tallest bar of the minimum-energy spectrum
  3. Compare the minimum-energy (least-squares) solution with the OMP solution using recovery error and sparsity
  4. Evaluate the rule \(m \ge C\,k\ln(N/k)\) against the success rates measured over 100 seeds, and estimate \(C\) for OMP
  5. Assess how measurement noise changes the recovery error and the support, and how extra measurements compensate

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a junior or senior digital signal processing course. Plan 25 to 30 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The DFT and its inverse, and the conjugate symmetry of the spectrum of a real signal
  • The sampling theorem and aliasing
  • Least squares for an overdetermined linear system

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Recovery below the Nyquist rate (5 min). Use the defaults: seed 1, \(k = 3\), \(m = 24\) random samples (19%), \(\sigma = 0\). The tones are at 16, 42 and 56 Hz, all above \(m/2 = 12\) Hz. The banner is green, OMP picked 42, 16 and 56 Hz and the recovery error is 0.0%. The minimum-energy solution has a recovery error of 92.0%. Its tallest bar is the strongest tone (42 Hz), but bars at frequencies that are not tones (9, 58 and 28 Hz) are taller than the bars at 16 and 56 Hz. Discuss why OMP still finds 16 Hz second: once the 42 Hz tone is fitted and subtracted, the interference it spread over the other bins disappears from the residual.

Activity 2: How many samples? (8 min). Keep \(k = 3\) and lower \(m\) one step at a time. Seed 1 is recovered down to \(m = 15\) and fails from \(m = 14\) down. The 100-seed line gives the success rate:

\(m\) 12 16 20 24 28 32 36 support recovered (\(k = 3\)) 6 37 72 91 98 99 100

The rule of thumb predicts 23 to 45 samples. Repeat with \(k = 5\) (rule: 32 to 65): 38, 65, 82, 95, 99 and 100 of 100 at \(m\) = 24, 28, 32, 36, 40 and 48. The success rate first reaches 95% at \(m = 28\) for \(k = 3\) and at \(m = 36\) for \(k = 5\); the read-out shows these as \(C = 2.5\) and \(C = 2.2\), inside the rule's range.

Activity 3: Random or evenly spaced? (7 min). Reload the page and set \(m = 32\). With random times, seed 1 is recovered and the 100-seed line reads 99 of 100. Choose Evenly spaced times: now every 4th sample is taken, 32 samples/s with a Nyquist frequency of 16 Hz. The minimum-energy spectrum shows equal copies of each tone (the 42 Hz tone at 10, 22, 42 and 54 Hz; the 56 Hz tone at 8, 24, 40 and 56 Hz). OMP picks 10, 16 and 8 Hz: the aliases \(|42 - 32| = 10\) and \(|56 - 64| = 8\), exactly as in the Sampling Theorem Explorer. The 16 Hz tone sits exactly at \(m/2\), so its stem stops just below its ring (0.45 instead of 0.47). Only 2 of 100 seeds are recovered. At \(m = 64\) evenly spaced, OMP picks 22, 16 and 8 Hz, and 12 of 100 seeds are recovered.

Activity 4: Noise (5 min). Reload, set \(m = 32\) and raise \(\sigma\). For seed 1 the recovery error is 5.9% at \(\sigma = 0.10\) and 11.7% at \(\sigma = 0.20\), and the support is still recovered. At \(\sigma = 0.30\) OMP picks 31 Hz instead of 56 Hz and the error jumps to 50.7%. Over 100 seeds: 99 of 100 (median error 5.0%) at \(\sigma = 0.10\), 99 (9.9%) at 0.20 and 93 (14.9%) at 0.30. Now raise \(m\) to 48 with \(\sigma = 0.30\): the support is recovered, the error is 12.9%, and all 100 seeds succeed.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. For \(k = 5\) tones and \(N = 128\), what range of \(m\) does \(m \ge C\,k\ln(N/k)\) with \(C\) = 2 to 4 predict, and how does the sim compare? Answer: \(k\ln(N/k) = 5\ln 25.6 = 16.2\), so 32 to 65 samples. The sim recovers 82 of 100 seeds at \(m = 32\), 95 at \(m = 36\) and all 100 at \(m = 48\).
  2. Why is the error of the minimum-energy solution close to \(\sqrt{1 - m/N}\)? Answer: by Parseval's theorem, minimizing the spectrum's energy minimizes the signal's energy, so the unmeasured samples are set to zero. The error is the energy of the missing samples, on average a fraction \(1 - m/N\) of the total. Seed 1 with \(k = 3\): 88.6% at \(m = 32\) (\(\sqrt{0.75} = 86.6\%\)) and 69.6% at \(m = 64\) (\(\sqrt{0.5} = 70.7\%\)).
  3. With 32 evenly spaced samples per second, OMP reports a 42 Hz tone as 10 Hz. Why do 32 random sample times not have this problem? Answer: on the uniform grid the DFT columns for \(f\), \(32 - f\), \(32 + f\) and \(64 - f\) have identical correlations with any real residual, so the 42 Hz tone is indistinguishable from 10 Hz. Random times make every column different; the aliasing becomes low-level interference spread over all frequencies, and the true tones stand out.
  4. Can \(m = 10\) samples recover \(k = 5\) tones? Answer: no. Five tones have 15 unknowns (5 frequencies, 5 amplitudes and 5 phases), more than the 10 equations; the sim recovers 0 of 100 seeds. In practice \(m \approx 2.2\,k\ln(N/k) = 36\) samples give 95% success.
  5. With the defaults, why is OMP's first pick 42 Hz? Answer: the first correlation is \(c(f) = \lvert\sum_i y_i e^{-j2\pi f t_i/N}\rvert\), which is \(N/2\) times the height of the minimum-energy bar at \(f\) (for 1 to 63 Hz). The tallest bar is at 42 Hz, the strongest tone (\(a = 0.92\)).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Compressed sensing beats the sampling theorem for any signal." It needs sparsity. With \(k = 10\) and \(m = 32\) only 1 of 100 seeds is recovered; with \(m = 64\) all 100 are. A signal with many tones needs many samples.

"Fewer samples just means a lower uniform sampling rate." Evenly spaced samples alias: at \(m = 32\) OMP returns the alias frequencies 10 and 8 Hz and only 2 of 100 seeds succeed. The same number of random samples succeeds for 99 of 100 seeds.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Compressed sensing - Wikipedia - sparsity, incoherent measurements and the \(m \ge C\,k\log(N/k)\) result
  2. Matching pursuit - Wikipedia - the greedy algorithm and its orthogonal variant (OMP) used in this sim
  3. Restricted isometry property - Wikipedia - the condition on \(\Phi\) that guarantees sparse recovery
  4. Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem - Wikipedia - the uniform-sampling limit that random sampling of a sparse spectrum gets around
  5. Sparse approximation - Wikipedia - finding a few columns of a dictionary that explain a measurement
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook on the DFT, sampling and aliasing

docs.title: A Convolutional Layer Is a Learned FIR Filter
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/conv-layer-as-filter/main.html" width="100%" height="702px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim trains a tiny one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) in the browser. The gradient descent is written by hand in the sketch, with no machine-learning library. Each input is a 64-sample segment that holds either a low tone (\(f = 0.08\) cycles/sample) or a high tone (\(f = 0.30\)) with a random phase, plus white Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\). The network has \(F\) kernels of \(K\) taps each:

\[z_f[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} w_f[k]\,x[n+k] + b_f, \qquad a_f = \max_n \mathrm{ReLU}\big(z_f[n]\big), \qquad p(\text{high}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\left(\sum_f v_f a_f + c\right)}}\]

Training minimizes the cross-entropy on 256 training segments, 16 per step, and accuracy is also measured on 256 separate test segments. The stem plots show each kernel \(w_f[k]\). The next plot shows its frequency response \(|H_f(f)| = \left|\sum_k w_f[k]\,e^{-j2\pi f k}\right|\), with gold markers at the two tone frequencies. The table lists each kernel's peak frequency, its gain ratio \(|H(0.30)|/|H(0.08)|\) in dB and its output weight \(v_f\). The loss and accuracy curves show training (solid) and test (dashed) results. Four test segments are drawn in blue over their clean tone (gold), with the network's prediction. Colored bars mark the \(K\) samples where each kernel responded most.

The MicroSim opens paused showing the untrained network. Run trains for up to 400 steps (about 7 s), Step applies one gradient step, Reset restores the starting weights, and New data draws a new training and test set. The sliders set the noise \(\sigma\) (0 to 2), the learning rate \(\eta\) (0.001 to 3), the kernel size \(K\) (5 to 16) and the number of filters \(F\) (1 to 3). A slider change restarts training from the same seeded weights. The output weights start at \(+0.5, -0.5, +0.5\).

This MicroSim is used in Chapter 15: Signal Processing Applications and AI Integration.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain how a convolutional layer computes \(z_f[n]\) as an FIR filter (written as a cross-correlation), followed by ReLU and global max-pooling
  2. Analyze a trained kernel's frequency response to decide which tone it detects, using the peak of \(|H(f)|\), the ratio \(|H(0.30)|/|H(0.08)|\) and the sign of its output weight \(v\)
  3. Relate the kernel length \(K\) to frequency resolution and predict when a kernel can form a peak at the low tone
  4. Evaluate how the learning rate and the noise level affect convergence, stability and test accuracy
  5. Design a hand-made kernel that detects the high tone and compare its frequency response with the learned kernel's

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate juniors and seniors in a digital signal processing or machine-learning-for-signals course. The four activities take about 40 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• FIR filters, convolution and correlation (Chapter 4)
  • The frequency response of an FIR filter (Chapters 6 and 9)
  • The idea of a classifier trained by gradient descent on a loss function

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
The defaults are \(\sigma = 1.00\), \(\eta = 0.1\), \(K = 12\), \(F = 2\) and data set 1. Reload the page to restore them. Every number below is reproducible because the data and the starting weights are seeded.

Activity 1: Watch a kernel become a filter (10 min).

  1. Press Reset. Before training, \(w_1\) peaks at \(f = 0.000\) and \(w_2\) at \(0.176\) cycles/sample, and the test accuracy is 69.5%.
  2. Press Step five times. \(w_1\) now peaks at 0.305 and \(w_2\) at 0.089, and the test accuracy is 85.9%. Each step moved a kernel toward one of the tones.
  3. Keep pressing Step: the test accuracy first reaches 95% at step 11 (95.7%). Then press Run. At step 400, \(w_1\) peaks at 0.304 cycles/sample with \(|H(0.30)|/|H(0.08)| = +30.4\) dB and \(v = +2.04\). \(w_2\) peaks at 0.081 with \(-26.7\) dB and \(v = -2.00\). The test accuracy is 96.5% (training 99.2%) and the losses are 0.027 (training) and 0.081 (test).
  4. Look at the \(w_1\) stems. They form a short burst of a sinusoid whose period is close to \(1/0.30 \approx 3.3\) samples.

Activity 2: How many filters does the task need? (8 min).

  1. Set \(F = 1\). The single kernel peaks at 0.306 with \(v = +2.42\), and the test accuracy falls to 90.2%. The network can only detect the high tone, so "low" means "no high tone found". The third test segment (a low tone) gets \(p(\text{high}) = 0.55\) and is misclassified.
  2. Set \(F = 3\). The test accuracy rises to 98.4%. \(w_1\) and \(w_3\) peak at 0.306 and 0.310 (high-tone detectors, \(v > 0\)) and \(w_2\) peaks at 0.073 (low-tone detector, \(v < 0\)). Each kernel's role follows the sign of its starting output weight.

Activity 3: Kernel length sets the frequency resolution (10 min).

  1. Set \(F = 2\) and \(K = 5\). \(w_1\) peaks at 0.269, but \(w_2\) peaks at \(f = 0.000\). Five taps hold only 0.4 of a period of the low tone, so that kernel becomes a smoothing (low-pass) filter. The test accuracy drops to 86.7%.
  2. Move the \(K\) slider to 6, 7 and 8, letting each run finish. The low-tone kernel peaks at 0.120, 0.086 and 0.084 cycles/sample.
  3. Set \(K = 16\). The peaks are 0.302 and 0.093 and the test accuracy is 99.2%. A \(K\)-tap kernel has a main lobe about \(2/K\) wide: 0.40 cycles/sample for \(K = 5\) and 0.125 for \(K = 16\). Compare those widths with the 0.16 gap between the low tone at \(+0.08\) and its mirror image at \(-0.08\).

Activity 4: Learning rate and noise (12 min). Start from \(K = 12\) and \(F = 2\).

  1. Set \(\eta = 0.001\). After 400 steps the test accuracy is only 85.2%, the training loss is still 0.593, and \(w_2\) rejects the high tone by only 5.9 dB. The kernels have barely moved.
  2. Set \(\eta = 1\), press Reset and press Step ten times. The test accuracy is 50% and \(w_2\)'s output weight has flipped from \(-0.50\) to \(+0.22\). Press Run: at step 400 both kernels are high-tone detectors (peaks 0.301 and 0.303) and the test accuracy is 88.3%.
  3. Set \(\eta = 3\). The weights blow up at step 11 and the sim reports that training diverged.
  4. Set \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(\sigma = 2.00\). The curves jump from step to step and the test accuracy ends at 63.3% (training 76.6%). With \(\eta = 0.01\) it ends at 71.1% (training 80.9%), and the kernels still peak at 0.313 and 0.087. With \(\sigma = 0.50\) and \(\eta = 0.1\), Reset followed by two Step presses already gives at least 95%, and the run ends at 100%.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With \(K = 12\), how many positions \(n\) does the global max-pool compare for each kernel, and which input samples does the winning position use? Answer: \(64 - 12 + 1 = 53\) positions. The winner \(n^*\) uses \(x[n^*], \dots, x[n^* + 11]\), the span marked by the colored bar.
  2. A trained kernel has \(|H(0.30)|/|H(0.08)| = +30\) dB and output weight \(v = +2.0\). Which class does a strong response support, and by what factor does the kernel pass the high tone more than the low tone? Answer: the high tone, because \(v > 0\) raises the logit. +30 dB is an amplitude ratio of \(10^{30/20} \approx 32\).
  3. For a kernel with \(a_f > 0\), the gradient is \(\partial L/\partial w_f[k] = (p - y)\,v_f\,x[n^* + k]\). Explain why gradient descent makes \(w_1\) (with \(v_1 > 0\)) look like the high tone. Answer: each step subtracts \(\eta (p - y) v_1\) times the winning input window. For a high-tone segment \((p - y) < 0\), so a copy of the 0.30 tone is added; for a low-tone segment \((p - y) > 0\), so a copy of the 0.08 tone is subtracted. The noise in these copies averages out, so the kernel becomes a band-pass filter matched to the high tone.
  4. Why does a 5-tap kernel trained on the low tone peak at \(f = 0\) instead of 0.08, and what is the smallest \(K\) in the sim whose low-tone kernel peaks near 0.08? Answer: five taps cover only 0.4 of a period, and the main lobe (about \(2/K = 0.4\) cycles/sample wide) merges the responses at \(+0.08\) and \(-0.08\) into one lobe at 0. In the sim \(K = 6\) gives a peak at 0.120 and \(K = 7\) gives 0.086.
  5. Design a 12-tap kernel that detects the high tone without training, and predict its frequency response. Answer: \(w[k] = \cos(2\pi \cdot 0.30\,k)\) for \(k = 0, \dots, 11\). Its \(|H(f)|\) peaks at 0.302 cycles/sample with a main lobe about \(2/12 \approx 0.17\) wide, close to the learned \(w_1\) (peak 0.304).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The weights of a neural network cannot be interpreted." The frequency-response plot shows that each trained kernel is an FIR band-pass filter. After pressing Run with the default settings the kernels peak at 0.304 and 0.081 cycles/sample, within 0.004 of the tones they vote for, and the sign of the output weight says which tone that is.

"A CNN convolution is the convolution of Chapter 4." Deep-learning layers compute \(\sum_k w[k]\,x[n+k]\), a cross-correlation with no kernel flip. Flipping a kernel in time changes only the phase of \(H(f)\), not \(|H(f)|\). So the learned kernel is the time-reversed impulse response of an ordinary FIR filter with the same magnitude response.

"A larger learning rate always trains faster." In Activity 4, \(\eta = 1\) flips the role of the second kernel and ends at 88.3% test accuracy instead of 96.5%, and \(\eta = 3\) diverges at step 11.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Convolutional neural network - Wikipedia - convolutional layers, shared weights, ReLU and pooling
  2. Finite impulse response - Wikipedia - FIR filters and their frequency response, the view used for every learned kernel
  3. Cross-correlation - Wikipedia - the operation a CNN layer actually computes, and how it differs from convolution
  4. Matched filter - Wikipedia - why a kernel shaped like the target signal maximizes the detection signal-to-noise ratio
  5. Gradient descent - Wikipedia - the update rule used to train the network and the role of the learning rate
  6. Cross-entropy - Wikipedia - the loss function plotted in the loss panel
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free textbook with chapters on FIR filters and on neural networks
