docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Convolution measures how much two functions overlap as one slides across the other. This MicroSim uses the simplest pair that shows the idea: a blue square \(f(x)\) that is 1 unit wide and 1 unit tall, and a red triangle \(g(x)\) with a base of 1 unit and a peak of 1 unit.

Drag the slider to move the square from left to right through the triangle. The purple triangle on the right is a gauge, not the final curve: its height is the area where the square and the triangle overlap, which is the value of \((f * g)(x)\) at the current position. The dashed outline marks the largest it can be, an area of 0.50 (the whole triangle, \(\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot 1\)), and the read-out under it shows the current area.

The slider runs from 0 to 270 in units chosen so that 60 units move the square by exactly its own width. The label under the slider also gives \(x\), the offset of the square's center from the triangle's center, in square widths. Overlap begins at slider 140 (\(x = -1\)), peaks at 200 (\(x = 0\)) and ends at 260 (\(x = 1\)).

This is the introductory picture. The Convolution Visualizer adds the flip step, more signal pairs and the full output curve. The idea is developed in Chapter 4: Convolution and Correlation.

The three panels

  • Left, blue: the square \(f(x)\), which the slider moves
  • Middle, red: the triangle \(g(x)\), which stays where it is
  • Right, purple: the gauge whose height is the overlap area, \((f * g)(x)\) at the current \(x\)

docs.title: Mathematical Connection
docs.text:
The convolution integral is

\[(f * g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau)\,g(x-\tau)\,d\tau\]

Convolution is commutative, \(f * g = g * f\), so the integral can be read with the roles swapped, \(\int g(\tau)\,f(x-\tau)\,d\tau\). That is the picture in the MicroSim:

  1. \(g(\tau)\) is the stationary triangle.
  2. \(f(x-\tau)\) is the square, flipped and shifted by \(x\). Flipping a symmetric square changes nothing, so only the shift is visible.
  3. The product \(g(\tau)\,f(x-\tau)\) equals \(g(\tau)\) where the square covers the triangle and \(0\) elsewhere, because \(f\) is 1 inside the square.
  4. The integral is the area under that product, which is the area of overlap.
  5. The slider sets \(x\), and the purple height at that position is \((f * g)(x)\).

The area is found by adding up 200 thin slices of the square. It agrees with the exact value to within 0.0001.

docs.title: Where Convolution Appears
docs.text:
• Image blurring in photo editing
  • Audio echo and reverberation effects
  • Signal filtering in communications
  • Data smoothing in statistics

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain convolution as a measure of how much a sliding function overlaps a stationary one
  2. Predict the slider positions at which the overlap begins, reaches its maximum and ends
  3. Interpret the height of the purple gauge as the area of overlap, not the height of overlap
  4. Calculate the overlap area at a given position from the geometry of the square and the triangle
  5. Connect the sliding-and-overlapping picture to the convolution integral

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students meeting convolution for the first time, in a signals and systems, signal processing or applied mathematics course. Allow 10 to 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Functions and their graphs
  • Area under a curve as an integral
  • Shifting a function, replacing \(x\) by \(x - x_0\)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Find the three landmarks (3 min). Drag the slider from 0 to 270 and watch the gauge. It stays at 0 until the right edge of the square meets the left corner of the triangle at slider 140 (\(x = -1.00\)). It reaches its full height at 200 (\(x = 0.00\)) and is back to 0 at 260 (\(x = 1.00\)). The output is non-zero over 120 slider units, which is 2 square widths: the width of the square plus the width of the triangle.

Activity 2: Read the values (5 min). Set the slider to 160, 180, 200, 220 and 240 and write down the area each time. The read-outs are 0.11, 0.39, 0.50, 0.39 and 0.11. Explain why the values on the two sides of 200 mirror each other.

Activity 3: Height versus area (3 min). Set the slider to 170. The right edge of the square sits exactly under the apex of the triangle, so the overlap already reaches the triangle's full height, yet the read-out is 0.25, half the maximum. Compare with slider 200, where the square covers the whole triangle and the area is 0.50. Say which quantity the gauge measures.

Activity 4: Predict, then plot (5 min). Before touching the slider, sketch \((f * g)(x)\) for \(x\) from \(-2\) to \(2\). Then set the slider to 140, 150, 160, ... 260 and plot the read-outs against \(x = (\text{slider} - 200)/60\). The points form a smooth bump, 2 widths wide, with a maximum of 0.50. It is not a triangle: near the start the area grows as the square of the overlap width (0.03, 0.11 and 0.25 at slider 150, 160 and 170).

Extension (homework).

  • Sketch the result for two squares, and for two triangles. Which is smoother?
  • Find a real-world example of convolution and say what slides over what.
  • Explain why the result is smooth even though the square has sharp edges.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. What is the overlap area at slider 200, and why can no other position give more? The area is 0.50, the full area of the triangle, \(\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot 1\). The square covers the whole triangle there, so nothing more can overlap.
  2. For which slider values is the output non-zero? From 140 to 260, a span of 120 units. This is \(x\) from \(-1\) to \(+1\) widths, so the output is as wide as the square plus the triangle.
  3. At slider 170 the square already touches the apex, but the gauge is only half its maximum height. Why? The square covers only the left half of the triangle's base. By symmetry that half has half the area, 0.25.
  4. The square is made twice as wide and still 1 tall. How do the maximum and the width of the output change? The maximum stays 0.50, because the triangle is already completely covered. The output is non-zero over 3 of the original widths (2 + 1) and has a flat top 1 width long while the triangle lies entirely inside the square.
  5. The convolution integral contains a flip, \(g(x-\tau)\). Why do you not see it in this MicroSim? Both shapes are symmetric about their centers, so the reversed shape looks the same. With an asymmetric function the flip matters, as the Convolution Visualizer shows.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "The gauge shows how high the shapes overlap." The gauge shows area. Compare slider 170, where the overlap already reaches the triangle's full height but the gauge is at half height, with slider 200.
  • "The purple triangle is the output signal." It is a gauge whose height is one value of the output at the current \(x\). The output itself is the smooth bump you get by plotting the gauge height against \(x\).
  • "Convolution multiplies the two functions at a point." At each \(x\) the product is a whole function of \(\tau\), and the output value is the integral of that product over all the overlapping points.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Convolution - Wikipedia - definition of the convolution integral, its properties and its graphical interpretation
  2. Chapter 6: Convolution - Steven W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - free online chapter that builds convolution from the impulse response
  3. Impulse response - Wikipedia - why convolution with \(h(t)\) describes what a linear system does to a signal
  4. Linear time-invariant system - Wikipedia - why the output of an LTI system is the convolution of the input with its impulse response
  5. But what is a convolution? - 3Blue1Brown - a visual explanation of the sliding-and-multiplying picture

docs.title: Convolution Theorem and Circular Convolution
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/convolution-theorem/main.html" width="100%" height="744px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim tests the convolution theorem for the discrete Fourier transform (DFT). The drop-down lists choose an input \(x[n]\) and an impulse response \(h[n]\): rectangle, triangle, exponential \(0.8^n\), alternating \((-1)^n\), a fixed random sequence, the impulse \(\delta[n]\), or a delayed impulse (a single 1 at the last sample). The N and M sliders set their lengths (1 to 16), and the Transform length L slider sets the DFT length, from \(\max(N, M)\) to 64. Both sequences are zero-padded to \(L\) samples.

The panels, from top to bottom:

  • \(x[n]\) (blue) and \(h[n]\) (purple)
  • the linear convolution \(y[n] = \sum_k x[k]\,h[n-k]\) (green), with \(N + M - 1\) samples
  • the \(L\)-point circular convolution \(y_c[n]\) (teal), with gold rings for \(\mathrm{IDFT}_L\{X[k]H[k]\}\)
  • the error \(e[n] = y_c[n] - y[n]\) (red)
  • the magnitudes \(|X[k]|\), \(|H[k]|\) and \(|Y[k]|\); point at a bin to read its values

Because the DFT treats each sequence as one period of a periodic signal, \(X[k]H[k]\) is the DFT of the circular convolution

\[y_c[n] = \sum_{m} y[n + mL], \qquad 0 \le n < L .\]

When \(L < N + M - 1\), the samples of \(y\) at \(n \ge L\) (red) do not fit in \(L\) samples: the arrows show them wrapping to \(n - L\) and adding to the samples there (time aliasing). The read-outs give the required length, the maximum error, and whether circular equals linear, which holds whenever \(L \ge N + M - 1\). The spectra are scaled by \(\max|X|\), \(\max|H|\) and \(\max|X|\cdot\max|H|\), so each maroon stem is the blue height times the purple height.

This MicroSim is used in Chapter 4: Convolution and Correlation.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the length \(N + M - 1\) of a linear convolution and the smallest DFT length \(L\) for which \(\mathrm{IDFT}_L\{X[k]H[k]\}\) equals it
  2. Explain circular convolution as linear convolution with its tail wrapped around, \(y_c[n] = \sum_m y[n + mL]\), and identify the time-aliased samples when \(L < N + M - 1\)
  3. Verify the convolution theorem \(Y[k] = X[k]H[k]\) by comparing the DFT route with the wrap-around sum and by reading \(|X[k]|\), \(|H[k]|\) and \(|Y[k]|\) at one bin
  4. Evaluate whether a transform length \(L\) is adequate for a given pair of sequences, including cases where the wrapped samples happen to be zero
  5. Predict that a delay becomes a circular shift (rotation) when \(L\) is too short

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a signals and systems or digital signal processing course (typically junior year). Plan 25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The convolution sum \(y[n] = \sum_k x[k]\,h[n-k]\)
  • The definition of the DFT and its inverse
  • Magnitude of a complex number

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Watch the tail wrap around (6 min). Start with the defaults: triangle \(x\) with \(N = 8\) (samples 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1), rectangle \(h\) with \(M = 4\), and \(L = 8\). The read-out says that \(L \ge 8 + 4 - 1 = 11\) is required. The linear result is 1, 3, 6, 10, 13, 14, 13, 10, 6, 3, 1. Its last three samples (6, 3 and 1, in red) wrap to \(n\) = 0, 1 and 2, so \(y_c\) = 7, 6, 7, 10, 13, 14, 13, 10 and the labels read 1+6=7, 3+3=6 and 6+1=7. The error panel shows +6, +3, +1 at the start and −6, −3, −1 at \(n\) = 8 to 10, so the maximum error is 6. Now raise \(L\) one step at a time: at \(L = 9\) the maximum error is 3, at \(L = 10\) it is 1, and at \(L = 11\) the status line turns green with a maximum error of 0. At \(L = 16\) the error is still 0; the extra samples are zeros.

Activity 2: The theorem in the frequency domain (6 min). Return to \(L = 8\). The gold rings sit on every circular sample, the red ones included, even though the result is wrong: in a window at least 700 px wide the circular-panel legend reports that the two routes differ by 1.8e−15, which is rounding error. Point at bin \(k = 0\): the read-out shows \(|X[0]| = 20.00\), \(|H[0]| = 4.00\) and \(|Y[0]| = 80.00\), the sums of \(x\), \(h\) and \(y_c\). Now choose the exponential for \(x\) and point at \(k = 2\): \(|X[2]| = 0.65\) but \(|H[2]| = 0.00\), so \(|Y[2]| = 0.00\). A 4-sample rectangle padded to 8 samples has zeros at \(k\) = 2, 4 and 6, and the product inherits every zero.

Activity 3: A delay becomes a rotation (5 min). Choose the triangle for \(x\) (\(N = 8\)) and the delayed impulse for \(h\) (\(M = 4\), so \(h[n] = \delta[n-3]\)), with \(L = 8\). The linear result is \(x\) delayed by three samples (0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1), but the circular result is 3, 2, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4: the last three samples have come around to the front, so the maximum error is 3. In the spectrum every purple stem has \(|H[k]| = 1\), because a delay changes only the phase, and the maroon stems match the blue ones. Set \(L = 11\) and the circular result becomes the true delay.

Activity 4: What the length rule really requires (5 min). Choose the impulse \(\delta[n]\) for \(x\) (\(N = 8\)) and the rectangle for \(h\) (\(M = 4\)) with \(L = 8\). The required length is still 11, but the status line is green: the three samples that wrap are all 0. Next choose the rectangle for both sequences with \(N = M = 16\): the required length is 31. At \(L = 16\) every circular sample equals 16 and the maximum error is 15. At \(L = 30\) only \(y[30] = 1\) wraps, so \(y_c[0] = 1 + 1 = 2\) and the maximum error is 1. At \(L = 31\), or at the FFT-friendly \(L = 32\), the error is 0.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. \(x[n]\) has 12 samples and \(h[n]\) has 5. What is the smallest \(L\) for which \(\mathrm{IDFT}_L\{X[k]H[k]\}\) equals the linear convolution, and what goes wrong at one less? Answer: \(L = 12 + 5 - 1 = 16\). At \(L = 15\) the last sample \(y[15]\) wraps onto \(y_c[0]\) (with the triangle and rectangle the sim shows a maximum error of 1).
  2. With the default settings (triangle \(N = 8\), rectangle \(M = 4\), \(L = 8\)), compute \(y_c[1]\) by hand. Answer: \(y_c[1] = y[1] + y[9] = 3 + 3 = 6\).
  3. If \(L = N + M - 2\), how many samples of the circular result are wrong? Answer: one. Only \(y[N + M - 2]\) wraps, so \(y_c[0]\) is too large by that amount and the last linear sample is missing (with the defaults and \(L = 10\): \(y_c[0] = 1 + 1 = 2\)).
  4. The gold rings always land on the circular result, even when the error panel is red. What does this show? Answer: the product of two \(L\)-point DFTs is always exactly the DFT of the circular convolution, for every \(L\). The theorem never fails; what fails for short \(L\) is the assumption that circular convolution equals linear convolution.
  5. With the 4-sample rectangle and \(L = 8\), \(|H[2]| = 0\). What is \(|Y[2]|\) for any input \(x\), and why? Answer: 0, because \(Y[k] = X[k]H[k]\) and a zero of either factor is a zero of the product.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Multiplying two FFTs gives the convolution." It gives the circular convolution. With the defaults and \(L = 8\) the gold rings agree with the wrap-around sum to about \(10^{-15}\), yet the error panel shows a maximum error of 6 against the linear result. The two agree only when \(L \ge N + M - 1\).

"Extra zero padding changes the answer." Compare \(L = 11\), \(L = 16\) and \(L = 64\) with the defaults: the same 11 samples appear, followed by zeros, and the maximum error stays 0. More padding only samples the spectrum at more frequencies; it does not change \(y[n]\).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Circular convolution - Wikipedia - definition of circular convolution and its relation to periodic summation of the linear result
  2. Convolution theorem - Wikipedia - convolution in time corresponds to multiplication of transforms, including the DFT form
  3. Discrete Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the DFT, its periodicity, and the circular convolution theorem
  4. Overlap-add method - Wikipedia - how zero padding to \(L \ge N + M - 1\) lets FFTs filter long signals block by block
  5. Chapter 18: FFT Convolution - Steven W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - free chapter on computing convolution with the FFT and the overlap-add method

docs.title: Convolution Visualizer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/convolution-visualizer/main.html" width="100%" height="632px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows how the convolution integral

\[y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)\,h(t-\tau)\,d\tau\]

builds one output value for each time \(t\). The two small plots at the top show the input \(x(t)\) in blue and the impulse response \(h(t)\) in red. The middle plot uses the integration variable \(\tau\). It shows \(x(\tau)\), the flipped and shifted copy \(h(t-\tau)\), and their product, shaded green where it is positive and salmon where it is negative. The signed area of the shaded region is \(y(t)\), plotted as the purple dot in the bottom plot. The bottom axis lines up with the middle axis, so the dashed marker sits at the same horizontal position in both. The output is drawn only up to the present time, so you can predict the next part of the curve before you reveal it.

  • Signals selects one of eight pairs of signals.
  • Time t sets the shift \(t\) from \(-2\) s to \(7\) s in steps of 0.05 s.
  • Play / Pause sweeps \(t\) automatically and Play speed sets the rate from 0.25× to 3×. The MicroSim starts paused.
  • < Step and Step > move \(t\) by 0.25 s. Reset returns \(t\) to \(-2\) s.

The line under the plots gives the current \(t\) and the exact value of the area. This simulation is used in Chapter 4: Convolution and Correlation.

docs.title: The Four Steps
docs.text:
1. Flip. Plot \(h\) against \(\tau\) and reverse it to get \(h(-\tau)\).
  2. Slide. Shift the flipped curve by \(t\) to get \(h(t - \tau)\). The dashed line marks \(\tau = t\), the place where the origin of \(h\) now sits.
  3. Multiply. Form the product \(x(\tau)\,h(t - \tau)\), shown as the shaded region.
  4. Integrate. The signed area of the shaded region is \(y(t)\).

docs.title: Signal Pairs
docs.text:
Signal pair What to look for Rectangle * Rectangle Equal widths give a triangle with its peak, 2, at full overlap (\(t = 2\) s) Wide rectangle * Narrow rectangle A trapezoid, flat at 1 from \(t = 1\) s to \(t = 3\) s while the narrow pulse is completely inside the wide one Rectangle * Exponential (RC filter) The output charges toward 1 and peaks at \(1 - e^{-2} = 0.865\) when the pulse ends at \(t = 2\) s, then decays Exponential * Exponential \(e^{-t}u(t) * e^{-2t}u(t) = (e^{-t} - e^{-2t})u(t)\), peak 0.25 at \(t = \ln 2 \approx 0.69\) s Triangle * Rectangle A 1 s average of a triangle: rounded corners, peak 0.75 at \(t = 1.5\) s, duration 3 s Triangle * Triangle A smooth bump, wider than either input: peak \(2/3\) at \(t = 2\) s, duration 4 s Sine burst * Rectangle (averager) A 0.5 s average (height 2, so unit area) passes a 1 Hz sine with gain \(2/\pi \approx 0.64\) and a 0.25 s delay Rectangle * Edge detector \(h(t)\) has zero area, so the output is zero wherever the input is constant

All signals are zero for \(t < 0\). The integral is evaluated numerically with the midpoint rule and a step of 0.005 s. For the three pairs made of rectangles (Rectangle * Rectangle, Wide * Narrow, Rectangle * Edge detector) the result is exact at every position of the Time slider, to floating-point rounding.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this activity, students will be able to:

  1. Explain each step of the convolution integral: flip, slide, multiply and integrate.
  2. Identify the range of \(t\) over which two finite-duration signals overlap, and so where the output is non-zero.
  3. Predict the shape of the output for simple pairs of signals before stepping through them.
  4. Calculate \(y(t)\) at one time from the overlap region and its area.
  5. Describe how the shape of an impulse response determines what a system does to its input.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a first signals and systems or signal processing course. Allow 20-25 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Time shifting and time reversal of signals
  • The impulse response of an LTI system
  • Integration as signed area

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min). Choose Rectangle * Exponential (RC filter). Press Reset, then press Step > repeatedly. The output stays at 0 until \(t = 0\), the first time the red curve touches the blue pulse. Compare the red curve with the small \(h(t)\) plot: it is mirrored left to right, with the sharp edge on the right at \(\tau = t\) and the tail on the left. Set Time t to 1.00, 2.00 and 3.00 s. The read-outs are 0.632, 0.865 and 0.318.

  2. Guided Practice (10 min). Before moving the slider, sketch the output on paper, then check it.

    • Rectangle * Rectangle: at \(t = 1\), \(2\) and \(3\) s the area is 1, 2 and 1. The output is non-zero for \(0 < t < 4\) s, which is the sum of the two pulse widths.
    • Wide rectangle * Narrow rectangle: the flat top of the trapezoid starts at \(t = 1\) s and ends at \(t = 3\) s. The read-out is 1.000 at \(t = 1.5\) s.
    • Exponential * Exponential: set \(t = 0.70\) s and read 0.250. Compare it with \(e^{-0.7} - e^{-1.4}\).
    • Gain and delay (5 min). Choose Sine burst * Rectangle (averager) and set Time t to 0.50, 1.00, 1.50 and 2.00 s. The read-outs alternate between +0.637 and −0.637. The input has amplitude 1, so the output amplitude is \(2/\pi = 0.64\). Its peaks fall at 0.5 s and 1.5 s, a quarter period after the input peaks at 0.25 s and 1.25 s. Step through one full period and watch the green and salmon regions partly cancel.
    • Zero-area impulse response (5 min). Choose Rectangle * Edge detector. The read-outs at \(t = 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00, 2.50\) s are +0.500, 0.000, 0.000, 0.000 and −0.500. Explain why the output is zero from \(t = 1\) s to \(t = 2\) s and where the positive and negative bumps come from.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Two rectangular pulses of duration 2 s and 3 s, both starting at \(t = 0\), are convolved. Over what range of \(t\) is the output non-zero? The output is non-zero for \(0 < t < 5\) s. Its duration is \(2 + 3 = 5\) s.
  2. For a rectangle \(x(t)\) of height 1 from 0 to 2 s and \(h(t) = e^{-t}u(t)\), find \(y(1)\) without the MicroSim. At \(t = 1\) the overlap is \(0 \le \tau \le 1\), so \(y(1) = \int_0^1 e^{-(1-\tau)}\,d\tau = 1 - e^{-1} = 0.632\).
  3. Why is the output of Rectangle * Edge detector exactly zero for \(1 \le t \le 2\) s? Over those times all of \(h(t-\tau)\), which spans \(\tau\) from \(t-1\) to \(t\), lies inside the flat part of \(x\). \(h\) has equal positive and negative areas, so the product has zero net area.
  4. What would a 1 s long averager do to a 1 Hz sine? It averages over exactly one full period, so the output is zero once the window lies completely inside the sine burst. Only the start-up and shut-down transients remain.
  5. Does flipping \(x\) instead of \(h\) change the answer? Which property of convolution does this show? No. Convolution is commutative, \(x * h = h * x\), so either signal can be the one that is flipped.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Convolution multiplies the two signals point by point." The shaded product is a whole function of \(\tau\) for one value of \(t\), and only its area is one point of the output. Move Time t and watch the product change shape.
  • "The output has the same duration as the input." In Rectangle * Rectangle two 2 s pulses give a 4 s output, and in Rectangle * Exponential the output keeps decaying long after the pulse has ended.
  • "The impulse response slides without being reversed." In the exponential pair, \(h(t)\) decays to the right but the red curve \(h(t-\tau)\) decays to the left, because it is a function of \(-\tau\).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Convolution - Wikipedia - definition of the convolution integral, its properties and its graphical interpretation
  2. Impulse response - Wikipedia - why \(h(t)\) characterizes a linear time-invariant system
  3. Linear time-invariant system - Wikipedia - why the output of an LTI system is the convolution of the input with \(h(t)\)
  4. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with a chapter on convolution
  5. Oppenheim, A. V., Willsky, A. S., & Nawab, S. H. (1997). Signals and Systems (2nd ed.). Prentice Hall. Chapter 2 covers the convolution sum and the convolution integral.

docs.title: Correlation and Matched Filtering
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/correlation-and-matched-filtering/main.html" width="100%" height="617px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A receiver knows the shape of the signal it is looking for, the template \(s[n]\) of length \(L\), but not when it arrives. The MicroSim hides one to five copies of a template in white Gaussian noise at unknown delays \(d_i\), so the received signal is

\[r[n] = \sum_i s[n - d_i] + w[n]\]

The plots, from top to bottom:

  • Received signal \(r[n]\) (600 samples). With True delays ticked, green bands show where the templates really are.
  • Template \(s[n]\) and the matched filter \(h[n] = s[L-1-n]\), the template reversed in time.
  • Normalized cross-correlation \(R_{rs}[m] = \sum_k r[k]\,s[k-m]\), divided by the template energy \(E_s = \sum_n s^2[n]\) so that a clean, isolated template gives a peak of exactly 1 at lag \(m = d_i\). It is computed only for lags \(0 \le m \le 600 - L\), where the whole template fits inside the record; the grey strip at the right marks the lags that have no full overlap.

A peak is declared wherever the correlation is a local maximum above the dashed Threshold. Each detected peak carries its lag \(m\) and its measured peak SNR. The summary box compares the measured SNR with the expected value \(\text{input SNR} + 10\log_{10}L\) and, with True delays ticked, reports how many signals were found, how many peaks are false alarms, and the largest timing error. Tick Moving average to overlay an \(L\)-sample averager scaled to the same output noise level and see why matching the template shape matters.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 4: Convolution and Correlation.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Choose a Template.
  2. Lower the Input SNR until you can no longer see the templates in the received signal. Check whether the correlation peaks still stand out.
  3. Set the Number of signals from 1 to 5. Delays are random and at least 1.5 template lengths apart.
  4. Adjust the Threshold and watch the trade-off between missed signals and false alarms in the summary box.
  5. Press New Noise for a new noise record and new delays.
  6. Untick True delays to hide the answers and try to locate the signals from the correlation alone.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
Filtering \(r[n]\) with the matched filter gives the same numbers as the cross-correlation, delayed by \(L - 1\) samples: \((r * h)[m + L - 1] = R_{rs}[m]\). Correlation and matched filtering are the same operation.

Define the input SNR as the average template power divided by the noise variance, \((E_s/L)/\sigma^2\). The peak SNR at the matched filter output is \(E_s/\sigma^2\), which is \(L\) times larger. In decibels the gain is \(10\log_{10}L\): 16.8 dB for the 48-sample templates and 17.2 dB for the 52-sample Barker code. No other linear filter does better in white noise. The noise in the normalized correlation has standard deviation \(\sigma_c = \sigma/\sqrt{E_s} = 1/\sqrt{L \cdot \text{SNR}}\), so \(\sigma_c = 0.14\) at 0 dB, 0.20 at \(-3\) dB and 0.46 at \(-10\) dB for \(L = 48\). The measured SNR printed beside each peak is \(20\log_{10}(\text{peak}/\sigma_c)\).

A plain \(L\)-sample moving average is the matched filter only for a rectangular pulse. For a template that changes sign it adds up positive and negative parts, so its peak is much smaller than the matched filter's 1.00: 0.11 for the sine burst, 0.16 for the chirp and 0.38 for the Barker code.

Template Samples Correlation peak shape (noise-free) Rectangular pulse 48 Triangle, 47 lags above 0.5, so noise easily shifts the maximum by several samples Sine burst (4 cycles) 48 Narrow main lobe but side peaks of 0.75 at \(\pm 12\) samples (one period) and negative lobes of \(-0.88\) at \(\pm 6\) Chirp, 0.02 to 0.25 cycles per sample 48 Single narrow peak (pulse compression); largest side lobe has magnitude 0.33 Barker-13 code, 4 samples per chip 52 Narrow peak; every side lobe is no larger than 1/13 = 0.077

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this activity, students will be able to:

  1. Explain how cross-correlation locates a known pattern inside a longer signal.
  2. Relate the matched filter to the time-reversed template and to cross-correlation.
  3. Calculate the expected peak SNR from the input SNR and the template length.
  4. Analyze how input SNR, template length and threshold affect missed detections and false alarms.
  5. Compare templates by the sharpness of their correlation peaks and the resulting timing accuracy.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in signals and systems or communications courses. Plan 20 to 30 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Discrete convolution and correlation
  • Signal energy and power, decibels
  • Basic idea of random noise and standard deviation

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Find the signals blind (5 min). Load the page and leave Chirp, Number of signals 3, Input SNR 0 dB and Threshold 0.50, but untick True delays. Can you find the three signals by eye in the top plot? Then read the lags of the three correlation peaks and tick True delays. On the first load the peaks are at lags 112, 358 and 476 with measured SNRs of 16.9, 15.8 and 17.4 dB, close to the expected \(0 + 16.8 = 16.8\) dB, and the summary reads "Detected 3 of 3 signals, 0 false alarms".

Activity 2: The threshold trade-off (10 min). Set Input SNR to \(-3\) dB (expected peak SNR \(-3 + 16.8 = 13.8\) dB). For each threshold below, press New Noise ten times and tally missed signals and false alarms in the summary box. Averaged over 500 noise records the chirp gives:

Threshold Signals missed False alarms per record 0.35 about 1% about 2.9 0.50 about 1% about 1.3 0.70 about 6.5% about 0.07 0.90 about 31.5% about 0.01

Your ten records will vary around these values. Explain why no threshold gives zero misses and zero false alarms at the same time.

Activity 3: Below the noise floor (5 min). Lower Input SNR to \(-10\) dB. The expected peak SNR is only \(-10 + 16.8 = 6.8\) dB, and \(\sigma_c = 0.46\), so noise peaks in the correlation are as tall as the signal peaks. Over 500 records the chirp misses about 45% of the signals and gives about 4.4 false alarms per record at every threshold from 0.20 to 0.70. Check this by changing the threshold between 0.20 and 0.70 over ten records, then raise it to 1.00. To get a usable detector at this noise level, would you rather lengthen the template or raise the input SNR? Answer with \(10\log_{10}L\).

Activity 4: Template shape and the moving average (10 min). Set Input SNR to 0 dB and Number of signals to 3.

  • Select Rectangular pulse and press New Noise ten times, reading the largest timing error in the summary box each time. Repeat with the Chirp. The pulse typically shows 1 to 6 samples (median 2 over 500 records); the chirp shows 0 in nearly every record.
  • Select Sine burst, set Input SNR to 20 dB and tick Moving average. The correlation peaks reach 1.0 while the dashed average stays below about 0.11, because four complete cycles sum to zero.
  • Select Rectangular pulse with Moving average ticked. The dashed curve lies exactly on the correlation, because the averager is the matched filter for a rectangle.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A 52-sample Barker template arrives at an input SNR of 3 dB. What peak SNR do you expect at the matched filter output? \(3 + 10\log_{10}52 = 3 + 17.2 = 20.2\) dB.
  2. Why is \(h[n] = s[L-1-n]\) called the matched filter, and how is its output related to the cross-correlation? Convolving \(r[n]\) with the time-reversed template gives \(\sum_k r[k]\,s[k-(n-L+1)] = R_{rs}[n-L+1]\), the cross-correlation delayed by \(L-1\) samples.
  3. At 0 dB the chirp usually shows 0 samples of timing error but the rectangular pulse shows several. Why? The chirp's correlation falls from 1 to 0.62 in one sample, so noise cannot move its maximum far; the pulse's correlation is a triangle 47 lags wide above half height, so a small noise bump moves the maximum several samples.
  4. At \(-3\) dB, raising the threshold from 0.35 to 0.70 removes almost all false alarms but misses about 6.5% of the signals. Why can you not have both zero misses and zero false alarms? Signal peaks sit at \(1 \pm 0.20\) and noise peaks of 0.35 to 0.70 also occur, so the two distributions overlap and any threshold trades one error for the other.
  5. With the sine burst and Moving average ticked, why is the averager output nearly flat where the signals are? Four complete cycles sum to zero, so an averager window covering the whole burst outputs about zero; its largest value is 0.11, against 1.00 for the matched filter.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Any smoothing filter detects as well as a matched filter." Tick Moving average with the chirp, sine burst or Barker template: the averager peak is 0.16, 0.11 or 0.38 of the matched filter's peak. Only the rectangular pulse is matched by an averager.
  • "A signal below the noise level cannot be detected." At \(-3\) dB the noise power is twice the template power and the received trace shows no obvious pattern, yet with the threshold at 0.70 about 93.5% of the signals are found with almost no false alarms.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Matched filter - Wikipedia - definition of the matched filter and its SNR optimality
  2. Cross-correlation - Wikipedia - definition, properties and use in pattern detection
  3. Barker code - Wikipedia - binary codes with side lobes no larger than 1/N
  4. Pulse compression - Wikipedia - why a chirp gives a long pulse and a narrow correlation peak
  5. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on convolution and correlation
  6. Turin, G. L. (1960). An introduction to matched filters. IRE Transactions on Information Theory, 6(3), 311-329. - the classic tutorial paper
  7. Oppenheim, A. V., & Schafer, R. W. (2010). Discrete-Time Signal Processing (3rd ed.). Pearson. - standard textbook treatment of convolution and correlation

docs.title: DCT Basis Explorer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/dct-basis-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="668px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows the discrete cosine transform (DCT-II) with orthonormal scaling, the form used by JPEG. The View drop-down list switches between a 1-D view and a 2-D view.

1-D view. The top row shows the eight basis functions \(\phi_k[n] = c_k\cos\big(\pi k(2n+1)/16\big)\) for \(N = 8\). The Signal list picks an 8-sample signal \(x[n]\) (ramp, smooth bump, step edge, a pure basis function, one cosine period, alternating, or noise); drag any blue sample to make your own. The maroon bars are the coefficients \(X[k]\), and the K slider keeps the first \(K\) of them. The purple curve is the reconstruction \(x_K[n]\) and the red panel is the error \(e[n] = x[n] - x_K[n]\). The top read-out (and, on wide screens, the chart at the lower right) gives the fraction of the energy \(\sum x^2\) in the first \(K\) DCT coefficients and in the first \(K\) DFT coefficients, taken from low to high frequency (\(0, \pm1, \pm2, \pm3, 4\)). Click a basis function or a bar to highlight it; the gold dashed curve is its contribution \(X[k]\,\phi_k[n]\).

2-D view. The grid shows the 64 basis images \(\phi_u[m]\,\phi_v[n]\) of the 8×8 DCT. The Block list picks a synthetic 8×8 block. The Quantization step Q slider replaces each coefficient \(C\) by \(Q\cdot\mathrm{round}(C/Q)\), so every coefficient with \(|C| < Q/2\) becomes 0 (its basis image fades). The sim shows the reconstructed block, the pixel error and the PSNR.

\[X[k] = c_k \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\cos\!\left[\frac{\pi k(2n+1)}{2N}\right], \qquad c_0 = \sqrt{1/N},\; c_k = \sqrt{2/N}\] \[C = D\,X\,D^{T}, \qquad \mathrm{PSNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{255^2}{\mathrm{MSE}}\]

Here \(D\) is the 8×8 DCT matrix with rows \(\phi_k\), and \(X\) is the block minus 128 (JPEG's level shift). Because the basis is orthonormal, \(\sum_k X[k]^2 = \sum_n x[n]^2\) (Parseval). The error energy therefore equals the energy of the dropped coefficients.

This MicroSim is used in Chapter 8: Advanced Transforms.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Describe the N = 8 DCT-II basis functions and relate the index \(k\) to the number of half-cycles of the cosine across the block
  2. Calculate the fraction of the energy held by the first \(K\) DCT coefficients and use Parseval's relation to predict the energy of the reconstruction error
  3. Compare the energy compaction of the DCT and the DFT for the same signal, and explain the difference with the mirror (even) extension versus the periodic extension
  4. Apply uniform quantization with step \(Q\) to the 2-D DCT of an 8×8 block and relate the number of nonzero coefficients to the PSNR
  5. Explain why JPEG transforms 8×8 blocks with the DCT before quantizing them

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a digital signal processing or multimedia course (typically junior or senior year). Plan 30 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The definition of the DFT and Parseval's theorem
  • Inner products and orthogonal bases
  • Signal energy \(\sum x[n]^2\) and uniform quantization (Chapter 5)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Read the basis (6 min). Look at the top row. \(\phi_0[n] = 1/\sqrt{8} \approx 0.354\) for every \(n\), and \(\phi_k\) is a cosine with \(k\) half-cycles across the block: \(\phi_1\) falls once from 0.49 to −0.49. Choose pure basis k = 3. The bar chart shows a single bar, \(X[3] = 6.00\), and every other coefficient is 0.00. Move K: the DCT energy read-out is 0.00% for \(K \le 3\) and jumps to 100.00% at \(K = 4\). The basis functions are orthogonal, so this signal has no component along any other \(\phi_k\). The DFT of the same signal is spread out: its first 4 bins hold 53.55% and its first 7 hold 95.48%.

Activity 2: Energy compaction of a ramp (8 min). Choose ramp (\(x[n] = n - 3.5\)) with \(K = 3\). Only the odd coefficients are nonzero: \(X[1] = -6.44\), \(X[3] = -0.67\), \(X[5] = -0.20\), \(X[7] = -0.05\). The ramp is antisymmetric about its centre and the even \(\phi_k\) are symmetric. The read-out shows DCT 98.82% against DFT 65.03%. The error panel reports \(\sum e^2 = 0.50\), which is 1.18% of \(\sum x^2 = 42.00\): exactly the energy of the dropped \(X[3]\), \(X[5]\) and \(X[7]\). At \(K = 4\) the DCT holds 99.90% and the DFT 74.56%. The DFT magnitudes decay slowly (3.70, 3.70, 2.00, 2.00, 1.53, 1.53, 1.41). The DFT treats the block as periodic, so the ramp jumps from 3.5 back to −3.5. The DCT-II implies a mirror extension with no jump.

Activity 3: When the DFT wins (6 min). Choose cosine, one period (\(3\cos(2\pi n/8)\)) with \(K = 3\): the DFT holds 100.00%, all of it in bins ±1, while the DCT holds 96.33%. Its coefficients are \(X[1] = 1.99\), \(X[2] = 5.54\), \(X[3] = -1.13\), and so on. Now choose step edge. At \(K = 2\) the DCT leads (82.11% vs 42.68%), at \(K = 3\) the DFT is ahead (85.36% vs 82.11%, because \(X[2] = 0\)), and at \(K = 4\) the DCT leads again (92.23% vs 85.36%).

Activity 4: Quantizing an 8×8 block (10 min). Switch the view to 2-D 8×8 block. With the smooth blob and \(Q = 20\), only 4 of 64 coefficients survive: \(C[0,0] = -240\), \(C[0,2] = C[2,0] = -220\) and \(C[2,2] = 140\). The PSNR is 40.3 dB with a maximum pixel error of 6. The gold-framed basis image (0, 2) is highlighted by default: its coefficient \(C = -228.46\) is quantized to \(20\cdot\mathrm{round}(-11.42) = -220\). At \(Q = 1\) there are 13 nonzero coefficients and the reconstruction is exact (PSNR ∞). At \(Q = 50\) the same 4 coefficients survive but the PSNR falls to 34.5 dB, and at \(Q = 100\) it is 29.5 dB with a maximum error of 16. Then compare the blocks at \(Q = 20\):

  • horizontal gradient: 3 nonzero, all in row \(u = 0\), PSNR 44.2 dB
  • vertical edge: 5 nonzero, all in row \(u = 0\), PSNR 42.1 dB
  • diagonal edge: 32 nonzero, PSNR 35.2 dB
  • random noise: 56 nonzero, PSNR 34.0 dB

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. For \(N = 8\), what is \(\phi_0[n]\), and what does \(X[0]\) measure? Answer: \(\phi_0[n] = 1/\sqrt{8} \approx 0.354\) for every \(n\), so \(X[0] = \sum x[n]/\sqrt{8} = \sqrt{8}\times\) (mean of \(x\)). For the smooth bump, \(X[0] = 5.44\) and the mean is 1.92.
  2. A signal has \(\sum x^2 = 42\) and its first three DCT coefficients are 0, −6.44 and 0. What fraction of the energy do they hold, and what is the error energy if only they are kept? Answer: \(6.44^2/42 \approx 41.50/42 = 98.8\%\); the error energy is about \(42 - 41.50 = 0.50\), the energy of the dropped coefficients (the sim shows 98.82% and \(\sum e^2 = 0.50\)).
  3. Why does the DCT compact the energy of a ramp better than the DFT? Answer: the DFT implicitly repeats the block periodically, so the end of the ramp jumps back to its start, and that discontinuity needs many high-frequency bins. The DCT-II corresponds to a mirror (even) extension with no jump, so its coefficients fall off quickly (−6.44, −0.67, −0.20, −0.05).
  4. With quantization step \(Q = 20\), which coefficients become 0? What happens to \(C = -228.46\)? Answer: every coefficient with \(|C| < Q/2 = 10\) becomes 0. \(C = -228.46\) becomes \(20\cdot\mathrm{round}(-11.42) = -220\).
  5. Why does JPEG apply the DCT to 8×8 blocks before quantizing? Answer: in smooth image regions most of the energy falls in a few low-frequency coefficients (the blob keeps 4 of 64 at \(Q = 20\) with a PSNR of 40.3 dB). After quantization most coefficients are 0, and long runs of zeros compress very well with run-length and entropy coding.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The DCT always compacts energy better than the DFT." Choose cosine, one period with \(K = 3\): the DFT holds 100.00% and the DCT 96.33%. With the step edge at \(K = 3\) the DFT is also ahead (85.36% vs 82.11%). The DCT's advantage is for smooth, correlated signals such as image rows, not for every signal.

"The highest-frequency DCT basis function is the alternating sequence \((-1)^n\)." Choose alternating ±2: \(X[7] = 5.13\) holds only 82.11% of the energy, and \(X[5] = 1.80\), \(X[3] = 1.20\) and \(X[1] = 1.02\) hold the rest. The DFT puts all of it in bin 4. Compare the \(k = 7\) panel with the blue samples: \(\phi_7\) alternates in sign, but its amplitude follows a slow cosine envelope.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Discrete cosine transform - Wikipedia - definitions of the DCT-II, orthonormal scaling, the 2-D separable DCT and the basis images
  2. JPEG - Wikipedia - how JPEG level-shifts, transforms and quantizes 8×8 blocks with the DCT
  3. Transform coding - Wikipedia - why compacting energy into a few coefficients makes lossy compression efficient
  4. Peak signal-to-noise ratio - Wikipedia - the PSNR formula used to score the reconstructed block
  5. Parseval's theorem - Wikipedia - why the error energy equals the energy of the dropped coefficients
  6. Chapter 27: Data Compression - Steven W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - free chapter section on JPEG transform compression with 8×8 DCT blocks

docs.title: DFT Explorer: Probing a Signal with Rotating Phasors
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/dft-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="744px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The discrete Fourier transform

\[X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\,e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\]

is a sum of \(N\) complex numbers, and this MicroSim draws every one of them. The signal \(x[n]\) (blue stems) is the sum of up to three sinusoids at whole-number bins \(m\). Each drop-down list picks a cosine (\(m = 0 \ldots N/2\)) or a sine (\(m = 1 \ldots N/2-1\)), and each slider sets its amplitude \(A\) (0 to 2). The Bin k slider chooses the probing frequency, and N sets the length to 8, 16 or 32.

The unit circle shows the phasor \(e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\) for every \(n\). It turns clockwise by \(360^\circ\,k/N\) per sample, and samples that land on the same point share a label. On screens at least 600 px wide, a panel below the signal plots its real part \(\cos(2\pi kn/N)\) and imaginary part \(-\sin(2\pi kn/N)\).

The Running sum plane places the products \(x[n]\,e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\) head to tail (green). The maroon arrow from the origin to the end of the chain is \(X[k]\), and its length is the highlighted bar of the magnitude spectrum \(|X[k]|\). When \(k\) matches a frequency in the signal, the products keep pointing the same way and add up. When it does not, they wind around into a closed loop and \(X[k] = 0\). Animate adds the products one sample at a time; Step adds one per click and starts again at \(n = 0\) after a finished sum. Clicking a bar selects that bin.

Inverse DFT rebuilds the signal from the bins you keep, \(x_r[n] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\ \text{kept}} X[k]\,e^{+j2\pi kn/N}\), and draws its real part as maroon rings. Click bars to remove or restore bins. The sim shows the error \(e[n] = x[n] - \mathrm{Re}\,x_r[n]\), the fraction of the energy kept, and a warning when \(x_r[n]\) is complex.

This simulation is used in Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain how \(X[k]\) is formed by multiplying each sample \(x[n]\) by a phasor that turns \(k/N\) of a revolution per sample and adding the products
  2. Predict the non-zero DFT values of a sum of whole-bin sinusoids: \(AN/2\) at bins \(m\) and \(N - m\), or \(AN\) when \(m = 0\) or \(m = N/2\)
  3. Distinguish a matching bin, where the products line up and add, from a non-matching bin, where they close into a loop, and relate this to the orthogonality of the DFT phasors
  4. Interpret the phase of \(X[k]\): a cosine gives a real \(X[m]\) and a sine gives \(X[m] = -jAN/2\)
  5. Analyze an inverse DFT built from a subset of bins by predicting its error and energy, and explain why bins \(k\) and \(N - k\) must be kept together for a real result

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a first digital signal processing or signals and systems course (sophomore or junior engineering, physics or computer science). Plan 25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex numbers in polar form and Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta\)
  • Discrete-time sinusoids such as \(\cos(2\pi mn/N)\)
  • Summation notation

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Products that add up and products that cancel (7 min). Start from the defaults: \(N = 16\), \(x[n] = \cos(2\pi\cdot 2n/16) + 0.5\cos(2\pi\cdot 5n/16)\) and \(k = 2\). The green products march to the right and the arrow ends at \(X[2] = 8.00 + j0.00\) ("the products add up"). Move \(k\) to 3: the chain closes into a loop and the read-out shows \(X[3] = 0.00 + j0.00\) ("the products cancel"). Sweep \(k\) from 0 to 15 and list the non-zero bins: \(X[2] = X[14] = 8.00\) and \(X[5] = X[11] = 4.00\). Check them against \(AN/2\): \(1 \times 16/2 = 8\) and \(0.5 \times 16/2 = 4\).

Activity 2: One sample at a time (6 min). With \(k = 2\), press Step and watch the gold point on the unit circle move \(-45.0^\circ\) per sample. After \(n = 0\) the partial sum is \(1.50 + j0.00\), which is just \(x[0]\) because the phasor starts at 1. After \(n = 0\ldots3\) it is \(2.04 + j0.16\), after \(n = 0\ldots7\) it is \(4.50 + j0.32\), and after all 16 samples it is \(8.00 + j0.00\). The highlighted spectrum bar grows toward its dashed final height. Once the sum is complete, set \(k = 3\) and press Animate: the bar rises and then falls back to zero as the chain closes.

Activity 3: Phase, negative frequencies and special bins (6 min). Set \(A_3 = 1.00\) (component 3 is \(\sin(2\pi\cdot 3n/16)\)) and \(k = 3\). The arrow points straight down: \(X[3] = 0.00 - j8.00\), phase \(-90.0^\circ\). Move to \(k = 13\): \(X[13] = 0.00 + j8.00\), phase \(90.0^\circ\), and the circle reports "\(-292.5^\circ = +67.5^\circ\) per sample", a counter-clockwise turn: bins above \(N/2\) are negative frequencies. Set \(A_3\) back to 0 and \(A_2\) to 0, choose "cos, m = 8" for component 1 and set \(k = 8\). Now \(x[n] = (-1)^n\) and \(X[8] = 16.00\), not 8: bins \(m\) and \(N - m\) are the same bin. Choosing "cos, m = 0" with \(k = 0\) also gives \(X[0] = 16.00\).

Activity 4: Rebuilding the signal (6 min). Reload the page to restore the defaults and check Inverse DFT. With all 16 bins kept, the rings sit on the stems: max \(|e[n]| = 0.000\) and energy kept 100.0%. Click bars 5 and 11 to remove them: the rings follow \(\cos(2\pi\cdot 2n/16)\) alone, max \(|e[n]| = 0.500\) and energy kept 80.0%. Click bar 5 to restore it while bar 11 stays removed: the warning reports that \(x_r[n]\) is complex (max \(|\mathrm{Im}| = 0.250\)), max \(|e[n]| = 0.250\) and energy kept 90.0%.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With \(N = 16\), what are the DFT values of \(x[n] = 2\cos(2\pi\cdot 3n/16)\)? Answer: \(X[3] = X[13] = AN/2 = 2 \times 16/2 = 16\), and every other bin is 0.
  2. For the default signal, \(X[3] = 0\) although \(x[n]\) is not zero. Why exactly zero? Answer: multiplied by the probing phasor, each cosine becomes two phasors that make \(m - k\) and \(m + k\) whole turns over the \(N\) samples, and \(\sum_n e^{j2\pi qn/N} = 0\) for any whole \(q\) that is not a multiple of \(N\). For \(k = 3\) the turn counts are \(-1\) and 5 (from \(m = 2\)) and 2 and 8 (from \(m = 5\)), so every part sums to zero and the chain returns to the origin.
  3. Why does \(x[n] = \cos(\pi n)\) with \(N = 16\) give \(X[8] = 16\) instead of \(N/2 = 8\)? Answer: here \(m = N/2 = 8\), so bins \(m\) and \(N - m\) are the same bin and both halves of the cosine land in it: \(X[8] = AN = 16\).
  4. What is \(X[3]\) for \(x[n] = \sin(2\pi\cdot 3n/16)\), and what does its phase mean? Answer: \(X[3] = -j8\), phase \(-90^\circ\): a sine is a cosine delayed by a quarter cycle. The mirror bin is \(X[13] = +j8\).
  5. In Inverse DFT mode with the default signal, you remove bins 2 and 14 and keep the rest. Predict the largest error and the energy kept. Answer: \(x_r[n] = 0.5\cos(2\pi\cdot 5n/16)\) and \(e[n] = \cos(2\pi\cdot 2n/16)\), so max \(|e[n]| = 1.000\); the energy kept is \((4^2 + 4^2)/(8^2 + 8^2 + 4^2 + 4^2) = 32/160 = 20.0\%\).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A cosine at bin \(m\) makes one spike at \(m\)." The spectrum always shows two bars, at \(m\) and \(N - m\), each \(AN/2\) tall. At \(k = N - m\) the unit circle turns counter-clockwise, which is the negative-frequency half of \(\cos\theta = (e^{j\theta} + e^{-j\theta})/2\). Removing only one of the pair in Inverse DFT mode makes \(x_r[n]\) complex, and the sim warns you.

"If \(k\) does not match, \(X[k]\) is small but not zero." For whole-bin sinusoids the chain closes exactly and the read-out shows \(0.00 + j0.00\). Non-zero values between peaks (spectral leakage) appear only when a frequency falls between bins, which this MicroSim does not generate.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Discrete Fourier transform - Wikipedia - definition of \(X[k]\) and the inverse DFT, with the orthogonality of the basis phasors
  2. Root of unity - Wikipedia - the points \(e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\) on the unit circle are \(N\)-th roots of unity
  3. Euler's formula - Wikipedia - why a cosine is the sum of two counter-rotating phasors
  4. Negative frequency - Wikipedia - why bins above \(N/2\) mirror the positive frequencies of a real signal
  5. Parseval's theorem - Wikipedia - the energy-kept read-out in Inverse DFT mode
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT and its properties

docs.title: Probability Distribution Explorer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/distribution-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="642px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim draws random samples from the distributions used most often in signal processing and compares them with the theory. The drop-down list selects uniform \(U(a, b)\), Gaussian \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), exponential \(\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)\), binomial \(B(n, p)\) (Bernoulli when \(n = 1\)), Poisson \(\mathrm{Pois}(\lambda)\), or the central-limit mode, in which every sample is the sum \(S = U_1 + \dots + U_n\) of \(n\) independent \(U(0, 1)\) values. The two parameter sliders change with the distribution.

The plot shows the theoretical PDF (or the PMF of a discrete distribution) in maroon and a blue histogram of the first \(N\) samples, with \(N\) from 10 to 10000. Continuous histograms are density-scaled with bin width \(h = 3.49\,\sigma N^{-1/3}\) (Scott's rule). Show CDF switches to the cumulative distribution \(F(x) = P(X \le x)\) and the empirical CDF of the samples. The gold band marks \(\mu \pm k\sigma\) (slider Band k) and is labelled with the probability it holds,

\[P(\mu - k\sigma \le X \le \mu + k\sigma) = F(\mu + k\sigma) - F(\mu - k\sigma).\]

Gaussian overlay adds, in green, the Gaussian with the same mean and variance. The table compares the theoretical mean, variance and standard deviation with the sample mean \(\bar{x}\), the sample variance \(s^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2\) and \(s\), and the band probability with the fraction of samples in the band. It also shows the standard error of the mean \(\sigma/\sqrt{N}\).

All samples come from a seeded generator (Mulberry32 uniforms, the Box–Muller transform for Gaussians, the inverse CDF for exponentials), so the page always opens with the same samples (seed 1). New samples moves to the next seed. Raising \(N\) keeps the first samples and adds new ones.

This simulation is used in Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain the difference between a PDF or PMF and a CDF, and compute an interval probability as \(F(b) - F(a)\)
  2. Calculate the mean, variance and standard deviation of the uniform, Gaussian, exponential, binomial and Poisson distributions from their parameters
  3. Apply the 68–95–99.7 rule to Gaussian signals and compare it with the band probabilities of non-Gaussian distributions
  4. Describe how the sample mean and variance approach the true values as \(N\) grows, using the standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{N}\)
  5. Explain the central limit theorem by observing that a sum of \(n\) uniform variables approaches a Gaussian with mean \(n/2\) and variance \(n/12\)

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a first signal processing, signals and systems, or engineering probability course. Plan 30–40 minutes for the four activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Integrals and sums as areas
  • The definitions of mean, variance and standard deviation (Chapter 1)
  • Reading a histogram

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
All sample values below are what the MicroSim shows for seed 1, the samples drawn when the page loads. After New samples the sample column changes; the theory column does not.

Activity 1: The 68–95–99.7 rule (8 min). Keep the Gaussian with \(\mu = 0.0\) and \(\sigma = 1.00\) and set \(N = 10000\). Step Band k through 1, 2 and 3. The theoretical probabilities are 0.683, 0.954 and 0.997, and the fractions of samples in the band are 0.684, 0.956 and 0.998. Now set \(\mu = 1.0\) and \(\sigma = 2.00\): the band at \(k = 1\) moves to \([-1, 3]\), but its probability is still 0.683 (and 0.954 at \(k = 2\)), because the probability depends only on \(k\). Check Show CDF with \(k = 1\): \(F(\mu - \sigma) = 0.159\) and \(F(\mu + \sigma) = 0.841\), so \(\Delta F = 0.683\), the same area.

Activity 2: Sample statistics converge (8 min). Return to \(\mu = 0.0\), \(\sigma = 1.00\), \(k = 1\), and step \(N\):

\(N\) Sample mean Sample variance Fraction in \(\mu \pm \sigma\) Standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{N}\) 10 −0.285 1.473 0.500 0.3162 100 0.210 0.980 0.690 0.1000 1000 −0.029 0.968 0.689 0.0316 10000 0.016 0.998 0.684 0.0100

The error of the sample mean shrinks roughly like \(\sigma/\sqrt{N}\). At \(N = 10\) press New samples a few times and watch how far the sample mean and the histogram move from one seed to the next.

Activity 3: Same mean, different shape (10 min). Use \(N = 10000\).

  1. Exponential, \(\lambda = 1.00\): mean and standard deviation are both 1.000 (sample 0.995 and 0.985). The band holds 0.865, 0.950 and 0.982 for \(k\) = 1, 2 and 3, not 0.683, 0.954 and 0.997: the exponential is skewed, with a long right tail.
  2. Set \(\lambda = 0.50\): the theoretical mean becomes 2.000 and the variance 4.000 (\(1/\lambda\) and \(1/\lambda^2\)). The sample mean doubles exactly to 1.990, because the same uniform numbers are rescaled, and the band probability stays 0.865.
  3. Uniform, \(a = -2.0\), \(b = 2.0\): variance \((b - a)^2/12 = 1.333\) (sample 1.327). The band holds only 0.577 at \(k = 1\) and 1.000 at \(k = 2\), because \(\mu \pm 2\sigma = \pm 2.309\) covers the whole support.
  4. Poisson, \(\lambda = 4.0\): mean and variance are both 4.000 (sample 3.992 and 4.007). The band \([2, 6]\) holds 0.798 of the probability.
  5. Binomial, \(n = 1\), \(p = 0.30\) (Bernoulli): mean \(p = 0.300\) and variance \(p(1 - p) = 0.210\) (sample 0.297 and 0.209).

Activity 4: The central limit theorem (10 min). Choose CLT: sum of n uniforms, check Gaussian overlay, and set \(N = 10000\), \(k = 1\). Step Terms n and record the read-outs:

\(n\) \(\mathrm{Var}(S) = n/12\) \(P(\mu \pm \sigma)\), theory Sample fraction Largest gap between \(F\) and \(\Phi\) 1 0.083 0.577 0.584 0.0572 2 0.167 0.650 0.659 0.0164 3 0.250 0.667 0.670 0.0099 6 0.500 0.674 0.676 0.0048 12 1.000 0.679 0.681 0.0023 30 2.500 0.681 0.684 0.0009

The histogram is flat for \(n = 1\), triangular for \(n = 2\) and already bell-shaped for \(n = 3\). The band probability climbs toward the Gaussian 0.683, and from \(n = 3\) on the largest gap between the exact CDF and the Gaussian CDF roughly halves each time \(n\) doubles (0.0099 at \(n = 3\), 0.0048 at \(n = 6\), 0.0023 at \(n = 12\)). With \(n = 12\) and \(k = 2\) the band holds 0.955, against 0.954 for a Gaussian.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Thermal noise is Gaussian with \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 2\) mV. What fraction of noise samples lies between −4 and +4 mV? Answer: ±4 mV is \(\mu \pm 2\sigma\), so 0.954 (95.4%); the MicroSim shows 0.954 for any \(\sigma\) when \(k = 2\).
  2. Waiting times are exponential with a mean of 2 s. What are \(\lambda\), the variance and the probability that a wait lies within one standard deviation of the mean? Answer: \(\lambda = 0.5\) per second, variance \(1/\lambda^2 = 4\) s², \(\sigma = 2\) s; the band \([0, 4]\) s holds \(1 - e^{-2} = 0.865\).
  3. For a Poisson variable with \(\lambda = 4\), the band \(\mu \pm \sigma\) holds 0.798 instead of 0.683. Give two reasons. Answer: the band is the closed interval \([2, 6]\) and \(X\) takes only integer values, so both end points count in full (\(P(X = 2) = 0.147\), \(P(X = 6) = 0.104\)); and the Poisson distribution is not Gaussian (it is discrete and skewed).
  4. \(S\) is the sum of 12 independent \(U(0, 1)\) values. Give \(E[S]\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(S)\), and explain why \(S - 6\) is a quick approximate standard Gaussian. Answer: \(E[S] = 12 \times 0.5 = 6\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(S) = 12 \times \tfrac{1}{12} = 1\), so \(S - 6\) has mean 0 and variance 1, and by the central limit theorem its CDF is within 0.0023 of \(\Phi\).
  5. With \(N = 100\) the sample mean of a \(N(0, 1)\) source was 0.210. Is the generator biased? Answer: not necessarily. The standard error is \(\sigma/\sqrt{N} = 0.100\), so 0.210 is 2.1 standard errors from 0, unusual but possible; at \(N = 1000\) and \(N = 10000\) the sample means are −0.029 and 0.016, within 1 and 1.6 standard errors.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"68% of the values always lie within one standard deviation of the mean." That holds only for the Gaussian. The MicroSim shows 0.577 for the uniform distribution, 0.865 for the exponential and 0.798 for Poisson with \(\lambda = 4\). The sum of \(n\) uniforms moves toward 0.683 only as \(n\) grows, as the central limit theorem predicts.

"The sample mean and variance are the mean and variance of the distribution." They are estimates. With \(N = 10\) Gaussian samples (\(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma = 1\)) the sample mean is −0.285 and the sample variance 1.473, and New samples changes both. Only as \(N\) grows do they settle near the true values.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Probability distribution - Wikipedia - PDFs, PMFs and CDFs of discrete and continuous random variables
  2. Normal distribution - Wikipedia - the Gaussian density, its moments and why it models thermal noise
  3. 68–95–99.7 rule - Wikipedia - the probabilities within one, two and three standard deviations of a Gaussian mean
  4. Central limit theorem - Wikipedia - why sums of independent random variables approach a Gaussian
  5. Irwin–Hall distribution - Wikipedia - the exact distribution of a sum of \(n\) uniform variables used in the CLT mode
  6. Poisson distribution - Wikipedia - counts of random events, with mean equal to variance
  7. Box–Muller transform - Wikipedia - how the sketch turns uniform random numbers into Gaussian ones
  8. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook; its chapter on statistics, probability and noise covers histograms, the PDF and the Gaussian

docs.title: Euler's Formula Explorer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/euler-formula-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="602px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim demonstrates Euler's formula, one of the most important equations in signal processing:

\[e^{i\theta} = \cos(\theta) + i\sin(\theta)\]

The left panel shows the complex plane with a green vector of length 1 that points at angle \(\theta\) from the positive real axis. Its tip is the complex number \(e^{i\theta}\). The blue dot is the projection of the tip onto the real axis, which is \(\cos(\theta)\). The red dot is the projection onto the imaginary axis, which is \(\sin(\theta)\). The right panel plots the two projections against \(\theta\): a faint curve shows one full period and a bold curve shows the part swept out so far. A dashed level line connects each plot's current point to its value axis. The box under the circle reports \(\theta\) in radians and degrees, \(\cos(\theta)\), \(\sin(\theta)\) and the number \(e^{i\theta}\) in rectangular form.

Use Play to rotate the vector, the Angle slider to set \(\theta\) yourself, and the Speed slider to change how fast it turns. This simulation supports the section on Euler's formula in Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
Left panel: unit circle

  • The unit circle in the complex plane (radius = 1)
  • The rotating green vector from the origin, whose tip is \(e^{i\theta}\)
  • A blue point on the real axis showing \(\cos(\theta)\) and a red point on the imaginary axis showing \(\sin(\theta)\)
  • Dashed lines connecting the tip to its two axis projections
  • An arc marking the angle \(\theta\)

Right panel: wave traces

  • A cosine plot (blue) and a sine plot (red) against \(\theta\) from 0 to \(2\pi\)
  • The current point on each plot, with its value printed beside it
  • A dashed level line from each plot's value axis to the current point

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Control Function Play / Pause Start or stop the automatic rotation Angle slider Set \(\theta\) from 0 to \(2\pi\) in steps of \(0.01\pi\) (1.8°); moving it while the animation runs pauses the animation Speed slider Set the rotation speed from 0.1x to 5.0x; at 1.0x the vector turns at 1.2 rad/s, so one revolution takes about 5.24 s Reset Return to \(\theta = 0\), clear the traces and pause (the speed setting is kept)

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
Euler's formula connects three fundamental ideas:

  • Exponentiation (\(e^x\))
  • Trigonometry (\(\cos\), \(\sin\))
  • Complex numbers (\(i\))

It matters in signal processing because it allows us to:

  1. Represent sinusoids compactly: \(A\cos(\omega t + \phi) = \text{Re}\left[Ae^{i(\omega t + \phi)}\right]\)
  2. Simplify calculations: multiplying complex exponentials adds their phases, \(e^{i\theta_1} e^{i\theta_2} = e^{i(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}\)
  3. Understand frequency analysis: the Fourier transform decomposes signals into complex exponentials

Because \(\cos^2(\theta) + \sin^2(\theta) = 1\), the tip always lies on the unit circle: \(|e^{i\theta}| = 1\) for every \(\theta\). As \(\theta\) increases from 0 to \(2\pi\) the tip travels once around the circle counterclockwise, the real part completes one cycle of cosine and the imaginary part completes one cycle of sine. A point that rotates at a steady rate is called a complex sinusoid or phasor.

\(\theta\) Angle slider \(e^{i\theta}\) \(\cos(\theta)\) \(\sin(\theta)\) 0 0.00π 1 1 0 \(\pi/2\) 0.50π \(i\) 0 1 \(\pi\) 1.00π \(-1\) \(-1\) 0 \(3\pi/2\) 1.50π \(-i\) 0 \(-1\) \(2\pi\) 2.00π 1 1 0

docs.title: Applications in Signal Processing
docs.text:
• Phasors: in AC circuit analysis a sinusoidal voltage or current is represented by a phasor \(Ve^{i\phi}\), which turns impedance calculations into complex arithmetic.
  • Fourier transform: the transform uses \(e^{-i\omega t}\) as its basis functions and decomposes a signal into frequency components.
  • Modulation: AM, FM and PM can be understood as varying the amplitude, frequency or phase of a complex exponential.
  • Filter design: transfer functions and frequency responses are written with complex exponentials, which makes their analysis tractable.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain how the rotating green vector on the unit circle represents \(e^{i\theta}\), with its real-axis projection tracing \(\cos(\theta)\) and its imaginary-axis projection tracing \(\sin(\theta)\)
  2. Predict the values of \(\cos(\theta)\) and \(\sin(\theta)\) at \(\theta\) = 0, \(\pi/2\), \(\pi\) and \(3\pi/2\), then confirm them with the angle slider and the read-out box
  3. Explain why the sine and cosine traces are identical curves offset by a quarter turn, given that they are projections of the same rotating vector onto perpendicular axes
  4. Trace how advancing \(\theta\) through a full \(2\pi\) rotation generates exactly one complete cycle of each wave
  5. Evaluate Euler's identity by setting \(\theta = \pi\) and confirming that \(e^{i\pi} = -1\)

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College-level signal processing, complex analysis or pre-calculus courses. Plan 15-25 minutes for self-directed exploration, or about 45 minutes with instructor-led discussion of the assessment questions.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex numbers and the complex plane (see the Complex Plane MicroSim)
  • Basic trigonometry: sine, cosine and the unit circle
  • Familiarity with exponential functions

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Trace the circle (5 min). Set the speed to 0.5x and press Play. One revolution takes about 10.5 s. Watch the green tip travel counterclockwise, watch the blue and red dots slide along the axes and watch the bold traces build up on the right. Press Pause at any point and read the box under the circle.

Activity 2: Find the special points (5-10 min). Press Reset, then use the angle slider.

  • Set the angle to 0.25π (45°). The read-out shows \(\cos(\theta) = 0.7071\) and \(\sin(\theta) = 0.7071\), so \(e^{i\theta} = 0.71 + 0.71i\).
  • Set 0.50π. The blue dot sits at the origin, \(\cos(\theta) = 0.0000\) and \(\sin(\theta) = 1.0000\).
  • Set 1.50π. \(\cos(\theta) = 0.0000\) again and \(\sin(\theta) = -1.0000\).
  • Find every setting where \(|\cos(\theta)| = |\sin(\theta)|\): 0.25π, 0.75π, 1.25π and 1.75π, where both read-outs are \(\pm 0.7071\).

Activity 3: Phase relationship (5 min). Set the angle to 0.00π: cosine is at its maximum (1.0000) while sine is 0. Now set 0.50π: sine is at its maximum (1.0000) while cosine is 0. The sine curve reaches each feature a quarter turn (\(\pi/2\)) later than the cosine curve, so \(\sin(\theta) = \cos(\theta - \pi/2)\).

Activity 4: Euler's identity (5 min). Set the angle to 1.00π. The read-out shows \(\cos(\theta) = -1.0000\), \(\sin(\theta) = 0.0000\) and \(e^{i\theta} = -1.00 + 0.00i\). The tip is at the left end of the real axis, so \(e^{i\pi} = -1\), or equivalently \(e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0\).

Activity 5: Frequency connection (5 min). Press Reset, set the speed to 5.0x and press Play. The vector turns at \(1.2 \times 5 = 6.0\) rad/s, which is \(6.0 / 2\pi \approx 0.95\) revolutions per second, so one full cycle of each wave takes about 1.05 s. At 1.0x the rate is 1.2 rad/s, or about 0.19 Hz. The frequency of the sinusoids is the rotation rate of the phasor.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. What is the value of \(e^{i\pi}\)? Explain it geometrically. (Answer: \(-1\). The angle \(\pi\) points the unit vector along the negative real axis, so \(\cos(\pi) = -1\) and \(\sin(\pi) = 0\).)
  2. Why does the point move counterclockwise as \(\theta\) increases? (Answer: Positive angles are measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis. Just after \(\theta = 0\) the cosine falls slightly below 1 while the sine becomes positive, which moves the tip up and to the left.)
  3. How does multiplying two complex exponentials \(e^{i\theta_1} \cdot e^{i\theta_2}\) relate to their angles? (Answer: The angles add, giving \(e^{i(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}\). For example, \(0.25\pi + 0.25\pi = 0.50\pi\), and the result is \(i\).)
  4. At \(\theta = 0.75\pi\) what are \(\cos(\theta)\), \(\sin(\theta)\) and \(|e^{i\theta}|\)? (Answer: \(\cos(\theta) = -0.7071\), \(\sin(\theta) = 0.7071\) and \(|e^{i\theta}| = \sqrt{0.5 + 0.5} = 1\).)
  5. Why is Euler's formula useful for representing AC signals? (Answer: A sinusoid \(A\cos(\omega t + \phi)\) is the real part of the rotating phasor \(Ae^{i(\omega t + \phi)}\), so amplitude and phase combine into one complex number and time shifts become multiplications.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Sine and cosine are two separate waves." They are two projections of one rotating vector. Press Play and watch the blue and red dots: they move together because they are driven by the same angle, and the sine curve is the cosine curve delayed by a quarter turn.

"The vector gets longer or shorter as it rotates." Its length is always 1. Compare the vector at 0.25π (both projections 0.7071) with the vector at 0.00π (projections 1 and 0): \(\cos^2(\theta) + \sin^2(\theta) = 1\) in every case, so only the direction changes.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Euler's formula - Wikipedia - statement, proofs and applications of the formula
  2. Euler's identity - Wikipedia - the special case \(e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0\) explored in Activity 4
  3. Unit circle - Wikipedia - the circle on which the point \(e^{i\theta}\) travels
  4. Phasor - Wikipedia - representing sinusoids as rotating complex numbers
  5. Sine and cosine - Wikipedia - projections of a point on the unit circle and the quarter-turn offset between the two functions
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on complex numbers and the complex exponential
  7. Oppenheim, A. V., & Schafer, R. W. (2010). Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed. - Pearson - standard text that develops complex exponential sequences
  8. Nahin, P. J. (2006). Dr. Euler's Fabulous Formula - Princeton University Press - book-length treatment of the formula and its uses
  9. Euler, L. (1748). Introductio in analysin infinitorum - the original publication of the formula

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text:
Version history

Version 2.0.0 (2026-10-14). Ported from p5.js 1.11.10 to p5.js 2.3.2. Layout fixes: the read-out box no longer overlaps the circle, the lower plot is no longer clipped by the control region, the projection labels no longer collide at \(\theta = 0\), and the title shrinks to fit narrow screens. The traces are now computed from the current angle (a faint full period plus a bold swept portion) instead of a stored history, so they stay correct when the angle slider is dragged, and no spurious line is drawn when the animation wraps from \(2\pi\) to 0. The angle slider is now expressed in units of \(\pi\) so that \(\pi/2\), \(\pi\) and \(3\pi/2\) can be set exactly. Moving the angle slider while the animation runs now pauses it. Added the \(e^{i\theta}\) read-out and quarter-turn tick labels on the \(\theta\) axes.

docs.title: Even and Odd Signal Decomposition

Copy this iframe to your website:
