docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim generates a pure sine wave \(x(t) = A\sin(2\pi f t)\), plays it through your speakers, and shows it two ways at once. The top plot (green) is the time domain: a 20 ms window of the waveform, triggered on a rising zero crossing so the wave holds still like an oscilloscope trace. The bottom plot (purple) is the frequency domain: the magnitude spectrum from 0 to 2100 Hz computed by a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT).

  • Frequency slider (20-2000 Hz, default 440 Hz) sets \(f\). The wave completes \(f \times 0.020\) cycles in the window, and the spike moves to \(f\).
  • Amplitude slider (0-1, default 0.5) sets \(A\). The wave height and the spike height both scale with \(A\); the spike does not move.
  • Start/Pause turns the tone on and off. Reset returns the sliders to 440 Hz and 0.5.

The read-out above the spectrum gives the centre frequency and height of the strongest FFT bin. The FFT uses \(N = 16384\) points, so its bins are \(\Delta f = f_s / N\) apart: 2.93 Hz when your audio device runs at \(f_s = 48\) kHz (2.69 Hz at 44.1 kHz). The sample rate and bin width are printed under the spectrum on wide screens. A 440 Hz tone falls between two bins, so at 48 kHz the read-out shows 439.5 Hz. Heights are scaled so that a sine of amplitude 1 centred on a bin reaches 1.0; because the browser applies a Blackman window, a tone that falls between bins reads up to about 12% lower. The speakers play the tone at half the displayed amplitude to protect listeners; the FFT analyses the full signal.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  1. Explain that the FFT decomposes a time-domain waveform into the frequencies it contains
  2. Predict that raising the frequency slider shortens the period in the time-domain plot and shifts the spectral peak to the right in the frequency-domain plot
  3. Predict that increasing the amplitude slider raises both the waveform and the spectral peak in proportion while leaving the peak's frequency unchanged
  4. Distinguish the time-domain display, which plots amplitude against time, from the frequency-domain display, which plots magnitude against frequency
  5. Identify the frequency of a pure sine wave from the location of its single spectral peak and from the number of cycles in the 20 ms window

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College freshmen in an introductory signal processing course. The lab takes about 20 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Basic trigonometry
  • Familiarity with sine waves (period, frequency, amplitude)

docs.title: Materials and Setup
docs.text:
• Computer with a web browser and audio output
  • This MicroSim
  • Headphones or speakers (optional but recommended)
  • The student worksheet in the activities below
  • Whiteboard or projector for demonstrations

Student setup. Open the MicroSim, set the computer volume to a comfortable level, and find the two plots (top and bottom), the two sliders, the Start and Reset buttons, and the red PAUSED status indicator.

Instructor setup. Project the MicroSim for a class demonstration, have the example frequencies 220 Hz, 440 Hz and 880 Hz ready, and prepare simple sine-wave sketches on the whiteboard.

docs.title: Lesson Introduction
docs.text:
Hook: the musical connection. Ask: "When you hear a musical note, what makes it different from noise?" Students may mention pitch, tone or harmony. Lead toward the idea that a musical note has a specific frequency.

Core concept. "Today we will analyse a signal - music, voice, or an electronic signal - by breaking it into its frequency components."

Key terms. Write these on the board:

  • Time domain: how a signal changes over time (what an oscilloscope shows)
  • Frequency domain: which frequencies are present in a signal and how strong each one is
  • FFT (Fast Fourier Transform): a fast algorithm that converts a sampled time-domain signal into the frequency domain

The read-outs quoted below were measured with a 48 kHz audio device. On a 44.1 kHz device the frequencies differ by up to about 3 Hz and the heights by a few hundredths, because the bins fall in different places.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Interface tour and first observations (8 min).

  1. Before pressing Start (440 Hz, amplitude 0.5): the top plot is a flat line and the spectrum is empty. Ask: "What do you see in both displays right now?"
  2. Press Start. A green sine wave appears with 8.8 cycles in the 20 ms window (\(440 \times 0.020\)), and a purple spike appears at 440 Hz. The read-out shows Strongest bin: 439.5 Hz, magnitude 0.49. Ask: "Where is the spike? Why there?"
  3. Set the frequency to 220 Hz. The wave stretches out to 4.4 cycles and the spike moves left (read-out 219.7 Hz).
  4. Set the frequency to 880 Hz. The wave compresses to 17.6 cycles and the spike moves right (read-out 878.9 Hz). Ask: "Can you predict the pattern?"

Key point: one sine wave in time always produces exactly one spike in frequency.

Activity 2: Amplitude exploration (7 min).

  1. Set the frequency to 440 Hz and change the amplitude from 0.5 to 0.1. The wave shrinks to peaks of \(\pm 0.1\) and the spike drops to a height of 0.10. Ask: "What changed? What stayed the same?"
  2. Set the amplitude to 1.0. The wave reaches the \(\pm 1\) gridlines and the spike reaches 0.98.
  3. Worksheet: set the frequency to 500 Hz and complete the table.
Amplitude Time-domain wave height Frequency spike height 0.1 0.3 0.7 1.0

Expected spike heights: 0.09, 0.28, 0.66 and 0.95. Each is about 0.95 times the amplitude (500 Hz falls between two bins), so the spike height is proportional to the amplitude. Key point: amplitude changes the height in both domains but not the frequency location.

Activity 3: Frequency prediction (5 min).

  1. Set the frequency to 100 Hz and press Start. The window holds exactly 2 cycles and the spike is at the far left (read-out 99.6 Hz).
  2. Predict where the spike and the wave will be at 200 Hz, then test it. The spike moves to 199.2 Hz and the window holds 4 cycles.
  3. Find the setting that puts the spike on the 1000 Hz tick. At 1000 Hz the read-out shows 999.0 Hz: discuss why the FFT reports the nearest bin rather than the exact frequency.

Activity 4: Musical notes (5 min). Set each note and listen while you watch the spike:

  • C4: 262 Hz (read-out 260.7 Hz)
  • E4: 330 Hz (read-out 331.1 Hz)
  • G4: 392 Hz (read-out 392.6 Hz)
  • C5: 523 Hz (read-out 524.4 Hz)

Higher pitch puts the spike further to the right. C5 is one octave above C4, and its spike sits at almost exactly twice the frequency (\(523 / 262 \approx 2.0\)).

docs.title: Class Discussion and Wrap-up
docs.text:
Ask students to share:

  • "What surprised you most about the relationship between time and frequency?"
  • "How would you explain the FFT to a friend in simple terms?"

Connect to the real world:

  • Music production: equalizers and spectrum analysers show frequency content
  • Medical imaging: MRI reconstructs images with Fourier transforms
  • Communication: mobile networks place many signals in separate frequency channels
  • Audio compression: MP3 encoders use frequency analysis to discard sounds we cannot hear

Preview of the next lesson: "What will the frequency domain look like when two sine waves play at the same time?"

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A student sets the frequency to 250 Hz. Where does the spike appear, and how many complete cycles fit in the 20 ms window? (Answer: at 250 Hz (the read-out shows 249.0 Hz at 48 kHz); \(250 \times 0.020 = 5\) cycles.)
  2. At a fixed frequency the amplitude is changed from 0.2 to 0.6. What happens to the height and the position of the spike? (Answer: the height triples because the spectrum magnitude is proportional to amplitude; the position does not change.)
  3. You count 6 complete cycles in the 20 ms window. What frequency is the generator set to? (Answer: \(6 / 0.020\ \text{s} = 300\) Hz; the spike confirms it, with a read-out of 298.8 Hz at 48 kHz.)
  4. Why does the read-out show 439.5 Hz rather than 440 Hz for a 440 Hz tone at \(f_s = 48\) kHz? (Answer: the FFT measures only at bins spaced \(48000 / 16384 \approx 2.93\) Hz apart. 440 Hz lies between bin 150 (439.45 Hz) and bin 151 (442.38 Hz), and the read-out reports the centre of the stronger bin.)
  5. Predict the spectrum of a signal that contains 300 Hz at amplitude 0.5 and 900 Hz at amplitude 0.25. (Answer: two spikes, one at 300 Hz and one at 900 Hz, with the second about half as tall as the first.)

Assessment rubric (formative, during the lesson).

  • Excellent (4): correctly predicts the effects of frequency and amplitude and explains the reasoning
  • Proficient (3): makes correct observations with minimal guidance
  • Developing (2): participates but needs significant guidance
  • Beginning (1): struggles to make basic observations

Worksheet assessment.

  • Understanding of the FFT: identifies that a sine wave creates a single spike, explains the relationship between the two domains, and shows that amplitude affects height, not position
  • Problem solving: makes accurate predictions about frequency changes, uses the MicroSim to test hypotheses, and records observations accurately

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Higher frequency means a taller spike." Frequency moves the spike sideways; only the amplitude changes its height. With the amplitude at 0.5, move the frequency from 220 Hz to 880 Hz: the spike moves right while its height stays near 0.5 (0.50 and 0.47).

"The time-domain wave and the frequency spike should look similar." They show different information. A smooth wave with 8.8 cycles in the window becomes one narrow spike at 440 Hz.

"The FFT creates the frequencies." The FFT only reveals frequencies that are already in the signal, the way a prism reveals colours already present in white light. Press Pause: the signal goes silent and the spike decays to nothing.

docs.title: Extension Activities
docs.text:
For advanced students:

  1. Research challenge: look up the definition of the discrete Fourier transform. How does the bin spacing \(f_s/N\) explain the read-out values in Activity 3?
  2. Real-world connection: find an example of frequency analysis in your own field (engineering, music, medicine).

For students needing support:

  1. Visual summary: draw a sine wave and its frequency spike, with labelled axes.
  2. Analogy: invent an analogy that explains why we need both the time and the frequency representation.

docs.title: Homework
docs.text:
1. In your own words, explain what the Fast Fourier Transform does and why it is useful.
  2. Describe a situation where you would analyse a signal in the frequency domain rather than the time domain.
  3. Using the MicroSim, put the spike on the 1000 Hz mark. Explain how you found the setting and why the read-out may not show exactly 1000 Hz.
  4. Creative application: if you were designing a music app, how could you use frequency-domain analysis? Describe at least two features.

docs.title: Instructor Notes
docs.text:
• Audio not working: students must click Start (browsers block sound until a click) and check that the tab is not muted. The speakers play the tone at half the displayed amplitude.
  • Display too small: use browser zoom, or open the MicroSim full screen.
  • Running behind: skip the worksheet table in Activity 2.
  • Ahead of schedule: discuss frequency resolution. This MicroSim uses a 16,384-point FFT, giving 2.93 Hz bins at 48 kHz; a 1,024-point FFT would give 46.9 Hz bins (\(48000 / 1024\)), too coarse to separate 440 Hz from 460 Hz.
  • Differentiation: visual learners can sketch both plots; auditory learners can listen with headphones while sweeping the frequency; kinesthetic learners can explore freely with the sliders.
  • Accommodations: allow verbal worksheet answers, give English-language learners a vocabulary list of the key terms, and ask advanced students about sampling rate and frequency resolution.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the algorithm that computes the spectrum shown in the bottom plot
  2. Discrete Fourier transform - Wikipedia - definition of the frequency bins and their spacing \(f_s/N\)
  3. Frequency domain - Wikipedia - time-domain and frequency-domain views of the same signal
  4. Window function - Wikipedia - the Blackman window and why a tone between bins reads slightly low
  5. AnalyserNode - MDN Web Docs - the browser FFT that p5.sound uses for the spectrum and the waveform
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT and the FFT

docs.title: FFT Butterfly
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fft-butterfly/main.html" width="100%" height="582px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim traces the first job of a radix-2 decimation-in-time FFT: putting the \(N\) input samples into bit-reversed order before the butterfly stages combine them. Each circle is one sample \(x[n]\) labelled with its index \(n\) (at \(N = 32\), read the binary labels). The orange column is the natural order \(x[0], x[1], \dots, x[N-1]\).

  • Start / Next Step adds one column. Each step splits every group into its even-indexed samples (top half of the group) and its odd-indexed samples (bottom half). Navy lines show where each sample moves, and gray bars mark the boundaries of the new groups.
  • Reset returns to the natural order.
  • FFT Size (4, 8, 16 or 32) chooses \(N\) and resets the diagram.

The diagram has \(\log_2 N\) columns: the natural order plus \(\log_2 N - 1\) splits. The last split would only turn pairs into single samples, which does not change the order. The green column therefore holds \(N/2\) pairs of samples that are \(N/2\) apart, such as \(x[0], x[4]\) for \(N = 8\); each pair feeds one butterfly of the first stage. The binary labels show why the result is called bit-reversed: read across a row and the bits on the right are the bits on the left in reverse order. For \(N = 8\), row 1 (001) receives \(x[4]\) (100).

Each split rests on the decimation-in-time identity, where \(E[k]\) and \(O[k]\) are the \(N/2\)-point DFTs of the even and odd samples:

\[X[k] = E[k] + W_N^k\,O[k], \qquad X[k + N/2] = E[k] - W_N^k\,O[k], \qquad W_N = e^{-j2\pi/N}\]

Repeating the split \(\log_2 N\) times costs \((N/2)\log_2 N\) complex multiplications instead of \(N^2\): 12 instead of 64 for \(N = 8\), and 80 instead of 1024 for \(N = 32\).

This MicroSim supports Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Describe one decimation-in-time step as splitting every group of samples into its even-indexed and odd-indexed halves
  2. Calculate the number of columns (\(\log_2 N\)), the number of splits (\(\log_2 N - 1\)) and the group size after split \(s\) (\(N/2^s\)) for a given FFT size
  3. Predict the row that sample \(x[n]\) occupies in the final column by reversing the bits of \(n\), and verify the prediction in the diagram
  4. Explain why the final pairs \(x[m]\) and \(x[m + N/2]\) are the inputs of the first butterfly stage
  5. Compare the \((N/2)\log_2 N\) complex multiplications of the radix-2 FFT with the \(N^2\) of the direct DFT

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in an introductory digital signal processing course, during the lesson on the FFT. Plan 15-20 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The definition of the DFT and its \(N^2\) cost
  • Binary representation of integers
  • Even and odd indices of a sequence

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: One split at a time (5 min). Keep FFT Size at 8 and press Start. The middle column holds 0, 2, 4, 6 above the gray bar and 1, 3, 5, 7 below it: the even and the odd samples. Press Next Step. Each group of 4 splits again and the green column reads 0, 4, 2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 7. Ask: which samples feed each 4-point DFT, and which feed each 2-point DFT?

Activity 2: Read the bits (5 min). At the last step for \(N = 8\), compare the binary labels across each row. Row 3 shows 011 on the left and 110 on the right, so it receives \(x[6]\). Find the samples that end in the row where they started: \(x[0]\), \(x[2]\), \(x[5]\) and \(x[7]\), whose 3-bit patterns (000, 010, 101, 111) read the same in both directions.

Activity 3: Count the steps (5 min). Select each FFT Size and press Next Step until nothing changes. The title stops at Step 2 of 2 for \(N = 4\), Step 3 of 3 for \(N = 8\), Step 4 of 4 for \(N = 16\) and Step 5 of 5 for \(N = 32\). Record \(N\), the number of splits and the group size after each split. Each doubling of \(N\) adds one split, and one butterfly stage.

Activity 4: Predict before you click (5 min). Select \(N = 16\). Before stepping, reverse four bits to predict the final rows: \(x[3]\) (0011) goes to row 12 (1100), \(x[5]\) (0101) to row 10 (1010) and \(x[11]\) (1011) to row 13 (1101). Step to the end and check the green column. Which four samples end in their own row? (\(x[0]\), \(x[6]\), \(x[9]\) and \(x[15]\).)

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. For \(N = 32\), how many splits does the diagram show, and what are the groups after the second split? (Answer: \(\log_2 32 - 1 = 4\) splits; after the second split there are 4 groups of 8 samples.)
  2. For \(N = 16\), which sample sits in row 2 of the final column? (Answer: row 2 is 0010; reversed it is 0100 = 4, so \(x[4]\). The green column reads 0, 8, 4, 12, ...)
  3. After the first split for \(N = 8\), the top group is \(x[0], x[2], x[4], x[6]\). What is computed from these samples, and how is it combined with the bottom group? (Answer: the 4-point DFT \(E[k]\) of the even samples. It is combined with the odd-sample DFT \(O[k]\) as \(X[k] = E[k] + W_8^k O[k]\) and \(X[k+4] = E[k] - W_8^k O[k]\).)
  4. How many complex multiplications does a radix-2 FFT need for \(N = 32\), compared with the direct DFT? (Answer: \((32/2) \times 5 = 80\) versus \(32^2 = 1024\), about 13 times fewer.)
  5. Is the green column the FFT output \(X[k]\)? (Answer: no. It holds the same input samples in a new order; no arithmetic has been done yet. The butterfly stages that follow compute \(X[k]\), which comes out in natural order.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Bit-reversed order means the list is reversed." Reversing the list would put \(x[7]\) first. In the diagram \(x[0]\) and \(x[7]\) stay at the top and bottom while \(x[4]\) moves up to row 1: the bits of each index are reversed, not the list.

"The right-hand column is the FFT result." The green circles carry the same sample labels as the orange ones. Reordering only moves data; the multiplications and additions happen in the butterfly stages that follow.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - overview of FFT algorithms and their \(O(N \log N)\) cost
  2. Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm - Wikipedia - the radix-2 decimation-in-time recursion into even and odd samples
  3. Bit-reversal permutation - Wikipedia - the input order shown in the green column and how it is computed
  4. Butterfly diagram - Wikipedia - the two-input butterfly that combines each pair after the reordering
  5. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook; Chapter 12 explains the FFT's interlaced decomposition and bit-reversal sorting

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text: Version 2.0 (October 2026) ported the sketch to p5.js 2.3.2 and removed the unused p5.sound library. The intermediate columns now follow the textbook decimation-in-time split (whole sequence first, then each half); the earlier version built the same bit-reversed order from the smallest groups upward. The binary labels, the group bars and the caption under the diagram were added, and the column headings were renamed from "Inputs"/"Outputs" to "Natural order"/"Bit-reversed order", because the right-hand column is not the FFT output.

docs.title: FFT Live Audio from Microphone
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fft-live-audio/main.html" width="100%" height="482px" scrolling="no" allow="microphone"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a live spectrum analyzer for your computer's microphone. Press Start and allow microphone access when the browser asks. The purple bars show the magnitude spectrum of the last fraction of a second of sound, computed by a fast Fourier transform (FFT), from 0 Hz up to the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\). The vertical axis is in decibels: \(-100\) dB is an empty bar and anything louder than \(-30\) dB fills the plot. A gold marker and the Strongest peak read-out show the loudest frequency above 50 Hz, and moving the mouse over the plot reads out the frequency under the cursor.

Control What it does Start / Stop Opens or closes the microphone. Sound is analyzed in your browser only; nothing is recorded, sent or played back. Smoothness (0 to 0.95) Averages each new spectrum with the previous ones. High values steady the display but make it slow to follow sudden sounds. FFT Size (128 to 16384 bins) Sets how many frequency bins divide the range from 0 Hz to \(f_s/2\). Reset Returns to Smoothness 0.50 and 1024 bins.

The line above the plot shows the quantities that the FFT Size controls. With \(N\) bins and sample rate \(f_s\),

\[\Delta f = \frac{f_s}{2N}, \qquad T_{\text{window}} = \frac{2N}{f_s}.\]

For example, 1024 bins at \(f_s = 48\) kHz gives a bin width of 23.4 Hz and needs a window of 2048 samples (42.7 ms). Finer frequency resolution always costs a longer window, which is the time-frequency trade-off.

This simulation is used in Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis. If you embed it on another site, keep allow="microphone" on the iframe.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Identify the frequency of a sustained whistle as the strongest narrow peak in the live spectrum.
  2. Calculate the bin width \(f_s/(2N)\) and window length \(2N/f_s\) for a given FFT size and sample rate.
  3. Predict how raising the Smoothness slider toward 0.95 steadies the spectrum but slows its response to sudden sounds.
  4. Explain the trade-off between frequency resolution and time resolution when the FFT size changes.
  5. Compare the spectra of a whistle, a sung vowel and a hissed "sss" to distinguish tonal sounds from broadband noise.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in an introductory signal processing, audio engineering or music technology course. Plan 15-20 minutes. A computer with a working microphone is required.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Frequency, amplitude and the idea of a sinusoid
  • Sampling and the Nyquist frequency (Chapter 5)
  • What a magnitude spectrum is and the decibel scale

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Find your whistle (5 min). Press Start with Smoothness 0.50 and FFT Size 1024 bins. Whistle a steady note. A single narrow peak appears with the gold marker on it; read its frequency from the Strongest peak read-out, then whistle higher and lower and watch the peak move. At 48 kHz the read-out moves in steps of the 23.4 Hz bin width.

Activity 2: Resolution in steps (5 min). Keep whistling the same note and move FFT Size from 128 to 16384 bins. At 128 bins (bin width 187.5 Hz at 48 kHz) the peak is a wide block and the read-out jumps in 187.5 Hz steps. At 16384 bins the bin width is 1.46 Hz, so the read-out is much more precise, but the analysis window is 32768 samples (683 ms) long.

Activity 3: Smoothness and time (5 min). Set FFT Size to 1024 bins and Smoothness to 0.00, then clap once: the bars flash and disappear. Set Smoothness to 0.95 and clap again: the bars fade slowly. Each display frame the analyzer keeps the fraction \(\tau\) (the Smoothness value) of the previous magnitude, so after a sound ends the bars fall by \(20\log_{10}\tau\) dB per frame: about 6 dB per frame at 0.50 but only 0.45 dB per frame at 0.95, which at 60 frames per second takes about 2.6 s to cross the 70 dB height of the plot.

Activity 4: Tones versus noise (5 min). With Smoothness 0.50 and 2048 bins, compare a whistle, a long sung "ah" and a long hissed "sss". The whistle gives one peak, the vowel gives a row of evenly spaced peaks (harmonics of the voice's fundamental frequency), and the hiss spreads energy over many kilohertz with no single peak.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. At \(f_s = 48\) kHz with FFT Size 1024 bins, what is the bin width? Answer: \(48000 / (2 \times 1024) = 23.4375\) Hz, about 23.4 Hz.
  2. With 1024 bins at \(f_s = 48\) kHz, the strongest peak is in bin 85. What frequency is that? Answer: \(85 \times 23.4375 = 1992.2\) Hz.
  3. At \(f_s = 44.1\) kHz with 4096 bins, how long is the analysis window? Answer: \(2 \times 4096 = 8192\) samples, and \(8192 / 44100 = 0.186\) s, about 186 ms.
  4. With Smoothness 0.80, how many display frames does it take a bar to fall by 20 dB after a sound stops? Answer: each frame falls by \(20\log_{10}0.8 = 1.94\) dB, so about \(20 / 1.94 \approx 10\) frames, roughly 0.17 s at 60 frames per second.
  5. Why does a clap stay on the display much longer at 16384 bins than at 128 bins, even with Smoothness 0? Answer: 16384 bins needs a 32768-sample window (683 ms at 48 kHz), so the clap stays inside the analyzed window for a large part of a second; the 128-bin window is only 256 samples (5.3 ms).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A bigger FFT size shows higher frequencies." The frequency axis always runs from 0 Hz to the Nyquist frequency; move the FFT Size slider and the axis does not change. Only the bin width and the window length change.

"Smoothness filters the sound." Smoothness only averages successive spectra over time for display. Whistle with Smoothness 0.00 and then 0.95: the peak appears at the same frequency both times. At 0.95 it only rises and fades more slowly, because the averaging changes how the display follows time, not which frequencies are present.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the algorithm that computes the spectrum shown here
  2. Short-time Fourier transform - Wikipedia - spectra of a sliding window of a live signal and the time-frequency trade-off
  3. Window function - Wikipedia - the Blackman window that the browser analyzer applies before the FFT
  4. Spectrum analyzer - Wikipedia - what instruments and software that display a live spectrum do
  5. AnalyserNode - MDN - the Web Audio node behind the analyzer, including fftSize and smoothingTimeConstant
  6. MediaDevices: getUserMedia() method - MDN - how a web page asks for microphone access
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT and FFT
  8. p5.sound.js - Processing Foundation - the audio library used by this MicroSim

docs.title: Microphone Frequency Visualization with FFT
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fft-mic/main.html" allow="microphone" width="100%" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim turns your computer's microphone into a real-time spectrum analyzer. Press Start and allow microphone access when the browser asks. Every frame the sketch computes a fast Fourier transform (FFT) of the most recent microphone samples and draws one bar per frequency bin. Bar height is the bin's level in decibels, from −100 dB (empty) to −30 dB (full height). Bar color runs from blue at the low end of the displayed range to red at the high end. A gold triangle marks the strongest bin, and the Peak read-out gives its frequency.

Control What it does Start / Stop Opens the microphone and starts the analysis. Stop releases the microphone and freezes the last spectrum so you can study it. Max Freq slider Sets the highest frequency on the horizontal axis, from 2 kHz to 24 kHz in 0.5 kHz steps (default 8 kHz). The axis never extends past the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\).

The analyzer returns 512 bins evenly spaced from 0 Hz to the Nyquist frequency, so bin \(k\) is centered on

\[f_k = k \cdot \frac{f_s}{2 \cdot 512}\]

At the common sample rate \(f_s = 48\) kHz the bin width is 46.875 Hz; at 44.1 kHz it is 43.07 Hz. The level is \(20\log_{10}|X_k|\). A full-scale sine wave reads about −14 dB, because half of its energy belongs to the negative frequency and the analyzer's Blackman window has a coherent gain of 0.42. Successive spectra are averaged with a smoothing constant of 0.8. The peak search skips the 0 Hz (DC) bin and the leakage around it.

Sound is analyzed only inside your browser; nothing is recorded or uploaded. Browsers allow microphone access only on pages served over https or from localhost.

This simulation is used in Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Identify the dominant frequency of a whistled or hummed sound using the Peak read-out and the gold marker.
  2. Calculate the center frequency of an FFT bin from its index, the sample rate and the number of bins, and use it to explain why the read-out differs from the true frequency of a tone.
  3. Compare the spectra of a hummed note, a whistle and a hissed "sss" by the number, spacing and spread of their peaks.
  4. Predict how the Max Freq slider rescales the frequency axis, and explain why the axis cannot extend past the Nyquist frequency.
  5. Interpret the decibel scale of the vertical axis, including the 6 dB rise that comes from doubling a tone's amplitude.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in an introductory signal processing, audio engineering or music technology course. Plan 15-20 minutes. Each student (or pair) needs a computer or phone with a microphone.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Frequency, amplitude and the idea of a sinusoid
  • Sampling and the Nyquist frequency (Chapter 5)
  • What a spectrum is and what the DFT computes (Chapter 6)
  • Decibels as a logarithmic measure of amplitude

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Hiss versus hum (5 min). Leave Max Freq at 8 kHz and press Start. Stay quiet for a few seconds and note the background level. Then say a long "sss", and afterwards sing a steady "ooo". The "sss" raises a broad band of bars with no distinct peaks, typically strongest in the right half of the plot (above about 4 kHz). The "ooo" produces a row of narrow, evenly spaced peaks, typically with most of the energy below 1 kHz.

Activity 2: Harmonics of a hummed note (5 min). Set Max Freq to 2 kHz. Hum a steady low note and press Stop while humming to freeze the spectrum. Read the positions of the first four peaks on the axis. The peaks are evenly spaced, and the spacing equals the frequency of the first peak (the fundamental). For example, a fundamental near 200 Hz gives further peaks near 400, 600 and 800 Hz.

Activity 3: Frequency resolution (5 min). Use a tone-generator app on a phone to play a steady 440 Hz sine wave near the microphone. At \(f_s = 48\) kHz the Peak read-out shows 422 Hz, not 440 Hz: \(440 / 46.875 = 9.39\), so the strongest bin is bin 9, centered on \(9 \times 46.875 = 421.9\) Hz. Change the tone to 1000 Hz and the read-out shows 984 Hz (bin 21). On a computer that runs audio at 44.1 kHz the same tones read 431 Hz and 991 Hz. On wide screens the note below the plot ("fs = ..., bin width ...") tells you which case applies.

Activity 4: The Nyquist limit (5 min). Drag Max Freq all the way to 24 kHz. At \(f_s = 48\) kHz the right edge of the plot is exactly the Nyquist frequency, and on wide screens the plot is labeled "right edge = Nyquist (fs/2)". At \(f_s = 44.1\) kHz the label stops at 22.05 kHz however far you drag the slider. Notice how little energy everyday sounds have in the upper half of this range.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With \(f_s = 48\) kHz and 512 bins spanning 0 Hz to the Nyquist frequency, what is the bin width, and what frequency is bin 100 centered on? (Answer: \(48000 / 1024 = 46.875\) Hz; \(100 \times 46.875 = 4687.5\) Hz.)
  2. You whistle a steady 1000 Hz tone and the sample rate is 48 kHz. What does the Peak read-out show, and why? (Answer: 984 Hz. \(1000 / 46.875 = 21.3\), so the strongest bin is bin 21, centered on 984.4 Hz; the read-out can only report bin center frequencies.)
  3. A hummed note shows peaks near 150, 300, 450 and 600 Hz. What is its fundamental frequency, and what are the other peaks? (Answer: 150 Hz; the other peaks are its 2nd, 3rd and 4th harmonics.)
  4. A tone's amplitude doubles. How far does its bar rise on the decibel axis? (Answer: \(20\log_{10} 2 \approx 6\) dB, which is 6/70 of the plot height on this −100 to −30 dB scale.)
  5. Why can this display never show frequencies above 24 kHz when the sample rate is 48 kHz? (Answer: the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2 = 24\) kHz is the highest frequency a signal sampled at 48 kHz can represent.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The Peak read-out is the exact pitch." The FFT measures energy in bins 46.9 Hz wide (at 48 kHz), and the read-out reports the center of the strongest bin. Activity 3 exposes this: a 440 Hz tone reads 422 Hz.

"A voice is a single frequency." A hummed or sung note is a fundamental plus a family of harmonics at whole-number multiples of it. Activity 2 freezes the spectrum so students can see and measure the evenly spaced peaks.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the algorithm that computes the spectrum shown here
  2. Spectrum analyzer - Wikipedia - instruments and software that display a live spectrum like this one
  3. Nyquist frequency - Wikipedia - why the frequency axis stops at half the sample rate
  4. Harmonic series (music) - Wikipedia - why one sung note produces several evenly spaced peaks
  5. Window function - Wikipedia - the Blackman window, its coherent gain and spectral leakage
  6. Decibel - Wikipedia - the logarithmic scale used on the vertical axis
  7. AnalyserNode - MDN - the browser FFT analyzer (window, smoothing, decibel conversion) underneath p5.sound
  8. MediaDevices: getUserMedia() method - MDN - how a page asks for microphone access and why it needs a secure context
  9. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT and FFT

docs.title: FFT Size MicroSim
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fft-size/main.html" width="100%" height="582px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim plays a pure sine wave \(x(t) = A\sin(2\pi f t)\) and analyses it with a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) whose size you choose, to show how the FFT size sets the frequency resolution: the spacing of the frequency bins and the width of the spectral peak.

  • Frequency slider (20-2000 Hz, default 440 Hz) sets \(f\); Amplitude slider (0-1, default 0.5) sets \(A\).
  • FFT Size radio buttons choose 512, 1024, 2048 (default), 4096 or 8192 bins. The size is the number of bins between 0 Hz and the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\); each spectrum is computed from the most recent \(N = 2 \times \text{size}\) samples.
  • Start/Pause turns the tone on and off. Reset returns the sliders to 440 Hz and 0.5.

The top plot (green) shows a stretch of the waveform one window long, \(T = N/f_s\). The bottom plot (purple) draws one bar per frequency bin. A gold triangle marks the strongest bin and a gold bracket marks the peak width at half height. Below the spectrum the MicroSim prints that width and the bin width

\[\Delta f = \frac{f_s}{N}.\]

Because \(T = N/f_s\), the product \(\Delta f \cdot T = 1\): each doubling of the FFT size halves the bin width and the peak width, and doubles the length of signal the FFT must see. The browser applies a Blackman window, so the peak is always about 2.4 bins wide at half height. A sine of amplitude 1 centred on a bin reaches a height of 1.0; the speakers play the tone at half the displayed amplitude.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the bin width \(\Delta f = f_s/N\) and the window length \(T = N/f_s\) for a given FFT size and sample rate
  2. Predict how doubling the FFT size changes the bin width, the width of the spectral peak and the length of the analysis window
  3. Explain the time-frequency trade-off: a larger FFT resolves frequency more finely only by analysing a longer stretch of signal, because \(\Delta f \cdot T = 1\)
  4. Explain why the strongest bin can differ from the true tone frequency by up to half a bin width
  5. Determine which FFT sizes can separate two tones a given distance apart, using the measured peak width

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in an introductory signal processing course who have just met the FFT.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sine waves: frequency, period and amplitude
  • Sampling and the sample rate \(f_s\)
  • What an FFT spectrum shows (for example, the Basic FFT MicroSim)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
The numbers below were measured with a 48 kHz audio device. The MicroSim prints the sample rate in the Freq Resolution line; on a 44.1 kHz device the bins are 8% narrower and the read-outs differ slightly.

Activity 1: Interface tour.

  1. Press Start with the defaults (440 Hz, amplitude 0.5, 2048 bins). The Freq Resolution line reads 48000 / 4096 = 11.72 Hz/bin, and the time axis spans 85.3 ms, so the window holds \(440 \times 0.0853 = 37.5\) cycles.
  2. Read the spectrum: the strongest bin is at 445.3 Hz, not 440 Hz. Ask why. (\(440 / 11.72 = 37.55\), so the tone lies between bin 37 at 433.6 Hz and bin 38 at 445.3 Hz.)
  3. Change the amplitude to 0.1 and then to 1.0. The peak height changes from 0.09 to 0.90, but the peak width stays at 28.9 Hz: the width depends on the FFT size, not on the amplitude.

Activity 2: Peak width and FFT size. Keep 440 Hz and amplitude 0.5. Select each FFT size in turn and fill in the table. Expected values at 48 kHz:

FFT size (bins) N (samples) Window \(T\) \(\Delta f\) (Hz/bin) Strongest bin (Hz) Peak width at half height (Hz) 512 1024 21.3 ms 46.88 421.9 113.8 1024 2048 42.7 ms 23.44 445.3 55.6 2048 4096 85.3 ms 11.72 445.3 28.9 4096 8192 170.7 ms 5.86 439.5 13.9 8192 16384 341.3 ms 2.93 439.5 6.9

Each doubling halves \(\Delta f\) and the peak width and doubles \(T\). At 512 bins the peak is built from a handful of wide bars; at 8192 bins it is a thin spike. The width is always about 2.4 bins, so the width in hertz is set by \(\Delta f\). (At 44.1 kHz: \(\Delta f\) = 43.07, 21.53, 10.77, 5.38 and 2.69 Hz; peak widths 102.1, 52.9, 25.5, 12.8 and 6.7 Hz.)

Activity 3: How accurate is the strongest bin? Set the frequency to 1000 Hz.

  1. At 512 bins the strongest bin reads 984.4 Hz, an error of 15.6 Hz.
  2. At 2048 bins it reads 996.1 Hz; at 8192 bins, 999.0 Hz.
  3. Repeat at 100 Hz: 93.8 Hz, 105.5 Hz and 99.6 Hz. In every case the error is less than half a bin width (\(\Delta f/2\)), because the read-out reports the centre of the bin nearest the tone.

Activity 4: The time-frequency trade-off. Set 440 Hz and select 8192 bins.

  1. Drag the amplitude slider quickly to 0 and back to 0.5 (about a tenth of a second). The time plot shows a gap in the wave that travels from the right edge (newest samples) to the left across the 341 ms window, and the spectral peak drops while the gap is inside the window.
  2. Select 512 bins and repeat. The 21 ms window is shorter than the gap, so no single frame shows the whole change: the wave simply shrinks, vanishes and returns.
  3. Discuss: a long window gives a sharp peak but cannot say exactly when something happened inside it; a short window locates changes in time but gives a wide peak. This trade-off is the reason a spectrogram (short-time Fourier transform) needs a window-length setting.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With \(f_s = 48\) kHz and an FFT size of 4096 bins, what are the bin width and the window length? (Answer: \(N = 8192\) samples, so \(\Delta f = 48000 / 8192 = 5.86\) Hz and \(T = 8192 / 48000 = 170.7\) ms.)
  2. At \(f_s = 44.1\) kHz you need bins no wider than 5 Hz. Which is the smallest FFT size in this MicroSim that meets the requirement? (Answer: \(\Delta f = 44100 / (2 \times \text{size}) \le 5\) requires size \(\ge 4410\), so 8192 bins (\(\Delta f = 2.69\) Hz). 4096 bins gives 5.38 Hz, which is too wide.)
  3. Two equal-strength tones at 440 Hz and 460 Hz are analysed at 48 kHz. Which FFT sizes show two separate peaks? (Answer: 4096 and 8192 bins, whose single-tone peaks are 13.9 Hz and 6.9 Hz wide at half height, narrower than the 20 Hz spacing. At 512 to 2048 bins the peaks are 28.9 Hz or wider and generally merge into one.)
  4. Why does a 440 Hz tone read 421.9 Hz at 512 bins and 48 kHz? (Answer: the bins are 46.88 Hz apart. 440 Hz lies at bin 9.39, between bin 9 (421.9 Hz) and bin 10 (468.8 Hz), and bin 9 is the stronger. The error, 18.1 Hz, is less than half a bin, 23.4 Hz.)
  5. A student wants 1 Hz frequency resolution and also wants to see when a 10 ms click occurs. Can one FFT do both? (Answer: no. \(\Delta f = 1\) Hz needs \(T = 1/\Delta f = 1\) s of signal, so the click is somewhere inside a 1 s window and its timing is lost. Because \(\Delta f \cdot T = 1\), finer frequency resolution always costs time resolution.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A bigger FFT is always better." A larger FFT gives narrower peaks only because it analyses a longer stretch of signal. In Activity 4, at 8192 bins each spectrum depends on 341 ms of signal, so a short gap is spread across the whole analysis; at 512 bins the window is only 21 ms. Larger FFTs also cost more computation, \(O(N \log N)\) per spectrum.

"The FFT reports the exact frequency of the tone." The FFT measures only at the bin frequencies \(k f_s/N\). At 512 bins a 440 Hz tone appears at 421.9 Hz; the read-out approaches 440 Hz only as the bins get narrower.

"The peak should be a single thin line." Any finite window spreads a pure tone over several bins: about 2.4 bins at half height for the Blackman window. The peak narrows in hertz as \(N\) grows, but it never becomes a single bin.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Bin width: \(\Delta f = f_s/N\). Doubling the FFT size halves the bin width.
  • Peak width: a pure tone's peak is a fixed number of bins wide (about 2.4 at half height here), so it narrows in proportion to \(\Delta f\).
  • Time-frequency trade-off: the FFT needs \(T = N/f_s\) seconds of signal, and \(\Delta f \cdot T = 1\). Fine frequency detail costs time detail.
  • Amplitude and width are independent: amplitude sets the height of the peak; the FFT size sets its width.

docs.title: Extension Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict and verify: before changing the FFT size, predict the new Freq Resolution and peak width, then check them on screen.
  2. Two tones: what would the spectrum look like if a second oscillator played 460 Hz? Sketch it for 1024 and 8192 bins, then compare with the two-oscillator FFT MicroSim.
  3. Real-world choices: a guitar tuner must distinguish notes about 6% apart, while a speech analyser must follow changes every 10-20 ms. Which needs a larger FFT, and why?

docs.text:
1. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the algorithm that computes the spectrum, with its \(O(N \log N)\) cost
  2. Discrete Fourier transform - Wikipedia - definition of the frequency bins and their spacing \(f_s/N\)
  3. Window function - Wikipedia - the Blackman window and its main-lobe width, which sets the peak width in bins
  4. Spectral leakage - Wikipedia - why a pure tone spreads over several bins
  5. Short-time Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the time-frequency resolution trade-off explored in Activity 4

docs.text:

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a small music player that shows what you are hearing. Pick a track from the Track list and press Play. The red bars are the magnitude spectrum computed by a fast Fourier transform (FFT): each bar shows how much energy the music has at one frequency. The black line is the waveform, the air pressure over the last instant of time. The spectrum updates continuously as the music changes.

Control What it does Track Chooses a song from the list. A newly chosen track starts from the beginning. Play / Pause Starts and pauses the music. Switching tracks while playing keeps playing. Volume Sets the playback level (it does not change the shape of the spectrum, only how loud you hear it). Range Zooms the frequency axis: 0-5 kHz, 0-10 kHz or the full range up to the Nyquist frequency. Your file Loads an audio file from your own computer to analyze.

The analyzer uses an FFT of 1024 bins that spans 0 Hz up to the Nyquist frequency, half the sample rate, so each bin is \(f_s / (2 \times 1024)\) wide: about 23.4 Hz at a 48 kHz sample rate.

This simulation is used in Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Describe what the red spectrum bars and the black waveform line each represent.
  2. Identify the frequency range that contains most of a track's energy.
  3. Compute the frequency of an FFT bin from its index, the FFT size and the sample rate.
  4. Compare the spectra of different recordings and explain the differences.
  5. Predict what the spectrum of a recording will look like before playing it, then check the prediction.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College-level introductory signal processing, audio engineering or music technology students. Plan 15-20 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Frequency, amplitude and the idea of a sinusoid
  • The sampling theorem and the Nyquist frequency (Chapter 5)
  • What a spectrum is (Chapter 7 introduction)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Where is the energy? (5 min). Play Classical Pop (Instrumental) with the range set to 0-10 kHz. Note the highest frequency where bars are clearly visible. Most of the visible energy lies below about 3 kHz, with only isolated small peaks higher up.

Activity 2: Zoom in (5 min). Change the range to 0-5 kHz. The tall bars bunch together at low frequencies. Look for groups of peaks that are evenly spaced: these are the harmonics of a single note.

Activity 3: Waveform vs spectrum (5 min). Pause the music. The waveform and spectrum freeze. Press Play and watch both for a few seconds. Which of the two changes more smoothly, and why?

Activity 4: Your own sound (5 min). Use Your file to load a spoken-voice recording or a different style of music. Before it plays, sketch the spectrum you expect. Then compare.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. At a 48 kHz sample rate and an FFT of 1024 bins covering 0 Hz to the Nyquist frequency, what frequency is bin 100? (Answer: \(100 \times 24000 / 1024 = 2343.75\) Hz.)
  2. What is the highest frequency this player can show for a recording sampled at 44.1 kHz? (Answer: the Nyquist frequency, 22.05 kHz.)
  3. The waveform looks like a smooth wiggle but the spectrum has many tall bars. How can both describe the same sound? (Answer: the waveform is the sum of many sinusoids; the spectrum lists how strong each one is.)
  4. Why does lowering the Volume not change the shape of the spectrum bars much? (Answer: Volume scales the whole signal; the bars are drawn on a decibel scale, so a uniform scaling moves every bar by the same amount.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text: Students often assume a tall bar at one frequency means the music contains one note there. A single musical note produces a peak at its fundamental frequency and further peaks at whole-number multiples of it (its harmonics), so one note appears as a family of evenly spaced bars.
