docs.title: FFT Spectrum Analyzer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fft-spectrum-analyzer/main.html" width="100%" height="607px" scrolling="no" allow="microphone"></iframe>

The allow="microphone" attribute lets the microphone source work when the MicroSim is embedded in a page on another site.

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A spectrum analyzer takes a frame of \(N\) samples, multiplies it by a window function \(w[n]\) and computes the DFT

\[X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\,w[n]\,e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\]

with a Fast Fourier Transform. This MicroSim does exactly that, with its own radix-2 FFT, on every frame.

  • Upper plot: the frame of \(N\) samples before the window (grey) and after it (blue), with time in milliseconds.
  • Lower plot: the spectrum from 0 to \(f_s/2\). Bin \(k\) sits at frequency \(f = k\,\Delta f\), where \(\Delta f = f_s/N\) is the bin spacing shown in the yellow banner.
  • Orange markers label up to four peaks. Move the mouse over the spectrum to read one bin: its number \(k\), its frequency, the raw \(\lvert X[k]\rvert\), the amplitude in linear units and dB, and the phase.

Controls. Source chooses the input signal. Run / Pause lets time advance (the MicroSim starts paused). Signal frequency f sets the tone from 50 to 3900 Hz (it is greyed out for the chirp and the microphone). FFT size N chooses 128 to 4096 samples. Window chooses rectangular, Hamming, Hanning, Blackman or Kaiser (\(\beta = 8.6\)). Display shows the magnitude on a linear scale, in dB or the phase, and Spectrogram adds a scrolling time-frequency image.

The MicroSim illustrates frequency bins, the amplitude scaling of the DFT, spectral leakage, window functions, frequency resolution and the trade-off between frequency and time resolution. It is used in Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals.

docs.title: How the Vertical Axis Is Scaled
docs.text:
A sine of amplitude \(A\) whose frequency falls exactly on a bin gives \(\lvert X[k]\rvert = A\,N/2\) with a rectangular window, and \(A\,N/2\) times the mean of the window otherwise. The magnitude displays divide that out:

\[\text{amplitude} = \frac{2\,\lvert X[k]\rvert}{N \cdot \text{mean of } w[n]}\]

so a bin-centred sine reads its own amplitude whatever the FFT size and window. The readout line also gives the raw \(\lvert X[k]\rvert\). The dB display is \(20\log_{10}\) of this amplitude (0 dB = amplitude 1), and the phase display shows \(\angle X[k]\) only for the bins that hold more than 5% of the peak amplitude (the phase of an empty bin is only numerical noise).

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
The generated signals are computed in the browser at \(f_s = 8000\) Hz. They are analysed, not played through the speakers.

Source What it shows Sine One spectral line, and leakage when the frequency is not on a bin Two tones (\(f\) and \(f + 100\) Hz, amplitudes 1 and 0.5) Frequency resolution: the tones separate only when the FFT is long enough Square wave Odd harmonics with amplitudes \(4/(\pi k)\) Sawtooth wave All harmonics with amplitudes \(2/(\pi k)\) Sine + white noise A tone of amplitude 1 in Gaussian noise of standard deviation 1; a longer FFT lowers the noise in each bin Chirp A sweep from 100 to 3900 Hz every 4 s (950 Hz per second); use it with the spectrogram Microphone Live audio at the sampling rate of your sound card, shown up to 8 kHz

The square and sawtooth waves are built from their harmonics below \(f_s/2\), so they contain no aliased components.

docs.title: Spectrogram
docs.text: Tick Spectrogram and press Run. Every 50 ms of signal a new row is added at the top, and the image holds the last 5 s: frequency runs across, time runs downward and colour shows the level from −80 dB (dark) to 0 dB (bright).

docs.title: Microphone
docs.text: The microphone opens only after you choose Microphone, press Run and allow access in the browser. The sound is analysed in your browser and is never played back or sent anywhere. The analyzer reads the raw signal, with the browser's echo cancellation and noise suppression switched off. Pause freezes the last frame; choosing another source closes the microphone. At a 48 kHz sound card rate and \(N = 1024\) the bin spacing is 46.875 Hz.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this activity, students will be able to:

  1. Compute the bin spacing and frame length of an FFT from the sampling rate and the FFT size.
  2. Use the relation \(\lvert X[k]\rvert = A\,N/2\) to read the amplitude of a tone from an FFT.
  3. Compare the leakage of rectangular, Hamming, Hanning, Blackman and Kaiser windows.
  4. Explain the trade-off between frequency resolution and time resolution when the FFT size changes.
  5. Interpret a spectrogram of a steady tone, a frequency sweep and live sound.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in signals and systems or digital signal processing. Plan 25-30 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sampling and the Nyquist frequency
  • The DFT and the idea of a frequency bin
  • Decibels

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Bins and amplitude scaling (5 min). Choose the sine at 1000 Hz with the rectangular window. For each FFT size from 128 to 4096, record \(\Delta f\), the frame length, the bin number of the peak and the raw \(\lvert X[k]\rvert\) from the readout. Expected: \(\Delta f\) halves from 62.5 Hz to 1.953 Hz, the frame grows from 16 ms to 512 ms, the peak moves from bin 16 to bin 512, and \(\lvert X[k]\rvert = N/2\) every time (64 at \(N = 128\), 512 at \(N = 1024\), 2048 at \(N = 4096\)) while the amplitude reads 1.000.

Activity 2: Leakage and windows (10 min). With \(N = 1024\), move the tone to 1004 Hz, about half-way between bins 128 and 129.

  • The peak now reads about 0.65 (−3.7 dB) with the rectangular window, 0.86 (−1.4 dB) with Hanning and 0.89 (−1.0 dB) with Blackman.
  • Switch to dB and point at a bin 20 bins from the peak. The level is roughly −36 dB (rectangular), −53 dB (Hamming), −87 dB (Hanning) and −95 dB (Blackman). Which window would you choose to find a weak tone next to a strong one?
  • Return to 1000 Hz: every window now reads amplitude 1.000, and the rectangular window shows a single bin.

Activity 3: Resolution, harmonics and noise (10 min).

  • Choose the two-tone source at 1000 Hz with the Hanning window. At \(N = 128\) only one peak is found; at \(N = 256\) two appear, near 1000 Hz and 1100 Hz. Relate this to \(\Delta f\).
  • Choose the square wave at 250 Hz and \(N = 4096\). The first three peaks read 1.273, 0.424 and 0.255, matching \(4/(\pi k)\) for \(k = 1, 3, 5\). Switch to the phase display before pressing Run: every harmonic is at −90°, because the square wave is a sum of sines.
  • Choose sine + white noise with the rectangular window. Compare \(N = 128\) and \(N = 4096\) in dB: the tone stays near amplitude 1 while the noise level in each bin falls by about 15 dB.

Activity 4: Time against frequency (5-10 min). Tick Spectrogram, choose the chirp, the Hanning window and press Run. At \(N = 256\) (a 32 ms frame) the sweep moves only 30 Hz per frame and the peak reads about 0.9. At \(N = 4096\) (a 512 ms frame) the frequency rises 486 Hz during one frame, so the energy spreads over a band a few hundred hertz wide and the peak reads only about 0.13. Then choose Microphone, press Run and whistle a rising note or hold a long vowel. A steady note is a vertical line in the spectrogram; a hissing "s" is a broad band of energy at high frequencies.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A signal is sampled at \(f_s = 8000\) Hz and analysed with \(N = 2048\). What are the bin spacing and the frame length? (Answer: \(\Delta f = 8000/2048 = 3.906\) Hz and \(N/f_s = 256\) ms.)
  2. A sine of amplitude 1 at 1000 Hz is analysed with \(N = 1024\) and a rectangular window. Which bin holds the peak, and what is \(\lvert X[k]\rvert\)? (Answer: \(k = 1000/7.8125 = 128\) and \(\lvert X[128]\rvert = N/2 = 512\).)
  3. Why does a 1004 Hz tone read about 0.65 instead of 1 with the rectangular window at \(N = 1024\)? (Answer: 1004 Hz lies about half-way between two bins, so the frame does not hold a whole number of cycles; the energy leaks into neighbouring bins and no single bin sees the full amplitude. A Hanning or Blackman window reduces this scalloping loss.)
  4. Two tones 100 Hz apart are analysed with a Hanning window at \(f_s = 8000\) Hz. Why are they resolved at \(N = 256\) but not at \(N = 128\)? (Answer: at \(N = 128\), \(\Delta f = 62.5\) Hz and the tones are only 1.6 bins apart, inside one Hanning main lobe (4 bins wide); at \(N = 256\), \(\Delta f = 31.25\) Hz and they are 3.2 bins apart, so two separate peaks form.)
  5. Why does the noise in each bin fall by about 15 dB from \(N = 128\) to \(N = 4096\) while the tone does not change? (Answer: the noise power is shared among about \(N/2\) bins, so its amplitude per bin falls as \(1/\sqrt{N}\); \(10\log_{10}(4096/128) = 15\) dB. The tone's energy stays in one bin, and the scaling keeps its amplitude at 1.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "The height of an FFT peak is the amplitude of the tone." The raw DFT value grows with \(N\): the readout shows \(\lvert X[k]\rvert = 512\) at \(N = 1024\) and 2048 at \(N = 4096\) for the same unit sine. Only after dividing by \(N/2\) (and the window's mean) does it read 1.
  • "Leakage is an error in the FFT algorithm." The same FFT gives one clean line at 1000 Hz and a spread-out peak at 1004 Hz. Leakage comes from cutting a frame that does not hold a whole number of cycles, and the window choice trades a wider main lobe for lower side lobes.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Window function - Wikipedia - definitions and leakage properties of the Hamming, Hanning, Blackman and Kaiser windows
  2. Spectral leakage - Wikipedia - why a tone between bins spreads into its neighbours
  3. Kaiser window - Wikipedia - the Bessel-function window and its \(\beta\) parameter
  4. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the algorithm behind the analyzer, including the radix-2 Cooley-Tukey FFT
  5. Spectrogram - Wikipedia - the time-frequency image shown by the Spectrogram option
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT, FFT and windows
  7. p5.sound.js - Processing Foundation - the audio library used to read the microphone
  8. Harris, F. J. (1978). On the use of windows for harmonic analysis with the discrete Fourier transform. Proceedings of the IEEE, 66(1), 51-83. - the classic comparison of window functions
  9. Cooley, J. W., & Tukey, J. W. (1965). An algorithm for the machine calculation of complex Fourier series. Mathematics of Computation, 19(90), 297-301. - the paper that introduced the FFT
  10. Oppenheim, A. V., & Schafer, R. W. (2010). Discrete-Time Signal Processing (3rd ed.). Pearson. - Chapter 10 covers Fourier analysis of signals using the DFT

docs.title: FFT Waveform Types
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fft-waveform-types/main.html" width="100%" height="532px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows how the shape of a periodic waveform determines its harmonic content. The top plot (green) is the time domain: 50 ms of a sine, square, triangle or sawtooth wave with peak amplitude 1, with a read-out of the period \(T = 1/f\). The bottom plot (purple) is the frequency domain: one vertical line for every harmonic \(f_n = n f\) from 0 to 500 Hz, labelled with its harmonic number \(n\) when there is room.

  • Waveform radio buttons choose the shape. The caption above the spectrum summarizes the rule, for example Odd harmonics, 1/n decay.
  • Frequency slider (0-500 Hz, default 50 Hz) sets the fundamental \(f\). Every harmonic line moves with it, so fewer harmonics fit below 500 Hz as \(f\) rises.
  • Hover over (or tap) a spectral line to highlight it in gold and read its frequency and exact relative magnitude, for example n = 3: 300 Hz, magnitude 1/3 = 0.333.

Line heights are relative to the fundamental (the \(n = 1\) line always reaches 1), so you can compare how fast the harmonics decay: \(1/n\) for the square and sawtooth waves, \(1/n^2\) for the triangle wave. A small dot on the baseline marks every harmonic that is present, even when its line is too short to see. The spectrum is computed from the Fourier series rather than by running an FFT on samples; it shows the peak heights an ideal FFT would report for a window that holds a whole number of periods, without leakage or aliasing.

This MicroSim supports the Fourier series section of Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals.

docs.title: Fourier Series of the Four Waveforms
docs.text:
For a wave of peak amplitude 1 and angular frequency \(\omega = 2\pi f\):

\[\text{Square} = \frac{4}{\pi}\left[\sin(\omega t) + \frac{1}{3}\sin(3\omega t) + \frac{1}{5}\sin(5\omega t) + \frac{1}{7}\sin(7\omega t) + \cdots\right]\] \[\text{Triangle} = \frac{8}{\pi^2}\left[\sin(\omega t) - \frac{1}{9}\sin(3\omega t) + \frac{1}{25}\sin(5\omega t) - \frac{1}{49}\sin(7\omega t) + \cdots\right]\] \[\text{Sawtooth} = \frac{2}{\pi}\left[\sin(\omega t) - \frac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega t) + \frac{1}{3}\sin(3\omega t) - \frac{1}{4}\sin(4\omega t) + \cdots\right]\]

The factor in front sets the absolute size of the fundamental (\(4/\pi \approx 1.27\), \(8/\pi^2 \approx 0.81\), \(2/\pi \approx 0.64\)); the MicroSim divides it out so that only the decay pattern remains. The MicroSim draws the triangle and sawtooth starting from \(-1\) at \(t = 0\). That is a time shift, which changes the phases of the harmonics but not their magnitudes.

Why only odd harmonics? Square and triangle waves have half-wave symmetry: shifting them by half a period flips their sign, \(x(t + T/2) = -x(t)\). Every even harmonic fails that test, so its coefficient is zero. The sawtooth has no such symmetry, so all harmonics appear.

Why does the triangle decay faster? The square and sawtooth waves jump (the signal itself is discontinuous), which gives coefficients that fall as \(1/n\). The triangle wave never jumps; only its slope changes abruptly at the corners, which gives \(1/n^2\). In general, the smoother a waveform is in time, the faster its spectrum falls off in frequency. When a jump is rebuilt from a finite number of harmonics, the partial sum overshoots by about 9% of the jump near the edge (the Gibbs phenomenon); this MicroSim shows the ideal waveforms, not partial sums.

Connection to sound. Instruments playing the same note share the fundamental but differ in harmonic content, which we hear as timbre. Sine tones sound pure, triangle waves soft, square waves hollow and buzzy, and sawtooth waves bright, which is why subtractive synthesizers start from a sawtooth and filter harmonics away.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Compare the harmonic spectra of sine, square, triangle and sawtooth waves at the same fundamental frequency
  2. Explain why square and triangle waves contain only odd harmonics while sawtooth waves contain every integer harmonic
  3. Distinguish the \(1/n\) amplitude decay of a square wave from the \(1/n^2\) decay of a triangle wave in the spectrum plot
  4. Predict how raising the fundamental frequency slider rescales the position of every harmonic line
  5. Relate jumps and corners of a waveform in the time domain to the amount of high-frequency energy in its spectrum

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in an introductory signal processing, electronics or music technology course. Plan 20 minutes of guided exploration.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Basic trigonometry: sine waves, frequency and period
  • The idea of a spectrum as a plot of magnitude against frequency (see the Basic FFT MicroSim)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Square versus triangle (5 min). Set the frequency to 100 Hz and select Square. Lines appear at 100, 300 and 500 Hz with relative heights 1, 0.333 and 0.200. Switch to Triangle: the lines stay at the same frequencies but shrink to 1, 0.111 and 0.040. Hover over each line to read the exact values. Ask: "Which wave has more high-frequency energy, and which one has sharper features in the time plot?"

Activity 2: The missing even harmonics (5 min). At 100 Hz select Sawtooth: five lines appear at 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz with heights 1, 0.5, 0.333, 0.25 and 0.2. Switch to Square: the 200 Hz and 400 Hz lines vanish. Ask students to sketch the square wave shifted by half a period and explain the symmetry that removes them.

Activity 3: Frequency scaling (5 min). Select Square at 50 Hz: the period read-out shows 20.0 ms, the window holds 2.5 cycles, and five lines appear at 50, 150, 250, 350 and 450 Hz. Move to 100 Hz: the period halves to 10.0 ms, the window holds 5 cycles, and only three lines remain (100, 300, 500 Hz). Every harmonic frequency doubled; none of the relative heights changed.

Activity 4: A crowded spectrum (5 min). Select Sawtooth at 20 Hz. Exactly one ramp fills the 50 ms window (period 50.0 ms), and 25 lines fill the spectrum, the last at 500 Hz with height 0.040. Then select Sine: a single line at 20 Hz remains. Discuss why a pure sine is the only waveform with one line.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A square wave has a fundamental of 60 Hz. Which lines appear between 0 and 500 Hz, and what are their relative heights? (Answer: 60, 180, 300 and 420 Hz, with heights 1, 0.333, 0.200 and 0.143; the next odd harmonic, 540 Hz, is off the plot.)
  2. What is the relative magnitude of the 5th harmonic of a triangle wave, and how does it compare with the 5th harmonic of a square wave? (Answer: \(1/25 = 0.04\) for the triangle and \(1/5 = 0.2\) for the square, five times larger.)
  3. Why does a 100 Hz square wave have no line at 200 Hz? (Answer: it has half-wave symmetry, \(x(t + T/2) = -x(t)\), which forces every even-harmonic coefficient to zero.)
  4. How many lines does a 125 Hz sawtooth produce between 0 and 500 Hz? (Answer: four, at 125, 250, 375 and 500 Hz, with heights 1, 0.5, 0.333 and 0.25.)
  5. The time plot shows exactly 4 complete cycles in its 50 ms window. What are the fundamental frequency and the period? (Answer: \(f = 4 / 0.050\ \text{s} = 80\) Hz and \(T = 12.5\) ms; the read-out confirms it.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Harmonics are extra tones the analyser adds to every signal." Harmonics are part of the waveform's shape. Select Sine at any frequency: only one line appears. The harmonics appear only when the shape departs from a sinusoid.

"Square and triangle waves have the same spectrum because both contain only odd harmonics." The lines sit at the same frequencies but decay at different rates. At 100 Hz, hover over the 300 Hz line: 0.333 for the square wave, 0.111 for the triangle wave.

docs.title: Extension Activities
docs.text:
• Predict the spectrum of a half-amplitude square wave. (The relative heights do not change; only the absolute scale does.)
  • Add a dB magnitude scale (an extension to the code) so that the small triangle-wave harmonics become visible.
  • Add audio output so that students can hear the timbre of each waveform at the same pitch.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fourier series - Wikipedia - the decomposition of a periodic signal into harmonics that this MicroSim plots
  2. Square wave - Wikipedia - odd-harmonic series with \(1/n\) amplitudes
  3. Triangle wave - Wikipedia - odd-harmonic series with \(1/n^2\) amplitudes and alternating signs
  4. Sawtooth wave - Wikipedia - series containing every integer harmonic
  5. Gibbs phenomenon - Wikipedia - the overshoot when a jump is rebuilt from a finite number of harmonics
  6. Timbre - Wikipedia - how harmonic content shapes the character of a sound
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on Fourier analysis and harmonics

docs.title: Filter Bank and Polyphase Explorer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/filter-bank-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="664px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim builds an \(M\)-channel uniform filter bank from one low-pass prototype filter \(p[n]\) and shows both what the bank does and how it is implemented efficiently. With \(f_s = 8\) kHz, channel \(k\) covers \(k f_s/2M\) to \((k+1) f_s/2M\) and is centred on \((2k+1) f_s/4M\).

  • Upper left: the magnitude response \(|H_k(e^{j\omega})|\) of every analysis filter in its own colour, with the channel number above its centre and dashed lines at the test frequencies. The maroon strip underneath is the overall analysis-synthesis response \(|T(e^{j\omega})|\); a perfect bank would give a flat 0 dB line.
  • Upper right: the energy of the test signal in each subband, in dB of the input energy, and their sum.
  • Lower left: the prototype \(p[n]\) with every tap coloured by its phase \(m = n \bmod M\), and below it the \(M\) polyphase components \(E_m[q] = p[qM + m]\).
  • Lower right: 8 ms of the input \(x[n]\) and the output \(\hat{x}[n]\) shifted back by the bank delay \(N-1\), with the error on a magnified scale.
  • Read-outs: the prototype cutoff, the reconstruction error in dB, the range of \(|T|\), the worst alias term, and the multiplications per output sample for direct and polyphase decimation.

Channels M (2, 4, 8) sets the number of subbands. Prototype length N (16-128 taps) sets the length of \(p[n]\). Test signal chooses four tones (0.3, 1.0, 2.3 and 3.4 kHz with amplitudes 1.0, 0.7, 0.5 and 0.3), a linear chirp from 0 to 4 kHz, or a single tone whose frequency is set by the Tone slider. Tuned cutoff adjusts the prototype cutoff so that neighbouring channels cross at \(-3\) dB; unchecked, the cutoff is \(\pi/2M\) and they cross at \(-6\) dB. Hover over the response plot to read the two strongest channel gains.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 10: Advanced Filter Design and Implementation.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
The prototype is a Hamming-windowed sinc of length \(N\) with cutoff \(\omega_c\), scaled so that \(\sum_n p[n] = 1\). Cosine modulation shifts it to each channel centre (a pseudo-QMF bank):

\[h_k[n] = 2\,p[n]\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi(2k+1)}{2M}\left(n - \frac{N-1}{2}\right) + \phi_k\right), \qquad \phi_k = (-1)^k \frac{\pi}{4}\]

Each channel output is kept at every \(M\)-th sample, \(v_k[m] = (h_k * x)[mM]\). The synthesis filters \(f_k[n]\) use the same cosine with phase \(-\phi_k\) and gain \(2M\) (which undoes the \(1/M\) of decimation), and the output is the sum of the channels:

\[\hat{x}[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1} \sum_{m} v_k[m]\, f_k[n - mM], \qquad \hat{X}(z) = T(z)X(z) + \sum_{l=1}^{M-1} A_l(z)\,X(zW^l)\]

with \(T(z) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_k F_k(z)H_k(z)\), \(A_l(z) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_k F_k(z)H_k(zW^l)\) and \(W = e^{-j2\pi/M}\). The phases \(\pm\phi_k\) make the large alias terms between neighbouring channels cancel; what remains is set by the prototype's stop band. \(T\) is flat only if neighbouring channels are power complementary, \(|P(e^{j\omega})|^2 + |P(e^{j(\pi/M - \omega)})|^2 \approx 1\), which requires \(|P(e^{j\pi/2M})| = 1/\sqrt{2}\) (\(-3\) dB) at the band edge. With Tuned cutoff the sketch finds that \(\omega_c\) by bisection. The reconstruction error is

\[E = 10\log_{10}\frac{\sum_n \left(\hat{x}[n + N - 1] - x[n]\right)^2}{\sum_n x[n]^2}\ \text{dB}\]

over a 2048-sample record. The polyphase form writes \(P(z) = \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} z^{-m}E_m(z^M)\). Filtering at \(f_s\) and then discarding \(M-1\) of every \(M\) outputs costs \(N\) multiplications per input sample, which is \(N \cdot M\) per output sample. The polyphase decimator runs its \(M\) branches of \(N/M\) taps at \(f_s/M\) and computes only the samples that are kept: \(N\) multiplications per output sample, or \(N/M\) per input sample, a saving of a factor \(M\).

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the edges \(k f_s/2M\) and centre \((2k+1) f_s/4M\) of every channel and predict which channel or channels a tone falls into
  2. Explain why the subband energies add up to the input energy when neighbouring channels cross at \(-3\) dB, and to less when they cross at \(-6\) dB
  3. Analyze how the prototype length \(N\) and the cutoff tuning change the overall response \(|T|\), the worst alias term and the reconstruction error
  4. Decompose a prototype filter into its \(M\) polyphase components \(E_m[q] = p[qM + m]\) and state their length \(N/M\)
  5. Calculate the multiplications per output sample for direct and polyphase decimation and explain where the factor \(M\) comes from

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a junior- or senior-level digital signal processing course. Plan about 40 minutes for the four activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• FIR filters, the windowed-sinc design method and magnitude responses in dB
  • Downsampling by \(M\) and aliasing (see the Multirate Sample Rate Converter)
  • Modulation: multiplying by a cosine shifts a spectrum up and down in frequency

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
All values are those the sim displays. Start from the defaults: M = 4, N = 64, multi-tone, Tuned cutoff checked.

Activity 1: Where does the energy go? (10 min). The channels are 1 kHz wide and centred on 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 kHz.

  • The bars read \(-1.7\), \(-8.7\), \(-8.6\) and \(-13.1\) dB and sum to 100.1 %. Predict them yourself: a tone of amplitude \(A\) has power \(A^2/2\), so the four tones carry 0.5, 0.245, 0.125 and 0.045 (total 0.915). The 1.0 kHz tone sits exactly on the edge between channels 0 and 1 and is split equally, so channel 0 holds \((0.5 + 0.1225)/0.915\), which is \(-1.7\) dB.
  • Set M = 8 (0.5 kHz channels). The bars read \(-2.6\), \(-8.7\), \(-8.7\), \(-57.4\), \(-8.6\), \(-35.9\), \(-13.5\) and \(-23.5\) dB. Channel 3 (1.5-2.0 kHz) contains no tone; its \(-57.4\) dB is leakage through the filters' stop bands.
  • Set M = 4 and choose the linear chirp. Every bar is close to \(10\log_{10}(1/4) = -6.0\) dB (\(-6.2\), \(-5.8\), \(-5.8\), \(-6.2\); the outer two are lower because the chirp fades in and out at 0 and 4 kHz).

Activity 2: The \(-3\) dB crossover (10 min). Choose single tone at 1.00 kHz with M = 4 and N = 64.

  • With the cutoff tuned (\(\omega_c = 0.138\pi\), \(|P| = -3.0\) dB at the band edge), channels 0 and 1 each read \(-3.0\) dB, the sum is 100.0 % and the reconstruction error is \(-68.8\) dB.
  • Uncheck Tuned cutoff (\(\omega_c = \pi/2M = 0.125\pi\), \(|P| = -6.0\) dB). The two bars drop to \(-6.0\) dB, the sum to 50.1 %, the maroon strip dips to \(-6.01\) dB at every band edge (0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 kHz), and the error is \(-6.0\) dB: half of the tone's amplitude is lost.
  • Still untuned, move the tone to 1.50 kHz, the centre of channel 1. The error improves to \(-64.2\) dB. Switch to the multi-tone signal: the error is \(-11.7\) dB untuned against \(-62.0\) dB tuned.

Activity 3: Prototype length, aliasing and the error floor (10 min). Choose the linear chirp, M = 8, tuned, and step N:

N Reconstruction error Worst alias term Overall response \(\lvert T \rvert\) 16 \(-3.1\) dB (cannot tune) \(-9.7\) dB \(+3.56\) dB everywhere 32 \(-25.0\) dB \(-29.2\) dB \(+0.00\) to \(+0.62\) dB 48 \(-44.2\) dB \(-46.5\) dB \(+0.00\) to \(+0.07\) dB 64 \(-51.2\) dB \(-63.8\) dB \(+0.00\) to \(+0.04\) dB 128 \(-45.6\) dB \(-69.5\) dB \(+0.00\) to \(+0.10\) dB

At N = 16 the prototype is too short to be narrower than one 0.5 kHz channel, so the channels overlap heavily (the bars sum to 150.7 %). Up to N = 48 the error tracks the worst alias term. Beyond that the alias term keeps falling but the error levels off between \(-45\) and \(-51\) dB: a windowed-sinc prototype is only approximately power complementary, so \(|T|\) keeps a ripple of a few hundredths to a tenth of a dB. Now set M = 2: the worst alias term reads below \(-120\) dB because the two-channel bank cancels aliasing exactly, and the error with the multi-tone signal and N = 64 is \(-55.4\) dB.

Activity 4: Polyphase bookkeeping (10 min). Return to M = 4, N = 64.

  • Each polyphase component \(E_0 \ldots E_3\) has \(64/4 = 16\) taps. Compare \(E_0\) with \(E_3\) and \(E_1\) with \(E_2\): each pair are mirror images, \(E_m[q] = E_{M-1-m}[N/M - 1 - q]\), because \(p[n]\) is symmetric.
  • The read-out gives \(N \cdot M = 256\) multiplications per output sample for the direct decimator and \(N = 64\) for the polyphase one (4 times fewer); per input sample that is 64 against 16.
  • Set M = 8, N = 128: 1024 against 128 per output sample, and 128 against 16 per input sample.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With \(f_s = 8\) kHz and M = 8, which frequencies does channel 5 cover, and where is its centre? Answer: the channels are \(f_s/2M = 0.5\) kHz wide, so channel 5 covers 2.5 to 3.0 kHz and is centred on \((2 \cdot 5 + 1) \cdot 8/32 = 2.75\) kHz.
  2. With M = 4 and the tuned cutoff, a single tone is set to 2.00 kHz. Which bars rise, and to what level? Answer: 2.0 kHz is the edge between channels 1 and 2. Each channel passes it at \(|H| = -3\) dB, so each holds half of the power: both bars read \(-3.0\) dB and the error is \(-68.8\) dB.
  3. Why does the untuned bank lose 6 dB at a band edge rather than 3 dB? Answer: at the edge each of the two channels has gain 0.5 in the analysis filter and 0.5 in the synthesis filter, so each path contributes 0.25 and the two paths sum to 0.5, which is \(-6\) dB. With the tuned cutoff each gain is \(1/\sqrt{2}\), each path contributes 0.5, and the sum is 1.
  4. A 128-tap filter decimates by M = 8. How many multiplications does each output sample cost in the direct and the polyphase form? Answer: direct \(128 \times 8 = 1024\) (seven of every eight filter outputs are thrown away); polyphase 128, from 8 branches of 16 taps running at \(f_s/8\). Per input sample that is 128 against 16.
  5. Doubling N from 64 to 128 with M = 8 makes the chirp's reconstruction error worse (\(-51.2\) to \(-45.6\) dB). Why does a longer prototype not guarantee a better bank? Answer: the longer prototype lowers the alias terms (\(-63.8\) to \(-69.5\) dB), but the error is then set by the ripple of \(|T|\) (+0.04 dB at N = 64, +0.10 dB at N = 128). That ripple depends on how closely the tuned windowed sinc approaches power complementarity, not on its length. A lower floor needs an optimized prototype or a perfect-reconstruction design.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Splitting a signal into M decimated subbands throws information away." The bank keeps \(M\) subbands at \(f_s/M\) each, exactly as many samples as the input. With the default settings the output matches the input to \(-62.0\) dB; the residual error comes from the prototype design, not from decimation.

"A polyphase filter is a different filter." \(E_0 \ldots E_{M-1}\) are the taps of \(p[n]\) dealt out like cards (the colours in the lower-left panel). The polyphase decimator performs the same multiplications as the direct filter for every output sample that is kept, and skips only the outputs that downsampling would discard.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Filter bank - Wikipedia - analysis and synthesis banks, uniform DFT and cosine-modulated banks, and perfect reconstruction
  2. Polyphase quadrature filter - Wikipedia - the near-perfect-reconstruction pseudo-QMF bank built here, as used in MPEG audio coding
  3. Quadrature mirror filter - Wikipedia - the two-channel bank in which aliasing cancels exactly (compare M = 2)
  4. Downsampling (signal processing) - Wikipedia - decimation, aliasing and the polyphase implementation of a decimator
  5. Sub-band coding - Wikipedia - why audio and image coders split signals into subbands before quantizing them
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on windowed-sinc filters

docs.title: FIR Filter Design Comparison Tool
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fir-filter-design-comparison-tool/main.html" width="100%" height="667px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim designs two odd-length, linear-phase FIR filters, A (solid blue) and B (dashed maroon), for the same specification and overlays them so that you can compare design methods directly.

  • Filter type (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass) and the cutoff sliders \(\omega_{c1}\), \(\omega_{c2}\) (in units of \(\pi\) rad/sample) set the shared specification. The grey line is the ideal brick-wall response.
  • Each design has its own method, taps \(N\) (odd, 11-127) and one shape parameter:
    • Window: \(h[n] = h_d[n]\,w[n]\) with \(h_d[n] = \sin(\omega_c(n-M))/(\pi(n-M))\), \(M = (N-1)/2\), and a rectangular, Hann, Hamming, Blackman or Kaiser window (slider \(\beta\) for Kaiser).
    • Frequency sampling: \(N\) amplitude samples \(H[k]\) at \(\omega_k = 2\pi k/N\) (1 in the pass band, 0 in the stop band) followed by an inverse DFT. The transition sample \(T_1\) sets the first stop-band sample next to each band edge.
    • Parks-McClellan: the optimal equiripple design for pass and stop bands separated by a transition band of width \(\Delta\omega\) centered on the cutoff, with equal weights.
  • The right plot shows \(|H(e^{j\omega})|\) evaluated at 2049 frequencies in dB, on a linear scale, or zoomed on the passband. The left plot shows the impulse response \(h[n]\), the zeros of \(H(z)\), the phase or the group delay.
  • The table reports each design's transition width \(\Delta\omega\), passband ripple and stop-band attenuation. For a Kaiser window it also prints the prediction of Kaiser's formulas.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 10: Advanced Filter Design and Implementation.

docs.title: How the read-outs are measured
docs.text:
• \(\delta_p\) is the largest passband deviation \(\big||H|-1\big|\) and \(\delta_s\) the largest stop-band \(|H|\). Passband ripple \(= 20\log_{10}\frac{1+\delta_p}{1-\delta_p}\) dB and stop-band attenuation \(A_s = -20\log_{10}\delta_s\) dB.
  • The pass band ends at the last ripple peak before the cutoff and the stop band starts at the first null after it. \(\Delta\omega\) runs from the frequency where \(|H|\) falls below \(1-\delta_p\) to the frequency where it reaches \(\delta_s\) (the coloured bars at the top of the magnitude plot).
  • Kaiser's formulas: \(\beta = 0.1102(A-8.7)\) for \(A > 50\) dB, \(\beta = 0.5842(A-21)^{0.4} + 0.07886(A-21)\) for \(21 \le A \le 50\) dB, and \(\Delta\omega \approx (A-7.95)/(2.285\,(N-1))\).
  • Every design is symmetric, so \(H(e^{j\omega}) = A(\omega)e^{-j\omega M}\): the phase is linear and the group delay is \(M = (N-1)/2\) samples at every frequency.
  • Parks-McClellan limits: the sketch narrows the requested \(\Delta\omega\) if the band edges would remove more than half of a pass band or stop band, or if Kaiser's estimate \(2.285\,\Delta\omega\,(N-1) + 7.95\) exceeds 130 dB (a wider band would need a ripple smaller than double-precision arithmetic can resolve). The table and a footnote show the width used.
  • Hann and Blackman windows are zero at both ends, and some cutoffs make the end taps of \(h_d[n]\) zero (for example \(\omega_c = 0.40\pi\) with \(N = 51\), because \(\sin(10\pi) = 0\)). Such a filter has fewer than \(N-1\) zeros.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  1. Apply the window method to design a low-pass, high-pass or band-pass FIR filter and read its transition width, passband ripple and stop-band attenuation
  2. Compare how the rectangular, Hann, Hamming, Blackman and Kaiser windows trade transition width against stop-band attenuation at a fixed number of taps
  3. Predict the stop-band attenuation and transition width of a Kaiser-window design from \(\beta\) and \(N\) with Kaiser's formulas, and check the prediction against the measurement
  4. Explain how the transition sample \(T_1\) changes the stop-band attenuation of a frequency-sampling design, and find the value that maximizes it
  5. Evaluate which design method meets a given specification with the fewest taps, using Parks-McClellan as the optimal benchmark

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate engineering and computer science students in a digital signal processing course (typically third year). The activities take about 40 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The z-transform and the frequency response \(H(e^{j\omega})\) of an FIR filter
  • The ideal low-pass impulse response (the sinc function) and the DFT
  • Decibels and the idea of passband and stop-band tolerances

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
All activities start from the default settings: low-pass, \(\omega_c = 0.40\pi\), \(N = 51\) for both designs, A = Hamming window, B = frequency sampling with \(T_1 = 0.40\). The table reports the values quoted below.

Activity 1: Window comparison (10 min). Set Design A's window to each option in turn and copy the table row.

Window (N = 51) Transition \(\Delta\omega\) Passband ripple Stop-band attenuation Rectangular 0.037π 1.60 dB 21.1 dB Hann 0.125π 0.110 dB 43.9 dB Hamming 0.133π 0.030 dB 53.7 dB Blackman 0.223π 0.0031 dB 75.3 dB

Every step down the table buys more attenuation and less ripple with a wider transition band. Switch the left plot to Zeros: with the Blackman window the stop-band zeros on the unit circle start at a higher angle than with the rectangular window, matching its later stop-band edge.

Activity 2: Taps versus window shape (10 min). Keep A on Hamming and set \(N\) = 21, 51 and 101. The transition width falls from 0.333π to 0.133π to 0.067π, so \(\Delta\omega\,(N-1) \approx 6.7\pi\) stays constant, while the attenuation stays near 54 dB (53.6, 53.7 and 53.9 dB). Now choose the Kaiser window with \(N = 51\). At \(\beta = 5.0\) the table shows 54.0 dB and 0.129π, and the footnote predicts 54.1 dB and 0.128π. At \(\beta = 8.0\) it shows 80.9 dB and 0.204π (predicted 81.3 dB and 0.204π). The shape parameter \(\beta\), not \(N\), sets the attenuation.

Activity 3: The transition sample (10 min). Watch Design B (frequency sampling, \(N = 51\)). Set \(T_1 = 0\): the attenuation drops to 16.4 dB and the passband ripple grows to 2.29 dB, even though every frequency sample is exactly 0 or 1. Sweep \(T_1\) upward: the attenuation peaks at 42.9 dB for \(T_1 = 0.38\) (39.7 dB at 0.40) and falls again to 22.0 dB at \(T_1 = 0.70\). Use Passband zoom to see the ripple between the samples.

Activity 4: Which method needs the fewest taps? (10 min). Keep A at Hamming, \(N = 51\) (53.7 dB, \(\Delta\omega =\) 0.133π). Set B to Parks-McClellan with \(\Delta\omega = 0.13\pi\). At \(N = 51\), B reaches 58.4 dB with 0.021 dB ripple. Lower B's taps: at \(N = 47\) it still gives 54.7 dB with 0.032 dB ripple, beating A with four fewer taps and a slightly narrower transition band. At \(N = 45\) it falls to 53.1 dB. Switch the left plot to Group delay: B's delay drops from 25 to 23 samples.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A Hamming design with \(N = 51\) has \(\Delta\omega = 0.133\pi\) and 53.7 dB attenuation. Predict both values for \(N = 101\). (Answer: the transition width scales as \(1/(N-1)\), so \(0.133\pi \times 50/100 \approx 0.067\pi\); the attenuation is set by the window and stays near 54 dB. The sim shows 0.067π and 53.9 dB.)
  2. You need at least 60 dB of stop-band attenuation with \(N = 51\) taps. Which Kaiser \(\beta\) do you choose, and what transition width do you expect? (Answer: \(\beta = 0.1102(60-8.7) = 5.65\), so set \(\beta = 5.7\); \(\Delta\omega \approx (60-7.95)/(2.285 \times 50) = 0.456\) rad \(= 0.145\pi\). The sim measures 60.1 dB and 0.146π.)
  3. Why does a frequency-sampling design with \(T_1 = 0\) reach only about 16 dB of attenuation, and how does \(T_1 = 0.38\) help? (Answer: between the samples the response is an interpolation of the abrupt 1-to-0 step, which oscillates like the response of a rectangular window. A transition sample makes the step gradual, so the interpolation ripple shrinks and the attenuation rises to 42.9 dB at the cost of a wider transition band.)
  4. A 51-tap linear-phase filter runs at \(f_s = 8\) kHz. How long is its delay, and does it depend on frequency? (Answer: \(M = 25\) samples, or \(25/8000 = 3.125\) ms, at every frequency, because the symmetric impulse response gives a phase of \(-25\omega\).)
  5. Why does a 47-tap Parks-McClellan design beat a 51-tap Hamming design? (Answer: Parks-McClellan spreads the error evenly (equiripple) across both bands, while a window design's ripples decay away from the band edge, so most of its stop band has more attenuation than the specification needs and the taps are used less efficiently.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"More taps give more stop-band attenuation." With the window method the window shape sets the attenuation and the number of taps sets the transition width. In Activity 2 the Hamming design stays between 53.6 and 53.9 dB from \(N = 21\) to \(N = 101\) while \(\Delta\omega\) shrinks by a factor of five.

"A frequency-sampling filter equals the ideal response because it matches it at every sample." It matches only at \(\omega_k = 2\pi k/N\). With \(T_1 = 0\) the samples are exactly 1 and 0, yet the response between them ripples by 2.29 dB in the pass band and rises to −16.4 dB in the stop band.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Finite impulse response - Wikipedia - FIR filters, the window method and frequency sampling
  2. Window function - Wikipedia - definitions and side-lobe levels of the rectangular, Hann, Hamming and Blackman windows
  3. Kaiser window - Wikipedia - the Bessel-function window and the formulas that relate \(\beta\), attenuation and filter length
  4. Parks-McClellan filter design algorithm - Wikipedia - the optimal equiripple design used for method three
  5. Remez algorithm - Wikipedia - the exchange algorithm behind Parks-McClellan
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on windowed-sinc and custom FIR filters

docs.title: FIR vs IIR Filters
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fir-vs-iir/main.html" width="100%" height="702px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim designs two low-pass filters for the same cutoff \(f_c\) and draws them on shared axes. The FIR filter (blue) is a windowed sinc with \(N\) taps, \(h[n] = 2f_c\,\mathrm{sinc}\big(2f_c(n-M)\big)\,w[n]\) with \(M = (N-1)/2\) and a Hamming window, scaled so that its DC gain is exactly 1. Its taps are symmetric, so its phase is exactly linear. The IIR filter (green) is a Butterworth filter: analog poles spaced evenly on a circle of radius \(\Omega_c = 2\tan(\pi f_c)\) (pre-warped), mapped to the \(z\)-plane by the bilinear transform, with every zero at \(z = -1\).

The sliders set the cutoff (0.02 to 0.45 of \(f_s\)), the FIR length \(N\) (5 to 101, odd) and the IIR order (1 to 8). The panels show the magnitude in dB, the unwrapped phase, the group delay, the first 64 samples of each impulse response, and the IIR pole-zero plot. The table gives the multiplies per output sample (FIR: \(N\); IIR: \(2N+1\) in direct form, 5 per biquad plus 3 for a first-order section in cascade form), the group delay at DC, \(|H|\) at \(f_c\) and \(2f_c\), and the largest pole radius. Note that the two filters define "cutoff" differently: the windowed sinc is about 6 dB down at \(f_c\), the Butterworth exactly 3 dB. Hover over any plot to read values at one frequency or sample.

Quantize IIR to B bits rounds the IIR coefficients to \(B\)-bit fixed point (4 to 16 bits), either as one direct-form polynomial or as cascaded biquads. Each coefficient list shares one binary point, placed so its largest value fits, and \(a_0 = 1\) stays exact. Red marks show the new poles and zeros; direct-form roots are found with the Durand-Kerner iteration. If any pole reaches the unit circle, the filter is unstable and no frequency response is drawn.

This simulation is used in Chapter 9: Filter Design Fundamentals.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Compare the magnitude, phase and group delay of an FIR and an IIR low-pass filter with the same cutoff, and explain why a symmetric FIR has a constant group delay of \((N-1)/2\) samples
  2. Distinguish a finite impulse response from an infinite one, and relate the decay of \(h[n]\) to the largest pole radius
  3. Calculate the multiplies per output sample of an FIR filter, a direct-form IIR filter and a cascade of biquads
  4. Evaluate which filter type is cheaper for a given attenuation, and explain why the FIR's cost grows as the cutoff narrows
  5. Analyze how rounding IIR coefficients to \(B\) bits moves the poles, and explain why cascaded biquads stay stable where a high-order direct form fails

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduates in a first digital signal processing course (junior or senior electrical engineering, computer engineering or computer science). Plan 25 to 30 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The \(z\)-transform, poles and zeros, and the unit-circle stability test (Chapter 8)
  • Difference equations and convolution with an impulse response
  • Frequency response in decibels and normalized frequency \(f/f_s\)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Same cutoff, different trade-offs (7 min). Start from the defaults (\(f_c = 0.100\,f_s\), \(N = 31\), IIR order 4, direct form). The table shows \(|H(f_c)|\) = −6.1 dB for the FIR and −3.0 dB for the IIR, and \(|H(2f_c)|\) = −70.6 dB and −28.0 dB. The FIR costs 31 multiplies per sample, the IIR 9 (10 as biquads). In the group-delay panel the FIR is a flat line at 15 samples, while the IIR starts at 4.02 samples at DC, peaks at about 6.5 samples near \(0.09\,f_s\) and falls below 1 sample at high frequencies. Hover the phase panel at \(f = 0.100\,f_s\): the FIR phase is \(-3.00\pi\) rad (\(= -2\pi \cdot 0.1 \cdot 15\)) and the IIR phase is \(-1.00\pi\). Set \(N = 101\): the FIR delay becomes 50.0 samples. Set the order to 8: the IIR delay at DC rises to 7.89 samples and its peak to about 15.7 samples.

Activity 2: Finite versus infinite (5 min). With the defaults, the dashed blue line marks where the FIR ends (\(n = 30\)); the IIR \(h[n]\) keeps going and is still nonzero at \(n = 63\) (hover: about \(-2 \times 10^{-7}\)). Now set \(f_c = 0.020\,f_s\), \(N = 101\) and order 8. The largest pole radius is 0.9758, close to the unit circle, so the IIR response is still ringing at \(n = 63\) (\(h \approx 0.0120\)), and its group delay peaks near 74 samples at \(0.019\,f_s\).

Activity 3: Which filter is cheaper? (8 min). At \(f_c = 0.100\,f_s\) with order 4, the IIR gives −28.0 dB at \(2f_c\) for 9 multiplies. Lower \(N\) until the FIR just beats it: \(N = 15\) gives −34.2 dB, while \(N = 13\) gives only −27.4 dB. Repeat at \(f_c = 0.020\,f_s\): the order-4 IIR gives −24.2 dB, and the FIR needs \(N = 57\) (−24.5 dB; \(N = 55\) gives −23.1 dB), so 57 multiplies and 28 samples of delay against 9 multiplies.

Activity 4: Rounding the coefficients (10 min). Return to the defaults and tick Quantize IIR to B bits (8 bits, direct form). The filter is stable (largest pole radius 0.7630 instead of 0.7954) but its DC gain is about +1.9 dB. At \(B = 6\) the radius is 0.9809, the response has a +13.8 dB peak near \(0.106\,f_s\) and \(h[n]\) rings. At \(B = 5\) the radius is 1.0268: UNSTABLE. Switch to Cascaded biquads at \(B = 5\): radius 0.7906, stable. Set the order to 8: the direct form needs 13 bits (12 bits gives 1.0074, unstable; 13 bits gives 0.9099), while biquads are stable even at 4 bits (0.8660). Finally set \(f_c = 0.020\,f_s\): the order-8 direct form is unstable even at 16 bits (1.2987); biquads are stable at 8 bits (0.9763), and at 7 bits one pole lands exactly on \(z = 1\).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A symmetric FIR filter has 41 taps. What is its group delay, and does it depend on frequency? Answer: \((41 - 1)/2 = 20\) samples at every frequency, because symmetric taps give exactly linear phase.
  2. How many multiplies per output sample does an order-6 Butterworth filter need in direct form, and as cascaded biquads? Answer: \(2 \cdot 6 + 1 = 13\) in direct form and \(3 \times 5 = 15\) as three biquads.
  3. At \(f_c = 0.020\,f_s\) and order 8 the IIR impulse response is still ringing at \(n = 63\), but at \(f_c = 0.100\,f_s\) and order 4 it has died out. Why? Answer: \(h[n]\) decays roughly like \(r^n\) for the largest pole radius \(r\). \(0.9758^{63} \approx 0.21\), but \(0.7954^{63} \approx 5 \times 10^{-7}\).
  4. A design needs cutoff \(0.02\,f_s\) and at least 24 dB attenuation at \(0.04\,f_s\). Compare the two filter types. Answer: an order-4 Butterworth reaches −24.2 dB with 9 multiplies (10 as biquads); the Hamming FIR needs 57 taps, 57 multiplies and 28 samples of delay. Choose the IIR unless linear phase is required.
  5. With \(f_c = 0.100\,f_s\) and order 8, the direct form needs 13 bits to stay stable while biquads are stable at 4 bits. Explain the difference. Answer: the roots of a high-order polynomial with clustered poles are extremely sensitive to small changes in its coefficients. Each biquad holds only two poles, set by its own \(a_1\) and \(a_2\), so a rounding error moves those two poles only a little.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A zero outside the unit circle makes the filter unstable." Tick Quantize IIR to B bits at the defaults: rounding the direct-form numerator splits the four zeros at \(z = -1\) into reciprocal pairs, two of them at radius 1.375, outside the circle. The table still reports a stable filter (largest pole radius 0.7630). Stability depends only on the poles.

"Cutoff means the same thing for every filter." At the same \(f_c\) the FIR is 6.1 dB down and the Butterworth 3.0 dB down. When you compare designs, compare the attenuation at the frequencies that matter, as in Activity 3, not the labels.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Finite impulse response - Wikipedia - FIR structure, linear phase from symmetric taps, and the window design method
  2. Infinite impulse response - Wikipedia - recursive filters, transfer functions and pole-based stability
  3. Butterworth filter - Wikipedia - maximally flat response and poles evenly spaced on a circle
  4. Bilinear transform - Wikipedia - mapping an analog prototype to the z-plane with frequency pre-warping
  5. Digital biquad filter - Wikipedia - second-order sections and why cascades are less sensitive to coefficient quantization
  6. Group delay and phase delay - Wikipedia - definition of the group delay plotted in the sim
  7. Durand–Kerner method - Wikipedia - the root-finding iteration used for the quantized direct-form poles
  8. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free textbook with chapters on windowed-sinc and recursive filters
