docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fourier-series-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="627px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A periodic signal can be rebuilt from sinusoids whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of the fundamental \(f_0 = 1/T\). This MicroSim keeps only the first \(N\) of those harmonics and draws the partial sum (red) on top of the original waveform (grey) over two periods. Choose a square, triangle, sawtooth or pulse-train waveform, or drag in the time plot to draw one period of your own. Add harmonics with Step >, Play or the slider and watch the sum converge.

Below the time plot, the magnitude spectrum shows the amplitude of every harmonic and the phase spectrum shows its angle. A checkbox swaps them for bar charts of the cosine and sine coefficients \(a_n\) and \(b_n\). A banner reports the rms error and, for waveforms with a jump, the Gibbs overshoot. Hover over a bar to read that harmonic's coefficients and see its sinusoid in orange. Click a bar to switch the harmonic off and see what it contributes.

This simulation is used in Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals.

docs.title: Fourier Series
docs.text:
A periodic signal with period \(T\) has the Fourier series

\[x(t) = a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[a_n\cos(n\omega_0 t) + b_n\sin(n\omega_0 t)\right], \qquad \omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{T}\]

The three plots are:

  1. Time plot: the waveform, the partial sum, and in orange the single harmonic that is currently selected.
  2. Magnitude spectrum: the amplitude \(\sqrt{a_n^2 + b_n^2} = 2\lvert c_n\rvert\) of each harmonic. Bar 0 is the DC term \(a_0\).
  3. Phase spectrum: the angle of the complex coefficient \(c_n = (a_n - jb_n)/2\). No stem is drawn for a harmonic whose amplitude is zero.

Bars in colour are included in the sum. Pale bars are harmonics above \(N\). Hollow bars are harmonics you switched off.

The coefficients of the four standard waveforms (amplitude from \(-1\) to \(+1\), except the pulse train which goes from 0 to 1) are:

Waveform \(a_0\) \(a_n\) \(b_n\) Amplitudes fall as Square 0 0 \(\dfrac{4}{\pi n}\) for odd \(n\), 0 for even \(n\) \(1/n\) Triangle 0 0 \(\dfrac{8}{\pi^2 n^2}(-1)^{(n-1)/2}\) for odd \(n\), 0 for even \(n\) \(1/n^2\) Sawtooth 0 0 \(\dfrac{2}{\pi n}(-1)^{n+1}\) \(1/n\) Pulse train, duty cycle \(d = 0.25\) \(d\) \(\dfrac{2}{\pi n}\sin(\pi n d)\) 0 \(1/n\) with a sinc-shaped envelope

The custom waveform starts as a half-wave rectified sine. Drag in the time plot to draw one period of your own. Its coefficients are found by evaluating the coefficient integrals numerically over 512 samples of the curve you drew.

Convergence and the Gibbs phenomenon. The banner reports the rms error between the waveform and the partial sum. For waveforms with a jump it also reports how far the highest peak of the partial sum overshoots the waveform. Adding harmonics makes the ripple narrower but not lower: the overshoot settles at about 9% of the jump height however many harmonics are used. The triangle wave has no jump, so its series converges quickly and without overshoot.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
1. Pick a Waveform. Press Step > to add one harmonic at a time, or Play to add them automatically (Play starts paused).
  2. Drag the Number of harmonics N slider to set \(N\) directly from 1 to 50.
  3. Move the mouse over a bar to select that harmonic. Its sinusoid is drawn in orange and its coefficients are listed under the time plot.
  4. Click a bar to switch that harmonic off and on again, and see what it contributes to the shape.
  5. Tick Show individual harmonics to draw every sinusoid in the sum.
  6. Tick Show aₙ and bₙ to replace the magnitude and phase plots with bar charts of the cosine and sine coefficients.
  7. Reset returns to five harmonics, switches every harmonic back on and restores the default custom waveform.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this activity, students will be able to:

  1. Explain a Fourier series as a sum of harmonics of the fundamental frequency.
  2. Compare the harmonic content of square, triangle, sawtooth and pulse waveforms.
  3. Describe how the partial sum converges as harmonics are added, and what the Gibbs phenomenon is.
  4. Relate the coefficients \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) to the amplitude and phase of each harmonic.
  5. Predict from the symmetry of a waveform whether its series has cosine terms, sine terms or both.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in a signals and systems or introductory signal processing course. Plan 20 to 25 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sinusoids: amplitude, frequency and phase
  • Even and odd functions
  • Complex numbers in polar form

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Which harmonics are present? (5 min). Choose Square wave, set the slider to \(N = 1\) and press Step > eight times to reach \(N = 9\). The red curve changes at \(N = 3, 5, 7\) and \(9\) but not at \(N = 2, 4, 6\) and \(8\), and the rms error in the banner is the same at \(N = 1\) and \(N = 2\). Why does adding an even harmonic change nothing?

Activity 2: Read the coefficients (5 min). Hover over bars 1, 3 and 5 with the square wave.

  • The readout gives \(b_1\), \(b_3\) and \(b_5\) = 1.2732, 0.4244 and 0.2546. Check them against \(4/(\pi n)\).
  • Switch to the triangle wave. \(b_1\), \(b_3\) and \(b_5\) become 0.8106, −0.0901 and 0.0324. The sign alternates and the amplitudes fall as \(1/n^2\).
  • Switch to the sawtooth and look at the phase spectrum. The phase alternates between \(-90°\) (odd \(n\)) and \(+90°\) (even \(n\)). Why?

Activity 3: Convergence and the Gibbs overshoot (10 min). Choose Square wave and use the slider to set \(N = 1, 3, 5, 9, 21\) and \(50\). Record the rms error and the peak overshoot from the banner.

\(N\) rms error peak overshoot 1 0.435 13.7% 3 0.315 10.0% 5 0.259 9.4% 9 0.201 9.1% 21 0.136 9.0% 50 0.090 9.0%

The rms error keeps falling but the overshoot levels off at about 9% of the jump. In the time plot the ripple gets narrower and moves toward the jump, but its height does not shrink. Which quantity goes to zero as \(N\) grows, and which does not?

Activity 4: Smoothness, symmetry and your own waveform (10 min).

  • Compare the triangle wave and the square wave at \(N = 5\). The rms error is 0.016 for the triangle and 0.259 for the square. Use the rate at which the amplitudes fall to explain the difference.
  • Choose the Pulse train and tick Show aₙ and bₙ. Only the cosine coefficients are non-zero. Harmonics 4, 8, 12 and so on are missing. Relate this to the 25% duty cycle.
  • Choose Custom, and before drawing anything read \(a_0\), \(b_1\) and \(a_2\): 0.3183, 0.5 and −0.2122. Check them against \(1/\pi\), \(1/2\) and \(-2/(3\pi)\), the known results for a half-wave rectified sine.
  • The square wave has only sine terms and the pulse train only cosine terms. What symmetry of each waveform explains that? Drag in the time plot to draw a waveform that needs both.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Which harmonics does the square wave contain, and how do their amplitudes fall with \(n\)? Answer: only the odd harmonics. Their amplitude is \(4/(\pi n)\), so it falls as \(1/n\) (1.2732, 0.4244, 0.2546 for \(n = 1, 3, 5\)).
  2. At \(N = 50\) the square wave's rms error is 0.090, yet the overshoot is still about 9.0%. Why does the overshoot not disappear? Answer: the error shrinks because the ripple becomes narrower, but its peak height stays at about 9% of the jump. This is the Gibbs phenomenon.
  3. Why is the triangle wave's rms error at \(N = 5\) (0.016) so much smaller than the square wave's (0.259)? Answer: the triangle wave is continuous and its amplitudes fall as \(1/n^2\), so the omitted harmonics carry very little. The square wave's amplitudes fall only as \(1/n\).
  4. Which harmonics of the 25% duty-cycle pulse train are zero, and why? Answer: \(n = 4, 8, 12, \dots\). The coefficient is proportional to \(\sin(\pi n d)\) with \(d = 1/4\), which is zero whenever \(n\) is a multiple of 4.
  5. Does a half-wave rectified sine need cosine terms, sine terms or both? Answer: both, plus a DC term. It is neither even nor odd, and the simulation shows \(a_0 = 0.3183\), \(b_1 = 0.5\) and \(a_2 = -0.2122\).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Enough harmonics will remove the overshoot at a jump." The rms error keeps falling, which makes it look as though the overshoot should too. Step the square wave from \(N = 9\) to \(N = 50\) and watch the banner: the overshoot stays at about 9% while the rms error falls from 0.201 to 0.090.

"Every periodic waveform contains every harmonic." Many waveforms leave out whole families of harmonics. Step through the square wave and the even bars are all zero. The 25% duty-cycle pulse train has no bar at \(n = 4, 8, 12, \dots\).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fourier series - Wikipedia - definition of the series, coefficient formulas and convergence
  2. Gibbs phenomenon - Wikipedia - the overshoot of about 9% of the jump near a discontinuity
  3. Square wave - Wikipedia - the series with only odd harmonics falling as \(1/n\)
  4. Sawtooth wave - Wikipedia - the series with all harmonics and alternating signs
  5. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook covering the Fourier transform family
  6. Oppenheim, A. V., Willsky, A. S., & Nawab, S. H. (1997). Signals and Systems (2nd ed.). Prentice Hall. Chapter 3 covers the Fourier series of periodic signals.
  7. Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals - this textbook - the chapter that embeds this MicroSim

docs.title: Fourier Transform Pairs
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/fourier-transform-pairs/main.html" width="100%" height="672px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A Fourier transform pair links a signal \(x(t)\) to its spectrum

\[X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\,e^{-j2\pi ft}\,dt, \qquad x(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(f)\,e^{j2\pi ft}\,df .\]

The drop-down list picks one of five pairs: rectangle ↔ sinc, with \(\operatorname{sinc}(u) = \sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)\); Gaussian ↔ Gaussian; one-sided exponential \(e^{-at}u(t)\) ↔ \(1/(a + j2\pi f)\), whose power \(|X(f)|^2\) has the Lorentzian shape; cosine ↔ two impulses; and impulse train ↔ impulse train. The top plot shows \(x(t)\), the middle plot \(|X(f)|\) and the bottom plot the phase \(\angle X(f)\). Both axes run from −4.25 to 4.25 (seconds and hertz), so equal widths look equal.

  • Time scale T (0.25 to 2 s) replaces \(x(t)\) with \(x(t/T)\), which transforms to \(T\,X(fT)\): a shorter signal has a wider, lower spectrum.
  • Shift t₀ (−2 to 2 s) delays the signal: \(x(t - t_0) \leftrightarrow e^{-j2\pi f t_0}X(f)\). The magnitude stays the same and the phase gains a ramp of \(-360°\,t_0\) per hertz.
  • Show phase hides or shows the phase plot.

Maroon curves are the analytic transforms. Green dots are a numerical estimate: the sketch samples \(x(t)\) every \(\Delta t = 1/128\) s over a 128 s window, takes a 16384-point FFT and multiplies by \(\Delta t\). The bottom read-out gives the largest difference between the two. Impulses are arrows whose height is their area; for the two periodic pairs the window holds exactly 64 periods (\(\Delta t = T/256\)) and each green dot is an FFT bin times its width \(\Delta f\). Gold bars mark a width in each domain, and the first read-out line compares them. The phase is drawn only where \(|X|\) exceeds 2% of \(X(0)\).

This MicroSim is used in Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Identify the transform of a rectangular pulse, a Gaussian, a one-sided exponential, a cosine and an impulse train
  2. Predict how the height and width of \(|X(f)|\) change when a signal is compressed or stretched in time, using \(x(t/T) \leftrightarrow T\,X(fT)\)
  3. Calculate the phase that a time shift adds at a given frequency, using \(x(t - t_0) \leftrightarrow e^{-j2\pi f t_0}X(f)\)
  4. Explain why the Gaussian reaches the smallest time-bandwidth product, \(\sigma_t\sigma_f = 1/(4\pi)\)
  5. Read a transform pair backwards, identifying \(x(t)\) from a given \(X(f)\) (the inverse Fourier transform)

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a signals and systems or introductory signal processing course (sophomore or junior engineering, physics or computer science). Plan 25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex exponentials and Euler's formula
  • The unit step \(u(t)\) and the unit impulse \(\delta(t)\)
  • The definition of the Fourier transform (Chapter 6)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Compress in time, expand in frequency (6 min). Choose Rectangle ↔ sinc with \(T = 1.00\) s and \(t_0 = 0\). The first zero of the sinc is at 1.00 Hz and \(X(0) = 1.00\), the area of the pulse. Set \(T = 0.50\) s: the pulse is half as wide, \(X(0)\) drops to 0.50 and the first zero moves out to 2.00 Hz. Set \(T = 2.00\) s: \(X(0) = 2.00\) and the first zero is at 0.50 Hz. The product of the width and the first-zero frequency stays 1. With \(T = 1.00\) s, look at the phase plot: 0° in the main lobe and 180° in the lobes between 1 and 2 Hz, 3 and 4 Hz, where the sinc is negative.

Activity 2: A delay is a phase ramp (6 min). Keep the rectangle with \(T = 1.00\) s and set \(t_0 = 0.50\) s. The green magnitude dots do not move at all, but the phase becomes a ramp of −180° per hertz: −45° at 0.25 Hz and −90° at 0.5 Hz. Set \(t_0 = -1.00\) s (an advance): the ramp is now +360° per hertz and the phase at 0.25 Hz is +90°.

Activity 3: The Gaussian time-bandwidth product (6 min). Choose Gaussian ↔ Gaussian with \(T = 1.00\) s. The two plots have the same shape because \(e^{-\pi t^2} \leftrightarrow e^{-\pi f^2}\), and the measured rms widths are \(\sigma_t = 0.282\) s and \(\sigma_f = 0.282\) Hz. Set \(T = 0.50\) s (\(\sigma_t = 0.141\) s, \(\sigma_f = 0.564\) Hz) and then \(T = 2.00\) s (\(\sigma_t = 0.564\) s, \(\sigma_f = 0.141\) Hz). The product stays \(\sigma_t\sigma_f = 0.0796 = 1/(4\pi)\). Now choose the exponential with \(T = 1.00\) s: \(|X|\) falls to \(X(0)/\sqrt{2}\) at \(a/(2\pi) = 0.159\) Hz, where the phase is about −45°.

Activity 4: Impulses and periodic signals (7 min). Choose Cosine ↔ two impulses with \(T = 0.50\) s: impulses of area ½ sit at ±2.00 Hz. Set \(t_0 = 0.10\) s: the areas do not change and the phases become −72° at +2 Hz and +72° at −2 Hz. Choose Impulse train ↔ impulse train with \(T = 2.00\) s: the spectrum is a train of impulses every 0.50 Hz, each of area 0.50. Set \(T = 1.00\) s and \(t_0 = 0.25\) s: the phases are −90° at 1 Hz, 180° at 2 Hz and +90° at 3 Hz. Finally set \(t_0 = 1.00\) s, one whole period: every phase returns to 0° and the read-out reports that nothing changed.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A rectangular pulse lasts 2 ms. At what frequency is the first zero of its spectrum, and what is \(X(0)\)? Answer: at \(1/T = 500\) Hz; \(X(0) = T = 0.002\) s (the area of the pulse).
  2. A signal is compressed in time by a factor of 3, from \(T = 1.5\) s to \(T = 0.5\) s. How do the height and the width of its spectrum change? Check with the rectangle. Answer: \(X(0)\) falls from 1.50 to 0.50 (one third) and the first zero moves from 0.667 Hz to 2.00 Hz (three times wider).
  3. Which signal has the transform \(X(f) = 0.5\,\operatorname{sinc}(0.5f)\,e^{-j\pi f}\)? Answer: \(e^{-j\pi f} = e^{-j2\pi f(0.5)}\), so it is a rectangular pulse of width 0.5 s delayed by 0.5 s, running from 0.25 s to 0.75 s. Setting \(T = 0.50\) s and \(t_0 = 0.50\) s in the sim gives a phase ramp of −180° per hertz.
  4. A signal is delayed by 0.25 s. What happens to its magnitude spectrum, and what phase is added at 2 Hz? Answer: the magnitude is unchanged; the added phase is \(-360° \times 2 \times 0.25 = -180°\).
  5. A Gaussian pulse has an rms duration \(\sigma_t = 1\) ms. What is its rms bandwidth \(\sigma_f\), and can any pulse with \(\sigma_t = 1\) ms have \(\sigma_f = 50\) Hz? Answer: \(\sigma_f = 1/(4\pi \times 0.001) = 79.6\) Hz. No: \(\sigma_t\sigma_f\) would be 0.05, below the minimum \(1/(4\pi) = 0.0796\).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Delaying a signal changes its spectrum." Only the phase changes. Drag the shift slider with any pair selected: the green magnitude dots stay exactly where they are, while the phase plot tilts into a steeper or shallower ramp.

"A narrower pulse has a narrower spectrum." The opposite is true. Lower \(T\) for the rectangle or the Gaussian: the pulse narrows while the spectrum spreads out and drops in height, because the product of the two widths is fixed.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fourier transform - Wikipedia - definition, inverse transform, scaling and shift properties, and a table of transform pairs
  2. Sinc function - Wikipedia - the normalized sinc and its role as the transform of a rectangular pulse
  3. Gaussian function - Wikipedia - the Gaussian and why its Fourier transform is another Gaussian
  4. Dirac comb - Wikipedia - the impulse train and its transform, an impulse train with reciprocal spacing
  5. Cauchy distribution - Wikipedia - the Lorentzian shape of the power spectrum of a decaying exponential
  6. Uncertainty principle - Wikipedia - the time-bandwidth limit that the Gaussian attains
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on Fourier transform pairs and properties

docs.title: Frequency Detection
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/frequency-detection/main.html" width="100%" height="597px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim builds the Fourier transform from one idea: wrap a signal around a spinning circle and see where its center of mass lands. A sine wave with period \(T_s\) (the shaded curve in the Cartesian Coordinates graph; its left edge is "now") is sampled and wound onto the Polar plot. Each sample becomes a point whose distance from the center is the sample value and whose angle makes one full turn every circle period \(T_c\). The Center of Mass panel repeats the wound curve, marks the average of all its points with a yellow dot, and prints that dot's distance from the center as \(|\text{COM}|\).

  • Circle period (0.10–2.00 s) sets \(T_c\). The blue marker shows \(T_c\) on both graphs, which span 0–2 s; the blue lines in the Cartesian graph mark each completed turn.
  • Signal period (0.1–1.0 s) sets \(T_s\). Resolution (10–300 points/s) is the sampling rate. Speed scales simulated time.
  • AutoPoll sweeps \(T_c\) from 0.10 to 2.00 s in 0.05 s steps at 20× speed. It records each strength once it stops changing; press it again to stop. Show Spin rotates the drawing instead of the pen.

The Frequency Strength graph plots \(|\text{COM}|\) against \(T_c\), and its header names the strongest period and its frequency \(f_c = 1/T_c\). With \(t_n = n/R\) for resolution \(R\), the simulation computes

\[|\text{COM}(T_c)| = \left|\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n=0}^{M-1} x(t_n)\,e^{-i2\pi f_c t_n}\right|,\]

a sampled, averaged form of the Fourier transform \(X(f) = \int x(t)\,e^{-i2\pi f t}\,dt\) at \(f = f_c\). For \(x(t) = \sin(2\pi t/T_s)\) it settles at \(1/2\) when \(T_c = T_s\) and falls to zero otherwise.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 6: Fourier Analysis Fundamentals.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  1. Explain how winding a signal around a spinning circle turns it into a center of mass whose distance from the origin measures the strength of one frequency
  2. Predict that the center of mass stays about 0.5 from the origin only when the circle period equals the signal period, and keeps returning to the origin otherwise
  3. Interpret the AutoPoll frequency-strength graph to find the period and frequency of a sine wave
  4. Relate the center-of-mass average to the Fourier transform integral \(X(f) = \int x(t)e^{-i2\pi f t}\,dt\)
  5. Identify an alias peak caused by a low resolution (sampling rate) and compute where it appears

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in a first signals and systems course, after complex numbers and before the discrete Fourier transform. Plan 20–30 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex numbers in polar form and Euler's formula \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\)
  • Period and frequency of a sinusoid, \(f = 1/T\)
  • The center of mass (average position) of a set of points

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: A mismatched winding (5 min). Keep the defaults (\(T_s\) = 0.50 s, \(T_c\) = 0.30 s, Resolution 300, Speed 1.00x) and press Play. The wound curve becomes a three-lobed rose that is balanced around the center. \(|\text{COM}|\) is about 0.15 after 0.5 s and 0.08 after 1 s, then returns to 0.000 at 1.5 s, the first time that both 3 signal periods and 5 turns of the circle are complete. It returns to zero every 1.5 s after that.

Activity 2: A matched winding (5 min). Press Reset, set the circle period to 0.50 s and press Play. The positive and the negative half of every cycle now land on the same side of the center (a negative radius flips a point to the opposite side), so the curve is a single circle that passes through the center. \(|\text{COM}|\) settles at 0.50 (0.498 after 1 s). Now set \(T_c\) = 1.00 s. The curve becomes a four-petal rose, and \(|\text{COM}|\) is back to 0.000 after every whole second. Check Show Spin: the red dot on the polar plot now moves straight up and down in step with the red dot at the left edge of the Cartesian graph.

Activity 3: Detect the frequency (8 min). Press Reset, then AutoPoll, and wait for the sweep to reach 2.00 s (about 13 s). One stem stands out at 0.50 s with a strength of about 0.51, and the header reads 0.50 s = 2.00 Hz. Its neighbors at 0.45 s and 0.55 s reach only about 0.11, and the rest stay below about 0.1. Set the signal period to 0.8 s and run AutoPoll again (about 22 s): the peak moves to 0.80 s, which is 1.25 Hz.

Activity 4: An alias (7 min). Set Resolution to 10 pts/s and the signal period to 0.3 s, so a 3.33 Hz sine is sampled only 3 times per period (the Cartesian graph shows a jagged three-point wave). Run AutoPoll. Two stems of about 0.5 appear: at 0.30 s (3.33 Hz) and at 0.15 s (6.67 Hz). They are equally strong, so the header may name either one. The 0.15 s stem is an alias at \(f_s - f = 10 - 3.33 = 6.67\) Hz. At 10 samples per second, winding at 6.67 Hz cannot be told apart from winding at \(-3.33\) Hz.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A sine wave is wound with \(T_c = T_s\). Where does its center of mass end up, and why? (Answer: about 0.5 from the center. Each turn of the circle covers exactly one cycle, and the negative radius flips the other half-cycle onto the same side of the center, so nothing cancels. The wound curve is a single circle through the center whose center of mass is 0.5 away.)
  2. AutoPoll shows a single peak at \(T_c\) = 0.25 s. What is the frequency of the signal? (Answer: \(f = 1/0.25\ \text{s} = 4\) Hz.)
  3. With \(T_s\) = 0.5 s and \(T_c\) = 0.3 s, why does \(|\text{COM}|\) return to exactly zero every 1.5 s? (Answer: 1.5 s is the least common multiple of the two periods. It holds 3 whole signal periods and 5 whole turns, and over such a span the sum of \(\sin(2\pi t/T_s)\,e^{-i2\pi t/T_c}\) is zero whenever \(1/T_c \ne 1/T_s\) (and no alias is involved). This is the orthogonality of sinusoids.)
  4. Explain why the AutoPoll stems at 0.45 s and 0.55 s are not zero when the signal period is 0.5 s. (Answer: AutoPoll watches each \(T_c\) for only a few signal periods. At \(T_c\) = 0.55 s, \(|\text{COM}|\) is still 0.49 after 1 s and 0.30 after 3 s, and reaches 0 only at 5.5 s, so nearby frequencies need a long observation to tell apart. This is spectral leakage, and frequency resolution is about \(1/T\) for observation time \(T\).)
  5. At Resolution 10 pts/s, a 3.33 Hz signal produces a second peak at \(T_c\) = 0.15 s. Explain it. (Answer: sampling at \(f_s\) = 10 Hz makes winding at 6.67 Hz identical to winding at \(6.67 - 10 = -3.33\) Hz. A real sine has a component at \(-3.33\) Hz, so the alias appears at \(1/6.67 = 0.15\) s.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The horizontal axis of the strength graph is frequency." It is the circle period \(T_c\), so frequency \(f_c = 1/T_c\) decreases to the right. The header converts the peak to hertz (0.50 s = 2.00 Hz). Compare the 0.80 s peak in Activity 3 with the 0.50 s peak: the slower signal appears farther right.

"Only the exact matching period gives a large center of mass." Close periods look matched for a while. Set \(T_s\) = 0.5 s and \(T_c\) = 0.55 s and press Play: \(|\text{COM}|\) starts near 0.49 and decays only slowly (0.42 at 2 s, 0.17 at 4 s), reaching zero at 5.5 s. Telling close frequencies apart takes a long observation.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the integral \(X(f) = \int x(t)e^{-i2\pi ft}\,dt\) that the winding average approximates
  2. But what is the Fourier Transform? A visual introduction - 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson) - the "winding machine" and center-of-mass picture this MicroSim animates
  3. Center of mass - Wikipedia - the average position shown by the yellow dot
  4. Aliasing - Wikipedia - why a low resolution produces the extra peak in Activity 4
  5. Rose (mathematics) - Wikipedia - the petal curves \(r = \sin(k\theta)\) traced when \(T_c/T_s = k\)
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free textbook with chapters on the DFT and spectral leakage

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/graph-viewer/main.html" width="100%" height="702px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This viewer draws the learning graph of this course: a directed network of the 200 concepts taught in the book, joined by 262 arrows. Each node is a concept. An arrow runs from a prerequisite to a concept that depends on it, so the arrow from Real Numbers to Complex Numbers means that Real Numbers should be understood first. The color of a node shows its taxonomy category, and the layout comes from a force-directed physics solver, so the position of a node on the screen carries no meaning.

  • Legend checkboxes show or hide every concept in one category. Check All and Uncheck All set all 12 at once.
  • Search box lists the visible concepts whose names contain the text you type, with the category code in parentheses. Click a result to zoom to that node and select it. Hidden categories are not searched.
  • Graph Statistics counts the visible nodes, the visible edges (both ends must be visible) and the orphans (visible nodes that have no visible edge).
  • Menu button (the button at the top left) collapses the sidebar to give the graph the full width. On a narrow screen the sidebar starts collapsed.
  • Mouse: drag a node to move it, scroll to zoom and drag the background to pan.

The viewer reads learning-graph.json from the learning-graph folder, so it always shows the current graph of the book.

docs.title: The 12 Categories
docs.text: Code Category Color Concepts MATH Mathematical Foundations dark red #8B0000 25 SIG Signal Fundamentals orange-red #FF4500 25 SYS System Properties gold #FFD700 20 CONV Convolution and Correlation lime green #32CD32 10 SAMP Sampling and Quantization blue #1E90FF 15 FOUR Fourier Analysis purple #9370DB 20 XFRM Advanced Transforms deep pink #FF1493 15 FILT Filter Design turquoise #00CED1 25 ADAP Adaptive Processing pink #FF69B4 10 RAND Stochastic Processes brown #8B4513 10 ADVN Advanced Topics indigo #4B0082 15 APPL Applications and AI dark slate #2F4F4F 10

docs.title: Ways to Use It
docs.text:
• Course planning: show only the categories of one unit to design a lesson sequence.
  • Concept exploration: search for a concept and see which concepts feed into it and which depend on it.
  • Gap analysis: a nonzero orphan count after you choose a set of categories means that the set is missing prerequisites or dependents.
  • Progressive learning: start with the foundation categories and enable the advanced ones gradually.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  • Identify the prerequisites of a concept by tracing the arrows that point into its node.
  • Use the legend checkboxes to isolate one category and predict the node, edge and orphan counts before reading them from the statistics.
  • Explain why the orphan count rises when a category is hidden, even though the full graph has no orphans.
  • Locate a concept with the search box and state which category it belongs to.
  • Evaluate a study sequence by deciding which categories must be shown together so that no visible concept is missing a prerequisite.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students and instructors in a first signal processing course who want to see how the concepts of the book depend on each other, and course designers who plan the order of topics.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: No signal processing background is needed. Students should know what a prerequisite is and should be able to read a directed graph (a node-and-arrow diagram).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Read the whole graph (5 min). Open the viewer with all 12 boxes checked. The statistics read Nodes 200, Edges 262 and Orphans 0. Click Uncheck All: all three counts fall to 0 and the canvas is empty. Check only Mathematical Foundations: the counts become Nodes 25, Edges 27 and Orphans 0.

Activity 2: Why orphans appear (10 min). Click Uncheck All and check only System Properties. The counts are Nodes 20, Edges 5 and Orphans 14. Predict what happens when you also check Signal Fundamentals, then try it: the counts become Nodes 45, Edges 46 and Orphans 0. Nineteen arrows run from Signal Fundamentals into System Properties, and they were hidden because one end of each was hidden.

Activity 3: Find a concept (5 min). Click Check All, click the search box and type convolution. Five concepts are listed: Convolution, Discrete Convolution, Circular Convolution and Convolution Theorem (all CONV), and Convolutional Neural Networks (APPL). Click Convolution: the view zooms to the node and the edges that touch it are drawn thicker and grey. Now uncheck Convolution and Correlation and type convolution again: only Convolutional Neural Networks (APPL) is listed.

Activity 4: Plan a study path (10 min). Select Convolution with the search box and count the arrows that point into it: three, from Integral Calculus (MATH), Signals (SIG) and Systems (SIG). Click Uncheck All and check only Convolution and Correlation and Signal Fundamentals: Nodes 35, Edges 34 and Orphans 2. The two orphans are Unit Step Function and Unit Impulse Function, whose prerequisite Real Numbers is hidden. Check Mathematical Foundations as well: Nodes 60, Edges 70 and Orphans 0.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With all 12 categories checked, what do the three statistics read?

    Nodes 200, Edges 262 and Orphans 0.

  2. Only System Properties is checked and the viewer reports 14 orphans, although the full graph has none. Explain.

    An orphan is a visible node with no visible edge. Most arrows that touch System Properties concepts come from Signal Fundamentals (19 of them), which is hidden. Checking Signal Fundamentals restores the arrows and the orphan count falls to 0.

  3. Which three concepts are direct prerequisites of Convolution?

    Integral Calculus, Signals and Systems.

  4. With Convolution and Correlation unchecked, how many concepts match the search text convolution, and which?

    One: Convolutional Neural Networks (APPL). The search covers visible nodes only.

  5. A student wants to study Fourier Analysis. Which other categories must be shown so that no Fourier Analysis concept is missing a prerequisite, and what do the statistics read?

    Mathematical Foundations and Signal Fundamentals. The statistics read Nodes 70, Edges 81 and Orphans 0.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"An arrow points from a concept to the things it needs." The arrows point from a prerequisite to the concept that depends on it. Search for Real Numbers: it has no arrow pointing in, and 13 arrows leave it. It is the only concept in the graph with no prerequisite.

"Orphans are the concepts that nothing else depends on." In this viewer an orphan has no visible edge at all, in either direction, so the full graph has 0 orphans. The learning-graph quality report counts a different thing: 112 concepts that no other concept depends on. Hide a category and the orphan count tells you which concepts have lost all of their neighbors.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Directed acyclic graph - Wikipedia - the graph structure that a learning graph uses so that prerequisites never form a cycle
  2. Concept map - Wikipedia - the node-and-link diagram idea that a learning graph formalizes
  3. Knowledge space - Wikipedia - the theory of prerequisite structure among concepts that underlies adaptive learning
  4. Topological sorting - Wikipedia - how a valid study order is derived from the arrows
  5. vis-network documentation - vis.js project - the library that draws the graph

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text:
• The viewer loads vis-network 10.0.2 (pinned; the page used to load whatever version unpkg served as "latest").
  • Files: main.html (entry point), script.js (data loading, legend, search, statistics) and local.css.
  • The data path is ../../learning-graph/learning-graph.json, relative to docs/sims/graph-viewer/. The viewer uses vis.DataSet for nodes and edges and the node hidden property to filter by category.
  • The group colors and category names come from the groups object of learning-graph.json.

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer V1
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/graph-viewer-v1/main.html" width="100%" height="807px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Superseded by the Learning Graph Viewer

This is the deprecated first version (v1) of the learning graph viewer. It is superseded by the current Learning Graph Viewer, which adds search, taxonomy filtering and graph statistics. This page, and the earlier view-graph* experiments it links to, are kept for reference only.

This MicroSim draws the learning graph of this textbook: 200 concepts (nodes) joined by 370 directed prerequisite edges, read from signal-processing-concepts.json. Each arrow points from a concept to one of its prerequisites, so an arrowhead lands on the idea that must be understood first. Node color is the taxonomy group named in the legend (12 groups, from Math Foundations to AI & Machine Learning).

The layout is computed in two steps. A force-directed solver (ForceAtlas2) first lets every node settle. Physics is then switched off, the 27 Math Foundations nodes are pinned to the left edge, and the 10 Applications and AI & Machine Learning nodes are pinned to the right edge. Read from right to left, the arrows run from the goal concepts back to the mathematics they rest on.

The viewer has no sliders. Drag a node to move it, drag the background to pan, scroll to zoom, and click a node to select it and highlight its edges. The ☰ button hides or shows the legend. The mathematical background behind the left column is covered in Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations, and the way learning graphs are built is described on the Learning Graph page.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, a student can:

  • Identify the taxonomy group of a concept from its node color and the legend.
  • Trace a prerequisite chain by following arrows from a concept back to a Math Foundations node.
  • Explain how fixed: { x: true, y: false } pins a node to a column while leaving it free to move vertically.
  • Compare the number of arrows arriving at hub concepts such as Filtering and Signals with the number arriving at a typical concept to judge which concepts are most foundational.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in an introductory signal processing course, and instructors who are designing a learning graph for an intelligent textbook.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Directed-graph vocabulary: node, edge, arrow, path.
  • Familiarity with the list of topics in the course description.
  • Optional: basic JavaScript, for the code-reading questions.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the legend. Match each of the 12 legend colors to nodes in the graph. Expected: the red Math Foundations nodes form one column on the left edge and the green Applications and purple AI & Machine Learning nodes form one column on the right edge. Labels in the two columns overlap, so drag nodes up or down to read them.
  2. Trace a prerequisite chain. Start at Fast Fourier Transform (yellow, Fourier Analysis) and follow one arrow at a time: Fast Fourier Transform, Discrete Fourier Transform, Fourier Transform, Fourier Series, Periodic Signals, Signals, Real Numbers. Expected: 6 arrows, ending on a red node in the left column. Following every arrow from Fast Fourier Transform reaches 10 distinct prerequisite concepts.
  3. Compare pinned and free nodes. Drag Trigonometry (red, left column) diagonally toward the center. Expected: it slides only up or down and its horizontal position does not change. Now drag Unit Circle (gray, Other Transforms) the same way. Expected: it follows the pointer in both directions.
  4. Find the hubs. Click Filtering (lavender). Expected: 37 edges are highlighted, 35 arrows that arrive at it from concepts that list Filtering as a prerequisite and 2 that leave it. Repeat for Signals (28 arrows arrive, 29 edges highlighted), Fourier Transform (21 arrive, 24 highlighted) and Systems (17 arrive, 18 highlighted), the next three busiest prerequisites.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Which taxonomy groups are pinned, and to which side of the graph?

    Math Foundations (group MATH) is pinned to the left. Applications (APP) and AI & Machine Learning (AI) are pinned to the right.

  2. In the data file an edge reads {"from": 2, "to": 1}, joining Complex Numbers (2) and Real Numbers (1). At which node is the arrowhead drawn, and what does that say about the two concepts?

    At Real Numbers. Complex Numbers depends on Real Numbers, so Real Numbers is the prerequisite.

  3. Why does the code use fixed: { x: true, y: false } instead of fixed: true?

    The nodes must stay in their column, so x is locked, but y is left free so that the overlapping labels in the column can be pulled apart by dragging.

  4. Why does the script wait for the stabilizationIterationsDone event before pinning the nodes?

    Physics runs first with every node free, so the solver can settle the whole graph. Only afterwards is physics switched off and the pinned groups moved to x = -1200 and x = 1200 and locked in x.

  5. Which concepts have no prerequisites at all?

    Real Numbers, Vectors, Differential Calculus, Integral Calculus, Probability Theory and Trigonometry. All six are Math Foundations nodes and have no outgoing arrow.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Arrows point from a prerequisite to the concept it unlocks." In this graph the arrowhead is at the prerequisite. Following arrows takes you down toward the basics, as Activity 2 shows.
  • "A node's horizontal position tells how advanced it is." Only the pinned columns are placed by rule (left for Math Foundations, right for Applications and AI). Every other position comes from the physics layout and changes from one page load to the next. Group membership is carried by color, not by position.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. vis-network documentation - visjs.org - options for physics, node fixing and interaction used by this viewer
  2. vis-network on GitHub - GitHub - source and release history of the library, pinned here at version 9.1.9
  3. Force-directed graph drawing - Wikipedia - background on the layout algorithm family that ForceAtlas2 belongs to
  4. Directed acyclic graph - Wikipedia - the structure of a prerequisite graph
  5. Concept map - Wikipedia - the educational tool that learning graphs formalize

docs.title: How the pinning works
docs.text:
The current graph-viewer.js waits for the physics solver to stabilize, then fixes the x position of the Math Foundations group on the left and the Applications and AI groups on the right:

network.once('stabilizationIterationsDone', function () {
  network.setOptions({ physics: { enabled: false } });
  const updatedNodes = [];
  nodes.forEach(function (node) {
    if (node.group === "MATH") {
      updatedNodes.push({ id: node.id, x: -1200, group: node.group, fixed: { x: true, y: false } });
    } else if (node.group === "APP" || node.group === "AI") {
      updatedNodes.push({ id: node.id, group: node.group, x: 1200, fixed: { x: true, y: false } });
    }
  });
  nodes.update(updatedNodes);
});

docs.title: Earlier generations
docs.text:
Before the group-based pinning above, the first experiment changed a standard vis.js template to pin nodes in the found (foundation) group to the left and nodes in the goal group to the right, drawn as red boxes and gold stars:

// Extract nodes from the JSON data
const nodes = new vis.DataSet(data.nodes);

// Function to fix the x positions for foundation and goal groups after JSON load
// and set red boxes for foundation and gold stars for goals
nodes.forEach(function (node) {
    if (node.group === "found") {
        node.x = -900;
        node.fixed = { x: true, y: false }; // Fix x, but let y be adjusted by physics
        node.shape = "box";
        node.color = "red";
        node.font = {"color": "white"};
    } else if (node.group === "goal") {
        node.x = 900;
        node.fixed = { x: true, y: false }; // Fix x, but let y be adjusted by physics
        node.shape = "star";
        node.color = "gold";
    }
});

The three earlier viewer pages are kept in this directory unchanged apart from pinning the library version. They read a graph-data.json file that is no longer in the directory, so they currently show an empty network.

  • View JSON Graph V1
  • View JSON Graph V2
  • View Learning Graph with Sidebar V3

docs.title: Huffman Coding
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/huffman-coding/main.html" width="100%" height="752px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim builds a Huffman code step by step. The Source list chooses the symbol probabilities: a skewed five-symbol source, powers of 1/2, a uniform eight-symbol source, two symbols with \(p = 0.9\) and \(0.1\), approximate English letter counts per 1000 letters, or Count the characters of my message, which counts every character (spaces included) of the text in the Message box (up to 30 characters). With a preset, the box holds a sample message that is encoded with the preset's code.

Each press of Next merge joins the two least-probable nodes, ringed in gold, into a new node whose probability is their sum. Build tree does all remaining merges, Undo takes one back and Reset returns to the separate symbols. Ties are broken by a fixed rule (single symbols first, then alphabetical order, then the oldest merged node), so the tree is always the same. The table under the leaves lists \(p_i\) (or the count \(n_i\)), the ideal length \(-\log_2 p_i\), the codeword and its length \(\ell_i\). Every merge puts one bit, 0 for the left branch and 1 for the right, in front of the codeword of each symbol below it.

The side panel compares the entropy and the average code length,

\[H = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i, \qquad L = \sum_i p_i\,\ell_i, \qquad H \le L < H + 1,\]

and shows the efficiency \(H/L\), the fixed-length code of \(\lceil \log_2 K \rceil\) bits for \(K\) symbols, and the compression ratio (fixed-length bits divided by Huffman bits). The bottom panel encodes the message into a bit stream, counts its bits, and decodes it by walking down the tree. Point at a leaf to trace its path.

This MicroSim is used in Chapter 13: Multirate Signal Processing and Compression.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Construct a Huffman code by repeatedly merging the two least-probable nodes and reading the codewords from the root
  2. Calculate the entropy \(H\), the average code length \(L\), the efficiency \(H/L\) and the compression ratio against a fixed-length code
  3. Verify the bound \(H \le L < H + 1\) and identify the distributions for which \(L = H\) exactly
  4. Explain why a prefix-free code can be decoded without separators between codewords
  5. Analyze why Huffman coding is inefficient for very skewed sources and how coding blocks of symbols improves it

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a digital signal processing, communications or information theory course (junior or senior engineering or computer science). Plan 25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Probability of discrete events and the base-2 logarithm
  • Binary numbers and binary trees
  • The idea of lossless compression (Chapter 13)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Build the tree by hand (7 min). Choose Skewed: 5 symbols (\(p\) = 0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1) and press Reset. Before each press of Next merge, predict the next pair. The four merges are D + E → 0.2, B + C → 0.4, DE + A → 0.6 and BC + DEA → 1.0; the second and third merges are ties, settled by the tie rule. After each merge "L so far" reads 0.200, 0.600, 1.200 and 2.200: every merge adds its probability to \(L\). The final code is A = 11, B = 00, C = 01, D = 100, E = 101, with \(H = 2.122\) and \(L = 2.200\) bits/symbol, an efficiency of 96.5 % and a compression ratio of \(3/L = 1.36\). The message ACABADABCE needs 22 bits instead of \(10 \times 3 = 30\).

Activity 2: When does L equal H? (6 min). Choose Powers of 1/2. Every \(-\log_2 p_i\) (1, 2, 3, 4, 4) is an integer and equals \(\ell_i\), so \(L = H = 1.875\) bits/symbol and the efficiency is 100.0 %. Choose Uniform: 8 symbols: \(L = H = 3.000\), every codeword has 3 bits and the ratio is 1.00, so there is nothing to gain over a fixed-length code. Now choose Count the characters of my message and type ABCDEF: six equally likely symbols give \(H = 2.585\) and \(L = 2.667\) (lengths 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3), and the message needs 16 bits instead of 18.

Activity 3: The one-bit floor (5 min). Choose Two symbols: 0.9 and 0.1. The entropy is only 0.469 bits/symbol, but each codeword needs at least one bit, so \(L = 1.000\) and the efficiency drops to 46.9 %, with no gain over the 1-bit fixed-length code. Huffman coding loses most when one symbol is very likely.

Activity 4: English letters and your own text (7 min). Choose English letters A–Z and press Build tree. The common letters E (100) and T (000) get 3 bits, while J, Q, X and Z get 9 bits; \(H = 4.173\), \(L = 4.202\) bits/letter (99.3 %), and the ratio against 5-bit codes is 1.19. The sample SHANNON needs 28 bits (4.000 bits/letter). Type HUFFMAN: it needs 32 bits (4.571 bits/letter), because F, U and M are less common. Finally choose Count the characters of my message and type MISSISSIPPI: S = 0, I = 11, M = 100, P = 101, \(H = 1.823\), \(L = 1.909\), and the message needs 21 bits instead of 22.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Symbols A–E have probabilities 0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1 and 0.1. What is \(L\) for the sim's Huffman code, and what is the compression ratio against a fixed-length code? Answer: lengths 2, 2, 2, 3, 3 give \(L = 0.8 + 0.4 + 0.4 + 0.3 + 0.3 = 2.2\) bits/symbol; a fixed-length code needs \(\lceil\log_2 5\rceil = 3\) bits, so the ratio is \(3/2.2 = 1.36\).
  2. For which probability distributions does a Huffman code reach \(L = H\) exactly? Answer: when every probability is a power of 1/2 (a dyadic distribution), because then \(-\log_2 p_i\) is an integer and Huffman's lengths equal it, as in the Powers of 1/2 preset (\(L = H = 1.875\)).
  3. The bit stream 110111100101 was made with the skewed code (A = 11, B = 00, C = 01, D = 100, E = 101). Decode it and explain why no separators are needed. Answer: 11 | 01 | 11 | 100 | 101 = A C A D E (12 bits). No codeword is the start of another, so the decoder knows a codeword has ended the moment it reaches a leaf; type ACADE in the Message box with the skewed preset to check.
  4. A source has \(p = 0.9\) and \(0.1\). Why is the Huffman efficiency only 46.9 %, and how could it be improved? Answer: \(H = 0.469\) bits/symbol, but every codeword needs at least one bit, so \(L = 1\). Coding pairs of symbols (probabilities 0.81, 0.09, 0.09, 0.01) gives lengths 1, 2, 3, 3, so \(L = 1.29\) bits per pair, or 0.645 bits/symbol; arithmetic coding gets closer still.
  5. With the English letter code, the message ZZZ needs 27 bits while a 5-bit fixed-length code needs 15. Does this contradict the claim that Huffman coding compresses? Answer: no. Huffman coding minimizes the average length over the source distribution (\(L = 4.202 < 5\) bits/letter); a message made of rare letters is atypical and can be longer than with a fixed-length code.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The Huffman code for a source is unique." The tie rule decides which of several equal-weight nodes is merged. For the skewed preset the sim gives lengths 2, 2, 2, 3, 3; preferring merged nodes in the ties gives lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 instead. Both have \(L = 2.2\) bits/symbol: the codes differ, but the average length is the same minimum.

"Huffman coding always reaches the entropy." It does only when every probability is a power of 1/2. The two-symbol preset shows \(L = 1.000\) against \(H = 0.469\), and every other preset shows \(L\) inside the shaded band from \(H\) to \(H + 1\) rather than at \(H\).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Huffman coding - Wikipedia - the merge algorithm, optimality among prefix codes, tie handling and minimum-variance codes
  2. Entropy (information theory) - Wikipedia - the definition \(H = -\sum p_i \log_2 p_i\) and its meaning as average information per symbol
  3. Shannon's source coding theorem - Wikipedia - why no lossless code can average fewer than \(H\) bits per symbol
  4. Prefix code - Wikipedia - the prefix property that lets a bit stream be decoded without separators
  5. Letter frequency - Wikipedia - typical relative frequencies of letters in English text, the basis of the English preset
  6. Arithmetic coding - Wikipedia - an entropy coder that avoids the one-bit-per-symbol floor of Huffman coding
  7. Chapter 27: Data Compression - Steven W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - free chapter covering Huffman coding and other compression methods

docs.title: IIR Prototype Comparison
docs.text:

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim compares the five classic analog low-pass prototypes that IIR filter design starts from: Butterworth, Chebyshev I, Chebyshev II, elliptic (Cauer) and Bessel (Thomson), all of the same order \(N\). Every plot is computed from the pole and zero lists of

\[H(s) = K\,\frac{\prod_i (s - z_i)}{\prod_k (s - p_k)},\]

so the magnitude (dB on a log frequency axis), phase, group delay \(\tau(\omega) = -d\phi/d\omega\), step response and s-plane plot of poles (×) and zeros (○) all describe the same filters.

  • Family checkboxes show or hide each family; colors match the legend and the table.
  • Order N (1 to 10) is the number of poles.
  • Ripple \(R_p\) (0.1 to 3 dB) is the passband tolerance; Chebyshev I and elliptic designs ripple by exactly \(R_p\).
  • Stopband \(A_s\) (20 to 80 dB) is the stopband attenuation that Chebyshev II and elliptic designs guarantee.
  • Scaling puts either the −3.01 dB point or the passband edge of every family at \(\omega = 1\) rad/s.
  • Zoom passband enlarges the passband to show the ripple.

The table lists \(\omega_p\) (where the loss first exceeds \(R_p\)), \(\omega_s\) (beyond which the loss stays at least \(A_s\)), the transition width \(\Delta\omega = \omega_s - \omega_p\), the ratio \(\omega_s/\omega_p\), the step overshoot and the 2% settling time. The smallest transition width, overshoot and settling time are highlighted in gold.

The elliptic poles and zeros are computed exactly from Jacobi elliptic functions (Landen transformations). The Bessel poles are the roots of the reverse Bessel polynomial (1 s group delay at DC), rescaled like the other families.

This simulation is used in Chapter 10: Advanced Filter Design and Implementation.

docs.title: Key Formulas
docs.text:
\[|H_{\text{Butterworth}}(j\omega)|^2 = \frac{1}{1 + (\omega/\omega_c)^{2N}} \qquad |H_{\text{Chebyshev I}}(j\omega)|^2 = \frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon^2 T_N^2(\omega/\omega_c)},\quad \varepsilon = \sqrt{10^{R_p/10} - 1}\]

For Chebyshev I, \(\omega_c\) is the ripple edge. Both Chebyshev types have \(\omega_s/\omega_p = \cosh\!\big(\cosh^{-1}(\varepsilon_s/\varepsilon)/N\big)\) with \(\varepsilon_s = \sqrt{10^{A_s/10} - 1}\); the elliptic ratio \(1/k\) solves the degree equation \(K'(k)/K(k) = K'(k_1)/\big(N K(k_1)\big)\) with \(k_1 = \varepsilon/\varepsilon_s\) and complete elliptic integrals \(K\), \(K'\).

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Compare the transition width \(\Delta\omega = \omega_s - \omega_p\) of the five prototype families at the same order and rank them from sharpest to gentlest
  2. Relate the pole and zero pattern in the s-plane (a circle, an ellipse, poles close to the \(j\omega\) axis, zeros on the \(j\omega\) axis) to flatness, ripple and notches in the magnitude response
  3. Analyze the trade-off between frequency selectivity and time-domain behavior: overshoot, settling time and group-delay variation
  4. Calculate Butterworth band edges and the minimum Butterworth order from \(|H|^2 = 1/(1 + \omega^{2N})\), and check them against the read-outs
  5. Evaluate which prototype best meets an application requirement, such as sharp channel selection or faithful pulse shape

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a junior- or senior-level signals and systems or digital signal processing course in electrical engineering, computer engineering or physics. Plan 30 to 40 minutes for the activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Laplace transform, transfer functions and the frequency response \(H(j\omega)\)
  • Poles, zeros and stability in the s-plane
  • Decibels, the step response and group delay
  • Filter specifications: passband, stopband and transition band (Chapter 9: Filter Design Fundamentals)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Rank the families by selectivity (8 min). Use the default settings: \(N = 4\), \(R_p = 1.0\) dB, \(A_s = 40\) dB, scaling "−3 dB point at ω = 1 rad/s", with Butterworth, Chebyshev I, elliptic and Bessel shown. Every curve passes through −3.01 dB at \(\omega = 1\). The dots on the dashed −40 dB line are the stopband edges: 1.459 (elliptic), 2.221 (Chebyshev I), 3.162 (Butterworth) and 4.724 rad/s (Bessel). The table gives the transition widths 0.496, 1.271, 2.318 and 4.130 rad/s. Look at the s-plane: the Butterworth poles lie on the unit circle, the Chebyshev I poles lie on a flattened ellipse closer to the \(j\omega\) axis, and only the elliptic filter has zeros, at \(\pm j1.55\) (on the plot) and \(\pm j3.39\) (listed under it). Those zeros are the two notches in the magnitude plot.

Activity 2: The same specification for two Chebyshevs (8 min). Check Chebyshev II and set Scaling to "Passband edge at ω = 1 rad/s". Now every family has exactly 1 dB loss at \(\omega = 1\), so \(\omega_p = 1.000\) for all of them and \(\omega_s\) equals the selectivity ratio: elliptic 1.515, Chebyshev I and Chebyshev II both 2.339, Butterworth 3.744 and Bessel 7.964. Check Zoom passband. Chebyshev I ripples between 0 and −1 dB and touches 0 dB at \(\omega = 0.383\) and \(0.924\) rad/s (where \(T_4(\omega) = 0\)). Chebyshev II is flat and monotonic in the passband because its ripple is in the stopband, where its zeros sit at \(\pm j2.53\) and \(\pm j6.11\). The two Chebyshevs have the same selectivity, but Chebyshev II overshoots only 13.0% and settles in 8.42 s, compared with 21.9% and 19.20 s for Chebyshev I.

Activity 3: The time-domain price of sharpness (8 min). Return to the default settings. In the table, overshoot grows as the transition narrows: Bessel 0.8%, Butterworth 10.8%, Chebyshev I 21.9% and elliptic 24.0%. The 2% settling times grow the same way: 3.88, 9.87, 20.22 and 23.12 s. In the group-delay plot the Bessel curve stays flat near 2.11 s through the passband, while the elliptic delay peaks near 11 s just below \(\omega = 1\). The delay peaks come from the poles closest to the \(j\omega\) axis. The Chebyshev I and elliptic step responses settle at 0.891, not 1, because an even-order equiripple design has a DC gain of \(10^{-R_p/20}\).

Activity 4: Raise the order (8 min). Keep the −3 dB scaling with \(R_p = 1.0\) dB and \(A_s = 40\) dB and move the Order slider. At \(N = 1\) all five families are the same first-order filter \(1/(s + 1)\): every row reads \(\Delta\omega = 99.49\) rad/s, 0.0% overshoot and 3.91 s settling. The elliptic transition width shrinks fastest: 4.977 (\(N = 2\)), 1.305 (\(N = 3\)), 0.496 (\(N = 4\)), 0.098 (\(N = 6\)) and 0.022 rad/s (\(N = 8\)). The Butterworth width falls more slowly: 9.286, 3.843, 2.318, 1.261 and 0.859 rad/s. Meanwhile the elliptic settling time grows from 23.12 s at \(N = 4\) to 57.73 s at \(N = 8\), and its group-delay peak runs off the chart ("peaks clipped"). Bessel overshoot stays below 1% at every order.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With \(N = 4\), \(R_p = 1\) dB and \(A_s = 40\) dB, a specification requires \(\omega_s/\omega_p \le 2\). Which families meet it? Answer: only the elliptic filter (1.515). Chebyshev I and II give 2.339, Butterworth 3.744 and Bessel 7.964.
  2. Use \(|H|^2 = 1/(1 + \omega^{2N})\) to find the Butterworth stopband edge for \(N = 4\) and \(A_s = 40\) dB, with the −3 dB point at 1 rad/s. Answer: \(10\log_{10}(1 + \omega_s^8) = 40\), so \(\omega_s = (10^4 - 1)^{1/8} = 3.162\) rad/s, which matches the table.
  3. What is the smallest Butterworth order that matches the selectivity of the 4th-order elliptic filter (\(\omega_s/\omega_p = 1.515\)) with \(R_p = 1\) dB and \(A_s = 40\) dB? Answer: \(N \ge \log_{10}\!\big((10^{4} - 1)/(10^{0.1} - 1)\big) / \big(2\log_{10} 1.515\big) = 12.7\), so \(N = 13\). Even at \(N = 10\) the sim shows a Butterworth ratio of 1.696.
  4. Why does the 4th-order Chebyshev I step response settle at about 0.89 instead of 1? Answer: for even \(N\) the equiripple passband starts at a ripple minimum, so the DC gain is \(1/\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon^2} = 10^{-1/20} = 0.891\) for \(R_p = 1\) dB. Overshoot is measured relative to this final value.
  5. A data-acquisition front end must pass rectangular pulses with as little ringing as possible. Which family would you choose at \(N = 4\), and what does it cost? Answer: Bessel, with 0.8% overshoot, 3.88 s settling and nearly constant group delay (the elliptic filter has 24.0% and 23.12 s). The cost is the widest transition band, \(\Delta\omega = 4.130\) rad/s against 0.496 rad/s for the elliptic filter.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The sharpest filter is the best filter." Sharpness is paid for in the time domain. In the default table the family with the narrowest transition (elliptic, 0.496 rad/s) also has the largest overshoot (24.0%) and the longest settling time (23.12 s). At \(N = 8\) its transition is only 0.022 rad/s wide, but it takes 57.73 s to settle and its group delay peak no longer fits on the plot.

"Chebyshev II gives up selectivity to get a flat passband." With "Passband edge at ω = 1 rad/s" scaling, Chebyshev I and Chebyshev II have exactly the same \(\omega_s = 2.339\). Type II does not lose selectivity. It moves the equiripple behavior from the passband to the stopband, and it rings less.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Butterworth filter - Wikipedia - the maximally flat magnitude response and its poles on a circle
  2. Chebyshev filter - Wikipedia - Type I and Type II responses, the ripple factor and the elliptical pole locus
  3. Elliptic filter - Wikipedia - equiripple passband and stopband, the elliptic rational function and the selectivity factor
  4. Bessel filter - Wikipedia - maximally flat group delay and the reverse Bessel polynomial
  5. Group delay and phase delay - Wikipedia - why constant group delay preserves pulse shape
  6. Jacobi elliptic functions - Wikipedia - the sn and cd functions behind the elliptic poles and zeros
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on Chebyshev filters and on step-response versus frequency-response trade-offs

docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim extends the 1-D Convolution Visualizer to images. The input \(x[m, n]\) is a 32 × 32 grayscale image built in code (0 = black, 255 = white): a bright square, a disc, a single bright pixel (an impulse), a one-pixel line and a horizontal ramp. Row \(m\) counts down and column \(n\) counts right. A kernel \(h[i, j]\), with \(i\) and \(j\) from \(-R\) to \(R\), produces

\[y[m, n] = \frac{1}{D}\sum_{i=-R}^{R}\sum_{j=-R}^{R} h[i, j]\,x[m - i, n - j].\]

The panels show the input with a 12 × 12 crop outlined, a zoom on the crop with the gold kernel window, the crop's output filling in as the window slides, and the full output. Below them, the rotated kernel, the pixels under the window and their products are laid out cell by cell, with the sum, the divisor \(D\) and \(y[m, n]\).

  • Kernel chooses identity, box blur 3×3 or 5×5, Gaussian, sharpen, Sobel x or y, Laplacian, emboss, or a custom 3 × 3 kernel typed into the grid (decimals or fractions such as 1/9). Editing a preset switches to Custom.
  • Play and Step move the window; so do clicks on any pixel and the arrow keys.
  • Edge padding repeats the border pixels instead of padding with zeros.
  • Normalise sets \(D\) to the sum of the weights (when that sum is not 0).
  • Flip kernel off computes the cross-correlation \(\sum h[i, j]\,x[m + i, n + j]\), as CNN layers do.
  • Add noise adds fixed Gaussian noise (\(\sigma = 12\)) and reports the noise level in and out.
  • Output display maps \(y\) to gray: clipped to 0–255, signed (0 = mid-gray) or \(|y|\); auto picks signed when the weights sum to 0.

This MicroSim is used in Chapter 15: Signal Processing Applications and AI Integration.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the output of a 3 × 3 kernel at one pixel by rotating the kernel, multiplying it with the neighbourhood and adding the products
  2. Predict the output of a kernel on a flat region from the sum of its weights, and explain why blur kernels are normalised
  3. Distinguish convolution from cross-correlation and identify the kernels for which the difference changes the result
  4. Compare how smoothing and derivative kernels respond to edges, thin lines, ramps and noise, using \(\sigma_{out} \approx \sigma_{in}\sqrt{\sum h^2}\)
  5. Evaluate the artifacts that zero padding and edge padding create at the image border

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a digital signal processing or image processing course (junior or senior year). Plan 25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• 1-D discrete convolution and the impulse response (Chapter 4)
  • A grayscale image as a 2-D array of numbers
  • Summation notation

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: One multiply-add by hand (6 min). Choose Box blur 3×3 and keep the default pixel (7, 13), just right of the square. The window holds 200 in its left column and 40 in the other six cells, so \(\Sigma = 3 \cdot 200 + 6 \cdot 40 = 840\), \(D = 9\) and \(y[7, 13] = 93.33\) (gray 93). Choose Gaussian 3×3: \(\Sigma = 4 \cdot 200 + 8 \cdot 40 + 4 \cdot 40 = 1280\) and \(y = 1280/16 = 80\). Go back to the box blur and uncheck Normalise: \(y[7, 13] = 840\), the flat background becomes \(9 \cdot 40 = 360\), almost everything turns white, and the status line reports \(y\) from 16 to 2160. The sum of the weights is the gain on flat regions.

Activity 2: Why convolution flips the kernel (7 min). Return to Sobel x with Flip kernel checked. The grid shows \(h\) with −1, −2, −1 on the left, but the arithmetic panel uses it rotated by 180°, so \(y[7, 13] = 4 \cdot 200 - 4 \cdot 40 = 640\). Uncheck Flip kernel: \(y = -640\). Check it again and click (7, 18), just right of the impulse at (7, 17), which is \(255 - 40 = 215\) above the background: \(y = 215 \cdot 2 = 430\). Click the eight other pixels around the impulse: the outputs are −215, 0, 215 / −430, 0, 430 / −215, 0, 215, which is \(215\,h\) exactly as typed in the grid. Without the flip the pattern is reversed. Convolving an impulse returns the kernel itself, which is why \(h\) is called the impulse response.

Activity 3: Edges, lines and ramps (6 min). Choose Sobel y and click (16, 10), (17, 10) and (18, 10), above, on and below the thin line: \(y\) = −640, 0 and 640. A line gives two responses of opposite sign. Choose Sobel x: \(y[17, 10] = 0\): along a horizontal line Sobel x responds only near the line's ends. Click the ramp at (26, 15), where the pixels to the left and right are 112 and 128: Sobel x gives \(4 \cdot 112 - 4 \cdot 128 = -64\), while Laplacian gives 0, because the second difference of a straight ramp is zero.

Activity 4: Borders and noise (6 min). Choose Box blur 3×3 and click the top-left pixel (0, 0). Five cells of the window lie outside the image (red dashed outlines) and read 0, so \(\Sigma = 160\) and \(y = 17.78\); the output gets a dark frame. Check Edge padding: those cells read 40 and \(y = 40\). With Sobel x and zero padding the largest output, 960, is not an edge at all but the right border of the ramp, \(4 \cdot 240\); edge padding lowers the maximum to 640. Finally uncheck Edge padding and check Add noise. The status line reports \(\sigma\) = 11.7 at the input and, at the output, 11.7 (identity), 3.8 (box 3×3), 4.2 (Gaussian), 2.3 (box 5×5), 38.7 (Sobel x) and 53.8 (Laplacian). For white noise the prediction \(\sigma_{in}\sqrt{\sum h^2}\) gives 3.9, 4.4, 2.3, 40.5 and 52.3: smoothing kernels suppress noise and derivative kernels amplify it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With the Gaussian 3×3 kernel, pixel (7, 12) has 200 in the left and middle columns of its window and 40 in the right column. What is \(y[7, 12]\)? Answer: \(\Sigma = 4 \cdot 200 + 8 \cdot 200 + 4 \cdot 40 = 2560\), so \(y = 2560/16 = 160\), as the sim shows.
  2. At the left edge of the square, pixel (7, 3) has 40 | 200 | 200 in every row of its window. What does Sobel x give with convolution, and with correlation? Answer: convolution uses the rotated kernel, \(4 \cdot 40 - 4 \cdot 200 = -640\); correlation gives \(+640\).
  3. Why is the Laplacian zero everywhere inside the ramp, while Sobel x is not? Answer: on \(x = 8n\) the second differences \(x[n-1] - 2x[n] + x[n+1]\) vanish in both directions, but the first difference does not: Sobel x gives \(4(x[n-1] - x[n+1]) = -64\).
  4. A video is a sequence of frames. How many multiplications per second does a 3 × 3 kernel need on 1920 × 1080 video at 30 frames per second, and how many if the kernel is separable? Answer: \(1920 \cdot 1080 \cdot 9 \cdot 30 = 559{,}872{,}000 \approx 5.6 \times 10^8\). A separable kernel such as the Gaussian, \([1\;2\;1]^T[1\;2\;1]\), needs 6 per pixel: \(3.7 \times 10^8\).
  5. CNN layers compute cross-correlation, not convolution. Does that matter? Answer: not for learned kernels, since learning \(h\) for correlation is the same as learning the rotated \(h\) for convolution. It matters when a fixed kernel such as Sobel x is copied between conventions: the output changes sign.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Convolution slides the kernel as it is written." True convolution rotates the kernel by 180° first. For the symmetric kernels (box, Gaussian, sharpen, Laplacian) the panel header reads "(= h)" and nothing changes, but for Sobel x the value at (7, 13) changes from 640 to −640 when Flip kernel is unchecked.

"A black output pixel means no response." Set Output display to clip to 0–255 with Sobel x: the left edge of the square (\(y = -640\)) and the flat background (\(y = 0\)) are both black. The signed display shows them as gray 43 and gray 128, and the right edge (\(y = 640\)) as gray 213.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Kernel (image processing) - Wikipedia - common 3 × 3 kernels, the convolution sum, edge handling and normalisation
  2. Sobel operator - Wikipedia - the Sobel kernels and the sign conventions that follow from flipping the kernel
  3. Gaussian blur - Wikipedia - Gaussian smoothing and why the kernel is separable
  4. Discrete Laplace operator - Wikipedia - the 5-point Laplacian kernel as a second difference
  5. Cross-correlation - Wikipedia - how correlation differs from convolution by the reflection of one signal
  6. Convolutional neural network - Wikipedia - convolutional layers, which apply learned kernels by cross-correlation
  7. Chapter 24: Linear Image Processing - Steven W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - free chapter on 2-D convolution, separability and image filters
