docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/impulse-and-frequency-response-analyzer/main.html" width="100%" height="627px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
An LTI system can be described in several equivalent ways. This MicroSim shows four of them at once for the same system. The two plots on the left are in the time domain and the two on the right are in the frequency domain:

  • Impulse response \(h(t)\) (top left) is the output for the input \(\delta(t)\).
  • Step response \(s(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} h(\tau)\,d\tau\) (bottom left) is the output for the input \(u(t)\). When you select a pulse or a square wave, this plot shows the output \(y(t) = x(t) * h(t)\) and draws the input in grey.
  • Magnitude \(|H(f)|\) in decibels (top right) and phase \(\angle H(f)\) in degrees (bottom right), where \(H(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}\,dt\). The frequency axis is logarithmic from 0.1 Hz to 100 Hz.

Use the System menu to choose a Butterworth low-pass filter, a Butterworth high-pass filter, a differentiator, an integrator or a second-order resonant system. The Cutoff slider sets the cutoff frequency \(f_c\) of a filter, the unity-gain frequency \(f_0\) of the differentiator and integrator, or the natural frequency \(f_n\) of the resonant system. The Filter order slider (\(N = 1\) to \(4\)) applies to the filters and the Damping ratio slider (\(\zeta = 0.05\) to \(2\)) applies to the resonant system. Controls the selected system does not use are greyed out. Hover over any plot to move the red cursor and read the values at that time or frequency.

The four views always agree because every curve is computed from the same closed-form expression for the selected system. This simulation supports the section on impulse, step and frequency response in Chapter 3: System Properties and Analysis.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
Every curve is drawn from a closed-form expression for the selected system, with \(\omega_c = 2\pi f_c\):

System Frequency response Impulse response Step response Low-pass, order 1 \(\dfrac{1}{1 + jf/f_c}\) \(\omega_c e^{-\omega_c t}u(t)\) \((1 - e^{-\omega_c t})u(t)\) High-pass, order 1 \(\dfrac{jf/f_c}{1 + jf/f_c}\) \(\delta(t) - \omega_c e^{-\omega_c t}u(t)\) \(e^{-\omega_c t}u(t)\) Differentiator \(jf/f_0\) \(\delta'(t)/(2\pi f_0)\) \(\delta(t)/(2\pi f_0)\) Integrator \(f_0/(jf)\) \(2\pi f_0\,u(t)\) \(2\pi f_0\,t\,u(t)\) Resonant \(\dfrac{1}{1 - (f/f_n)^2 + j2\zeta f/f_n}\) decaying sinusoid for \(\zeta < 1\) rises to 1, overshoots for \(\zeta < 1\)

The low-pass and high-pass filters are Butterworth filters of order \(N = 1\) to \(4\). Their magnitude responses are \(1/\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^{2N}}\) and \((f/f_c)^N/\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^{2N}}\), so the gain is always \(-3\) dB at \(f_c\) and the roll-off is \(20N\) dB per decade. Their impulse and step responses are computed from the filter poles by partial fractions.

Impulses cannot be plotted as ordinary curves, so they are drawn as arrows: a single arrow for \(\delta(t)\) and an up-down pair for the doublet \(\delta'(t)\).

The Input menu replaces the unit step with a 0.5 s rectangular pulse or a 1 Hz square wave of height \(\pm 1\). Both are sums of steps, so by linearity and time-invariance the output is the same sum of shifted step responses. For the pulse, \(y(t) = s(t) - s(t - 0.5)\). This equals the convolution \(y(t) = x(t) * h(t)\).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Choose a System and read its four plots.
  2. Hover over either time plot to move the time cursor, and over either frequency plot to move the frequency cursor. The red read-outs above the plots give the values at the cursor.
  3. Move Cutoff, Filter order and Damping ratio. The orange dotted line on the frequency plots marks the cutoff, natural or unity-gain frequency.
  4. Change the Input to see how the same system responds to a pulse or a square wave.
  5. Export h(t) as CSV downloads the regular part of the impulse response and the step response, sampled every 0.01 s from 0 to 2.5 s. Impulses and doublets are described in comment lines at the top of the file.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain why the impulse response completely characterizes an LTI system.
  2. Relate the step response to the impulse response through integration.
  3. Connect features of \(h(t)\) (decay rate, ringing) to features of \(H(f)\) (cutoff, resonant peak).
  4. Compare how low-pass, high-pass, differentiating, integrating and resonant systems change a signal in time and in frequency.
  5. Predict the response to a pulse or a square wave by superposing shifted step responses.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a signals and systems or introductory signal processing course. Plan 20-30 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The unit impulse and unit step functions
  • Convolution and the meaning of an impulse response
  • Complex numbers, magnitude and phase, and decibels

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Exploration (5 min). Select the low-pass filter with order \(N = 1\), \(f_c = 1\) Hz and the unit step input.

  • Put the time cursor near \(t = 0.16\) s, which is the time constant \(\tau = 1/(2\pi f_c) = 0.159\) s. The read-out shows \(s(t) \approx 0.63\).
  • Put the frequency cursor on 1 Hz (the orange line, where it starts). The read-out shows a gain of \(0.707 = -3.0\) dB and a phase of \(-45°\).

Activity 2: Bandwidth and speed (5 min). Keep \(N = 1\) and raise the cutoff from 1 Hz to 4 Hz.

  • The peak of \(h(t)\) is \(2\pi f_c\), so it grows from 6.28 to 25.1, and the impulse response becomes four times narrower.
  • The time constant falls from 0.159 s to 0.040 s, and the 10% to 90% rise time of \(s(t)\) falls from about 0.35 s to about 0.09 s.
  • State the rule: the rise time is about \(0.35/f_c\), so a wider bandwidth means a faster response.

Activity 3: Cost of a sharper cutoff (10 min). Set \(f_c = 1\) Hz and step the filter order from 1 to 4.

  • Hover on the magnitude plot at 10 Hz each time. The gain is \(-20\), \(-40\), \(-60\) and \(-80\) dB.
  • Read the phase at \(f_c\): it is \(-45°\), \(-90°\), \(-135°\) and \(-180°\).
  • Watch \(s(t)\). The step response overshoots by about 4% at \(N = 2\), 8% at \(N = 3\) and 11% at \(N = 4\), and the time to reach 50% grows from 0.11 s to 0.45 s. Describe what a sharper cutoff costs in the time domain.

Activity 4: Ringing and resonance (10 min). Select the resonant system with \(f_n = 1\) Hz and \(\zeta = 0.2\).

  • The magnitude plot has a peak of 8.1 dB near 0.96 Hz, and the step response overshoots by 53%.
  • \(h(t)\) crosses zero at 0.51 s and 1.53 s, so it rings with a period of about 1.02 s, close to \(1/f_n\).
  • Raise \(\zeta\) to 0.7 and then to 1.0. The peak disappears and the overshoot falls to about 5% and then to zero.

Activity 5: Inputs other than a step (5 min). Select the high-pass filter (\(N = 1\), \(f_c = 1\) Hz) with the square-wave input. Explain the output from the gain at low frequencies: the filter blocks the constant part of each half-cycle, so at every edge the output jumps by the same amount as the input (2 units at each edge after the first) and then decays toward 0 with a time constant of 0.16 s.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A first-order low-pass filter has \(f_c = 2\) Hz. What is its time constant, and what is \(s(t)\) at that time? (Answer: \(\tau = 1/(2\pi \cdot 2) = 0.080\) s, and \(s(\tau) = 1 - e^{-1} = 0.63\).)
  2. A fourth-order Butterworth low-pass filter has \(f_c = 1\) Hz. What is its gain at 10 Hz? (Answer: \(-80\) dB, because the roll-off is \(20N = 80\) dB per decade above \(f_c\).)
  3. A resonant system has \(f_n = 1\) Hz and \(\zeta = 0.2\). Estimate the height of the resonant peak and the step overshoot. (Answer: about 8.1 dB, which is a gain of about 2.5, and about 53% overshoot. Both come from the same lightly damped poles.)
  4. For the low-pass filter with \(N = 1\) and \(f_c = 1\) Hz, use \(s(t)\) to find the output of the 0.5 s pulse at \(t = 0.5\) s. (Answer: \(y(0.5) = s(0.5) - s(0) = 0.957\), which is the value read from the output plot.)
  5. Why is the impulse response of the differentiator drawn as a pair of arrows? (Answer: \(h(t)\) is the doublet \(\delta'(t)/(2\pi f_0)\), the derivative of an impulse. It is zero everywhere except at \(t = 0\) and cannot be drawn as an ordinary curve.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "The impulse response and the frequency response describe different things." They are the same system seen in two domains. Move the cutoff slider and watch both \(h(t)\) and \(|H(f)|\) change together.
  • "A sharper cutoff is free." Raise the filter order and the step response overshoots and rings, and it reaches 50% later.
  • "A wide bandwidth makes a system respond slowly." The opposite is true. Raise the cutoff and \(h(t)\) narrows and \(s(t)\) rises faster.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Impulse response - Wikipedia - definition of the impulse response and its role in characterizing LTI systems
  2. Step response - Wikipedia - the step response as the integral of the impulse response, with rise time and overshoot
  3. Frequency response - Wikipedia - magnitude and phase response and how they relate to the impulse response
  4. Butterworth filter - Wikipedia - the maximally flat filter used for the low-pass and high-pass systems
  5. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on linear systems and convolution
  6. Oppenheim, A. V., Willsky, A. S., & Nawab, S. H. (1997). Signals and Systems (2nd ed.). Prentice Hall. Chapters 2, 4 and 6 cover the impulse response, the Fourier transform, and time and frequency characterization of systems.

docs.text:

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim designs a digital filter at a sample rate of \(f_s = 8000\) Hz and shows it several ways at once. The magnitude plot (maroon) shows \(|H(f)|\) with the ideal brick-wall response as a dashed gray line and gold markers at the three test-tone frequencies. The lower plot shows the unwrapped phase, the group delay, the impulse response \(h[n]\) or the step response \(s[n]\). The pole-zero plot marks poles (×) and zeros (o) in the z-plane, with a number beside repeated roots. The read-out below it reports stability, the largest pole radius, the order, the −3 dB frequencies, the passband (gain within 3 dB of the peak) and the stopband (at least 40 dB below the peak). The bottom row filters the test signal \(x[n] = \sin(2\pi\,200\,n/f_s) + \sin(2\pi\,1000\,n/f_s) + \sin(2\pi\,3000\,n/f_s)\) sample by sample with the same coefficients. It shows 10 ms of input (gray) and output (blue) after a 2 s warm-up, and bars with the amplitude of each tone before and after the filter.

Control What it does Filter type Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop, notch, comb or all-pass Design IIR as a cascade of biquads, the same IIR multiplied out into one direct-form polynomial, or FIR (no feedback) Show Selects the lower plot: phase, group delay, impulse response or step response dB scale Magnitude in dB (−80 to +10 dB) or as a linear gain Cutoff fc / Centre f0 20–3500 Hz on a logarithmic slider Order N IIR: Butterworth order 1–8 (band-pass and band-stop have order 2N). FIR: order M = 8N Q Selectivity of the band-pass, band-stop, notch and all-pass sections Comb delay D, gain g Delay 2–64 samples and gain 0–0.95 of the comb filter Coeff. bits Rounds every coefficient to 4–24 bits; the right end (off) keeps 64-bit floating point

Sliders that do not apply to the chosen filter are grayed out. This MicroSim supports Chapter 9: Filter Design Fundamentals, in particular the sections on filter types, FIR and IIR structures, and filter stability.

docs.title: Design Equations
docs.text:
IIR filters start from an analog Butterworth prototype and use the bilinear transform with prewarping, \(\Omega = \tan(\pi f / f_s)\), so the −3 dB frequency lands exactly on the slider value. Each pair of complex poles becomes one second-order section (biquad). For order 2 this is exactly the RBJ cookbook low-pass:

\[b = \left[\tfrac{1-\cos\omega_0}{2},\ 1-\cos\omega_0,\ \tfrac{1-\cos\omega_0}{2}\right],\quad a = \left[1+\alpha,\ -2\cos\omega_0,\ 1-\alpha\right],\quad \omega_0 = \frac{2\pi f_c}{f_s},\ \alpha = \frac{\sin\omega_0}{2Q}\]

Higher even orders cascade sections with \(Q_k = 1/\left(2\cos\frac{(2k-1)\pi}{2N}\right)\); odd orders add a first-order section. Band-pass and band-stop filters use the low-pass-to-band-pass transformation, so order \(N\) gives \(N\) biquads; with \(N = 1\) they are the RBJ constant-0-dB-peak band-pass and notch sections. The notch is always one biquad. The all-pass cascades RBJ all-pass biquads (plus a first-order all-pass when \(N\) is odd), so its phase at \(f_0\) is \(-90N\) degrees. Every section is filtered with \(y[n] = \sum_k b_k x[n-k] - \sum_{k\ge 1} a_k y[n-k]\).

FIR filters are Hamming-windowed sinc filters of order \(M = 8N\) (\(M + 1\) taps). For a windowed sinc the cutoff is the half-amplitude (−6 dB) point, so the −3 dB frequency is lower than \(f_c\). The FIR band-pass and band-stop use edges \(f_1, f_2\) with \(\sqrt{f_1 f_2} = f_0\) and \(f_2 - f_1 = f_0/Q\). The FIR notch is the 3-tap filter \([1,\ -2\cos\omega_0,\ 1]\) scaled to a peak gain of 1.

Comb filters are \(y[n] = x[n] + g\,x[n-D]\) (FIR), with \(|H| = \sqrt{1 + g^2 + 2g\cos(\omega D)}\), and \(y[n] = (1-g)\,x[n] + g\,y[n-D]\) (IIR, peaks scaled to 0 dB). Both have peaks every \(f_s/D\) Hz and dips at odd multiples of \(f_s/(2D)\).

Coefficient rounding. Each coefficient vector (every numerator \(b\), and the feedback coefficients \(a_1 \ldots a_N\) of every section; \(a_0 = 1\) stays exact) is given a power-of-two scale \(2^e\) at least as large as its largest coefficient, and each coefficient is rounded to a multiple of \(2^e / 2^{B-1}\) (\(B\) bits including the sign). A biquad's \(a_1\) is always below 2 in magnitude, so its step is \(2^{-(B-2)}\). The coefficients of a high-order direct-form polynomial are much larger, so the same \(B\) gives a much coarser step.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Classify low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop, notch, comb and all-pass filters by which of the 200, 1000 and 3000 Hz test tones each one passes or removes
  2. Explain why raising the order of a Butterworth filter steepens the transition band without moving the −3 dB frequency
  3. Compare FIR and IIR designs using their pole locations, group delay and impulse responses
  4. Calculate the peak and dip frequencies of a comb filter from \(f_s/D\) and choose \(D\) to remove given tones
  5. Analyze how rounding the coefficients moves poles, and why a biquad cascade survives rounding that makes the same filter unstable in direct form

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate engineering and computer science students in a first digital signal processing course, after the z-transform has been introduced. Plan about 45 minutes for the four activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Difference equations and the z-transform
  • Poles, zeros and the unit circle
  • Frequency response, magnitude in decibels and phase
  • Sinusoids and sampling at a rate \(f_s\)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Filter families and the test signal (10 min). Start from the default settings (Low-pass, IIR biquad cascade, \(f_c\) = 500 Hz, N = 4). The tone bars read 1.00, 0.05 and 0.00: the 200 Hz tone passes, the other two are removed, and the blue output is a clean 200 Hz sinusoid. Set each row of the table and record the three bar values. Then compare each magnitude curve with its dashed ideal response.

Settings 200 Hz 1000 Hz 3000 Hz Read-out Low-pass, \(f_c\) = 500 Hz, N = 4 1.00 0.05 0.00 −3 dB at 500 Hz High-pass, \(f_c\) = 500 Hz, N = 4 0.02 1.00 1.00 Stopband 0–160 Hz Band-pass, \(f_0\) = 1000 Hz, Q = 2, N = 2 0.01 1.00 0.01 −3 dB at 797 and 1242 Hz Band-stop, \(f_0\) = 1000 Hz, Q = 1, N = 4 1.00 0.00 1.00 Stopband 866–1150 Hz Notch, \(f_0\) = 1000 Hz, Q = 10 1.00 0.00 1.00 −3 dB at 956 and 1046 Hz

The band-stop removes a wide band (866–1150 Hz is at least 40 dB down), while the notch is only 90 Hz wide at its −3 dB points. Both remove the 1000 Hz tone and keep the other two.

Activity 2: Order, phase, and FIR versus IIR (12 min).

  1. Low-pass, \(f_c\) = 500 Hz. Set N = 1, then 4, then 8. The −3 dB read-out stays at 500 Hz, but the 1000 Hz bar falls from 0.43 to 0.05 to 0.00, and the stopband starts at 3872, 1430 and 866 Hz. With Show: phase, the phase at 500 Hz is −45°, −180° and −360°: \(-45N\) degrees.
  2. Set N = 4 and Show: group delay. The IIR group delay peaks at about 10 samples (1.25 ms) near 450 Hz, so tones near the cutoff are delayed more than others.
  3. Change Design to FIR (order M = 32, 33 taps). The group delay becomes a flat line at 16 samples (2 ms), which is \(M/2\): linear phase. The pole-zero plot shows all 32 poles at \(z = 0\), and the read-out says STABLE. The −3 dB read-out is 398 Hz, because 500 Hz is the windowed sinc's −6 dB point. With Show: impulse response, the 33 taps are symmetric about n = 16.
  4. Notch, \(f_0\) = 1000 Hz. The IIR notch (Q = 10) gives bars 1.00, 0.00, 1.00. The FIR notch gives 0.16, 0.00, 0.83: its two zeros on the unit circle remove 1000 Hz but also cut most of the spectrum. The IIR notch places poles at radius 0.9652 right beside its zeros, which confines the notch to 956–1046 Hz.

Activity 3: Comb and all-pass filters (8 min).

  1. Comb, FIR, D = 4, g = 0.95. The read-out gives peaks every \(f_s/D\) = 2000 Hz (+5.8 dB) and dips at odd multiples of 1000 Hz (−26.0 dB). The bars read 1.85, 0.05, 0.05: the dips remove both the 1000 Hz and the 3000 Hz tones.
  2. Predict the bars for D = 8, then test. Now the peaks are every 1000 Hz, so the 1000 and 3000 Hz tones sit on peaks (1.95) and the 200 Hz tone reads 1.58.
  3. Switch to the IIR (feedback) comb with D = 8 and g = 0.90. It has narrow passbands at multiples of 1000 Hz, so the bars read 0.09, 1.00, 1.00, and the impulse response repeats every 8 samples (0.10, then 0.09, ...). Its 8 poles sit at radius \(0.9^{1/8} = 0.9869\).
  4. All-pass, \(f_0\) = 1000 Hz, Q = 2. For N = 1, 2 and 4 every bar reads 1.00, yet the read-out gives a phase at 1000 Hz of −90°, −180° and −360°. The output waveform changes shape because the three tones are delayed by different amounts.

Activity 4: Coefficient rounding and stability (15 min).

  1. Low-pass, \(f_c\) = 500 Hz, N = 8, IIR biquad cascade. Set Coeff. bits to 16. The filter stays STABLE with a largest pole radius of 0.9279, the same to four decimals as without rounding (step 1/16384).
  2. Change Design to IIR direct form, which is the same filter multiplied out into one 8th-order polynomial. At 16 bits the read-out says UNSTABLE with a pole radius of 1.0497. A cross sits outside the unit circle, the output bars turn red, and the output grows. The step is now 1/1024, because the direct-form coefficients are much larger. At 20 bits the direct form is stable again (0.9296), but the −3 dB point has moved to 493 Hz.
  3. Still in direct form, set Coeff. bits to off (64-bit floating point) and \(f_c\) = 20 Hz. The direct form is unstable even without deliberate rounding (radius 1.0032), while the biquad cascade at the same settings is stable (0.9969, a pole close to the unit circle).
  4. Biquad cascade, \(f_c\) = 100 Hz, N = 2, Coeff. bits = 8. Rounding puts a pole exactly on the unit circle at \(z = 1\). With Show: step response, the output keeps rising (6.37 at n = 127) instead of settling at 1. At 9 bits the filter is stable again (radius 0.9479).
  5. Return to FIR (low-pass, \(f_c\) = 500 Hz, N = 4) and set 6 bits. The filter stays STABLE, because all of its poles are at \(z = 0\). Only the stopband gets worse: it now ends at 3887 Hz instead of 4000 Hz.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With \(f_s\) = 8000 Hz, which delay D makes the FIR comb \(y[n] = x[n] + g\,x[n-D]\) remove the 1000 and 3000 Hz tones but keep 200 Hz? (Answer: D = 4. The dips are at odd multiples of \(f_s/(2D)\) = 1000 Hz, which are 1000 and 3000 Hz. With g = 0.95 the bars read 1.85, 0.05 and 0.05.)
  2. Use the prewarped frequencies \(\Omega = \tan(\pi f/f_s)\) to compute \(|H|\) at 1000 Hz for the 4th-order Butterworth low-pass with \(f_c\) = 500 Hz. (Answer: \(\Omega_c = \tan(\pi/16) = 0.1989\) and \(\Omega = \tan(\pi/8) = 0.4142\), so the ratio is 2.082 and \(|H| = 1/\sqrt{1 + 2.082^{8}} = 0.053\), which matches the 0.05 bar.)
  3. Why is the FIR low-pass group delay a flat 16 samples while the IIR group delay varies with frequency? (Answer: the 33 FIR taps are symmetric about n = 16, so \(H(e^{j\omega}) = e^{-j16\omega}A(\omega)\) with real \(A\): the phase is linear and every frequency is delayed by \(M/2\) = 16 samples (2 ms). The IIR poles make the phase nonlinear, and the delay is largest near the cutoff.)
  4. A 4th-order all-pass filter at \(f_0\) = 1000 Hz leaves all three bars at 1.00. What does it change, and what is its phase at 1000 Hz? (Answer: it changes only the phase, so each tone is delayed by a different amount and the waveform changes shape. The phase at 1000 Hz is −360°, that is −90° per order.)
  5. The same 8th-order low-pass (\(f_c\) = 500 Hz) is stable as a biquad cascade but unstable in direct form at 16 bits. Explain why. (Answer: the roots of a high-order polynomial with clustered roots are very sensitive to its coefficients. Rounding the large direct-form coefficients (step 1/1024) moves a pole to radius 1.0497. Each biquad places only one pole pair from two small coefficients rounded with step 1/16384, so its poles barely move.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A higher-order filter has a lower cutoff." For a Butterworth design the −3 dB frequency does not depend on the order. In Activity 2 it stays at 500 Hz for N = 1, 4 and 8. Only the transition band narrows: the stopband edge moves from 3872 Hz to 866 Hz.

"Coefficients rounded to 16 bits are practically exact, so the filter cannot change much." Whether rounding matters depends on the structure. At 16 bits the biquad cascade keeps its pole radius at 0.9279, while the direct form of the same filter becomes unstable (radius 1.0497). The pole-zero plot shows the cross leaving the unit circle.

"The cutoff of an FIR filter is its −3 dB frequency." For a windowed-sinc design the cutoff is the half-amplitude (−6 dB) point. With \(f_c\) = 500 Hz and M = 32 the −3 dB read-out is 398 Hz.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Digital biquad filter - Wikipedia - the second-order section used for every IIR design in this MicroSim, in direct forms I and II
  2. Audio EQ Cookbook - W3C (R. Bristow-Johnson) - the RBJ low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch and all-pass biquad formulas
  3. Butterworth filter - Wikipedia - maximally flat magnitude response, pole locations and the Q values of the cascaded sections
  4. Bilinear transform - Wikipedia - mapping analog prototypes to digital filters, with frequency prewarping
  5. Comb filter - Wikipedia - feedforward and feedback comb filters and their peak and dip frequencies
  6. All-pass filter - Wikipedia - unit magnitude response with frequency-dependent phase
  7. Finite impulse response - Wikipedia - FIR filters, the window design method and linear phase
  8. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on windowed-sinc and recursive filters

docs.text:

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim works in the z-plane, the domain of discrete-time systems. Poles (red crosses) and zeros (blue circles) are placed inside and around the green unit circle. Four plots show what they do: the magnitude response in dB, the phase response, the impulse response \(h[n]\) and the step response \(s[n]\). A banner states whether the causal system is stable, marginally stable or unstable.

Drag a pole or zero with the mouse, or select it and set its Radius and Angle with the sliders. Dragging snaps to the unit circle and to the real axis. System loads one of eight presets, and Add pole, Add zero and Remove edit the set (up to six items). Move the mouse over the magnitude or phase plot to place the orange point \(e^{j\omega}\) on the unit circle: the vectors from every pole and zero to that point are drawn, and the readout gives \(|H|\) and \(\angle H\) at that frequency.

The tool illustrates two ideas: the magnitude response is a ratio of distances from the zeros and poles to a point on the unit circle, and a causal system is stable when every pole lies strictly inside the unit circle. The gain is fixed at \(G = 1\) throughout.

This simulation is used in Chapter 8: Advanced Transforms.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
A rational transfer function is fixed, apart from the gain \(G\), by its zeros \(z_i\) and poles \(p_i\):

\[H(z) = G\,\frac{(z-z_1)(z-z_2)\cdots(z-z_M)}{(z-p_1)(z-p_2)\cdots(z-p_N)}\]

The frequency response is \(H(z)\) on the unit circle, \(z = e^{j\omega}\), with \(\omega\) in radians per sample from 0 to \(\pi\):

\[\lvert H(e^{j\omega})\rvert = \frac{\text{product of the distances from the zeros to } e^{j\omega}}{\text{product of the distances from the poles to } e^{j\omega}}\]

The phase is the sum of the angles of the zero vectors minus the sum of the angles of the pole vectors. A pole close to the unit circle gives a short vector in the denominator and therefore a resonance peak at that angle. A zero on the unit circle gives a vector of length zero and therefore a notch.

docs.title: Stability
docs.text:
For a causal discrete-time system, bounded-input bounded-output stability requires every pole to lie strictly inside the unit circle:

Pole location Banner Impulse response All poles inside the unit circle, \(\lvert p\rvert < 1\) Stable (green) Decays A simple pole on the unit circle, \(\lvert p\rvert = 1\) Marginally stable (amber) Neither decays nor grows Any pole outside the unit circle, \(\lvert p\rvert > 1\), or a repeated pole on it Unstable (red) Grows

Zeros do not affect stability. (For continuous-time systems, analyzed in the s-plane with the Laplace transform, the corresponding rule is that all poles lie in the left half-plane.) When the system is not stable its frequency response does not exist as a steady-state gain; the curves are then drawn dashed and grey to show only what the formula gives.

docs.title: Real Systems and the Origin
docs.text:
A system with real coefficients has poles and zeros that are either real or in complex-conjugate pairs. The tool enforces this: a pole or zero placed off the real axis always appears with its mirror image, and both move together.

The impulse and step responses come from the causal difference equation that has these poles and zeros. When the numbers of poles and zeros differ, a causal system has extra zeros or poles at \(z = 0\) to make them equal. They are drawn in grey with their count. They add delay and change the phase, but not the magnitude, since every point of the unit circle is at distance 1 from the origin.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this activity, students will be able to:

  1. Determine from a pole-zero plot whether a causal discrete-time system is stable.
  2. Explain the magnitude response as a ratio of distances from zeros and poles to a point on the unit circle.
  3. Relate the radius and angle of a pole pair to the decay rate and oscillation frequency of the impulse response.
  4. Design a simple resonator or notch by placing poles and zeros.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in signals and systems or digital signal processing. Plan 25-30 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex numbers in polar form
  • The z-transform and transfer functions
  • Impulse response and frequency response

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Resonance from geometry (7 min). Load Resonator (pole pair), which has \(r = 0.9\) and an angle of 45°. Hover over the magnitude plot until the readout says \(\omega = 0.25\pi\) and read \(|H|\): it is about 7.4 (17.4 dB). The nearer pole is \(1 - r = 0.1\) from \(e^{j\pi/4}\) and the other is about 1.35 away, and \(1/(0.1 \times 1.35) \approx 7.4\). Then set the radius to 0.5 and to 0.99. The peak of the magnitude plot rises from about 5.5 dB (a gain of 1.9) to 17.4 dB (7.4) to 37 dB (71). The closer the pole is to the circle, the sharper and taller the peak.

Activity 2: Oscillation, decay and stability (8 min). With the resonator at \(r = 0.9\), count the samples in one cycle of \(h[n]\): there are 8, which is \(2\pi/\omega_0\) for an angle of 45°. Set the angle to 90° (4 samples per cycle) and to 30° (12 samples). Return to 45° and raise the radius to 0.99: after 49 samples the envelope \(0.99^n\) is still about 0.6. Set the radius to 1.00: the banner turns amber and \(h[n]\) oscillates between \(\pm 1.41\) for ever. Set it to 1.05: the banner turns red, \(|h[49]|\) is about 15, and the magnitude curve turns dashed and grey.

Activity 3: Notch and FIR (8 min). Load Notch filter (a zero on the circle and a pole at \(r = 0.9\), both at 60°). Place the cursor at \(\omega = 0.33\pi\) (60° is \(\pi/3\)): \(|H|\) is 0 there and close to 1 elsewhere. Click the pole and raise its radius to 0.99: the \(-3\) dB width of the notch falls from about 0.21 to 0.02 rad/sample, ten times narrower. Then load Moving average of 4 (FIR). Its zeros are at \(z = \pm j\) and \(z = -1\), so \(|H| = 0\) at \(\omega = \pi/2\) and \(\omega = \pi\); \(h[n]\) is four ones and the step response settles at 4 (the DC gain with \(G = 1\)). Every pole is at \(z = 0\), so the banner reports an FIR system.

Activity 4: Zeros outside the circle, and a design task (7 min). Load All-pass (zeros at 1/r). The banner says stable although the zeros are at radius 1.25, and \(|H|\) is 1.56 (3.9 dB) at every frequency, because with \(G = 1\) the level is \(1/r^2\). Then design a filter that removes \(\omega = \pi/2\) and passes low frequencies with little change: put a zero pair on the circle at 90° and a pole pair at the same angle with \(r = 0.9\) (the readout at \(\omega = 0\) is about 1.1). Finally make an unstable system and repair it by moving a single pole.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A causal system has poles at \(0.6 \pm j0.7\). Is it stable? Yes. \(|p| = \sqrt{0.36 + 0.49} = 0.92 < 1\). Set the radius to 0.92 and the angle to 49° to confirm.
  2. A pole pair has radius 0.95 and angle 60°. What is the period of \(h[n]\), and where is the magnitude peak? The period is \(360/60 = 6\) samples and the peak is near \(\omega = \pi/3\), with \(|H| \approx 11.8\) (21.5 dB).
  3. Why can an FIR system never be unstable? All its poles are at \(z = 0\), inside the unit circle, and \(h[n]\) has finite length.
  4. The all-pass preset has zeros outside the unit circle. Why is it still stable? Stability depends only on the poles, which are at radius 0.8. Zeros shape the response but do not decide stability.
  5. Why does a zero on the unit circle produce a notch? The vector from the zero to \(e^{j\omega}\) has length 0 at that angle, so the product of distances, and with it \(|H|\), is 0.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A zero outside the unit circle makes the system unstable." Load the all-pass preset: the zeros sit at radius 1.25 and the banner stays green. Only poles decide stability.

"Stable means the poles are in the left half-plane." That rule belongs to the s-plane. In the z-plane the boundary is the unit circle. Load the high-pass preset, whose pole is at \(z = -0.8\) on the left side of the plane: it is stable. Drag the pole outward across the circle and watch the banner change.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Pole-zero plot - Wikipedia - poles and zeros in the s-plane and z-plane and what they say about a system
  2. Z-transform - Wikipedia - definition of the transform, the region of convergence and the transfer function \(H(z)\)
  3. BIBO stability - Wikipedia - the stability condition behind the green, amber and red banner
  4. All-pass filter - Wikipedia - why zeros at the reciprocal radius give a flat magnitude response
  5. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook; Chapter 33 covers the z-transform and pole-zero analysis
  6. Oppenheim, A. V., & Schafer, R. W. (2010). Discrete-Time Signal Processing (3rd ed.). Pearson. Chapters 3 and 5 cover the z-transform and the geometric evaluation of the frequency response.
  7. Proakis, J. G., & Manolakis, D. G. (2007). Digital Signal Processing (4th ed.). Pearson. Chapter 3 covers the z-transform and pole-zero analysis.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim computes two spectrograms of the same signal, panel A above panel B, each with its own short-time Fourier transform (STFT) settings:

\[X[m,k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n + mH]\,w[n]\,e^{-j2\pi kn/(PN)}, \qquad H = N(1 - \text{overlap})\]

Each panel has its own window length \(N\) (64 to 2048 samples), overlap (0 to 93.75%, so the hop \(H\) runs from \(N\) down to \(N/16\)), window (Hann, Hamming, Blackman or rectangular), zero-padding factor \(P\) (pad ×1 to ×8), dB floor (−120 to −20 dB) and color map (viridis, inferno, gray or jet). The line above each spectrogram reports the time span \(N/f_s\), the frequency resolution \(f_s/N\) (and the finer FFT bin spacing \(f_s/(PN)\) when zero padding is on), the frames per second \(f_s/H\) and the number of frames.

The Signal list offers a chirp, two close tones, a strong tone with a weak neighbor, tone bursts, a vibrato whistle (all 2 s long at \(f_s = 8000\) Hz) and the microphone. Start mic shows the last 2 s of live sound, filtered and resampled to about 8 kHz. The microphone is analyzed in your browser only and is never played back.

Guided challenges load a contrasting pair of settings and ask for a prediction; Reveal shows the answer. Pointing at a spectrogram moves a linked cursor through both panels. The line below them gives the level at that time and frequency in A and in B. The slice plot compares the two frame spectra under the cursor over a 1000 Hz span, with dots on the bins spaced \(f_s/N\) apart. Zoom magnifies the frequency axis up to ×8; click a spectrogram to center the zoom there. Levels are in dB relative to a sinusoid of amplitude 1.

This simulation is used in Chapter 14: Time-Frequency Analysis and Advanced Topics. The related Time-Frequency Analysis Explorer and Interactive STFT Spectrogram Analyzer focus on window length alone.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the time span \(N/f_s\), frequency resolution \(f_s/N\), hop size, frames per second and number of frames of an STFT from its window length, overlap and sampling rate.
  2. Analyze why neither a very short nor a very long window draws a chirp as a thin line, using the sweep during one window.
  3. Distinguish true frequency resolution (\(f_s/N\)) from the FFT bin spacing produced by zero padding (\(f_s/(PN)\)).
  4. Explain how overlap and window shape affect what a spectrogram shows (missed bursts, spectral leakage) without changing \(N/f_s\) or \(f_s/N\).
  5. Evaluate a set of spectrogram parameters (window, length, overlap, dB floor, color map) for a given signal and justify the choice.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in a digital signal processing course (junior or senior level). Plan 30-40 minutes for the four activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The DFT and FFT, and bin spacing \(f_s/N\)
  • Window functions and spectral leakage
  • The short-time Fourier transform and the spectrogram (Chapter 8)
  • Decibels

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Window length on a chirp (8 min). Choose challenge 1 (A: \(N = 256\), B: \(N = 2048\)), predict, then press Reveal. At \(t = 1\) s the slice shows A's peak about 60 Hz wide (6 dB down) and B's about 230 Hz wide: the chirp rises 1800 Hz/s, so it sweeps \(1800 \times 0.256 = 461\) Hz during one of B's windows. Step B's \(N\) down and read the peak of B's slice: −20.7 dB at 2048, −14.7 dB at 1024 and −8.8 dB at 512, against −6.2 dB for A. Then set A to \(N = 64\) with pad ×8: its peak widens to about 220 Hz. The best window for this chirp lies between these extremes.

Activity 2: Resolution versus zero padding (8 min). Choose challenge 2 (two tones 60 Hz apart). At \(t = 1\) s, B (\(N = 512\)) has two peaks, at 1000 Hz and 1062.5 Hz, with a dip to −35.2 dB between them, while A (\(N = 128\)) has one. Set A to \(N = 256\): still one peak, at 1031 Hz (the tones are only 1.9 bins apart). Set A to \(N = 512\): two peaks. Now choose challenge 3. A's caption reads "fs/N = 62.5 Hz (FFT bins 7.813 Hz)": its slice is smooth but remains a single peak about 130 Hz wide, while B's real 1024-sample window separates the tones with a dip of about 56 dB.

Activity 3: Overlap (7 min). Choose challenge 4 (bursts, \(N = 256\) in both panels). Both captions show \(N/f_s = 32\) ms and \(f_s/N = 31.25\) Hz, but A has 31.3 frames/s (62 frames) and B 125 frames/s (247 frames). Point at the brightest cell of each burst: in A the bursts peak between −10.1 and −36.0 dB (the cursor starts on the burst at 0.25 s, which falls on a frame boundary), in B between −10.1 and −11.3 dB. Set A's overlap to 50%: the range shrinks to −10.1 to −15.3 dB.

Activity 4: Window shape and dB floor (8 min). Choose challenge 5 (cursor at 1450 Hz, the weak tone). Switch A's window and read the A level: rectangular −36.5 dB, Hamming −49.5 dB, Blackman −56.9 dB, and Hann (panel B) −57.4 dB. Hamming's leakage at 1450 Hz (−54 dB, measured without the weak tone) is about as strong as the weak tone, so its line barely stands out; Hann and Blackman keep their leakage below −80 dB there and show it clearly. Then choose challenge 6: both panels read −57.4 dB at the cursor, but A's −40 dB floor paints the weak tone the floor color. Finish with challenge 9 and your own voice.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A 2 s signal at \(f_s = 8000\) Hz is analyzed with \(N = 512\) and 75% overlap. Give \(N/f_s\), \(f_s/N\), the hop, the frames per second and the number of frames. Answer: 64 ms, 15.625 Hz, \(H = 128\) samples, 62.5 frames/s, and \(\lfloor (16000 - 512)/128 \rfloor + 1 = 122\) frames (as panel B shows in challenge 2).
  2. Panel A uses \(N = 128\) with pad ×8. What are its FFT bin spacing and its frequency resolution at \(f_s = 8000\) Hz, and can it separate two tones 60 Hz apart? Answer: bins every \(8000/1024 = 7.8125\) Hz, but the resolution is still \(8000/128 = 62.5\) Hz, so no: zero padding interpolates the spectrum of the same 16 ms window.
  3. A chirp rises at 1800 Hz/s. How far does its frequency move during a 256 ms window, and what does this do to the spectrogram? Answer: \(1800 \times 0.256 = 461\) Hz; the energy of one frame spreads over that range, so the line widens (about 230 Hz at 6 dB down) and its peak drops (−20.7 dB versus −6.2 dB with \(N = 256\)).
  4. With a Hann window and 0% overlap, why can a short burst almost disappear, and what is the largest distance between a burst and the nearest frame center at 75% overlap with \(N = 256\)? Answer: the Hann window is close to zero at its ends, so a burst between two frames is multiplied by small window values in both; at 75% overlap the hop is 64 samples (8 ms), so every burst lies within 4 ms of a frame center.
  5. You must show a tone 50 dB below a strong tone 400 Hz away, with \(N = 256\). Rectangular or Hann, and why? Answer: Hann; the rectangular window's sidelobes from the strong tone are still about −37 dB at the weak tone's frequency, above the weak tone's −57 dB, while Hann's leakage there is below −80 dB.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Zero padding improves frequency resolution." Challenge 3 gives both panels a 1024-point FFT. A's zero-padded 128-sample window still shows one smooth peak about 130 Hz wide for two tones 60 Hz apart. In some frames a notch splits it into two bumps near 970 and 1090 Hz, 125 Hz apart, at the wrong frequencies. Only B's longer window separates the tones.

"More overlap gives a sharper spectrogram." In challenge 4 the captions show the same \(N/f_s\) and \(f_s/N\) in both panels whatever the overlap. Overlap only samples time more densely, which stops short bursts from slipping between frames.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Short-time Fourier transform - Wikipedia - definition of the STFT, hop size and the time-frequency resolution trade-off
  2. Spectrogram - Wikipedia - how spectrograms are computed and displayed, including wideband and narrowband speech spectrograms
  3. Window function - Wikipedia - Hann, Hamming, Blackman and rectangular windows, main-lobe width and sidelobe levels
  4. Spectral leakage - Wikipedia - why a rectangular window spreads a strong tone across the spectrum
  5. Chirp - Wikipedia - linear frequency sweeps like the test chirp used here
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT, windows and spectral analysis
  7. MediaDevices: getUserMedia() method - MDN - how a web page asks for microphone access and why it needs a secure context

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) cuts a signal into frames, multiplies each frame by a window \(w[n]\) and takes the DFT of every frame:

\[X[m,k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n+mH]\,w[n]\,e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\]

Here \(m\) is the frame index, \(k\) the frequency bin, \(N\) the window length and \(H\) the hop size. This MicroSim computes the STFT of one test signal twice, with window length A (teal) and window length B (purple), and stacks the two spectrograms on one time axis so they can be compared directly. Four checkboxes build the signal from two tones, two clicks, a chirp and noise. Two sliders set the tone spacing and the click spacing, and two more set the window lengths. Menus choose the window type and the hop size. Click a spectrogram to place a time and frequency cursor; the spectrum of the frame at the cursor is drawn beside each spectrogram. The display shows why a short window locates events in time, why a long window separates components in frequency, and why no window does both.

This simulation is used in Chapter 8: Advanced Transforms.

docs.title: The test signal
docs.text:
The sampling rate is \(f_s = 8000\) Hz. The signal lasts 1 s and the display shows 250 to 750 ms and 0 to 2000 Hz.

Component Description What it tests Two tones Steady sinusoids of amplitude 1 at 500 Hz and at 500 Hz plus the tone spacing Frequency resolution Two clicks Single-sample impulses at 500 ms and at 500 ms plus the click spacing Time resolution Chirp A tone that rises steadily at 800 Hz per second, from 1300 Hz at the left edge to 1700 Hz at the right edge Both at once Noise White Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.2 Robustness of what you see

docs.title: Reading the display
docs.text:
• The waveform at the top shows a teal bar and a purple bar: the samples that window A and window B use at the time cursor.
  • Each spectrogram caption gives the window's time span \(\Delta t = N/f_s\) and bin spacing \(\Delta f = f_s/N\), followed by the two spacings in the window's own units: the tone spacing in bins and the click spacing in window lengths.
  • Beside each spectrogram is the spectrum of the frame at the cursor, drawn sideways on the same frequency axis.
  • Colour runs from \(-60\) dB (dark) to 0 dB (bright), where 0 dB is a steady, bin-centred sinusoid of amplitude 1. Levels above 0 dB, such as two tones that merge and add, are drawn in the brightest colour.
  • The red line is the time cursor and the dashed line is the frequency cursor. The box at the upper right reports the cursor position and the distance from the cursor to the mouse pointer.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
1. Click in either spectrogram to place the cursor at a time and frequency. Click or drag in the waveform to move the time cursor only.
  2. Point at another feature without clicking. The box at the upper right reports the distance from the cursor to the pointer in milliseconds and hertz.
  3. Move the Window A and Window B sliders (32 to 2048 samples) and watch the two pictures and their captions.
  4. Change the Tone spacing (10 to 400 Hz) and the Click spacing (2 to 100 ms) to make the test easier or harder. Each slider is greyed out while its component is switched off.
  5. Tick Chirp or Noise to add components, and try the other Window types and Hop sizes.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
Two tones show as two separate lines only if they are about two or more bins apart. Two clicks show as two separate vertical lines only if they are about one window length or more apart. Since \(\Delta t \times \Delta f = 1\), making one of these easier makes the other harder. With the default spacings (100 Hz and 20 ms) window A separates the clicks and merges the tones, and window B does the opposite.

When both clicks fall inside one long window, the spectrum of that frame shows evenly spaced ripples. Two impulses \(\tau\) seconds apart have a spectrum that rises and falls every \(1/\tau\) hertz, so the spacing of the ripples still carries the time information that the picture has lost.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this activity, students will be able to:

  1. Compare spectrograms of one signal made with a short and a long window.
  2. Predict from the window length whether two tones or two clicks will be separated.
  3. Measure time and frequency separations on a spectrogram with cursors.
  4. Justify a choice of window length, window type and hop size for a given signal.
  5. Explain why the time span and the bin spacing of a window cannot both be made small.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in a digital signal processing, or signals and systems, course. Plan 25 to 30 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The DFT, bin spacing and window functions
  • The idea of a spectrogram
  • Sampling rate and sample period

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Two windows, two failures (5 min). Keep the default settings: tones 100 Hz apart, clicks 20 ms apart, \(N = 64\) in A, \(N = 1024\) in B, Hann window, hop \(N/4\).

  • Spectrogram A shows two thin vertical lines at 500 ms and 520 ms but one wide horizontal band around 500 to 600 Hz. Its caption reads "tones 0.8 bins apart, clicks 2.5 windows apart".
  • Spectrogram B shows two thin horizontal lines at 500 Hz and 600 Hz but one vertical band where the clicks are. Its caption reads "tones 12.8 bins apart, clicks 0.16 windows apart".
  • Click on a line in B and point at the other one. The box reports about 100 Hz. Click on a click line in A and point at the other: about 20 ms.

Activity 2: Find the window length that works (10 min). Step window A through \(N = 32, 64, 128, 256, 512\) with the defaults. Use the captions to fill in the first four columns, and the picture to fill in the last two.

\(N\) \(\Delta t\) \(\Delta f\) tones apart clicks apart tones separate? clicks separate? 32 4 ms 250 Hz 0.4 bins 5 windows no yes 64 8 ms 125 Hz 0.8 bins 2.5 windows no yes 128 16 ms 62.5 Hz 1.6 bins 1.25 windows no yes 256 32 ms 31.3 Hz 3.2 bins 0.63 windows yes no, only a shallow dip 512 64 ms 15.6 Hz 6.4 bins 0.31 windows yes no

No length separates both pairs cleanly. Now set the tone spacing to 200 Hz and window A to \(N = 128\). The tones are 3.2 bins apart and the clicks 1.25 windows apart, so both pairs are separated. Explain this with \(\Delta t \times \Delta f = 1\).

Activity 3: What the long window still knows (5 min). Untick Two tones, set the click spacing to 4 ms and window B to \(N = 1024\). Put the cursor on the clicks in B.

  • The two clicks are only 0.03 windows apart and appear as one vertical band, but across the band run horizontal stripes. The frame spectrum beside B has eight ripples between 0 and 2000 Hz.
  • Click on one stripe and point at the next: the box reports about 250 Hz, which is \(1/(4\ \text{ms})\).
  • Set the click spacing to 10 ms: the ripples are 100 Hz apart, and there are 20 of them.

Activity 4: A moving tone (5 min). Untick Two tones and Two clicks and tick Chirp. Set window A to \(N = 256\) and window B to \(N = 512\), then try \(N = 1024\) and \(N = 2048\) in B.

  • The ridge is thinnest at \(N = 512\). In the frame spectrum at the cursor, the ridge is about 64 Hz wide at \(N = 256\), 38 Hz wide at \(N = 512\) and 51 Hz wide at \(N = 1024\), measured where it has fallen to half its peak height (\(-6\) dB).
  • At \(N = 2048\) the ridge is smeared to about 102 Hz and its peak has fallen to about \(-11\) dB.
  • The chirp rises 800 Hz every second, so it moves 51 Hz during the 64 ms window of \(N = 512\). Why does a longer window smear it even though its bins are finer, and why is a shorter window coarse?

Activity 5: Window type and hop size (5 min).

  • Untick Two clicks and set window A to \(N = 256\). With Hann, the frame spectrum is above \(-60\) dB (the left edge of its plot) in only 11 of its 65 bins, a narrow skirt around the tones. With Rectangular it is above \(-60\) dB in all 65 and the curve runs across the whole plot. What happens to the area around the tones, and why?
  • Restore Hann and the clicks, set window A to \(N = 64\) and change the hop from \(N/4\) to \(N\) (no overlap). The click at 520 ms disappears from A. It falls on the first sample of a frame, where the Hann window is zero. Choose \(N/2\) and it returns.
  • Compare \(N/4\) with \(N/8\). The picture is smoother but the lines are no thinner. Does a smaller hop improve the resolution?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. With the default settings, which window separates the tones and which separates the clicks? Answer: window B (\(N = 1024\)) separates the tones, which are 12.8 bins apart, and merges the clicks, which are 0.16 windows apart. Window A (\(N = 64\)) separates the clicks (2.5 windows apart) and merges the tones (0.8 bins apart).
  2. What is the product of a window's time span and its bin spacing, and what does it imply? Answer: \(\Delta t \times \Delta f = (N/f_s)(f_s/N) = 1\) for every \(N\). Doubling the window length halves the bin spacing but doubles the time span, so improving one resolution worsens the other.
  3. What is the shortest window in the sliders that separates two tones 100 Hz apart with the Hann window, and why? Answer: \(N = 256\). The bin spacing is 31.25 Hz, so the tones are 3.2 bins apart and the frame spectrum shows two peaks with a valley about 9 dB deep. At \(N = 128\) they are 1.6 bins apart and merge into one peak.
  4. The tones are 200 Hz apart and the clicks 20 ms apart. Which single window length separates both pairs? Answer: \(N = 128\). The tones are 3.2 bins apart and the clicks 1.25 windows apart. \(N = 64\) puts the tones 1.6 bins apart, and \(N = 256\) puts the clicks 0.63 windows apart.
  5. Two clicks fall inside one long window and the frame spectrum has ripples 125 Hz apart. How far apart are the clicks? Answer: 8 ms, because the ripple spacing is \(1/\tau\) and \(1/(125\ \text{Hz}) = 8\) ms.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"There is one best window length for every signal." The best window depends on what must be separated. Compare window A and window B in Activity 1: each one fails at the task the other one does well.

"A smaller hop size improves time resolution." The hop only sets how many frames are drawn. Change the hop from \(N/2\) to \(N/8\) and the click and tone lines keep the same width; only the window length and type change the width.

"What a spectrogram does not show has been destroyed." Two clicks inside one long window merge in the picture, but their spacing is still present in the frame spectrum as ripples \(1/\tau\) hertz apart (Activity 3).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Short-time Fourier transform - Wikipedia - definition of the STFT, window and hop size
  2. Spectrogram - Wikipedia - the magnitude of the STFT displayed as an image
  3. Window function - Wikipedia - Hann, Hamming, Blackman and rectangular windows and their main lobes
  4. Chirp - Wikipedia - signals whose frequency changes with time
  5. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT, windows and spectral analysis
  6. Allen, J. B., & Rabiner, L. R. (1977). A unified approach to short-time Fourier analysis and synthesis. Proceedings of the IEEE, 65(11), 1558-1564.
  7. Cohen, L. (1995). Time-Frequency Analysis. Prentice Hall.
  8. Time-Frequency Analysis Explorer - this textbook - a single spectrogram with adjustable overlap, colour map and scale
  9. Chapter 8: Advanced Transforms - this textbook - the chapter that embeds this MicroSim

docs.title: Möbius Transform
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/mobius-transform/main.html" width="100%" height="632px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A Möbius (linear fractional) transformation maps each complex number \(z\) to

\[w = f(z) = \frac{Az + B}{Cz + D}, \qquad AD - BC \neq 0.\]

The left plot is the input \(z\)-plane and the right plot is the output \(w\)-plane, at the same scale. White dots on the left form a grid of \(z\) values; the white dots on the right are their images. The dashed circle is the unit circle.

  • Coefficients box: drag the colored dots to set \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) (parts from −1 to 1).
  • Preset: exact coefficients for the identity, a rotation with scaling, the inversion \(1/z\), the bilinear map and the Cayley map.
  • Draw in the input plane; its purple image appears on the right.
  • Scale sets the half-width of both plots (±1 to ±20); Density sets the dots per row (10 to 50).
  • Hover over the input plane to read \(z\) and \(f(z)\).

The read-outs show \(AD - BC\), the pole \(-D/C\) (red ×) and \(f(\infty) = A/C\) (black ○), where far-away inputs crowd. A Möbius map sends lines and circles to lines and circles and preserves angles (it is conformal).

Connection to IIR filter design. The bilinear transform in Chapter 10: Advanced Filter Design and Implementation, \(z = \frac{1 + sT/2}{1 - sT/2}\), is a Möbius map with \(A = T/2\), \(B = 1\), \(C = -T/2\), \(D = 1\). With \(T = 2\) it is the Bilinear preset: read the input as the analog \(s\)-plane and the output as the digital \(z\)-plane. The axis \(s = j\Omega\) lands on the unit circle at angle \(\omega = 2\arctan(\Omega T/2)\), the stable left half-plane lands inside the circle, and \(s = \infty\) lands at \(z = -1\): no aliasing, but warped frequency.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the pole \(-D/C\), the image of infinity \(A/C\) and the determinant \(AD - BC\) of a Möbius transformation from its coefficients
  2. Predict whether a line or circle in the \(z\)-plane maps to a line or a circle, from its position relative to the pole
  3. Explain how \(B\) translates the plane, \(A\) rotates and scales it, and a nonzero \(C\) bends lines into circles
  4. Demonstrate that the bilinear map \((1+s)/(1-s)\) sends the imaginary axis onto the unit circle and the left half-plane inside it
  5. Calculate the warped digital frequency \(\omega = 2\arctan\Omega\) of a point \(s = j\Omega\) under the bilinear map with \(T = 2\)

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate engineering, physics or mathematics students in a signals and systems or digital signal processing course, ideally just before the bilinear-transform method of IIR filter design. Plan 25 to 30 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex arithmetic in rectangular and polar form (see the Complex Plane MicroSim)
  • Poles of a rational function
  • Stability regions: the left half of the \(s\)-plane and the inside of the unit circle in the \(z\)-plane

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: The pole and the point at infinity (5 min). Choose Default example (\(A = 0.50 + 0.50i\), \(B = 0.30 + 0.20i\), \(C = -0.10 + 0.60i\), \(D = 0.20 - 0.50i\)) with Scale ±3. The read-outs show \(AD - BC = 0.50 - 0.31i\), the pole at \(z = 0.86 + 0.19i\) (red ×) and \(f(\infty) = 0.68 - 0.95i\) (black ○). The grid dots crowd around the ○, because the grid points farthest from the pole map closest to \(A/C\), while the dots next to the × are thrown out of view. Hover toward the ×: the \(w\) read-out grows without bound.

Activity 2: Lines become circles (7 min). Choose Inversion: w = 1/z and set Scale to ±2, so the grid lines sit at ±1. Trace the vertical grid line \(\mathrm{Re}\,z = 1\) from top to bottom. Its image is an arc of the circle with center \(0.5\) and radius \(0.5\); the missing piece near \(w = 0\) belongs to the parts of the line beyond \(|\mathrm{Im}\,z| = 2\). Hover at \(z = 2\) (the right edge of the input plane): \(w = 0.50\). Then trace the dashed unit circle: its image is the unit circle again, traversed in the opposite direction, because \(1/e^{i\theta} = e^{-i\theta}\).

Activity 3: The bilinear transform (8 min). Choose Bilinear: w = (1+z)/(1−z) with Scale ±3 and read the input plane as the \(s\)-plane. Trace the vertical axis from top to bottom: the image is an arc of the dashed unit circle from 143° through 0° to −143°. Draw a short stroke anywhere left of the vertical axis: its image lies inside the unit circle. Hover near \(z = i\): \(w \approx i\), an angle of \(2\arctan 1 = 90°\). Hover near the top of the axis, \(z \approx 3i\): \(w \approx -0.80 + 0.60i\), an angle of \(2\arctan 3 \approx 143.1°\). The pole × sits at \(s = 1\) and the ○ at \(w = -1\), where \(s = \infty\) lands.

Activity 4: One coefficient at a time (7 min). Choose Identity: w = z (\(A = D = 1\), \(B = C = 0\)); both plots look the same. Drag the green dot \(B\), on top at the origin, to about \(0.5\) on the real axis: every dot moves 0.5 to the right (a translation). Drag the blue dot \(C\), now alone at the origin, up to about \(0.5i\): a pole appears near \(z = -1/(0.5i) = 2i\), the ○ moves to about \(-2i\), and the straight grid rows bend into arcs. The Preset menu now reads Custom (dragged).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. For the Bilinear preset, \(f(z) = \frac{z + 1}{-z + 1}\), where is the pole and what is \(f(\infty)\)? Answer: the pole is \(z = -D/C = 1\) and \(f(\infty) = A/C = -1\).
  2. With the bilinear transform and \(T = 2\), where does the analog point \(s = j1\) land, and what digital frequency does it represent? Answer: \(z = (1 + j)/(1 - j) = j\), on the unit circle at \(\omega = 2\arctan 1 = \pi/2\) rad (90°).
  3. A student sets \(A = 0.5\), \(B = 1\), \(C = 0.5\), \(D = 1\). What does the output plane show, and why? Answer: \(AD - BC = 0.5 - 0.5 = 0\), so \(f(z) = (0.5z + 1)/(0.5z + 1) = 1\) for every \(z \neq -2\); all dots land on \(w = 1\) and the read-out warns that \(f\) is constant.
  4. Why do \(A = 0.5\), \(B = 0.5\), \(C = -0.5\), \(D = 0.5\) give exactly the same picture as the Bilinear preset? Answer: they are the preset's coefficients multiplied by 0.5; the common factor cancels between numerator and denominator, so \(f\) is unchanged (only \(AD - BC\) changes, from 2 to 0.5).
  5. Under \(w = 1/z\), what is the image of the line \(\mathrm{Re}\,z = 1\), and why is it not a straight line? Answer: the circle \(|w - 0.5| = 0.5\) (without the point \(w = 0\)). A line maps to a line only when it passes through the pole, here \(z = 0\), and \(\mathrm{Re}\,z = 1\) does not.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A Möbius transformation keeps straight lines straight." Activity 2 turns the line \(\mathrm{Re}\,z = 1\) into a circle. Only lines through the pole stay straight: with the Inversion preset, trace the real axis (it passes through the × at 0) and its image is the real axis again.

"The bilinear transform maps analog frequency evenly onto the unit circle." In Activity 3, the stretch of the imaginary axis from \(\Omega = 0\) to \(1\) covers 90° of the circle, from \(1\) to \(3\) only about 53°, and every \(\Omega > 3\) is squeezed into the last 37° before \(w = -1\). The dots crowding near the ○ at \(-1\) show the same compression. This is frequency warping, which pre-warping corrects at chosen frequencies.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Möbius transformation - Wikipedia - definition, the pole, the image of infinity and the circle-preserving property
  2. Bilinear transform - Wikipedia - the \(s\)-to-\(z\) mapping used in IIR filter design, and its frequency warping
  3. Conformal map - Wikipedia - why the right angles of the input grid survive the mapping
  4. Riemann sphere - Wikipedia - the point at infinity that a Möbius map sends to \(A/C\)
  5. Smith chart - Wikipedia - an engineering chart built on the Möbius map \(\Gamma = (z - 1)/(z + 1)\)
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to DSP, Chapter 33: The z-Transform - Steven W. Smith - free chapter on the \(z\)-plane and recursive (IIR) filter design

docs.text:
Prompt history

Version 2.0.0 (2026-10-14). Ported from p5.js 1.9.0 to p5.js 2.3.2 and made responsive; the entry file mobius-transform.html was renamed to main.html (the old name redirects). Changes from version 1:

  • The output plane was drawn upside down: it plotted the mirror image \(\overline{f(z)}\), with \(\mathrm{Im}\,w\) pointing down. It now uses the same orientation as the input plane.
  • The input and output planes are drawn at the same size, so magnification can be read directly (version 1 drew the same coordinate range at 150 px for the input and 300 px for the output).
  • A drawing now joins every pair of consecutive mouse points (version 1 used beginShape(LINES), which drew every other segment), it is drawn in purple so it stays visible on the axes, and its image is a continuous curve.
  • The grid dots sit at the centers of the grid cells, so the grid is symmetric about 0.
  • Added the preset menu, the pole and \(f(\infty)\) markers, the unit circle, the \(AD - BC\) read-out with a warning when it is zero, and the hover read-out.

Graph the coeffiecients as draggable vectors, and display a point domain of configurable scale and density.
Create a user drawable side canvas, map the drawn points back through the transform and displays it alongside the current point map visualization.
