docs.title: Multirate Sample Rate Converter
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/multirate-sample-rate-converter/main.html" width="100%" height="572px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a rational sample-rate converter that changes a signal's sample rate by the factor \(L/M\). The pipeline diagram shows three blocks: an upsampler \(\uparrow L\) that inserts \(L-1\) zeros between samples, a low-pass FIR filter (LPF), and a downsampler \(\downarrow M\) that keeps one sample in \(M\). The rate under each node follows the sliders; with \(f_s = 8\) kHz the output rate is \(f_s' = 8L/M\) kHz.

Below the diagram, four columns show the signal at the input \(x[n]\), after zero insertion \(u[k]\), after the filter \(v[k]\), and at the output \(y[m]\). Each column has a magnitude spectrum in dB, drawn from 0 Hz to that stage's own Nyquist frequency (the red value at the right end of the axis), above a 2 ms stem plot of the samples over the ideal continuous signal (gray). In the two high-rate columns, dashed lines mark the input Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\) (gray, "in") and the output Nyquist frequency \(f_s'/2\) (red, "out"). The gold curve is the filter response \(|H|/L\).

  • Upsample L and Downsample M (1-8 each) set the conversion ratio.
  • Filter length N (8-128 taps) sizes a Hamming-windowed sinc filter with cutoff \(\pi/\max(L, M)\) at the high rate and gain \(L\).
  • Low-pass filter on, when unchecked, bypasses the filter to expose raw images and aliases.
  • Input signal chooses a multi-tone (0.5, 1.2 and 3.1 kHz at amplitudes 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2), a linear chirp, or colored noise whose spectrum falls with frequency.

Read-outs give the output rate, the error against an ideal converter, the multiplications per output sample and, for the multi-tone input, the measured output peaks (aliases and images in red). Hover over a spectrum to read values.

This simulation supports Chapter 13: Multirate Signal Processing and Compression.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
Zero insertion compresses the spectrum by \(L\), so \(L-1\) images of the baseband appear at \(k f_s \pm f\):

\[u[k] = \begin{cases} x[k/L] & k = 0, \pm L, \pm 2L, \ldots \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad U(e^{j\omega}) = X(e^{j\omega L})\]

The filter runs at the high rate \(L f_s\). Its cutoff \(\omega_c = \pi/\max(L, M)\) removes the images (the \(L\) term) and everything above the output Nyquist frequency (the \(M\) term), and its taps are scaled so that \(\sum_j h[j] = L\):

\[v[k] = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} h[j]\, u[k-j], \qquad y[m] = v[mM], \qquad f_s' = f_s \frac{L}{M}\]

The sketch removes the filter's delay of \((N-1)/2\) high-rate samples so the four stages line up in time. The error read-out compares the output with an ideal converter, whose output \(y_{\text{ideal}}[m]\) is the input with every component at or above \(\min(f_s, f_s')/2\) removed, sampled at the output instants:

\[E = 10 \log_{10} \frac{\operatorname{mean}\left( (y[m] - y_{\text{ideal}}[m])^2 \right)}{\operatorname{mean}\left( x[n]^2 \right)} \ \text{dB}\]

A direct implementation computes every high-rate sample and then discards \(M-1\) of every \(M\), costing \(N \cdot M\) multiplications per output sample. A polyphase implementation computes only the kept samples and skips the inserted zeros, costing about \(N/L\). Each spectrum is computed from a 64 ms segment with a Blackman-Harris window and is scaled so a sinusoid of amplitude \(A\) reads \(20\log_{10} A\) dB (amplitude 0.5 reads \(-6.0\) dB).

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the sample rate at every node of an \(L/M\) converter, including the output rate \(f_s L/M\)
  2. Predict the frequencies \(k f_s \pm f\) of the spectral images created by inserting \(L-1\) zeros, and identify them on the spectrum after upsampling
  3. Predict where a component above the output Nyquist frequency lands after downsampling, and verify the alias frequency on the output spectrum
  4. Explain why the converter's single low-pass filter needs cutoff \(\pi/\max(L, M)\) and passband gain \(L\)
  5. Analyze how the filter length trades conversion error against multiplications per output sample, and compare direct and polyphase cost

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a junior- or senior-level digital signal processing course. Plan 45-50 minutes for the four activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The sampling theorem, the Nyquist frequency and aliasing
  • Reading a magnitude spectrum in decibels
  • FIR low-pass filters and the windowed-sinc design method

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
All activities use the multi-tone input unless stated otherwise. Readings are what the sim displays.

Activity 1: Zero insertion creates images (10 min). Set L = 3, M = 1, N = 48 and uncheck the filter.

  • The pipeline reads 8, 24, 24 and 24 kHz. In column 2 the three tones are still at 0.50, 1.20 and 3.10 kHz, but at \(-15.6\), \(-20.0\) and \(-23.5\) dB instead of \(-6.0\), \(-10.5\) and \(-14.0\) dB: each dropped by \(20\log_{10} 3 = 9.5\) dB.
  • Six new peaks appear at 4.90, 6.80, 7.50, 8.50, 9.20 and 11.10 kHz, which are \(8 \pm 3.1\), \(8 \pm 1.2\) and \(8 \pm 0.5\) kHz. The peak list marks them red and the error reads \(-1.8\) dB.
  • Check the filter box. The images fall below \(-70\) dB, the tones return to \(-6.0\), \(-10.4\) and \(-14.0\) dB because the filter has gain 3, and the error improves to \(-49.5\) dB.

Activity 2: Downsampling folds the spectrum (10 min). Set L = 1, M = 2, N = 48 and uncheck the filter.

  • The output rate is 4 kHz, so the output Nyquist frequency is 2 kHz. The 3.1 kHz tone cannot be represented and reappears at \(4 - 3.1 = 0.90\) kHz at \(-14.0\) dB (red in the peak list). The error reads \(-9.7\) dB.
  • Check the filter box (cutoff 2 kHz = \(\pi/2\)). The 0.90 kHz alias disappears, only 0.50 and 1.20 kHz remain, and the error improves to \(-50.9\) dB.
  • Now set M = 4 (output rate 2 kHz). Even with the filter on, a red alias remains at 0.80 kHz (\(-37.4\) dB) and the error is \(-33.1\) dB: the 1.2 kHz tone is only 0.2 kHz above the 1 kHz cutoff, closer than the 48-tap filter's transition band is wide.

Activity 3: Rational conversion, 3/2 versus 2/3 (10 min). Keep the filter on with N = 48.

  • L = 3, M = 2: the rates are 8, 24, 24 and 12 kHz, the cutoff is 4 kHz (\(\pi/3\), set by L), all three tones survive, and the error is \(-49.5\) dB. The cost is 96 multiplications per output sample direct and 16.0 polyphase.
  • L = 2, M = 3: the rates are 8, 16, 16 and 5.333 kHz, the cutoff is 2.667 kHz (\(\pi/3\), now set by M), and the 3.1 kHz tone is removed, so the output peaks are 0.50 and 1.20 kHz only. The error is \(-39.9\) dB; the cost is 144 direct and 24.0 polyphase.
  • Uncheck the filter at L = 2, M = 3. The error jumps to \(-3.0\) dB and red peaks appear at 0.43, 1.47, 2.17 and 2.23 kHz.
  • Finally set L = M = 3 with the filter off. The output equals the input sample for sample and the error reads "below \(-120\) dB". Explain why from \(y[m] = u[3m]\).

Activity 4: Filter length versus cost (10 min). Set L = 3, M = 2 with the filter on and step N through 8, 16, 32, 48, 64 and 128. Record the error and both costs:

N Error (dB) Direct N·M Polyphase N/L 8 -14.5 16 2.7 16 -19.9 32 5.3 32 -33.4 64 10.7 48 -49.5 96 16.0 64 -56.4 128 21.3 128 -62.5 256 42.7

At N = 16 an image survives at 4.90 kHz (\(-27.3\) dB, red) and the 3.1 kHz tone droops to \(-16.1\) dB because it sits in the filter's wide transition band. Switch to colored noise: the error is \(-33.3\) dB at N = 48 and \(-39.1\) dB at N = 128, worse than for the tones because the noise has energy right up to the 4 kHz cutoff.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A converter has \(f_s = 8\) kHz, L = 5 and M = 4. What are the rates at \(u\), \(v\) and \(y\), and what are the filter's cutoff and gain? (Answer: 40, 40 and 10 kHz; cutoff \(\pi/5\) at 40 kHz, which is 4 kHz, and gain 5. Set L = 5, M = 4 to check.)
  2. A 1.2 kHz tone sampled at 8 kHz is upsampled by L = 4. At which frequencies between 0 and the new Nyquist frequency do its images appear? (Answer: the new rate is 32 kHz, so the images are at \(8 \pm 1.2\) and \(16 - 1.2\): 6.8, 9.2 and 14.8 kHz, which is \(L - 1 = 3\) images.)
  3. With L = 1, M = 3 and the filter off, where does the 3.1 kHz tone appear in the output, and why? (Answer: the output rate is 2.667 kHz, so the tone folds to \(3.1 - 2.667 = 0.43\) kHz; it is above the output Nyquist frequency of 1.333 kHz.)
  4. Why must the interpolation filter have a passband gain of L? (Answer: inserting \(L-1\) zeros divides each component's amplitude by L and puts the rest of its energy into the \(L-1\) images; removing the images leaves amplitude \(A/L\), so the filter multiplies by L to restore \(A\).)
  5. For L = 3, M = 2 and N = 48, how many times cheaper is the polyphase implementation than the direct one, and where does the saving come from? (Answer: 96 versus 16 multiplications per output sample, six times cheaper, which is \(L \cdot M\): a factor M from not computing discarded outputs and a factor L from skipping the inserted zeros.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Upsampling adds detail to the signal." Raising the rate adds no new frequencies. Set L = 3, M = 1 with the filter on: the output rate is 24 kHz, but the output spectrum still holds only 0.5, 1.2 and 3.1 kHz, and nothing above 4 kHz rises above \(-70\) dB. The extra samples are interpolated, not measured.

"Downsampling just throws samples away, so it cannot hurt." With L = 1, M = 2 and the filter off, a 0.90 kHz component appears that was never in the input. Once aliased it sits among the wanted tones and no later filter can tell it apart, which is why the low-pass filter must come before the downsampler.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Sample-rate conversion - Wikipedia - rational L/M resampling and its applications, such as 44.1 kHz to 48 kHz audio
  2. Upsampling - Wikipedia - zero insertion, spectral images and the interpolation filter
  3. Downsampling (signal processing) - Wikipedia - decimation, aliasing and the anti-aliasing filter
  4. Aliasing - Wikipedia - why components above the Nyquist frequency fold back into the baseband
  5. Window function - Wikipedia - the Hamming window used in the filter and the Blackman-Harris window used for the spectra
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on windowed-sinc filters and sampling

docs.title: Noise Analysis and Reduction Tool
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/noise-analysis-and-reduction-tool/main.html" width="100%" height="672px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim generates a record of \(N\) noise samples \(w[n]\) at \(f_s = 1\) kHz, optionally adds a 5 Hz sinusoid \(s[n]\), and then reduces the noise. Four panels analyse the result:

  • Time series: the input \(x[n] = s[n] + w[n]\) (blue), the clean sinusoid (dashed) and the output \(y[n]\) (orange), for the first 1.02 s.
  • Histogram of \(w[n]\) with a Gaussian of the same mean and variance, plus the excess kurtosis (0 for Gaussian, \(-1.2\) for uniform).
  • Autocorrelation \(\rho[m]\) with the theoretical curve and the 95% band \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}\) expected for white noise.
  • Power spectral density by Welch's method on log-log axes, with the theoretical PSD and a fitted slope in dB/decade.

Noise type selects white Gaussian (Box-Muller), white uniform, pink (\(1/f\), a bank of one-pole filters), brown (\(1/f^2\), a leaky integrator), band-limited white noise (ideal low-pass at 50 Hz) or impulsive noise (5% spikes). Samples N and Noise RMS σ set the record length and level. Welch segments S averages \(S\) Hann-windowed segments of length \(M\); more segments smooth the estimate but widen the bins \(\Delta f = f_s/M\). Input SNR sets the sinusoid amplitude \(A = \sigma\sqrt{2\cdot 10^{\mathrm{SNR}/10}}\). Ensemble avg K averages \(K\) independent noisy copies, and Moving avg or Median with length L filters the result. New noise draws a new realization.

The banner measures each stage: \(\mathrm{SNR}_{out} = 10\log_{10}\!\left(P_s / \overline{(y-s)^2}\right)\). For white noise, ensemble averaging gains \(10\log_{10}K\) dB and an \(L\)-point moving average gains \(10\log_{10}L\) dB. This MicroSim supports Chapter 12: Stochastic Processes and Random Signals.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Classify a noise record as white, pink or brown from its measured PSD slope (0, −10 or −20 dB/decade) and its autocorrelation
  2. Distinguish Gaussian, uniform and impulsive white noise using the histogram and the excess kurtosis, even though their spectra are identical
  3. Explain the variance–resolution trade-off of Welch's method in terms of the number of segments \(S\) and the segment length \(M\)
  4. Predict the SNR gain of averaging \(K\) independent realizations (\(10\log_{10}K\)) and of an \(L\)-point moving average on white noise (\(10\log_{10}L\)), and explain why a moving average gains little against pink or brown noise
  5. Evaluate when a moving-average or median filter improves the output SNR, accounting for signal distortion at long \(L\) and for impulsive noise

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a signals and systems, digital signal processing or communications course. Plan 45–60 minutes for the four activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Mean, variance and the Gaussian distribution
  • Decibels and the definition of SNR
  • The discrete Fourier transform and the idea of a power spectral density
  • The autocorrelation function of a random process

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
All numbers below are what the MicroSim shows for the realization drawn when the page loads. After you press New noise they change by a random amount (a PSD slope typically by 1–2 dB/decade).

Activity 1: Fingerprint the noise colours (15 min). Uncheck Add 5 Hz sinusoid and set K = 1, L = 1, N = 8192, S = 16. Step through the noise types and record the PSD slope (header of the PSD panel), \(\rho[1]\) and the excess kurtosis.

Noise type PSD slope (dB/decade) \(\rho[1]\) Excess kurtosis White Gaussian +0.6 0.017 −0.04 White uniform −1.3 0.007 −1.20 Pink (1/f) −10.0 0.804 −0.08 Brown (1/f²) −19.7 0.999 +0.08 Band-limited (fit 1–30 Hz) +1.9 0.984 −0.23 Impulsive −0.3 −0.012 +45.4

The slopes match the theory: 0 dB/decade for white, −10 dB/decade (−3 dB/octave) for pink and −20 dB/decade (−6 dB/octave) for brown. The band-limited autocorrelation is a sinc: it crosses zero near lag 10 ms (\(1/(2B)\) with \(B = 50\) Hz; \(\rho[10] = 0.041\)) and dips to −0.196 at lag 15. Impulsive noise has a flat spectrum and \(\rho[1] \approx 0\), yet its kurtosis of 45.4 (theory 46.2) and its 1.7% of samples beyond ±4σ show that it is far from Gaussian.

Activity 2: Welch's trade-off (10 min). Choose White Gaussian, sinusoid off, N = 4096, K = 1, L = 1.

  1. S = 1: a single periodogram with M = 4096 and Δf = 0.24 Hz. The maroon curve scatters widely around the dashed theoretical level of −27 dB (\(10\log_{10}(2\sigma^2/f_s)\)), and the slope reads −2.1 dB/decade.
  2. S = 8: M = 512, Δf = 1.95 Hz. The curve is much smoother and the slope reads +0.9 dB/decade.
  3. S = 32: M = 128, Δf = 7.81 Hz. The curve is smoothest, but the slope fit now starts at 23 Hz and uses only 10 bins, so it reads +3.4 dB/decade.
  4. Switch to Pink and N = 256 with S = 32: M = 16 and Δf = 62.5 Hz, so no bins fall inside the 1–100 Hz fit band and the header reports too few bins.

Activity 3: Averaging against coloured noise (15 min). Sinusoid off, N = 8192, S = 16.

  1. Set K = 1 and Moving avg L = 16. The banner shows the noise reduction of the filter: White +11.95 dB (theory 12.04 dB), Pink +1.83 dB, Brown +0.01 dB, Band-limited +2.37 dB. Watch the orange autocorrelation of white noise become a triangle that reaches zero at lag 16.
  2. Set L = 1 and K = 16. Now every colour gains about 12 dB: White +12.01, Pink +11.18, Brown +11.14, Band-limited +12.09 dB.

A moving average only helps when neighbouring noise samples are uncorrelated. Pink and brown noise put most of their power at low frequencies, where the moving average passes everything. Independent realizations are uncorrelated with each other whatever their colour, so ensemble averaging always approaches \(10\log_{10}K\).

Activity 4: SNR, distortion and impulses (15 min). White Gaussian, sinusoid on, Input SNR = 0 dB, N = 4096, S = 8, K = 1, Moving avg.

  1. Step L through 1, 4, 16, 32, 64. The output SNR reads −0.10, 5.79, 12.03, 14.57 and 13.51 dB. It falls at L = 64 because the filter also attenuates the 5 Hz sinusoid (gain 0.84), and the resulting error is comparable to the remaining noise.
  2. Set Input SNR = +30 dB. L = 16 still helps (output 37.55 dB), but L = 64 drops the output SNR to 15.88 dB (filter gain −14.03 dB): at high SNR the distortion dominates.
  3. Return to 0 dB and choose Impulsive noise with L = 5. Moving avg gains +7.13 dB (output 7.22 dB); Median gains +14.89 dB (output 14.98 dB). Switch back to White Gaussian: now Moving avg gains +6.89 dB and Median only +5.36 dB.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A noise record shows a PSD slope of −9.6 dB/decade and \(\rho[1] = 0.80\). Which noise type is it, and how would brown noise differ? (Answer: pink noise; brown noise would have a slope near −20 dB/decade and \(\rho[1]\) very close to 1.)
  2. How many independent realizations must be averaged to improve the SNR of white noise by 15 dB? (Answer: \(10^{1.5} = 31.6\), so K = 32, which gives \(10\log_{10}32 = 15.05\) dB; the MicroSim shows +15.17 dB for the first-load realization.)
  3. Two white-noise records have the same flat PSD, but one has an excess kurtosis of 45. What kind of noise is it, and which filter in this MicroSim reduces it more? (Answer: impulsive noise; the median filter, because a few large spikes do not move the median of a window while they shift its mean.)
  4. With the SNR slider fixed, σ is doubled from 1.0 to 2.0. What happens to the PSD level, the PSD slope and the input SNR? (Answer: the PSD rises by \(20\log_{10}2 = 6.02\) dB (from −27.0 to −21.0 dB for white noise); the slope and the input SNR do not change, because the sinusoid amplitude is scaled with σ.)
  5. At 0 dB input SNR, why is the output SNR lower at L = 64 (13.51 dB) than at L = 32 (14.57 dB)? (Answer: the moving average's gain at 5 Hz drops to 0.84 at L = 64, so the output differs from the clean sinusoid by 16% of its amplitude; that distortion error adds to the noise and outweighs the extra noise reduction.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Averaging L samples always buys \(10\log_{10}L\) dB." That holds only when the noise samples are uncorrelated. In Activity 3 the same 16-point moving average gains 11.95 dB on white noise but only 1.83 dB on pink noise and 0.01 dB on brown noise, while averaging 16 independent realizations gains about 12 dB for every colour.

"White noise means Gaussian noise." Whiteness describes the spectrum and the autocorrelation; Gaussianity describes the amplitude distribution. White uniform and impulsive noise have the same flat PSD and delta-like autocorrelation as white Gaussian noise, but their histograms and kurtosis (−1.20 and +45.4) are very different.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Colors of noise - Wikipedia - white, pink and brown noise and their spectral slopes
  2. Welch's method - Wikipedia - averaging windowed, overlapping periodograms to reduce the variance of a PSD estimate
  3. Signal-to-noise ratio - Wikipedia - definitions of SNR in linear units and decibels
  4. Median filter - Wikipedia - the nonlinear filter that removes impulsive noise
  5. Box–Muller transform - Wikipedia - how the sketch turns uniform random numbers into Gaussian ones
  6. Kurtosis - Wikipedia - the fourth-moment statistic used to tell Gaussian, uniform and impulsive noise apart
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook; its chapter on moving average filters derives the \(\sqrt{L}\) noise reduction

docs.title: Nyquist-Shannon Sampling
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/nyquist-shannon-sampling/main.html" width="100%" height="502px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim samples a 5 Hz sine wave, \(x(t) = \sin(2\pi \cdot 5t)\), at the sampling rate \(f_s\) set by the slider (1 to 50 Hz in steps of 0.1 Hz) and shows one second of the result.

  • Upper plot: the original signal in black and its samples \(x[n] = x(n/f_s)\) as red dots.
  • Lower plot: two continuous signals rebuilt from the samples alone. The blue curve is the ideal (sinc) reconstruction that the sampling theorem promises. The gray curve joins neighboring samples with straight lines.

The read-out line gives the signal frequency \(f\), the Nyquist rate \(2f = 10\) Hz, the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\) and the number of samples per period \(f_s/f\). The colored status line is the Nyquist indicator: green when \(f_s > 2f\), gold when \(f_s = 2f\) exactly, and red when \(f_s < 2f\), in which case it reports the alias frequency.

This is the introductory sampling sim for the sections on the sampling theorem and aliasing in Chapter 5: Sampling and Quantization. The Sampling Theorem Explorer adds spectra and more controls.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
The blue curve is the Whittaker-Shannon interpolation of the samples,

\[x_r(t) = \sum_{n} x[n]\,\operatorname{sinc}(f_s t - n), \qquad \operatorname{sinc}(u) = \frac{\sin(\pi u)}{\pi u}.\]

The theorem needs every sample from \(n = -\infty\) to \(\infty\). The sim uses the samples in the window plus 2000 more on each side, which keeps the blue curve within 0.01 of the exact result for every slider setting.

When \(f_s > 2f\) the sum returns the original 5 Hz wave. When \(f_s < 2f\) the samples are identical to the samples of a slower sine at the alias frequency

\[f_a = |f - k f_s|,\]

where the integer \(k\) makes \(f_a \le f_s/2\), and the sum returns that alias instead.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. State the Nyquist criterion \(f_s > 2f\) and calculate the Nyquist rate of a sinusoid of known frequency
  2. Calculate the samples per period \(f_s/f\) and the Nyquist frequency \(f_s/2\) for a given sampling rate
  3. Predict the alias frequency \(f_a = |f - k f_s|\) when \(f_s < 2f\) and verify it by counting the cycles of the reconstruction
  4. Distinguish ideal (sinc) reconstruction from straight-line interpolation and explain why a jagged straight-line plot does not mean that information was lost
  5. Explain why sampling at exactly \(f_s = 2f\) can fail to capture a sine wave

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a first signals and systems or digital signal processing course. Plan 20 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Frequency and period of a sine wave (\(f = 1/T\))
  • Sampling as taking the values \(x[n] = x(nT_s)\) every \(T_s = 1/f_s\) seconds
  • Reading a plot of amplitude against time

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Above the Nyquist rate (5 min). Start at the default \(f_s\) = 22.0 Hz. The read-out shows 4.40 samples per period and \(f_s/2\) = 11.00 Hz, and the status line is green. The blue curve passes through every red dot and matches the black original, while the gray straight lines cut the corners off each peak. Lower \(f_s\) to 12.0 Hz (2.40 samples per period): the gray zigzag no longer looks like a sine, yet the blue curve is still the 5 Hz wave.

Activity 2: Find the edge (5 min). Set \(f_s\) = 10.5 Hz (2.10 samples per period): the status is still green and the blue curve still completes 5 cycles in one second. Set \(f_s\) = 10.0 Hz: the status turns gold, the 11 samples fall at \(t\) = 0, 0.1, ..., 1.0 s on zero crossings, and both reconstructions are flat lines. Set \(f_s\) = 9.5 Hz: the status turns red and reports a 4.5 Hz alias. The blue curve completes 4.5 cycles and starts downward instead of upward.

Activity 3: Predict the alias (5-10 min). Before moving the slider, compute \(f_a = |5 - k f_s|\) for \(f_s\) = 8.0, 6.0 and 4.5 Hz. Then check: at 8.0 Hz the status reports 3.0 Hz and the blue curve completes 3 cycles; at 6.0 Hz it reports 1.0 Hz and the blue curve completes one cycle; at 4.5 Hz it reports 0.5 Hz and the blue curve rises to +1 at \(t\) = 0.5 s and falls back to 0 at \(t\) = 1 s, half a cycle.

Activity 4: Samples that vanish (5 min). Set \(f_s\) = 5.0 Hz (1.00 sample per period). Every sample lands at the same point of the cycle, where \(\sin(2\pi n) = 0\), so the status reads "Every sample is 0" and the reconstruction is flat: the 5 Hz wave has aliased to 0 Hz. Try 2.5 Hz and 2.0 Hz and explain why the samples are again all zero.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A 5 Hz sine wave is sampled at 8 Hz. What frequency does the reconstruction show? Answer: 3 Hz, since \(|5 - 8| = 3\) Hz is below \(f_s/2 = 4\) Hz.
  2. What is the lowest sampling rate that captures a 5 Hz sine wave, and why does exactly 10 Hz fail in this sim? Answer: any rate above 10 Hz. At exactly 10 Hz the samples fall at \(t = n/10\), where \(\sin(\pi n) = 0\), so every sample is zero.
  3. At \(f_s\) = 12 Hz the gray curve looks nothing like a sine wave. Has information been lost? Answer: no. 12 Hz is above the 10 Hz Nyquist rate, and the blue sinc reconstruction recovers the 5 Hz wave; the distortion comes from straight-line interpolation, not from sampling.
  4. CD audio is sampled at 44.1 kHz. What is the highest frequency it can represent, and where does a 30 kHz tone appear if it reaches the converter unfiltered? Answer: 22.05 kHz; the 30 kHz tone aliases to \(|30 - 44.1| = 14.1\) kHz.
  5. How many samples per period does the default setting take, and how many does the Nyquist rate take? Answer: 4.4 samples per period at 22 Hz; exactly 2 at the 10 Hz Nyquist rate.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A sine wave needs many samples per period, say ten, to be captured." At \(f_s\) = 12 Hz there are only 2.4 samples per period and the straight-line plot looks badly distorted, but the blue sinc reconstruction is the original 5 Hz wave. The number of samples needed is set by the theorem, not by how the dots look when joined with straight lines.

"Sampling at exactly twice the frequency is enough." At \(f_s\) = 10.0 Hz every sample of this sine is zero and the wave disappears. The criterion is a strict inequality, \(f_s > 2f\), and practical systems sample well above it.

"Aliasing makes a signal look noisy." At \(f_s\) = 8.0 Hz the reconstruction is a clean, smooth sine wave. It is simply the wrong one: 3 Hz instead of 5 Hz. Nothing in the samples reveals that it is an alias.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem - Wikipedia - statement of the theorem, the condition \(f_s > 2B\), and sinc reconstruction
  2. Aliasing - Wikipedia - how frequencies above \(f_s/2\) fold to lower alias frequencies
  3. Nyquist rate - Wikipedia - the minimum sampling rate \(2B\) for a signal of bandwidth \(B\)
  4. Nyquist frequency - Wikipedia - the highest frequency \(f_s/2\) that a given sampling rate can represent
  5. Whittaker-Shannon interpolation formula - Wikipedia - the sinc sum used to draw the blue curve
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook; Chapter 3 (ADC and DAC) explains the sampling theorem and aliasing

docs.title: Development Notes
Index
docs.text:
Prompt

Please generate an SVG image of a LED circuit. It has a 5 volt power supply and a red LED. What resistor value should I use to get 20 milliamps of current?

To calculate the resistor value needed to achieve 20 mA current for a red LED powered by a 5V supply, we can use Ohm’s Law:

docs.title: Formula:
docs.text: \[ R = \frac{V_{supply} - V_{LED}}{I} \]

docs.title: Assumptions:
docs.text:
• Typical forward voltage for a red LED: ~2.0V
  • Desired current (I): 20 mA = 0.020 A
  • Supply voltage (Vsupply): 5V

docs.title: Calculation:
docs.text:
\[ R = \frac{5V - 2V}{0.020A} = \frac{3V}{0.020A} = 150\ \Omega \]

Resistor value needed: 150 ohms

Now I’ll generate an SVG schematic diagram of the LED circuit.

You should use a 150-ohm resistor to ensure 20 mA flows through a red LED powered by a 5V supply.

Prompt

Please generate a SchemaDraw file for this circuit.

from schemdraw import Drawing
import schemdraw.elements as elm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

with Drawing(file='led-circuit.svg') as d:
    # Vertical 5V DC voltage source on the left with "+" on top
    vsrc = d.add(elm.SourceV().up().label('+5V', loc='top'))

    # Top branch - just a wire
    d += elm.Line().right()

    # Right side of the circuit vertical resistor to LED
    d += elm.Resistor().down().label('150Ω')
    d += elm.LED().down().label('Red LED')

    # Horizontal line back toward the battery
    d += elm.Line().left().length(3)

    # Draw ground here
    gnd = d.add(elm.Ground())

    # Connect ground up to the negative battery terminal with a separate line
    # Draw a vertical line up from the ground to the negative terminal
    # Do not draw over the battery
    d += elm.Line().up().length(3)

    # Save PNG with white background
    fig = d.draw(show=False)
    fig.savefig('led-circuit.png', dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')

Prompt

Please generate a new schemadraw python program for the LED circuit. However, please place the 150K resistor vertically in the upper right and place the LED vertically under the resistor. Keep the ground on the bottom.

from schemdraw import Drawing
import schemdraw.elements as elm

with Drawing(file='led_circuit_vertical.svg') as d:
    d.config(unit=3)  # spacing between components
    d += elm.SourceV().at((0, 0)).up().label('+5V', loc='top')
    d += elm.Line().right(d.unit * 2)  # horizontal wire to the right
    d.push()  # save the position at top of resistor
    d += elm.Resistor().down().label('150Ω', loc='center')
    d += elm.LED().down().label('Red LED', loc='center')
    d += elm.Ground()
    d.pop()  # return to top of resistor
    d += elm.Line().left(d.unit * 2)  # wire returning to negative side of power
    d += elm.Line().down(d.unit * 3)  # connect back to ground line


from schemdraw import Drawing
import schemdraw.elements as elm

with Drawing(file='led_circuit_clean.svg') as d:
    d.config(unit=3)

    # Start at bottom (Ground)
    d += elm.Ground()                  # Ground
    d += elm.LED().up().label('Red LED', loc='right')   # LED pointing up
    d += elm.Resistor().up().label('150Ω', loc='right') # Resistor above LED

    d.push()  # Save position at top of resistor
    d += elm.Line().left(d.unit * 3)   # Horizontal line left to +5V line
    d += elm.SourceV().down().label('+5V', loc='left')  # Vertical power source back to ground
    d += elm.Line().right(d.unit * 3)  # Horizontal line to complete loop
    d.pop()                            # Restore top of resistor (to show full closed loop)

docs.title: Phase Spectrum: What the Magnitude Hides
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/phase-spectrum/main.html" width="100%" height="638px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A magnitude spectrum \(|X(f)|\) tells you which frequencies are present and how strong they are. The phase spectrum \(\angle X(f)\) tells you how those components line up in time, and that is what gives a signal its shape. The View radio buttons switch between three experiments.

A: Harmonics. The signal is \(x(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} A_k \cos(2\pi k f_0 t + \phi_k)\) with \(f_0 = 1\) Hz and fixed amplitudes \(A_k = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13\). Three sliders set the phases \(\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3\) (−180° to 180°), and the preset buttons load all 0°, a sawtooth (all −90°), a delay (−60°, −120°, −180°) or random phases. The magnitude bars never move, the RMS stays 0.825, but the waveform and its peak change. The dashed gray curve is the same magnitudes with every phase set to 0.

B: Time shift. A Gaussian pulse, rectangular pulse or sawtooth (100 samples over 1 s, so the DFT bins are 1 Hz apart) is delayed by \(\tau\). The shift theorem

\[x(t - \tau) \;\longleftrightarrow\; X(f)\,e^{-j2\pi f \tau}\]

leaves \(|X(f)|\) unchanged and adds a phase ramp of slope \(-2\pi\tau\) rad/Hz. The phase is shown wrapped to \((-\pi, \pi]\) or, with Unwrap phase, as a continuous line. A cursor reads \(|X|\) and \(\angle X\) at one frequency. Bins with \(|X|\) below 0.1% of the maximum have no meaningful phase and are marked ×.

C: Swap. Two signals A and B go through a 256-point DFT and are rebuilt from the magnitude of one and the phase of the other, from the magnitude alone (zero phase), or from the phase alone (\(|X| = 1\)). The read-outs give the correlation coefficient \(r\) of each rebuilt signal with A and with B.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain why signals with identical magnitude spectra can have very different waveforms and peak values
  2. Identify phases that grow linearly with frequency, \(\phi_k = k\,\phi_1\), as a pure time delay \(\tau = -\phi_1 / (360^\circ f_0)\)
  3. Calculate the phase \(-2\pi f \tau\) added by a delay \(\tau\) and the interval \(1/|\tau|\) at which the wrapped phase repeats
  4. Distinguish \(2\pi\) wrapping jumps from \(\pi\) jumps caused by sign changes of a real spectrum
  5. Analyze the swap experiment to conclude that the timing of a signal's features is carried by its phase

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a first signals and systems or digital signal processing course who have met the DFT. Plan 25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex numbers in polar form, magnitude and angle (see the Complex Plane MicroSim)
  • Sinusoids \(A\cos(2\pi f t + \phi)\) and what the phase \(\phi\) does to them
  • The DFT and the magnitude spectrum (Chapter 7)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Same magnitudes, different shapes (6 min). In view A the default phases are all −90° (the Sawtooth preset): the read-out shows peak \(|x|\) = 1.44 and RMS = 0.825. Press All 0°. The three cosines now peak together at \(t = 0\) and the peak rises to 1.83, yet the magnitude bars and the RMS (0.825) do not change. Press Delay (−60°, −120°, −180°): the blue curve is the dashed all-0° curve moved right by 0.167 s, and the peak is again 1.83. Set the phases to −45°, −90° and −135°: the note reports a pure delay of 0.125 s. Now move only \(\phi_2\) to −80°: the phases are no longer proportional to \(k\), and the shape changes.

Activity 2: A delay is a phase ramp (7 min). Choose view B with the Gaussian pulse and \(\tau\) = 0.05 s. The header reports slope \(-2\pi\tau\) = −0.314 rad/Hz (−18.0°/Hz) and a wrap every 20.0 Hz. With the cursor at 5 Hz the read-out shows \(\angle X\) = −90.0°; at 15 Hz it shows +90.0°, because −270° wraps to +90°. Check Unwrap phase: the same bin now reads −4.712 rad (−270.0°), and the dots form one straight line down to −12.252 rad at 39 Hz (bins 40-50 are marked undefined). Set \(\tau\) = 0.10 s: the slope doubles to −0.628 rad/Hz and the wrapped phase repeats every 10.0 Hz. Set \(\tau\) = −0.05 s: the phase now rises by 18° per hertz (+90.0° at 5 Hz). Through all of this \(|X(5\ \text{Hz})|\) stays at 0.895.

Activity 3: Not every jump is a wrap (6 min). Choose the sawtooth with \(\tau\) = 0: every defined bin from 1 to 48 Hz has phase +90°, a horizontal line. Choose the rectangular pulse, still at \(\tau\) = 0: the phase is 0° up to 9 Hz and 180° from 10 to 18 Hz, because the pulse's sinc-shaped spectrum is real and changes sign. Set \(\tau\) = 0.05 s with the cursor at 9 and then 10 Hz: the phase goes from −162° to 0° instead of falling another 18°. Check Unwrap phase: the dots follow the dashed line until 9 Hz, then climb by \(\pi\) at each sign change, while keeping the slope \(-2\pi\tau\) between the jumps.

Activity 4: The swap experiment (6 min). Choose view C with A = rectangular pulse, B = damped chirp and Swap the phases. \(|A|\) with \(\angle B\) oscillates like the chirp (\(r_A\) = −0.18, \(r_B\) = 0.64), and \(|B|\) with \(\angle A\) is a pulse between 0.10 and 0.25 s (\(r_A\) = 0.64, \(r_B\) = −0.08). Change A to the sawtooth burst: again each result follows its phase source (\(r_B\) = 0.74 and \(r_A\) = 0.74). Switch to Zero phase (|X| only): both rebuilt signals are symmetric about \(t = 0\) with their peak at \(t\) = 0.000 s, whatever the original timing. Switch to Phase only (|X| = 1): the rebuilt pulse is reduced to spikes at its edges, 0.10 and 0.25 s, and still correlates with A (\(r_A\) = 0.41).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. In view A, all-0° phases give a peak of 1.83 and all −90° phases give 1.44. Why is the RMS 0.825 in both cases? Answer: the power of a sum of sinusoids at different frequencies depends only on their amplitudes: \(\sqrt{(1^2 + 0.5^2 + 0.333^2)/2} = 0.825\). Phase moves energy around in time but does not change it.
  2. What waveform do the phases −45°, −90° and −135° produce for the 1, 2 and 3 Hz harmonics? Answer: the phases are \(k \times (-45^\circ)\), a linear phase, so the result is the all-0° waveform delayed by \(\tau = 45^\circ / (360^\circ \times 1\ \text{Hz}) = 0.125\) s, with the same peak of 1.83.
  3. A wrapped phase spectrum falls by 36° per hertz and wraps every 10 Hz. What delay produced it? Answer: slope \(-2\pi\tau\) = −36°/Hz gives \(\tau = 36/360 = 0.10\) s; the wrap interval \(1/\tau\) = 10 Hz agrees.
  4. A pulse is delayed by 0.02 s. What phase does the delay add at 50 Hz, and why can the wrapped phase at that one frequency not reveal the delay? Answer: \(-2\pi \times 50 \times 0.02 = -2\pi\) rad, which wraps to 0, exactly as for no delay. One wrapped phase only fixes \(\tau\) up to multiples of \(1/f\); the slope across many frequencies (unwrapped) is needed.
  5. A rebuilt signal uses the magnitude of a rectangular pulse and the phase of a damped chirp. Which original does it resemble, and what does that say about phase? Answer: the chirp (\(r_B\) = 0.64 against \(r_A\) = −0.18). Where edges and oscillations occur in time is encoded in the phase, so structure follows the phase.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The magnitude spectrum describes the signal; the phase is a minor detail." View A keeps \(|X|\) fixed while the peak moves between 1.44 and 1.83, and view C shows that a magnitude combined with someone else's phase looks like that someone else. With zero phase every signal collapses to a shape centred on \(t = 0\).

"Every jump in a phase plot is a \(2\pi\) wrap." Wrapping jumps are \(2\pi\) and disappear when you unwrap. The rectangular pulse in view B also has jumps of \(\pi\) where its spectrum changes sign; unwrapping cannot remove them, and they are not part of the delay.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Discrete Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the DFT used in views B and C, including its circular shift property
  2. Linear phase - Wikipedia - why a phase proportional to frequency is a pure delay that preserves waveform shape
  3. Group delay and phase delay - Wikipedia - delay as minus the slope of the phase, the quantity read from view B
  4. Phase unwrapping - Wikipedia - removing \(2\pi\) jumps and the ambiguities that remain
  5. Crest factor - Wikipedia - peak-to-RMS ratio, which changes with phase in view A while the RMS does not
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT, polar notation and phase

docs.title: Phasor Addition
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/phasor-addition/main.html" width="100%" height="612px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows that adding sinusoids of the same frequency is the same as adding vectors. Each sinusoid \(A_k\cos(\omega_1 t + \phi_k)\) is represented by its phasor \(A_k e^{j\phi_k}\), and

\[\sum_k A_k\cos(\omega_1 t + \phi_k) = \mathrm{Re}\Big\{\Big(\sum_k A_k e^{j\phi_k}\Big)e^{j\omega_1 t}\Big\} = |R|\cos(\omega_1 t + \angle R).\]

Engineers write \(j\) for \(\sqrt{-1}\), the \(i\) of Euler's formula. The left panel uses the colours of the Euler's Formula Explorer: a blue real axis, a red imaginary axis and a green vector, here the resultant \(R = \sum_k A_k e^{j\phi_k}\). Up to three phasors (orange, purple, brown) are drawn head to tail and turn together at \(\omega_1 = 2\pi f_1\). The blue dot is the resultant's projection on the real axis, which is the value of the sum at that instant. The right panel plots each waveform as a thin line, the sum as a thick green line, the envelope \(\pm|R|\) as dashed lines, and a gold cursor at the current time over an 8 s window.

Each phasor has a checkbox, an amplitude slider (0 to 2) and a phase slider (−180° to 180°). Speed sets \(f_1\) (0.10 to 2.00 Hz). The MicroSim opens paused at \(t = 0\), so each arrow sits at its phase angle \(\phi_k\); Play starts the rotation, Pause stops it, and Reset returns to \(t = 0\) and pauses. The read-out gives \(R\) in polar and rectangular form. Phasor 2 at f₂ makes phasor 2 turn at a second frequency \(f_2\). The resultant's length then changes with time, the dashed envelope becomes \(\pm|R(t)|\), and the read-out gives the beat frequency \(|f_2 - f_1|\).

This simulation is used in Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the resultant phasor \(R = \sum_k A_k e^{j\phi_k}\) for up to three sinusoids of one frequency and write their sum as \(|R|\cos(\omega t + \angle R)\)
  2. Predict from the phase difference whether two sinusoids reinforce, partly cancel or cancel completely, using \(|R| = 2A|\cos(\Delta\phi/2)|\) for equal amplitudes
  3. Demonstrate with the speed slider that the resultant amplitude and phase do not depend on the rotation rate \(\omega\) when every phasor shares that frequency
  4. Relate the projection of the rotating resultant onto the real axis to the value of the summed waveform at the cursor
  5. Analyze the sum of two sinusoids at different frequencies as a resultant whose length changes with time, and calculate the beat frequency \(|f_2 - f_1|\) and the envelope range

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a first signals and systems or circuits course. Plan about 25 minutes for the activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex numbers in rectangular and polar form (see the Complex Plane MicroSim)
  • Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta\)
  • Amplitude, frequency and phase of a sinusoid

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Two phasors at right angles (6 min). Start from the default settings: phasor 1 is \(1.00\angle 0°\), phasor 2 is \(1.00\angle 90°\), phasor 3 is off and \(f_1 = 0.50\) Hz. Press Reset: arrow 1 lies on the real axis and arrow 2 points straight up from its tip. The read-out shows \(R = 1.41\angle 45.0°\) \(= 1.00 + j1.00\), and the thick green sum peaks at 1.41, not 2: the sum is \(1.41\cos(\omega_1 t + 45.0°)\). At \(t = 0\) the blue dot sits at 1.00, the same value as the green dot on the cursor. Press Play and check that the two stay equal. Then move the speed from 0.50 Hz to 1.50 Hz: the plot shows 12 cycles in the 8 s window instead of 4 and \(\omega_1\) rises from 3.14 to 9.42 rad/s, but \(R\) stays \(1.41\angle 45.0°\).

Activity 2: The phase difference decides (5 min). Keep \(A_1 = A_2 = 1.00\) and \(\phi_1 = 0°\), and set \(\phi_2\) to each value below. Compare each read-out with \(|R| = 2\cos(\phi_2/2)\):

  • \(\phi_2 = 0°\): \(R = 2.00\angle 0.0°\), the amplitudes add
  • \(\phi_2 = 60°\): \(R = 1.73\angle 30.0°\)
  • \(\phi_2 = 120°\): \(R = 1.00\angle 60.0°\), the sum is no larger than either input
  • \(\phi_2 = 180°\): the read-out says \(R = 0\) and the green sum is flat

Activity 3: A balanced three-phase set (5 min). Check Phasor 3 and set all three amplitudes to 1.00 with \(\phi_1 = 0°\), \(\phi_2 = 120°\) and \(\phi_3 = -120°\). The three arrows close an equilateral triangle, \(R = 0\), and the sum is flat although each waveform has amplitude 1. This is why the currents of a balanced three-phase load cancel in the neutral wire. Now set \(A_3 = 0.50\): the triangle no longer closes and \(R = 0.50\angle 60.0°\) \(= 0.25 + j0.43\).

Activity 4: Beats (7 min). Set \(A_1 = A_2 = 1.00\), \(\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 0°\), phasor 3 off and \(f_1 = 1.00\) Hz. Check Phasor 2 at f₂ and set \(f_2 = 1.25\) Hz. Phasor 2 now gains a quarter turn per second on phasor 1, so the length of \(R\) swings between 0.00 and 2.00. The read-out gives a beat frequency of 0.25 Hz and a beat period of 4.00 s. In the first window the dashed envelope \(2|\cos(\pi \cdot 0.25\,t)|\) touches zero at \(t = 2\) s and \(t = 6\) s, and the sum reaches 2 at \(t = 0\), 4 and 8 s. Then set \(A_2 = 0.50\): \(|R(t)|\) now swings between 0.50 and 1.50 and the sum never dies out.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Write \(1.5\cos(\omega t) + 2\cos(\omega t + 90°)\) as a single sinusoid. Answer: \(R = 1.5 + j2.0 = 2.50\angle 53.1°\), so the sum is \(2.50\cos(\omega t + 53.1°)\). Check it with \(A_1 = 1.50\), \(A_2 = 2.00\), \(\phi_2 = 90°\).
  2. What is \(2\cos(\omega t + 30°) + 2\cos(\omega t - 30°)\)? Answer: \(|R| = 2 \cdot 2\cos 30° = 3.46\) and the imaginary parts cancel, so the sum is \(3.46\cos(\omega t)\).
  3. Phasors \(1\angle 0°\) and \(1\angle 90°\) are fixed. Which third phasor makes the sum zero? Answer: it must cancel \(R = 1.41\angle 45°\), so \(A_3 = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\) at \(\phi_3 = -135°\). The slider moves in 0.05 steps; \(A_3 = 1.40\) leaves \(|R| = 0.01\).
  4. Two tones of amplitude 1 and zero phase have frequencies 0.80 Hz and 1.00 Hz. What are the beat frequency and the beat period, and when does the sum first vanish? Answer: 0.20 Hz and 5.00 s. The envelope \(2|\cos(\pi \cdot 0.20\,t)|\) is first zero at \(t = 2.5\) s, and again at 7.5 s.
  5. Why can't the two tones in question 4 be replaced by one phasor? Answer: the angle between them grows by \(2\pi(f_2 - f_1)t\), so their vector sum has no fixed length. Its length, the envelope, varies between \(|A_1 - A_2|\) and \(A_1 + A_2\).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"The amplitudes of two sinusoids add." Only phasors that point the same way add their lengths. At the default settings \(1.00\angle 0°\) plus \(1.00\angle 90°\) gives a sum with amplitude 1.41. Only \(\phi_2 = 0°\) gives 2.00.

"The phase of the sum is the average of the phases." That is true only for equal amplitudes, as at the default settings (\(45°\) halfway between \(0°\) and \(90°\)). Set \(A_1 = 2.00\): the read-out shows \(R = 2.24\angle 26.6°\), because the longer arrow pulls the resultant toward itself.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Phasor - Wikipedia - phasor notation, phasor addition and the link to Euler's formula
  2. Euler's formula - Wikipedia - why \(A\cos(\omega t + \phi) = \mathrm{Re}\{Ae^{j\phi}e^{j\omega t}\}\)
  3. Beat (acoustics) - Wikipedia - interference of two tones and the beat frequency \(|f_1 - f_2|\)
  4. Three-phase electric power - Wikipedia - balanced phasors 120° apart that sum to zero
  5. Complex number - Wikipedia - rectangular and polar forms used in the read-out
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with a chapter on complex numbers

docs.title: Power Spectral Density and the Wiener-Khinchin Theorem
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/psd-wiener-khinchin/main.html" width="100%" height="786px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The Wiener-Khinchin theorem says that the power spectral density (PSD) of a wide-sense stationary process is the Fourier transform of its autocorrelation, \(S(\omega) = \sum_k r[k]\,e^{-j\omega k}\). This MicroSim estimates the PSD of a random record in two ways and compares both with the exact \(S(\omega)\).

The Process list offers white noise, a first-order autoregressive process AR(1) \(x[n] = a\,x[n-1] + w[n]\), a moving average of \(q\) noise samples, and a sinusoid in noise. The first slider sets \(a\) (−0.95 to 0.95), \(q\) (1 to 32) or the frequency \(\omega_0\). Every process is driven by the same unit-variance white noise \(w[n]\) from a seeded generator: New realization draws new noise and Reset seed returns to seed 1, so comparisons are reproducible. Record length sets \(N\) (64 to 4096) and Averages sets the number of segments \(K\).

  • Top: the first 512 samples of \(x[n]\), with the analysis segments in gold.
  • Middle: the biased sample autocorrelation \(\hat r[k] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_n x[n]\,x[n+k]\) (blue), the theoretical \(r[k]\) (black rings) and the lag window \(c[k]\) (gold).
  • Bottom: the PSD in dB for \(0 \le \omega \le \pi\) rad/sample. Maroon: the averaged periodogram of \(K\) segments of \(M\) samples, with Hann windows and 50% overlap (Welch) or rectangular windows without overlap (Bartlett). Green: the Wiener-Khinchin estimate \(\sum_{|k|<M} c[k]\,\hat r[k]\,e^{-j\omega k}\). Dashed: the theoretical \(S(\omega)\).

The lag window is matched to the segment window, so the two estimates have nearly the same mean. With one rectangular segment, \(c[k] = 1\) at every lag and the curves coincide exactly, because \(|X(\omega)|^2/N\) is the Fourier transform of \(\hat r[k]\). The read-outs give the RMS dB difference between the estimates and each one's RMS error against theory. Point at a lag to read \(\hat r[k]\) and \(r[k]\), or at the PSD to read the three values at one frequency.

This MicroSim is used in Chapter 12: Stochastic Processes and Random Signals.

docs.title: The Four Processes
docs.text:
With \(\sigma^2 = 1\):

Process Autocorrelation \(r[k]\) PSD \(S(\omega)\) White noise \(x[n] = w[n]\) \(\delta[k]\) \(1\) (0 dB) AR(1) \(x[n] = a\,x[n-1] + w[n]\) \(a^{\lvert k\rvert}/(1 - a^2)\) \(1/(1 - 2a\cos\omega + a^2) = 1/\lvert 1 - a e^{-j\omega}\rvert^2\) MA(q) \(x[n] = (w[n] + \dots + w[n-q+1])/\sqrt{q}\) \(1 - \lvert k\rvert/q\) for \(\lvert k\rvert < q\), else 0 \(\sin^2(q\omega/2)\,/\,\big(q\sin^2(\omega/2)\big)\) Sinusoid \(\sqrt{2}\cos(\omega_0 n + \phi) + w[n]\) \(\cos(\omega_0 k) + \delta[k]\) \(1 + \pi[\delta(\omega - \omega_0) + \delta(\omega + \omega_0)]\)

docs.title: How the Two Estimates Are Computed
docs.text:
The averaged periodogram uses segments of \(M = \lfloor N/K \rfloor\) samples (Bartlett) or \(M = \lfloor 2N/(K+1) \rfloor\) samples with a hop of \(M/2\) (Welch), a window \(v[n]\) with \(U = \sum_n v^2[n]\), and

\[\hat S_{\text{avg}}(\omega) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=0}^{K-1} \frac{1}{U}\left|\sum_{n=0}^{M-1} v[n]\,x[n + iD]\,e^{-j\omega n}\right|^2 .\]

Its mean is \(\sum_{|k|<M} c_v[k]\,r[k]\,e^{-j\omega k}\), where \(c_v[k] = \frac{1}{U}\sum_n v[n]\,v[n+|k|]\) is the autocorrelation of the window. Because \(E\{\hat r[k]\} = (1 - |k|/N)\,r[k]\), the Wiener-Khinchin estimate uses \(c[k] = c_v[k]\) for the Hann window and \(c[k] = (1 - |k|/M)/(1 - |k|/N)\) for the rectangular window. The Hann choice can never produce a negative PSD; the rectangular one can dip below zero at a few frequencies (this happens for the sinusoid with \(K\) = 2 to 5), and the read-out then says so. The RMS error against theory is measured where \(S(\omega)\) is within 40 dB of its maximum, which skips the exact zeros of the moving average.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain the Wiener-Khinchin theorem and verify that the periodogram of one rectangular segment equals the Fourier transform of the biased sample autocorrelation
  2. Calculate \(r[k]\), \(S(0)\) and \(S(\pi)\) for AR(1) and moving-average processes from their closed forms
  3. Analyze how the number of averaged segments \(K\) trades variance against frequency resolution, using the RMS error against theory and the depth of the moving-average nulls
  4. Relate features of an autocorrelation (decay rate, alternating sign, finite length, a component that never decays) to features of the PSD
  5. Distinguish agreement between two estimates from accuracy against the true PSD

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a digital signal processing, random signals or communications course (junior or senior year). Plan 30 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The DFT and decibels
  • Mean, variance and the autocorrelation of a wide-sense stationary process
  • Windowing a finite record (Chapter 7)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
All numbers below are for seed 1, the seed on page load (press Reset seed to return to it). Point at a lag in the autocorrelation panel, or at a frequency in the PSD panel, to read the values there.

Activity 1: The theorem, exactly (6 min). Keep the defaults (AR(1), \(a = 0.90\), \(N = 1024\)), choose Bartlett and drag \(K\) to 1. The gold lag window becomes a flat line at 1, the green curve lies exactly on the maroon one, and the read-out reports an RMS difference of 0.00 dB: the periodogram is the Fourier transform of \(\hat r[k]\), term by term. Both curves are nevertheless far from theory (RMS error 6.35 dB). Now set \(N\) = 64, 256 and 4096: the difference stays 0.00 dB and the error stays large (6.06, 5.40 and 6.33 dB). A longer record does not make a single periodogram more accurate.

Activity 2: Averaging trades variance for resolution (10 min). Choose Welch, \(N = 4096\), and step \(K\) through 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 and 63 (so \(M\) = 4096, 2048, 1024, 512, 256, 128). The Welch error against theory falls from 6.18 to 2.85, 1.72, 1.15, 0.73 and 0.57 dB, and the two estimates converge on each other (RMS difference 4.68, 1.51, 0.75, 0.43, 0.28, 0.19 dB). Now choose the moving average with \(q = 8\) and repeat \(K\) = 15, 31, 63. The exact PSD is zero at \(\omega = \pi/4\), but the Welch estimate there reads −33.03, −26.12 and −19.40 dB: shorter segments smear power into the null. The error against theory is smallest at \(K = 31\) (0.83 dB) and rises again at \(K = 63\) (1.14 dB), where this bias outweighs the lower variance.

Activity 3: Read the spectrum from the autocorrelation (8 min). Use Welch, \(N = 1024\), \(K = 7\). With \(a = 0.90\) the autocorrelation decays slowly (theory \(r[0] = 5.26\), \(r[1] = 4.74\); the record gives \(\hat r[1] = 4.31\)) and the PSD is low-pass: theory 20.00 dB at \(\omega = 0\) and −5.58 dB at \(\pi\) (the estimates read 20.39 and 18.52 dB at \(\omega = 0\)). Set \(a = -0.90\): \(\hat r[k]\) alternates in sign (\(\hat r[1] = -4.31\)) and the PSD flips to high-pass, 20.00 dB at \(\omega = \pi\). Set \(a = 0\): \(\hat r[k]\) is a single spike and the PSD is flat at 0 dB. Choose the moving average with \(q = 8\) and \(K = 15\): \(\hat r[k]\) is a triangle that reaches zero at \(|k| = 8\), and the theoretical PSD (9.03 dB at \(\omega = 0\)) has nulls at \(\omega = \pi/4\), \(\pi/2\) and \(3\pi/4\), the multiples of \(2\pi/q\).

Activity 4: A correlation that never dies (6 min). Choose the sinusoid with \(\omega_0 = 0.25\pi\), Welch, \(N = 1024\). The autocorrelation is a cosine with a period of 8 lags that does not decay: \(\hat r[0] = 1.98\) (power 1 from the sinusoid plus 1 from the noise), \(\hat r[4] = -0.98\), \(\hat r[8] = 0.95\). The PSD shows a line on a 0 dB floor. Point at \(\omega = 0.250\pi\) and step \(K\) through 1, 3, 7, 15 and 31: the Welch peak reads 25.22, 22.21, 19.26, 16.26 and 13.35 dB, about 3 dB lower each time \(M\) is halved, while the floor stays at 0 dB. The line's power is fixed; the estimate spreads it over a main lobe of width proportional to \(1/M\).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. An AR(1) process has \(a = 0.5\) and \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Find \(r[0]\), \(r[1]\), and \(S(\omega)\) at \(\omega = 0\) and \(\omega = \pi\) in dB. Answer: \(r[0] = 1/(1 - 0.25) = 1.33\) and \(r[1] = 0.67\); \(S(0) = 1/(1 - 0.5)^2 = 4\), or 6.02 dB; \(S(\pi) = 1/1.5^2 = 0.44\), or −3.52 dB. Pointing at \(\omega = 0\) in the sim shows a theory value of 6.02 dB.
  2. With Bartlett and \(K = 1\) the two curves coincide exactly. State the identity behind this. Answer: for a record of \(N\) samples, \(\frac{1}{N}|X(\omega)|^2 = \sum_{k=-(N-1)}^{N-1} \hat r[k]\,e^{-j\omega k}\) with the biased estimate \(\hat r[k] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_n x[n]\,x[n+|k|]\). It is the Wiener-Khinchin theorem applied to the data themselves.
  3. Why does the RMS error of a single periodogram stay near 6 dB when \(N\) grows from 64 to 4096, and what reduces it? Answer: a larger \(N\) gives more frequency samples but each still has a standard deviation about equal to its mean, so the estimate does not converge. Averaging \(K\) segments reduces the variance roughly \(K\)-fold, at the cost of resolution \(\propto 1/M\).
  4. For the moving average with \(q = 4\), give \(r[k]\) and the frequencies where \(S(\omega) = 0\). Why does the estimate not reach \(-\infty\) dB there? Answer: \(r[k]\) = 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25 for \(|k|\) = 0 to 3 and 0 beyond; nulls at \(\omega = \pi/2\) and \(\pi\). The window's main lobe and sidelobes leak power from neighbouring frequencies into the null (with \(N = 1024\) and Welch \(K = 15\) the estimate at \(\pi/2\) reads −27.40 dB).
  5. With the sinusoid, the Welch peak is 19.26 dB for \(M = 256\). Predict it for \(M = 128\), and explain why the peak height is not the sinusoid's power. Answer: about 3 dB lower; the sim shows 16.26 dB. A spectral line has a fixed power (its area); a window of \(M\) samples spreads that power over a main lobe of width about \(1/M\), so the peak height grows in proportion to \(M\).

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A longer record gives a more accurate periodogram." In Activity 1 the single-segment error stays between 5.4 and 6.4 dB from \(N = 64\) to \(N = 4096\). Only averaging reduces it: Welch with \(N = 4096\) and \(K = 63\) reaches 0.57 dB.

"If two PSD estimates agree, they are correct." With Bartlett and \(K = 1\) the two estimates differ by 0.00 dB, yet each is 6.35 dB RMS from the true PSD. Their agreement demonstrates the Wiener-Khinchin identity, not accuracy: both are computed from the same noisy record and make the same errors.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Wiener–Khinchin theorem - Wikipedia - the theorem that the PSD of a wide-sense stationary process is the Fourier transform of its autocorrelation
  2. Spectral density - Wikipedia - definition and properties of the power spectral density
  3. Periodogram - Wikipedia - the raw PSD estimate and why its variance does not fall as the record grows
  4. Welch's method - Wikipedia - averaging windowed, overlapping periodograms
  5. Bartlett's method - Wikipedia - averaging periodograms of non-overlapping segments, and its link to a triangular lag window
  6. Autoregressive model - Wikipedia - the AR(1) process, its autocorrelation \(a^{|k|}/(1-a^2)\) and its spectrum
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook covering the DFT, windows and noise spectra

docs.title: Quantization and Noise Shaping
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/quantization-and-noise-shaping/main.html" width="100%" height="632px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim quantizes a full-scale waveform with a uniform mid-rise quantizer and shows the result in the time domain and in the frequency domain. With \(b\) bits and a full-scale range \(V = 2\) (from \(-1\) to \(+1\)) there are \(2^b\) levels, a step size of

\[\Delta = \frac{V}{2^b}\]

and an error \(e[n] = x_q[n] - x[n]\) that is never larger than \(\Delta/2\). Everything on the screen is computed from the actual samples: the error spectrum comes from a radix-2 FFT and the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio (SQNR) is measured from it.

Five controls change the experiment:

  • Signal selects a sinusoid, a triangle wave or a three-harmonic waveform with a 547 Hz fundamental.
  • Oversampling sets the sampling rate to 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 times 40 kHz.
  • Bit depth b sets the number of bits from 1 to 16.
  • Noise shaping switches an error-feedback loop between off, 1st order and 2nd order.
  • Show low-pass filtered output adds the signal and the error left after an ideal 20 kHz low-pass filter.

The banner compares the SQNR measured in the 0 to 20 kHz signal band with the white-noise model, and the two numbers under the spectrum give the noise in the signal band and the total noise. This simulation supports the section on quantization in Chapter 5: Sampling and Quantization.

docs.title: The Four Plots
docs.text:
From top to bottom:

  1. Original signal \(x(t)\): the chosen waveform, four milliseconds of it.
  2. Quantized signal \(x_q[n]\), drawn as a staircase. The horizontal lines are the quantization levels (drawn up to 32 levels).
  3. Quantization error \(e[n]\), in units of the step size \(\Delta\).
  4. Spectrum of the error from 0 to \(f_s/2\), computed from the samples with an FFT. The shaded band from 0 to 20 kHz is the signal band. The dashed curve is the white-noise model described below.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
The white-noise model. If the error behaves like noise that is uniformly distributed over \([-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]\), its power is \(\sigma_e^2 = \Delta^2/12\) and it is spread evenly from 0 to \(f_s/2\). For a full-scale sinusoid this gives

\[\text{SQNR} \approx 6.02\,b + 1.76\ \text{dB}\]

The banner shows this prediction next to the value measured from the actual samples. The two agree well for many bits and drift apart for few bits, where the error of a simple waveform is not noise-like at all: it is a distortion locked to the signal.

Oversampling. Sampling at \(f_s = \text{OSR} \times 40\) kHz leaves the total error power unchanged but spreads it over a band that is OSR times wider. A digital low-pass filter that keeps only 0 to 20 kHz then removes all but \(1/\text{OSR}\) of it, a gain of 3 dB (half a bit) for every doubling of the sampling rate.

Noise shaping. A noise shaper feeds the previous quantization errors back to the quantizer input, so that the error appears at the output multiplied by a high-pass noise transfer function:

Modulator order Noise transfer function Total noise power In-band gain per doubling of OSR Off \(1\) \(\Delta^2/12\) 3 dB 1st order \(1 - z^{-1}\) \(2 \times \Delta^2/12\) about 9 dB 2nd order \((1 - z^{-1})^2\) \(6 \times \Delta^2/12\) about 15 dB

Noise shaping does not reduce the total noise. It increases it, and moves almost all of it above the signal band where the low-pass filter removes it. The two numbers under the spectrum (noise in the signal band and total noise) show this directly. Tick Show low-pass filtered output to see the filtered signal (green) and the error that is left.

With noise shaping the quantizer input can exceed full scale by up to \(\Delta/2\) (first order) or \(3\Delta/2\) (second order). The shaped quantizer is therefore given a few extra levels above and below full scale, drawn dashed; the caption reports how many levels are in use. Practical delta-sigma converters instead keep the input a little below full scale.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Leave oversampling at 1× and noise shaping off. Move the Bit depth slider and watch the staircase, the error and the SQNR.
  2. Choose an Oversampling ratio. The spectrum axis stretches to the new \(f_s/2\) while the shaded signal band stays at 20 kHz.
  3. Switch Noise shaping to 1st or 2nd order and compare the two noise figures under the spectrum.
  4. Tick Show low-pass filtered output to see what a decimation filter recovers.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this activity, students will be able to:

  1. Explain why quantization is irreversible and why the error is bounded by half a step.
  2. Predict the SQNR of a full-scale sinusoid from the bit depth.
  3. Describe the quantization error in time and in frequency, and say when the white-noise model fails.
  4. Explain how oversampling and noise shaping raise the SQNR in the signal band without lowering the total noise.
  5. Evaluate when noise shaping helps and when it makes the in-band SQNR worse.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in signals and systems or digital signal processing. Plan 20-25 minutes for the activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sampling and the Nyquist frequency
  • Decibels and signal power
  • The idea of a frequency spectrum

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Six decibels per bit (5 min). Choose Sinusoid, 1× oversampling, noise shaping off. Set the bit depth to 2, 4, 8 and 16. The step size reads 0.5, 0.125, 0.00781 and \(3.05\times10^{-5}\), and the measured SQNR is 12.8, 25.3, 49.6 and 97.5 dB (the rule \(6.02\,b + 1.76\) gives 13.8, 25.8, 49.9 and 98.1 dB). From 8 to 16 bits the SQNR rises by 47.9 dB, which is 6.0 dB per bit. The error plot always spans \(\pm\Delta/2\).

Activity 2: When the white-noise model fails (10 min). Keep Sinusoid and noise shaping off, set the bit depth to 4 and raise oversampling from 1× to 16×. The model promises a gain of 12 dB (25.8 to 37.9 dB), but the measured SQNR rises only from 25.3 to 28.5 dB and the total noise stays at -25.3 dBFS. Look at the error plot: it is a repeating sawtooth pattern locked to the signal, not noise, so much of its power falls inside the signal band. Now set the bit depth to 12: the measured value is 84.1 dB against 86.0 dB for the model, much closer, because the error has become noise-like.

Activity 3: Noise shaping needs oversampling (10 min). Set 4 bits, 16×, and step the noise shaping through Off, 1st order and 2nd order. The in-band SQNR is 28.5, 56.1 and 73.3 dB, while the total noise rises from -25.3 to -22.7 and -18.1 dBFS: the noise is moved out of the band, not removed. Now set oversampling to 1× and repeat: the SQNR falls to 25.3, 22.5 and 18.3 dB, because the signal band covers the whole spectrum and there is no empty band to push the noise into.

Activity 4: Few bits, high rate (5-10 min). Set 2 bits, 16×, 2nd-order noise shaping and tick the filtered output. The staircase uses 8 levels (4 plus headroom levels) and looks nothing like the input, yet the green filtered signal follows the input closely and the measured SQNR is 60.1 dB. A plain quantizer needs about 10 bits for this: 9 bits measure 55.6 dB and 10 bits measure 62.2 dB. Discussion: a delta-sigma audio converter uses a quantizer with very few bits at a sampling rate of several megahertz. Which part of the system turns that coarse stream into 16 or more useful bits? The digital low-pass (decimation) filter, which removes the shaped noise above the signal band and reduces the sampling rate.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A converter has 12 bits and a full-scale range of \(V = 2\). What are the step size and the predicted SQNR for a full-scale sinusoid? Answer: \(\Delta = 2/4096 = 4.88\times10^{-4}\) and SQNR \(\approx 6.02 \times 12 + 1.76 = 74.0\) dB. The simulation measures 74.8 dB.
  2. At 8 bits and 1× oversampling the sinusoid gives 49.6 dB but the triangle wave gives 47.7 dB. Why, when the step size is the same? Answer: the noise power is about the same (\(\Delta^2/12\)), but the triangle wave has less signal power (0.34 against 0.5), so the ratio is smaller.
  3. At 4 bits and 16× oversampling with noise shaping off, the model predicts 37.9 dB but the measured SQNR is 28.5 dB. Why is the model wrong here? Answer: the white-noise model assumes the error is spread evenly over 0 to \(f_s/2\). At 4 bits the error is a distortion locked to the signal, so a large part of its power lies inside the 20 kHz band and the filter removes little of it.
  4. At 4 bits and 16×, 2nd-order shaping raises the SQNR from 28.5 to 73.3 dB. Did the quantization noise decrease? Answer: no. The total noise rose from -25.3 to -18.1 dBFS (about 7 dB, a factor of about 5). The noise in the signal band fell because the shaping moved it above 20 kHz.
  5. At 4 bits and 1× oversampling, why does 2nd-order shaping lower the SQNR from 25.3 to 18.3 dB? Answer: at 1× the signal band is the whole spectrum up to \(f_s/2\). The noise transfer function has a gain above 1 for \(f > f_s/6\), so the noise is amplified in the band and there is no empty band to move it into.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Quantization error is always white noise that is unrelated to the signal." For few bits the error is a distortion that follows the signal. At 4 bits the error plot is a repeating sawtooth and the measured SQNR is 28.5 dB at 16×, 9.4 dB below the white-noise model. The model works well only when the bit depth is large enough.

"Noise shaping removes quantization noise." It moves noise. The total-noise figure under the spectrum goes up with shaping (from -25.3 to -18.1 dBFS at 4 bits) while the noise in the signal band goes down.

"Oversampling adds resolution without any filtering." The total noise does not depend on the oversampling ratio. The gain appears only when a low-pass filter discards the part of the noise above the signal band; tick the filtered output to see it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Quantization (signal processing) - Wikipedia - uniform quantization, step size and the error model
  2. Noise shaping - Wikipedia - error feedback and the noise transfer function
  3. Delta-sigma modulation - Wikipedia - oversampling converters that combine a coarse quantizer with noise shaping
  4. Oversampling - Wikipedia - why a higher sampling rate lowers the in-band quantization noise
  5. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook; Chapter 3 (ADC and DAC) covers quantization and oversampling
  6. Chapter 5: Sampling and Quantization - this textbook - where the MicroSim is used

Print references: Bennett, W. R. (1948), "Spectra of quantized signals", Bell System Technical Journal 27(3), 446-472. Oppenheim, A. V., and Schafer, R. W. (2010), Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., Pearson, Chapter 4.

docs.title: RC Low-Pass Filter Bode Plot
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/rc-lowpass-filter/main.html" width="100%" height="604px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim draws the Bode plot of the simplest analog filter: a resistor \(R\) in series with the signal and a capacitor \(C\) from the output to ground. The top plot is the gain in decibels and the bottom plot is the phase in degrees. Both share a logarithmic frequency axis from 1 Hz to 100 kHz.

  • Resistance R steps through the standard E12 resistor values from 10 Ω to 100 kΩ (12 values per decade).
  • Capacitance C steps through the E12 capacitor values from 1 nF to 100 µF.
  • Show straight-line asymptotes adds the grey dashed straight-line approximations that are used to sketch Bode plots by hand.

The read-outs at the top give the time constant \(\tau = RC\) and the corner frequency \(f_c = 1/(2\pi RC)\). The orange dashed line marks \(f_c\). The orange dots mark the two values that hold for every first-order low-pass filter: a gain of \(-3\) dB and a phase of \(-45°\) at \(f_c\). The black triangle spans one decade well above \(f_c\) and shows the gain falling by 20 dB across it. Hover over either plot to move the grey cursor and read the gain and phase at that frequency. The cursor snaps to \(f_c/10\), \(f_c\), \(10f_c\) and \(100f_c\), and it follows \(f_c\) when you move a slider.

This simulation supports the low-pass filter section of Chapter 9: Filter Design Fundamentals.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
The capacitor and resistor form a voltage divider whose ratio depends on frequency:

\[H(f) = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{1/(j2\pi f C)}{R + 1/(j2\pi f C)} = \frac{1}{1 + j f/f_c}, \qquad f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC} = \frac{1}{2\pi\tau}\]

The plotted gain and phase are

\[G(f) = 20\log_{10}|H(f)| = -10\log_{10}\left(1 + (f/f_c)^2\right) \text{ dB}, \qquad \angle H(f) = -\arctan(f/f_c)\]

At \(f = f_c\) the gain is \(-10\log_{10} 2 = -3.01\) dB (\(|H| = 1/\sqrt{2} = 0.707\)) and the phase is \(-45°\). Well above \(f_c\), \(|H(f)| \approx f_c/f\), so the gain falls by 20 dB for every factor of 10 in frequency (about 6 dB per octave) and the phase approaches \(-90°\). The straight-line asymptotes are 0 dB below \(f_c\) and \(-20\log_{10}(f/f_c)\) dB above it for the gain, and for the phase 0° below \(f_c/10\), \(-90°\) above \(10f_c\), and a straight line through \(-45°\) at \(f_c\) in between.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the time constant \(\tau = RC\) and the corner frequency \(f_c = 1/(2\pi RC)\) for given values of \(R\) and \(C\).
  2. Identify the \(-3\) dB gain and the \(-45°\) phase at the corner frequency on a Bode plot.
  3. Explain why the gain falls by 20 dB per decade and the phase approaches \(-90°\) well above \(f_c\).
  4. Predict how changing \(R\) or \(C\) moves the Bode plot along the frequency axis without changing its shape.
  5. Select standard E12 values of \(R\) and \(C\) that place the corner frequency near a target frequency.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a signals and systems, circuits, or introductory signal processing course. Plan 20-30 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complex numbers, magnitude and phase
  • Decibels and logarithms
  • The impedance of a resistor (\(R\)) and of a capacitor (\(1/(j2\pi fC)\))

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Find the corner (5 min). Start from the default \(R = 1\) kΩ and \(C = 1\) µF.

  • Confirm the read-outs: \(\tau = 1.00\) ms and \(f_c = 1/(2\pi \times 0.001) = 159\) Hz.
  • The cursor starts at \(f_c\). Read \(|H| = 0.707 = -3.01\) dB on the gain plot and \(-45.0°\) on the phase plot.

Activity 2: Measure the roll-off (5 min). Keep the default values and hover near the triangle.

  • Move the cursor to \(10f_c = 1.59\) kHz (it snaps there). The gain is \(-20.04\) dB (\(|H| = 0.0995\)) and the phase is \(-84.3°\).
  • Move it to \(100f_c = 15.9\) kHz. The gain is \(-40.00\) dB and the phase is \(-89.4°\). The triangle shows the same drop of \(-20.0\) dB over that decade.
  • Move it to \(f_c/10 = 15.9\) Hz. The gain is only \(-0.04\) dB and the phase is \(-5.7°\).

Activity 3: Only the product RC matters (5 min). Set \(R = 10\) kΩ and \(C = 1\) µF, then \(R = 1\) kΩ and \(C = 10\) µF.

  • Both give \(\tau = 10.0\) ms and \(f_c = 15.9\) Hz, and the two Bode plots are identical.
  • Now set \(R = 10\) kΩ and \(C = 10\) nF. Then \(\tau = 100\) µs and \(f_c = 1.59\) kHz: the whole curve moves two decades to the right without changing shape.

Activity 4: Design with standard parts (10 min). Choose components for a corner near 1 kHz with \(C = 100\) nF.

  • The exact value would be \(R = 1/(2\pi \times 1000 \times 100\text{ nF}) = 1.59\) kΩ, which is not an E12 value.
  • Try the neighbours: 1.5 kΩ gives \(f_c = 1.06\) kHz and 1.8 kΩ gives \(f_c = 884\) Hz.
  • Find another pair that comes closer (for example 3.3 kΩ with 47 nF gives \(f_c = 1.03\) kHz).

Activity 5: How good is the sketch? (5 min). Turn Show straight-line asymptotes on and compare the dashed lines with the curves.

  • The largest gain error is 3.01 dB, exactly at \(f_c\).
  • The largest phase error is 5.7°, at \(f_c/10\) and at \(10f_c\).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. A filter uses \(R = 4.7\) kΩ and \(C = 10\) nF. What are \(\tau\) and \(f_c\)? (Answer: \(\tau = 47\) µs and \(f_c = 1/(2\pi \times 47\ \mu\text{s}) = 3.39\) kHz.)
  2. What are the gain and the phase of any first-order RC low-pass filter at its corner frequency? (Answer: \(|H| = 1/\sqrt{2} = 0.707\), which is \(-3.01\) dB, and the phase is \(-45°\).)
  3. A filter has \(f_c = 200\) Hz. Estimate its gain at 20 kHz. (Answer: 20 kHz is two decades above \(f_c\), so the gain is about \(-40\) dB. The exact value is \(-40.0\) dB.)
  4. You double \(R\) and leave \(C\) unchanged. What happens to \(f_c\) and to the shape of the Bode plot? (Answer: \(f_c\) halves, so the curves move left by \(\log_{10}2 = 0.30\) decade. Their shape does not change.)
  5. Why does the gain fall by 20 dB per decade well above \(f_c\)? (Answer: for \(f \gg f_c\), \(|H(f)| \approx f_c/f\). A factor of 10 in \(f\) divides \(|H|\) by 10, which is \(20\log_{10}10 = 20\) dB.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "The cutoff frequency is where the filter stops passing signals." At \(f_c\) the output still has 70.7% of the input amplitude, and at \(2f_c\) it still has 44.7% (\(-6.99\) dB). Hover just above \(f_c\) and watch the gain fall gradually: an RC filter attenuates, it does not block.
  • "A larger resistor or capacitor raises the cutoff." Move either slider to the right and the orange line moves to the left. Because \(f_c = 1/(2\pi RC)\), a larger \(R\) or \(C\) means a slower filter and a lower corner.
  • "The straight-line sketch is the real response." Turn the asymptotes on: the true curve lies 3 dB below the corner of the sketch.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. RC circuit - Wikipedia - derivation of the RC low-pass transfer function, time constant and cutoff frequency
  2. Bode plot - Wikipedia - gain and phase plots on a logarithmic frequency axis and their straight-line approximations
  3. Low-pass filter - Wikipedia - first-order low-pass filters and the 20 dB per decade roll-off
  4. Cutoff frequency - Wikipedia - the -3 dB (half-power) definition of the corner frequency
  5. E series of preferred numbers - Wikipedia - the E12 values used by the R and C sliders
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on filters and on analog electronic filters

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text:
Version 2.0 (October 2026) rebuilt the original page, which used Plotly, as a p5.js 2.3.2 sketch. Changes from version 1:

  • The two number boxes and the Generate Bode Plot button were replaced by sliders that step through standard E12 values, so the plot updates as you drag. Values outside 10 Ω to 100 kΩ and 1 nF to 100 µF can no longer be entered.
  • The frequency axis now runs from 1 Hz to 100 kHz (it was 10 Hz to 100 kHz).
