docs.title: System Interconnections: Series, Parallel, Feedback
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/system-interconnections/main.html" width="100%" height="662px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim builds a system from two blocks, \(H_1\) and \(H_2\), and shows how the behavior of the whole follows from the parts. Everything runs in discrete time at \(f_s = 100\) Hz (\(T = 0.01\) s). Each block is one of:

  • Gain \(K\) (−2 to 2): \(y[n] = K\,x[n]\), so \(H(z) = K\)
  • Low-pass with time constant \(\tau\) (0.01 to 0.50 s): \(y[n] = a\,y[n-1] + (1-a)\,x[n]\) with \(a = e^{-T/\tau}\), so \(H(z) = (1-a)/(1 - a z^{-1})\)
  • Delay of \(D\) samples (1 to 50, that is 0.01 to 0.50 s): \(y[n] = x[n-D]\), so \(H(z) = z^{-D}\)

The Topology menu connects them in series, \(H = H_1 H_2\); in parallel, \(H = H_1 + H_2\); in a negative-feedback loop, \(H = H_1/(1 + H_1 H_2)\), with \(H_1\) in the forward path and \(H_2\) in the return path; or as a feedforward structure, \(H = 1 + H_1 H_2\), where the input reaches the summing junction both directly and through \(H_1\) then \(H_2\), and no signal travels backward.

The block diagram redraws as you change the menus and sliders, and the feedback loop turns red when it is unstable. Below it the sim prints the overall \(H(z)\), the difference equation that implements it, and the DC gain \(H(1)\). The pole-zero plot marks poles with × and zeros with ○, gives the largest pole magnitude, and shows a badge: stable (all poles inside \(|z| = 1\)), marginally stable (poles on the circle), unstable (a pole outside), or ill-posed (a loop with no delay in which \(1 + H_1 H_2 = 0\), so \(y[n]\) cannot be computed). The bottom plots show the step response \(s[n]\) and the impulse response \(h[n]\) from 0 to 2 s. Values beyond ±4 are clipped and drawn in red.

This simulation is used in Chapter 3: System Properties and Analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Calculate the overall transfer function of two blocks connected in series (\(H_1 H_2\)), in parallel (\(H_1 + H_2\)), in negative feedback (\(H_1/(1 + H_1 H_2)\)) and as a feedforward structure (\(1 + H_1 H_2\))
  2. Derive the difference equation of the combined system from \(H(z)\) and use it to predict the step and impulse responses
  3. Classify the combined system as stable, marginally stable or unstable from the largest pole magnitude
  4. Analyze how a delay inside a feedback loop produces oscillation, and instability when the loop gain exceeds 1, while the same blocks connected without a loop stay stable
  5. Explain the trade-off negative feedback makes between DC gain and speed of response

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a first signals and systems course (sophomore or junior engineering, physics or computer science). Plan 25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Impulse response, step response and BIBO stability (Chapter 3)
  • Difference equations and the meaning of \(z^{-1}\) as a one-sample delay
  • Complex numbers in polar form, for reading the pole-zero plot

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Series and parallel (5 min). Press Reset, then set H₁ = Gain with \(K_1 = 0.80\) and H₂ = Delay with \(D_2 = 10\) (these are the defaults). Choose Series: \(H(z) = 0.8z^{-10}\), the impulse response is a single spike of 0.8 at \(t = 0.10\) s, and the step response stays at 0 until 0.10 s and then holds at 0.8. Choose Parallel: \(H(z) = 0.8 + z^{-10}\), the impulse response has spikes of 0.8 at \(t = 0\) and 1 at \(t = 0.10\) s, and the step response steps to 0.8 and then to 1.8 (\(H(1) = 1.800\)). Both systems are FIR: the only poles are 10 poles at \(z = 0\), and the badge says stable.

Activity 2: Two low-pass blocks (5 min). Set both blocks to Low-pass with \(\tau = 0.10\) s, so each has \(a = 0.905\). In Series the read-out shows a double pole at \(z = 0.905\) and \(H(1) = 1.000\). The step response is S-shaped and first reaches 63% of its final value at \(t = 0.20\) s; a single block (change H₂ to Gain with \(K_2 = 1.00\)) reaches 63% at \(t = 0.09\) s. In Parallel with both blocks at \(\tau = 0.10\) s the two identical poles merge into one, \(H(z) = 0.19/(1 - 0.905z^{-1})\), and \(H(1) = 2.000\).

Activity 3: Feedback trades gain for speed (5 min). Choose Negative feedback, H₁ = Low-pass with \(\tau_1 = 0.10\) s and H₂ = Gain. With \(K_2 = 0\) there is no feedback: pole \(z = 0.905\) (\(\tau = 0.100\) s) and \(H(1) = 1.000\). With \(K_2 = 1.00\) the pole moves to \(z = 0.826\) (\(\tau = 0.052\) s), \(H(1) = 0.500\), and the step response reaches 63% of its final value at \(t = 0.05\) s. With \(K_2 = 2.00\) the pole is \(z = 0.760\) (\(\tau = 0.036\) s), \(H(1) = 0.333\) and the 63% point is at \(t = 0.03\) s. These are close to the continuous-time prediction \(\tau/(1 + K)\): 0.050 s and 0.033 s.

Activity 4: A delay in the loop (10 min). Press Reset (negative feedback, \(K_1 = 0.80\), \(D_2 = 10\)). The loop equation is \(y[n] = 0.8x[n] - 0.8y[n-10]\), so each correction arrives 0.10 s late. The step response alternates 0.80, 0.16, 0.672, 0.262 and settles toward \(H(1) = 0.444\); the 10 poles lie on \(|z| = 0.978\). Raise \(K_1\) to 1.00: the badge changes to marginally stable, the poles sit on the unit circle and the step response becomes a square wave between 1 and 0 with period 0.20 s that never decays. Raise \(K_1\) to 1.20: the poles move out to \(|z| = 1.018\), the oscillation grows, and the step response leaves the ±4 display range at \(t = 1.00\) s. Now keep \(K_1 = 1.20\) and switch the topology to Feedforward: \(H(z) = 1 + 1.2z^{-10}\) is stable, and its 10 zeros lie on \(|z| = 1.018\), exactly where the feedback loop put its poles. Finally return to Negative feedback and change H₂ to Gain (\(K_2 = 1.00\)): without the delay the loop is just the constant \(H = 1.2/2.2 = 0.545\), with no poles.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. H₁ is a gain of 2 and H₂ a gain of 1 in negative feedback. What is the overall system? Answer: \(H = 2/(1 + 2 \cdot 1) = 0.667\), a memoryless gain with no poles; the sim shows \(H(z) = 0.667\).
  2. H₁ is a gain of 0.5 and H₂ a delay of 5 samples in negative feedback. Find \(H(z)\), the pole magnitude and the DC gain. Answer: \(H(z) = 0.5/(1 + 0.5z^{-5})\). The poles solve \(z^5 = -0.5\), so all five have \(|z| = 0.5^{1/5} = 0.871\) and the system is stable, with \(H(1) = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333\).
  3. H₁ is a gain of −1 and H₂ a low-pass with \(\tau = 0.10\) s, connected in parallel. What are \(H(1)\) and \(h[0]\), and what kind of filter is this? Answer: \(H(1) = -1 + 1 = 0\) and \(h[0] = -1 + 0.0952 = -0.905\). The system blocks DC and passes sudden changes: it is an inverted high-pass filter, \(H(z) = (-0.905 + 0.905z^{-1})/(1 - 0.905z^{-1})\).
  4. A gain of 1.2 and a delay of 10 samples are unstable in negative feedback but stable in series, parallel and feedforward. Why? Answer: only the feedback connection has a loop. Its denominator \(1 + 1.2z^{-10}\) has poles at \(|z| = 1.2^{1/10} = 1.018\). In the other connections the denominator is just \(A_1 A_2 = 1\), so the poles are those of the blocks, all at \(z = 0\).
  5. In negative feedback with \(K_1 = -0.80\) and \(D_2 = 10\) (that is, positive feedback), what final value does the step response approach? Answer: \(H(1) = -0.8/(1 - 0.8) = -4.0\). The output moves toward −4 without oscillating and reads −3.95 at \(t = 1.99\) s.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Feedback always makes a system more stable." Negative feedback steadies the low-pass in Activity 3, but with a delay in the loop the same idea fails: the correction arrives late and pushes in the wrong direction. With \(K_1 = 1.20\) and \(D_2 = 10\) the badge reads unstable, while the same two blocks in series, parallel or feedforward are stable.

"Marginally stable means the output stays bounded." Set negative feedback with \(K_1 = -1.00\) and \(D_2 = 10\). The poles lie on the unit circle (one is at \(z = 1\)) and the badge says marginally stable, yet the step response steps down by 1 every 0.10 s and reaches −20 at \(t = 1.99\) s. A pole on the unit circle means the system is not BIBO stable, and \(H(1)\) is infinite.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Block diagram - Wikipedia - drawing systems as blocks joined by signal lines and summing junctions
  2. Negative feedback - Wikipedia - the closed-loop gain \(G/(1 + GH)\) and its trade-off between gain and speed
  3. Feed forward (control) - Wikipedia - systems that act on the input without a feedback loop
  4. Comb filter - Wikipedia - the feedforward and feedback forms of a gain plus a delay, as in Activity 4
  5. BIBO stability - Wikipedia - why poles must lie inside the unit circle for a bounded output
  6. Z-transform - Wikipedia - transfer functions in \(z^{-1}\), poles, zeros and the region of convergence
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on recursive filters and the z-transform

docs.title: System Property Explorer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/system-property-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="617px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Each system property is a statement that two signals must be equal. This MicroSim builds both signals for the system you select and overlays them on the output plot. When a property holds, the dashed orange curve lies exactly on the solid blue one. When it fails, the curves separate, and the panel below the plots reports the maximum difference and a one-line reason.

Use the System menu to choose one of eight example systems and the Test menu to run a linearity, time-invariance, causality or BIBO stability test. The Amplitude A, Frequency f and Time shift \(t_0\) sliders change the test input, so you can check whether a verdict depends on the input. The frequency slider is greyed out for the stability test, which uses a step. Five badges across the top give the true classification of the selected system, and the badge for the running test has a heavy outline.

The simulation illustrates superposition, time shifting, the rule that a causal output cannot depend on future input, and the definition of BIBO stability. It also makes a point of logic: one example can disprove a property but cannot prove it. It supports the section on system properties in Chapter 3: System Properties and Analysis.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
Test What is compared Input used Linearity \(\mathcal{T}[A x_1 + x_2]\) against \(A\,\mathcal{T}[x_1] + \mathcal{T}[x_2]\) \(x_1\) is a sine burst, \(x_2\) is a 2 s pulse starting at \(t_0\) Time-invariance \(\mathcal{T}[x(t - t_0)]\) against \(y(t - t_0)\) A sine burst of amplitude \(A\) Causality Outputs for two inputs that are identical up to \(t_0\) A sine burst, and the same burst with 1 added after \(t_0\) BIBO stability Whether the output stays bounded The bounded step \(A\,u(t - t_0)\)

The sine burst is \(\sin(2\pi f t)\) for \(0 \le t \le 4\) s and zero elsewhere. The badges give the true classification of the selected system:

System Linear Time-invariant Causal BIBO stable Memoryless Amplifier \(y(t) = 2x(t)\) yes yes yes yes yes Linear filter \(y(t) = \int_{t-1}^{t} x(\tau)\,d\tau\) yes yes yes yes no Time-varying multiplier \(y(t) = t\,x(t)\) yes no yes no yes Squarer \(y(t) = x^2(t)\) no yes yes yes yes Compressor \(y(t) = \tanh(x(t))\) no yes yes yes yes Predictor \(y(t) = x(t + 1)\) yes yes no yes no Integrator \(y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} x(\tau)\,d\tau\) yes yes yes no no Offset \(y(t) = x(t) + 1\) no yes yes yes yes

One example can disprove a property, but cannot prove it

A property must hold for every input. A single pair of curves that separate is enough to show that a property fails. Curves that match only show that the property holds for those inputs. For some slider settings a nonlinear system passes the linearity comparison by coincidence (try the squarer with \(A = 1\) and \(t_0 = 4\) s, where the burst and the pulse do not overlap). The MicroSim then reports that the system is not linear and that these inputs do not show it.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Choose a System and a Test.
  2. Compare the solid blue and dashed orange curves on the output plot. Read the verdict and the one-line reason in the panel below the plots.
  3. Move Amplitude, Frequency and Time shift to change the test input and check whether the verdict depends on the input.
  4. For the causality test the vertical dashed line marks \(t_0\), where the two inputs begin to differ. A thick red trace marks any output difference that appears before \(t_0\).
  5. For the stability test the dotted red lines mark the input bound \(\pm A\).

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this activity, students will be able to:

  1. Explain the superposition principle and test a system for linearity.
  2. Distinguish time-invariant systems from time-varying systems using a shifted input.
  3. Determine whether a system is causal by comparing outputs for inputs that agree up to a given time.
  4. Classify a system as BIBO stable or unstable from its response to a bounded input.
  5. Evaluate why a single matching example cannot prove that a system has a property.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in an introductory signals and systems course. Plan 20-25 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Signals as functions of time, time shifting
  • The unit step function
  • Basic integration

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Predict first (5 min). Before running any test, fill in a table of the four tested properties for \(y(t) = 2x(t)\), \(y(t) = t\,x(t)\), \(y(t) = x^2(t)\) and \(y(t) = x(t+1)\). Then select each system and read the badges.

  • The amplifier has all four properties.
  • The multiplier is linear and causal but not time-invariant and not BIBO stable.
  • The squarer is time-invariant, causal and stable but not linear.
  • The predictor is linear, time-invariant and stable but not causal.

Activity 2: Put a number on each failure (10 min). Keep the defaults \(A = 2\) and \(t_0 = 2\) s unless stated.

  • Select the time-varying multiplier and the time-invariance test. The maximum difference is 4.00. Explain this number from \(\mathcal{T}[x(t - t_0)] - y(t - t_0) = t_0\,x(t - t_0)\), whose peak is \(t_0 A\).
  • Select the offset system and the linearity test. The maximum difference is 2.00. Set \(A = 1\) and then \(A = 3\): it becomes 1.00 and 3.00, so it equals \(A\) for every setting. Explain why from the two expressions in the reason line.
  • Select the integrator and the stability test. The panel reports a magnitude of 16.0 at \(t = 10\) s. Compare it with \(A\,(10 - t_0) = 2 \cdot 8 = 16\).
  • Select the predictor and the causality test. The thick red trace runs from \(t = 1\) s to \(t = 2\) s and the difference is up to 1.00. Why does the trace start 1 s before \(t_0\)?

Activity 3: Matching curves that prove nothing (5 min). Select the squarer and the linearity test.

  • Set \(A = 1\) and \(t_0 = 4\) s. The curves coincide and the maximum difference is 0.00, but the verdict reads "Not linear, but these inputs do not show it".
  • Raise \(A\) to 2. The curves separate and the maximum difference becomes 2.00 (it is 6.00 when \(t_0 = 2\) s).
  • Switch to the compressor. With \(A = 1\) and \(t_0 = 4\) s it also passes; at \(A = 2\) the difference is 0.56.

Activity 4: Bounded or unbounded? (5 min). Run the stability test with \(A = 2\) and \(t_0 = 2\) s on four systems.

  • Linear filter: the magnitude never exceeds 2.00, which is \(A\) times the 1 s window.
  • Compressor: the magnitude never exceeds 0.96, which is \(\tanh(2)\).
  • Integrator: the output is still growing at \(t = 10\) s and has reached 16.0.
  • Time-varying multiplier: the output is still growing and has reached 20.0, which is \(A\,t\) at \(t = 10\) s.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. State both parts of linearity and say which one the offset system \(y(t) = x(t) + 1\) violates. (Answer: additivity, \(\mathcal{T}[x_1 + x_2] = \mathcal{T}[x_1] + \mathcal{T}[x_2]\), and homogeneity, \(\mathcal{T}[a x] = a\,\mathcal{T}[x]\). The offset system violates both: \(\mathcal{T}[x_1 + x_2] = x_1 + x_2 + 1\) but \(\mathcal{T}[x_1] + \mathcal{T}[x_2] = x_1 + x_2 + 2\), and \(\mathcal{T}[a x] = a x + 1\) but \(a\,\mathcal{T}[x] = a x + a\). The test shows a difference of \(A\).)
  2. Why is \(y(t) = t\,x(t)\) linear but time-varying? (Answer: the gain \(t\) multiplies every input in the same way, so superposition holds. Delaying the input gives \(t\,x(t - t_0)\), but delaying the output gives \((t - t_0)\,x(t - t_0)\). The two differ by \(t_0\,x(t - t_0)\), which peaks at 4.00 for \(A = 2\) and \(t_0 = 2\) s.)
  3. Give a bounded input that produces an unbounded output for the integrator. (Answer: the step \(A\,u(t - t_0)\) integrates to the ramp \(A\,(t - t_0)\), which grows without limit. At \(t = 10\) s with \(A = 2\) and \(t_0 = 2\) s it has reached 16.)
  4. The squarer passes the linearity comparison for \(A = 1\) and \(t_0 = 4\) s. Is the squarer linear? (Answer: no. The burst and the pulse do not overlap, so the cross term \(2A\,x_1 x_2\) is zero and \(A = 1\) hides the \(A^2 - A\) term. A counterexample such as \(A = 2\) disproves linearity; matching curves cannot prove it.)
  5. For \(y(t) = x(t + 1)\), which property fails and what does the red trace show? (Answer: causality. The output at time \(t\) uses \(x(t + 1)\), so inputs that differ only after \(t_0\) already give different outputs from \(t_0 - 1\) to \(t_0\). The red trace marks that interval.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "A system whose equation contains \(t\) multiplied by \(x(t)\) is nonlinear." Select the time-varying multiplier. The linearity curves coincide, but the time-invariance curves separate. The system is linear and time-varying.
  • "Adding a constant keeps a system linear." Select the offset system and the linearity test. The curves separate by \(A\) at every setting, because a zero input does not give a zero output.
  • "One passing example proves that a property holds." The squarer passes the linearity comparison at \(A = 1\) and \(t_0 = 4\) s. BIBO stability has the same limit: the MicroSim tests one bounded input, a step, whereas the definition requires a bounded output for every bounded input.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Linear time-invariant system - Wikipedia - definition of linearity and time invariance and the properties of LTI systems
  2. BIBO stability - Wikipedia - bounded-input bounded-output stability and its test for linear systems
  3. Causal system - Wikipedia - definition of causality and examples of non-causal systems
  4. Linear system - Wikipedia - the superposition principle behind the linearity test
  5. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on linear systems and convolution
  6. Oppenheim, A. V., Willsky, A. S., & Nawab, S. H. (1997). Signals and Systems (2nd ed.). Prentice Hall. Chapter 1 covers the basic system properties: memory, invertibility, causality, stability, time invariance and linearity.

docs.title: Time-Frequency Analysis Explorer
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/time-frequency-analysis-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="607px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A single Fourier transform says which frequencies a signal contains but not when they occur. The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) answers both questions by transforming one short, windowed frame after another:

\[X[m,k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n + mH]\,w[n]\,e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\]

Frame \(m\) holds \(N\) samples starting at sample \(mH\), where \(H\) is the hop size, multiplied by a window \(w[n]\). A spectrogram is a picture of \(\lvert X[m,k]\rvert\) with time across, frequency upward and colour for level.

The signal is one second long, sampled at \(f_s = 8000\) Hz. The display has three plots:

  1. Waveform with a red time cursor. The shaded band marks the \(N\) samples of the frame at the cursor.
  2. Spectrogram. Each frame is drawn at the centre of its \(N\) samples and each bin at its centre frequency, so every coloured rectangle is one value of \(X[m,k]\). The grey strips at the two ends are times for which no complete window fits.
  3. Spectrum at the cursor, drawn sideways so that it shares the frequency axis of the spectrogram. The dashed line marks the frequency the signal really has at that instant, and the colour bar underneath is the key to the spectrogram colours.

Choose the Signal and the Window type from the menus, set the Window length N (32 to 1024 samples) and the Overlap (0 to 90%) with the sliders, and pick the Colour map and Scale (magnitude in dB, linear magnitude or linear power). Click or drag in the waveform or the spectrogram to move the cursor. This MicroSim supports the section on spectral analysis in Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis.

docs.title: Mathematical Concepts
docs.text:
The trade-off. A window of \(N\) samples spans a time \(\Delta t = N/f_s\) and gives bins spaced \(\Delta f = f_s/N\) apart, so

\[\Delta t \times \Delta f = 1\]

whatever \(N\) is. A long window separates close frequencies but smears anything that changes during the window. A short window follows fast changes but gives wide frequency bins. This is the uncertainty principle of time-frequency analysis: both resolutions cannot be made fine together.

Window length \(N\) 32 64 128 256 512 1024 Time span \(\Delta t\) (ms) 4 8 16 32 64 128 Bin spacing \(\Delta f\) (Hz) 250 125 62.5 31.25 15.63 7.81

Overlap sets the hop size, \(H = N(1 - \text{overlap})\) rounded to a whole number of samples, and the number of frames is \(\lfloor (8000 - N)/H \rfloor + 1\). More overlap gives more frames and a smoother picture along the time axis, but it does not improve the resolution: that is fixed by \(N\).

Level. Amplitudes are scaled so that a steady sinusoid of amplitude 1 centred on a bin reads 0 dB, and the dB scale spans 80 dB (from \(-80\) dB to 0 dB). The windows are the periodic (DFT-even) forms, so a tone centred on a bin occupies exactly three bins with the Hann window.

Signals. The chirp sweeps linearly from 500 to 3500 Hz, so its frequency is \(500 + 3000\,t\) Hz. The frequency-shift-keyed (FSK) signal sends 16 bits, each 62.5 ms long, as a 1 kHz or a 2 kHz tone. The note sequence plays C5, E5, G5, C6 and G5, each 200 ms long, as a plucked tone with three harmonics. All three are synthesized by the MicroSim; no recorded audio is used.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click or drag in the waveform or the spectrogram to move the time cursor.
  2. Move the Window length slider and watch the cells of the spectrogram change shape: tall and narrow for a short window, flat and wide for a long one.
  3. Move the Overlap slider and read the hop size and the number of frames in the box at the upper right.
  4. Point at the spectrogram to read the time, frequency and level of the cell under the mouse.
  5. Change the Window, the Colour map and the Scale.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain why a spectrogram is needed for a signal whose frequency content changes with time.
  2. Compute the time span, bin spacing and hop size of an STFT from the window length, sampling rate and overlap.
  3. Analyze how the window length trades time resolution against frequency resolution.
  4. Choose STFT settings that suit a given signal.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a digital signal processing course. Plan 30 minutes for the activities below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The DFT, bin spacing and window functions
  • Spectral leakage
  • Sampling rate and sample period

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: What a spectrogram adds (5 min). Choose the chirp, the Hanning window, \(N = 256\) and 50% overlap. Drag the cursor from the left to the right of the spectrogram.

  • The dashed line in the side panel rises with the cursor. At the frame centred at \(t = 0.496\) s it reads 1988 Hz, which is \(500 + 3000 \times 0.496\).
  • The peak of the spectrum at the cursor sits on that line: its strongest bin is 2000 Hz, within half a bin (15.6 Hz) of the true value.
  • A single DFT of the whole second would show energy between 500 and 3500 Hz but nothing about when each frequency occurs.

Activity 2: The resolution trade-off (10 min). Keep the chirp and the Hanning window and step \(N\) from 32 to 1024.

  • Check the banner against the table above: \(\Delta t\) doubles and \(\Delta f\) halves at each step, and their product is always 1.
  • The ridge is thickest at \(N = 32\) (about 800 Hz wide, measured 20 dB below its peak) and thins as \(N\) grows. It is thinnest at \(N = 256\) (about 150 Hz), then widens again: about 175 Hz at \(N = 512\) and about 310 Hz at \(N = 1024\).
  • The chirp rises 3000 Hz per second, so during a 128 ms window it moves \(3000 \times 0.128 = 384\) Hz. The bins are narrow at \(N = 1024\), but the window is too long for the frequency to hold still. The best compromise is near the \(N\) at which the Hanning main lobe (\(4f_s/N\)) equals the sweep during the window (\(3000N/f_s\)), which is \(N \approx 292\).
  • With \(N = 256\), switch between the rectangular and Hanning windows on the dB scale. At 40 dB below the peak the Hanning ridge is about 260 Hz wide but the rectangular ridge is about 2100 Hz wide: its slowly decaying sidelobes show as a haze around the ridge.

Activity 3: Bits and notes (10 min). Use the Hanning window and 50% overlap.

  • Choose the FSK signal with \(N = 64\). Each bit lasts 62.5 ms, the window only 8 ms, so the bit edges are sharp. Each tone is a band of three bins (375 Hz) at 1000 or 2000 Hz.
  • Change to \(N = 1024\). Each tone is now a thin line, but the 128 ms window is longer than two bits, so the edges are blurred and in 8 of the 14 frames both tones are above \(-20\) dB at once. At \(N = 64\) only 6 of the 249 frames show both. Which \(N\) would you use to read the bits?
  • Choose the note sequence. Put the cursor at \(t \approx 0.24\) s (E5, 659 Hz) and at \(t \approx 0.44\) s (G5, 784 Hz). With \(N = 32\) both notes have the same strongest bin, 750 Hz. From \(N = 64\) upward they fall in different bins, and at \(N = 256\) the strongest bins are 656 Hz and 781 Hz, within 3 Hz of the true values.
  • At \(N = 1024\) find the harmonics of one note: G5 shows peaks near 784, 1568 and 2352 Hz.

Activity 4: What overlap does (5 min). With the chirp and \(N = 256\) change the overlap from 0% to 90%.

  • At 0% the hop is 256 samples (32 ms) and there are 31 frames. At 50% it is 128 samples and 61 frames. At 90% it is 26 samples (3.25 ms) and 298 frames.
  • The picture becomes smoother along the time axis, but the thickness of the ridge does not change. Overlap fills in the picture; only \(N\) and the window type change the resolution.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. For \(N = 512\) at \(f_s = 8000\) Hz, what are the time span and the bin spacing? \(\Delta t = 512/8000 = 64\) ms and \(\Delta f = 8000/512 = 15.6\) Hz; the product is 1.
  2. For \(N = 128\) and 75% overlap, what are the hop size and the number of frames in one second of signal? \(H = 128 \times 0.25 = 32\) samples (4 ms) and \(\lfloor (8000 - 128)/32 \rfloor + 1 = 247\) frames.
  3. Why does no window length give sharp time resolution and sharp frequency resolution together? Because \(\Delta t \times \Delta f = 1\): shortening the window to localize an event in time widens the bins by the same factor.
  4. For the chirp, why is the ridge thinner at \(N = 256\) than at \(N = 1024\) even though the bins are four times narrower at \(N = 1024\)? The frequency moves 384 Hz during the 128 ms window, which smears the ridge by more than the narrow bins save.
  5. Which window length would you choose to read the bits of the FSK signal, and which to measure the pitch of the notes? \(N = 64\) to \(128\) for the bits (8 to 16 ms against a 62.5 ms bit, and the tones are 8 to 16 bins apart); \(N = 256\) or more for the notes, where the bins are 31 Hz apart or less and the strongest bin lies within half a bin (16 Hz) of the pitch.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• A longer window always gives a better spectrogram. At \(N = 1024\) the chirp ridge is about twice as thick as at \(N = 256\) and the FSK bit edges are blurred over about 128 ms. Longer windows trade time resolution for frequency resolution.
  • Increasing the overlap improves the resolution. Move the Overlap slider: the hop and the number of frames change but the ridge keeps its thickness, because the resolution is set by \(N\) and the window.
  • The spectrogram shows the exact frequency at each instant. Compare the peak of the spectrum at the cursor with the dashed line: the peak is a bin centre, and each coloured cell stands for an interval of \(\Delta t\) and \(\Delta f\).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Short-time Fourier transform - Wikipedia - definition of the STFT, its frames, window and hop size
  2. Spectrogram - Wikipedia - how the squared magnitude of the STFT is displayed against time and frequency
  3. Window function - Wikipedia - Hann, Hamming, Blackman and rectangular windows and their sidelobes
  4. Chirp - Wikipedia - the linear sweep used as the first test signal
  5. Frequency-shift keying - Wikipedia - the two-tone digital signal used as the second test signal
  6. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT and on windows

Further reading (print): J. B. Allen and L. R. Rabiner, "A unified approach to short-time Fourier analysis and synthesis," Proceedings of the IEEE, 65(11), 1558-1564, 1977; A. V. Oppenheim and R. W. Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., Pearson, 2010, Chapter 10 (time-dependent Fourier analysis).

docs.title: Signal Processing Timeline
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/timeline-viewer/main.html" width="100%" height="752px"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

View the events in vis.js JSON format

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim is an interactive timeline of 50 milestones in the history of electronic signal processing. Each milestone is a box joined by a thin vertical line to a dot on the year axis. Boxes that would overlap are stacked in rows, so a year with several events (1996 has three) shows a column of boxes above one dot. The view opens on the years 1980 to 2000.

There are no buttons or sliders; you work directly on the timeline:

  • Pan: drag left or right to move through time. The timeline stops at 1800 and 2030.
  • Zoom: scroll the mouse wheel (or pinch on a touch screen) to widen or narrow the visible span. The span is limited to between 1 year and 40 years.
  • Read: the year axis at the bottom shows one label per year.

The events come from events.json, which lists an id, a text content and a start year for each milestone. The file was produced by an AI chatbot prompt (see Development Notes), so treat each year as a starting point for your own checking rather than as a citation.

The milestones touch many of the techniques taught in this book. This simulation belongs with Chapter 2: Introduction to Signals and Systems, and several entries point ahead to later chapters:

Milestone on the timeline Where this book covers the technique Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem Chapter 5: Sampling and Quantization Introduction of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis Development of Wavelet Transform for Signal Analysis Chapter 8: Advanced Transforms Introduction of Adaptive Filters, Invention of the Kalman Filter Chapter 11: Adaptive Signal Processing Invention of JPEG, Introduction of MPEG, Introduction of MP3 Chapter 13: Multirate Signal Processing and Compression

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Locate a milestone on the timeline by panning and zooming, and read its year from the axis.
  2. Compare the number of milestones in each decade and describe the pattern.
  3. Relate at least five milestones to the chapter of this book that covers the underlying technique.
  4. Evaluate the reliability of a one-year-per-event timeline by checking entries against an independent source.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates at the start of a signal processing course, or anyone using the book as a survey of the field. Plan 15 to 25 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: No mathematics is needed. Familiarity with the words sampling, filter and transform helps when relating milestones to chapters.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the opening view. Leave the timeline on its 1980 to 2000 opening view. Count the boxes dated 1980 to 1999: there are 17. Two more boxes, dated 2000 (First Software-Defined Radio and Multi-Input Multi-Output for Wireless Communication), sit on the right-hand edge. Find the year with three boxes: it is 1996 (digital hearing aids, HDTV standards and digital TV transmission), and the three connector lines meet the axis at a single dot.
  2. Zoom and pan across the whole list. Zoom out until the zoom stops at 40 years, then pan from the left limit to the right limit. The earliest entry is the telegraph (1837) and the latest is cloud-based signal processing (2022). Place a 40-year window at 1836 and both the telegraph (1837) and the telephone (1876) are visible, the longest gap between two consecutive event years in the list (39 years).
  3. Build a decade tally. Count the milestones in each decade and sketch a bar chart. Expected result: the 1990s have 11 milestones, the 1960s and the 1980s have 6 each, the 1970s, 2000s and 2010s have 5 each, and the 1950s have none. Discuss what could make a decade look busy or empty (see Common Misconceptions).
  4. Check three dates. Pick one entry that starts with "Invention of", one with "Introduction of" and one with "First". Look each up in an independent source (the Wikipedia articles under References are a start). Record the year you find and what that year marks: the first idea, a patent, a published standard, or a first product. Expected observation: you must decide which of these the entry means before you can say whether its year agrees.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. How many milestones does the timeline contain, and what are the earliest and latest years? 50 milestones, from 1837 (Invention of the Telegraph) to 2022 (First Commercial Use of Cloud-Based Signal Processing).
  2. Which decade contains the most milestones, and how many? The 1990s, with 11.
  3. "Introduction of Pulse Code Modulation (PCM)" is dated 1948 and "First Commercial Use of PCM in Telephone Systems" is dated 1968. How many years separate them, and what does that suggest about a single year per event? 20 years. An idea can be introduced long before it is deployed, so one year per event hides which stage the year marks.
  4. Which decades between the 1830s and the 2020s have no milestone at all? The 1840s, 1850s, 1860s, 1880s, 1910s and 1950s.
  5. Why should you check a date from this timeline against another source before citing it? The list was produced from a chatbot prompt with one year per entry and no sources, and its entries mix inventions, standards and first uses, so the year may refer to a different stage than you assume.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
• "The year on the timeline is when the technique was invented." Entries are worded differently ("Invention of", "Introduction of", "First Commercial Use of"), and the PCM pair shows a 20-year gap between introduction and commercial use. Zoom in on both entries and compare their wording.
  • "A busy decade means most progress happened then, and an empty decade means none did." The list was generated from a prompt asking for 50 milestones, so it is a sample. It has no entry for the 1950s and 11 for the 1990s, but the gap says only that the prompt's answer included none.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. vis-timeline Timeline documentation - visjs.github.io - the options and events used by this MicroSim (zoom limits, axis scale, item margins).
  2. vis-timeline on GitHub - GitHub - source and release history of the library loaded at version 7.7.3.
  3. Signal processing - Wikipedia - an independent overview for checking the scope and dates of milestones.
  4. Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem - Wikipedia - independent source for the first entry students can verify in Activity 4.
  5. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - independent source for the FFT entry and a bridge to Chapter 7.
  6. Fetch API - MDN Web Docs - the browser call the sketch uses to load events.json.

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text:
• Library: the page uses the standalone vis-timeline 7.7.3 build from a pinned CDN URL. It replaces the legacy vis 4.21.0 package. The new library reads a bare string such as "1980" as milliseconds, so timeline-viewer.js converts four-digit year strings to dates before building the timeline. events.json is unchanged.
  • Files: the entry page is main.html. timeline-viewer.html is a redirect stub so existing links keep working.
  • Iframe: the number of stacked rows depends on the page width, so the page height varies from about 700 px (wide) to about 1050 px (phone). The iframe is 752 px high, which fits widths of about 760 px and up, and it is left scrollable so narrower pages can still reach every row.
Prompt history
  • Timeline prompt page: the prompt that asked for 50 milestones in vis.js format.
  • ChatGPT dialog history

docs.title: Tone Generator MicroSim
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/tone-gen/main.html" width="100%" height="402px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim generates a pure sine tone \(x(t) = A\sin(2\pi f t)\), plays it through your speakers, and shows its magnitude spectrum from 0 to 10 kHz, computed live by a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Each blue bar shows the strongest FFT bin in a narrow band of frequencies. Heights are levels in decibels, \(L = 20\log_{10}(A)\) dB, so the top of the plot (0 dB) is a sine of amplitude 1.

  • Start/Stop turns the tone on and off. Nothing plays until you press Start.
  • Frequency (20 Hz to 10 kHz, default 440 Hz) sets \(f\). You can also press and drag horizontally across the plot: the frequency under the pointer is applied, so the peak follows the pointer.
  • Amplitude (0 to 0.50, default 0.20) sets \(A\). The default is deliberately quiet; set your volume low before you press Start.

The dashed line marks the frequency you set. The gold triangle marks the strongest FFT bin, and the read-out above the plot gives that bin's frequency and level. A tone of amplitude 0.20 reads -14.0 dB. The FFT uses \(N = 8192\) points, so it measures only at bins \(\Delta f = f_s/N\) apart: 5.86 Hz at a 48 kHz sample rate (5.38 Hz at 44.1 kHz). The read-out therefore differs from the set frequency by up to half a bin, and a tone that falls between two bins reads up to about 1 dB low because the browser applies a Blackman window. The sample rate and bin width are printed under the plot on wide screens.

This MicroSim supports Chapter 2: Signal Frequency and previews the spectra of Chapter 7: DFT, FFT and Frequency Domain Analysis.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  1. Identify the single spectral peak that a pure sine tone produces in the FFT display and read its frequency and level
  2. Predict how the FFT peak moves along the frequency axis as the tone sweeps from low to high frequency, and relate its position to the pitch they hear
  3. Explain how horizontal position on the plot maps linearly to a frequency between 20 Hz and 10 kHz
  4. Calculate the peak level \(20\log_{10}(A)\) dB for an amplitude \(A\) and verify that halving \(A\) lowers the peak by about 6 dB
  5. Explain why the read-out can differ from the set frequency by up to half a bin width (2.93 Hz at 48 kHz)

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in an introductory signal processing course. The activities take about 20 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sine waves: amplitude, frequency and period
  • Sound as a pressure wave; frequency and pitch
  • Base-10 logarithms (for decibels)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
The read-outs below were measured with a 48 kHz audio device. On a 44.1 kHz device the bins are 5.38 Hz apart, so the frequency read-outs differ from these by a few hertz; each is still within half a bin of the set frequency.

Activity 1: Hear the pitch, see the peak (5 min).

  1. Set your volume low and press Start (440 Hz, amplitude 0.20). One narrow peak appears on the dashed line, and the read-out shows FFT peak: 439.5 Hz, -14.0 dB.
  2. Set the frequency to 220 Hz. The pitch drops by one octave and the peak moves left (read-out 222.7 Hz).
  3. Set 880 Hz (read-out 878.9 Hz), then 1760 Hz (read-out 1757.8 Hz). Each doubling raises the pitch by one octave and doubles the peak's distance from 0 Hz.

Activity 2: Drag the tone across the spectrum (5 min). Press on the plot at the 1 kHz tick and drag slowly to the 6 kHz tick. The frequency label follows the pointer and the peak stays under it; release on the 6 kHz tick and the read-out shows close to 6000 Hz. Then compare two equal 1 kHz steps: drag from the 1 kHz tick to the 2 kHz tick, then from the 8 kHz tick to the 9 kHz tick. Both steps are the same width on the linear axis, but the first is a full octave (ratio 2) while the second is a ratio of only 1.125, about two semitones, so the first sounds like a much larger change in pitch.

Activity 3: Amplitude and decibels (5 min). Set the frequency to 1500 Hz (exactly on a bin at 48 kHz) and complete the table, then compare with \(20\log_{10}(A)\).

Amplitude Predicted level (dB) Read-out level (dB) 0.50 0.40 0.20 0.10 0.05

Expected read-outs: -6.0, -8.0, -14.0, -20.0 and -26.0 dB. Each halving of the amplitude (0.40 to 0.20, 0.20 to 0.10, 0.10 to 0.05) lowers the peak by 6.0 dB, and the peak never moves sideways.

Activity 4: Frequency resolution (5 min). Read the bin width under the plot (\(48000 / 8192 = 5.86\) Hz). Set 1500 Hz: the read-out is exactly 1500.0 Hz because \(1500 / 5.859375 = 256\) is a whole bin. Set 1000 Hz: the read-out is 1002.0 Hz, the centre of bin 171, because \(1000 / 5.859375 = 170.7\). Set 220 Hz: the read-out is 222.7 Hz (bin 38). In every case the error is at most half a bin, 2.93 Hz.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. The amplitude is set to 0.25. What level will the FFT peak show at 1500 Hz? (Answer: \(20\log_{10}(0.25) = -12.0\) dB; the read-out shows -12.0 dB.)
  2. With \(f_s = 48\) kHz and \(N = 8192\), what is the bin width, and why does a 1000 Hz tone read 1002.0 Hz? (Answer: \(48000/8192 = 5.86\) Hz. 1000 Hz lies between bin 170 (996.1 Hz) and bin 171 (1002.0 Hz); it is closer to bin 171, so that bin is the strongest.)
  3. You change the frequency from 440 Hz to 880 Hz without touching the amplitude. What happens to the pitch, the position of the peak and its height? (Answer: the pitch rises one octave, the peak moves right to twice the frequency (878.9 Hz), and the height stays the same (-14.0 dB before, -14.1 dB after).)
  4. The plot spans 0 to 10 kHz across its width. Where must you press to set about 2500 Hz? (Answer: one quarter of the way from the 0 tick to the 10 kHz tick, halfway between the 2 and 3 kHz ticks, because the axis is linear.)
  5. After you press Stop, the peak sinks and disappears within a fraction of a second. What does this tell you about where the peak comes from? (Answer: the FFT only reveals frequencies that are present in the signal; when the tone is silent there is nothing at 440 Hz to show.)

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"A louder tone has a higher frequency." Amplitude and frequency are independent. At 440 Hz, change the amplitude from 0.10 to 0.40: the peak rises from -20.0 dB to -8.0 dB but stays at 439.5 Hz, and the pitch does not change.

"Doubling the amplitude doubles the level in decibels." Decibels are logarithmic: doubling the amplitude adds \(20\log_{10}(2) = 6.0\) dB. Activity 3 shows -20.0 dB at 0.10 and -14.0 dB at 0.20, not -40 dB.

"The FFT measures the exact frequency." It measures the energy in bins a fixed distance apart. A 1000 Hz tone reads 1002.0 Hz at 48 kHz because the nearest bin centre is at 1002.0 Hz.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Sine wave - Wikipedia - amplitude, frequency and period of the pure tone the oscillator generates
  2. Pitch (music) - Wikipedia - how the frequency of a tone relates to the pitch we hear, including octaves
  3. Decibel - Wikipedia - the \(20\log_{10}\) amplitude ratio used for the level axis
  4. Fast Fourier transform - Wikipedia - the algorithm that computes the spectrum
  5. Window function - Wikipedia - the Blackman window and why a tone between bins reads slightly low
  6. OscillatorNode - MDN Web Docs - the Web Audio source behind the p5.sound oscillator
  7. The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing - Steven W. Smith - free online textbook with chapters on the DFT and the FFT

docs.title: Wavelet Explorer: CWT Scalogram and Haar DWT
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/wavelet-explorer/main.html" width="100%" height="594px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows two ways to analyze a signal at several resolutions. Every signal has 256 samples at \(f_s = 256\) Hz, so it lasts 1 s. Choose it from the second list: two tones (8 Hz + 32 Hz), a linear chirp whose frequency rises as \(f(t) = 4 + 56t\) Hz, an 8 Hz tone with a spike of height 3 at \(t = 0.625\) s, a step at \(t = 0.41\) s, or a 4 Hz sine with Gaussian noise (\(\sigma = 0.3\)).

CWT scalogram mode computes

\[W(a,b) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} \sum_n x[n]\,\psi\!\left(\frac{n-b}{a}\right)\]

at 32 log-spaced scales \(a\) (in samples) for the Morlet \(\psi(t) = e^{-t^2/2}\cos 5t\), the Mexican hat \(\psi(t) = (1-t^2)e^{-t^2/2}\) or the Haar wavelet. The color map shows \(|W|\) with time on the x axis. The y axis is labeled with the pseudo-frequency \(f = f_c f_s / a\) on the left and the scale \(a\) on the right, where \(f_c\) is the frequency at which the wavelet's spectrum peaks (0.796, 0.225 and 0.742). The Scale and Position sliders, or a click on the scalogram, choose \((a, b)\): the gold curve on the signal is the dilated wavelet (peak scaled to fit), and the read-outs give \(W(a,b)\) and the largest \(|W|\) in that row. dB color scale maps the top 40 dB of \(|W|\), which reveals weak features. The signal is mirror-extended at both ends.

Haar DWT mode splits the signal into detail coefficients \(d_1 \ldots d_L\) and an approximation \(a_L\) (\(L\) = 1 to 5) with \(a[k] = (x[2k] + x[2k+1])/\sqrt{2}\) and \(d[k] = (x[2k] - x[2k+1])/\sqrt{2}\). Each bar is as wide as the samples its coefficient covers. Details with \(|d| \le T\) are set to zero (gray bars), and the maroon curve is the reconstruction, with its mean squared error (MSE).

This MicroSim supports Chapter 8: Advanced Transforms.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Explain why scale is inversely related to frequency, and convert between scale and pseudo-frequency with \(f = f_c f_s / a\)
  2. Interpret a scalogram to locate a chirp's changing frequency, a tone's band and a transient's time of occurrence
  3. Compare the time and frequency resolution of the Morlet, Mexican hat and Haar wavelets
  4. Calculate Haar approximation and detail coefficients, and the number of coefficients at each level
  5. Analyze how the number of levels and the hard threshold trade noise removal against signal distortion

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Undergraduate students in a signals and systems or digital signal processing course (junior or senior engineering, physics or computer science). Plan 25 minutes for the four activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Sinusoids, frequency and sampling (\(f_s\), samples per cycle)
  • Convolution and correlation as sliding sums
  • The Fourier transform and the idea of a spectrum (Chapters 6 and 7)

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activity 1: Scale and pseudo-frequency (5 min). Start with the defaults: chirp, Morlet, scale \(a = 6.49\) samples, position \(b = 0.500\) s. The read-out converts the scale to \(f = 0.796 \times 256 / 6.49 = 31.4\) Hz, and the largest \(|W|\) in that row is 3.13 at \(t = 0.492\) s; the chirp reaches 31.4 Hz at \((31.4 - 4)/56 = 0.489\) s. Move the scale slider right to \(a = 12.7\) samples: the row is now 16.0 Hz and its maximum moves to 0.219 s (predicted 0.215 s). Larger scale, lower frequency, earlier in the chirp.

Activity 2: Time and frequency resolution (7 min). Choose two tones. With the Morlet wavelet the 8 Hz and 32 Hz tones form two separate bands with a dark gap between them. At \(a = 24.8\) samples (8.2 Hz) the row maximum is 6.20; at \(a = 6.49\) samples (31.4 Hz) it is 3.18. The tones have equal amplitude, but \(|W|\) grows as \(\sqrt{a}\) for a sinusoid, and \(\sqrt{24.8/6.49} = 1.96\). Switch to the Mexican hat and then Haar: the bands spread out and the gap fills in (poorer frequency resolution), and with the Mexican hat the brightest part of the low band sits near 7 Hz, a reminder that pseudo-frequency is approximate. Now choose tone + spike, the Morlet wavelet and dB color scale. The spike draws a cone that is narrow at small scales. Move the scale slider fully left (\(a = 2.12\) samples, 96.0 Hz): the row maximum is 2.06 at \(t = 0.625\) s, and at \(b = 0.645\) s (5 samples later) \(W\) is only 0.09. At \(a = 6.49\) samples the spike gives \(W = 1.18\) at 0.625 s, smaller by \(\sqrt{6.49/2.12}\), while a tone's response grows with scale.

Activity 3: Sparsity and perfect reconstruction (6 min). Choose Haar DWT, step edge, \(L = 5\), \(T = 0\). The read-out shows 10 nonzero coefficients out of 256 (5 approximation + 5 detail) and MSE = 0 (perfect reconstruction): each detail row holds a single bar at the edge (values −0.707, −0.500, −0.354, −1.75 and −1.59 for \(d_1\) to \(d_5\)). With \(L = 1\) the count is 77, and with \(L = 3\) it is 22. Set \(T = 0.40\): only \(d_3\) is removed, 9 coefficients remain and MSE = 0.0005, which equals \(0.354^2/256\).

Activity 4: Denoising by hard thresholding (7 min). Choose noisy sine and \(L = 3\). At \(T = 0\) the error against the clean sine equals that of the noisy input, 0.0821. Raise the threshold: the error falls to 0.0564 at \(T = 0.50\) and 0.0385 at \(T = 1.00\) (the universal threshold \(\sigma\sqrt{2 \ln N} = 0.3\sqrt{2 \ln 256} = 1.00\)). From \(T = 1.05\) every detail is removed and the 32 approximation coefficients alone give 0.0350. Now set \(L = 5\): the error is lowest near \(T = 0.65\) (0.0462) and climbs to 0.0965 at \(T = 2.00\), worse than doing nothing. Over all settings the lowest error is 0.0265, at \(L = 2\) with \(T \ge 1.05\).

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. For the Morlet wavelet (\(f_c = 0.796\)) and \(f_s = 256\) Hz, what scale corresponds to 20 Hz? Answer: \(a = f_c f_s / f = 0.796 \times 256 / 20 = 10.2\) samples.
  2. Two tones have equal amplitudes, at 8 Hz and 32 Hz. Why does the 8 Hz band of the Morlet scalogram reach about twice the \(|W|\) of the 32 Hz band? Answer: with the \(1/\sqrt{a}\) normalization a sinusoid gives \(|W| \propto \sqrt{a}\); the 8 Hz tone matches a scale 4 times larger, so its response is \(\sqrt{4} = 2\) times larger (the sim shows 6.20 and 3.18).
  3. A 256-sample signal is decomposed with \(L = 3\). How many coefficients are in \(d_1\), \(d_2\), \(d_3\) and \(a_3\)? Answer: 128, 64, 32 and 32, which add up to 256.
  4. For the step, \(T = 0.75\) removes \(d_1\), \(d_2\) and \(d_3\) (−0.707, −0.500 and −0.354). Predict the MSE without running the reconstruction. Answer: the Haar DWT is orthonormal, so the squared error equals the energy of the removed coefficients: \((0.5 + 0.25 + 0.125)/256 = 0.0034\), which the sim shows.
  5. At \(L = 5\) and \(T = 2.00\) the denoised sine has a larger error (0.0965) than the noisy input (0.0821). Why? Answer: the large \(d_4\) and \(d_5\) coefficients carry the 4 Hz sine itself; removing them leaves only 8 block averages, each 32 samples long, which is half a period of the sine.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
"Each bright stripe along a band is a separate event." All three wavelets here are real, so \(W(a,b)\) follows the oscillation of the signal and \(|W|\) rises and falls twice per cycle. With two tones the 8 Hz band shows 16 bright patches per second although the tone is steady. Drag the position slider along that row (\(a = 24.8\) samples): the read-out \(W(a,b)\) changes sign 16 times in the 1 s signal, once per half cycle.

"A larger threshold always removes more noise and gives a cleaner signal." Hard thresholding also removes signal. In Activity 4 the error at \(L = 5\) first falls from 0.0821 to 0.0462 and then rises to 0.0965 as \(T\) grows, because the threshold starts deleting the coefficients that describe the sine.

docs.title: Signal Processing Word Cloud
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/signal-processing/sims/wordcloud/main.html" width="100%" height="512px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim displays 51 key terms from signal processing as a word cloud. In the embedded view each term is drawn at a font size equal to half its weight in pixels. The weights run from 18 to 80, so "Signal Processing" (weight 80) is drawn at 40 px and the smallest terms, such as "Notch Filter" (weight 18), are drawn at 9 px. In a larger window, such as fullscreen, every word is scaled up by the same factor so the cloud still fills the window. Each word has a 50% chance of being turned through 90 degrees and receives a random dark color, so every load gives a different arrangement while the size ordering never changes.

There are no sliders or buttons. The only interaction is to reload the page, which runs the placement algorithm again. The terms and weights are stored in words.json in this folder and are drawn with the wordcloud2.js library.

The cloud previews the vocabulary of the book: transforms (Fourier, Z, Laplace, wavelet, Hilbert), filters (lowpass, bandpass, notch, Butterworth, Chebyshev), sampling and rate conversion (aliasing, decimation, interpolation) and system properties (impulse response, causality, linear time-invariance). The weights are rough estimates of how often a term is mentioned in a typical college-level signal processing textbook. They were suggested by an AI assistant and were not counted from a real corpus, so read size as relative emphasis, not as a measured frequency.

The terms are introduced throughout the book, starting with Chapter 2: Introduction to Signals and Systems.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After using this MicroSim, students will be able to:

  1. Recall at least 15 of the 51 signal processing terms shown in the cloud.
  2. Classify the terms into families such as transforms, filters, and sampling and rate conversion.
  3. Relate a word's weight to its rendered font size and compare two words by that ratio.
  4. Evaluate what a word cloud does and does not show, separating how often a term is mentioned from how important it is.
  5. Predict the chapter of this book that introduces a given term.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: College undergraduates in electrical engineering, computer science, data science or applied mathematics at the start of a signal processing course, or reviewing its vocabulary before an exam.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: None. Students do not need to know what any of the terms mean yet.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Reload and compare (3 minutes). Reload the page three times. Positions, rotations and colors change each time, but "Signal Processing" is always the largest word (40 px) and "Filter" (35 px) is always the second largest. Which words are always among the smallest? "Notch Filter", "Phase Shift" and "Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)" share the lowest weight, 18, so they are drawn at 9 px.
  2. Sort into families (10 minutes). On paper, group the 51 terms into families. Count the terms containing the word "Transform" and the terms containing the word "Filter". Seven terms contain "Transform" and seven contain "Filter" (the plain term "Filter" included).
  3. Predict the chapter (10 minutes). For each of Convolution, Aliasing, Z-Transform, Butterworth Filter and Decimation, write down the chapter you expect to introduce it, then check the chapter pages. Convolution is in Chapter 4, Aliasing in Chapter 5, Z-Transform in Chapter 8, Butterworth Filter in Chapter 10 and Decimation in Chapter 13.
  4. Find the gaps (10 minutes). The cloud has "Lowpass Filter", "Bandpass Filter" and "Notch Filter" but no "Highpass Filter", "FIR Filter" or "IIR Filter". Which important terms would you add, and what weight would you give them? Chapter 9 lists High-Pass Filters, FIR Filters and IIR Filters as concepts; Chapter 14 lists Spectrogram. Weights are a judgment call, so justify yours.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
1. Which term is drawn largest, and at what font size? "Signal Processing", weight 80, drawn at 40 px.
  2. "Sinc Function" and "Butterworth Filter" both have weight 30. How large is their text relative to "Signal Processing"? 30 / 80 = 0.375 of its size: 15 px against 40 px.
  3. "Sampling" has weight 60 and "Sampling Theorem" has weight 25. What font size does each get? 30 px and 12.5 px, because size is half the weight.
  4. Why do the positions change on every reload while the sizes do not? Placement and color are chosen at random each time the cloud is drawn; size comes only from the fixed weight in words.json.
  5. A classmate says that because "Noise" (65) is drawn larger than "Convolution" (60), noise is more important to learn. Respond. Size shows an estimate of how often a term is mentioned, not how much effort it takes to learn or how much later material depends on it. A term can be mentioned often and still be easy, or rarely and still be foundational.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
1. "Bigger word means more important topic." Size here encodes an estimated frequency of mention. Reloading shows that size is fixed by weight alone, and Assessment question 5 asks students to separate frequency from importance.
  2. "Words that sit close together are related." Position is random. Reload and the same two words land in different places, so proximity carries no meaning in this cloud.

docs.text: The word list and weights were first generated with an AI assistant; the prompt and response are kept on the Wordcloud prompt page. Earlier experiments placed the words with vis-network text nodes; that page explains why wordcloud2.js, which places the words much better, is the library used here.

docs.title: Signal Processing Stories
docs.text: These stories were created mostly by generative AI. I used a generative AI to generate some story ideas and then wrote some detailed prompts that created a narrative for the stories. Each story also included narratives that were fed into the OpenAI DALL-E 3 text to image system. You can see examples of the narrative prompts, the image prompts and the reference prompts.

docs.title: Frequency Hopping: The Untold Story of Hedy Lamarr, Engineer and Hollywood Star
docs.text:
In the glittering world of 1940s Hollywood, Hedy Lamarr led an extraordinary double life - by day, she was a glamorous movie star dubbed "the most beautiful woman in the world," but by night, she was a brilliant inventor whose mind would revolutionize modern technology. After escaping her controlling first husband, an Austrian arms manufacturer where she secretly absorbed technical knowledge about weapons systems, Hedy fled to America and became a film star. During World War II, she conceptualized frequency-hopping technology to prevent enemy jamming of radio-controlled torpedoes, collaborating with composer George Antheil to develop a synchronization method inspired by player pianos. Though their 1942 patent was initially dismissed by the U.S. Navy, who couldn't fathom that an actress could contribute to military technology, their groundbreaking invention eventually became the foundation for secure military communications, GPS, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi used by billions today. Hedy's remarkable story exemplifies the qualities of a great engineer - curiosity, creativity, persistence, and courage - and stands as a powerful reminder that innovation can come from unexpected places, regardless of gender or profession.

Read the Frequency Hopping Story

docs.title: Algorithm of the Century: Cooley and Tukey's FFT Revolution
docs.text:
This tells the story of how James Cooley and John Tukey revolutionized signal processing by developing the Fast Fourier Transform algorithm in 1965 during the Cold War. Born from the practical need to detect Soviet nuclear tests, their breakthrough reduced calculation time from N² to N log N operations, making previously impossible computations feasible on 1960s computers. The algorithm spread rapidly across scientific disciplines after being published, enabling real-time signal analysis for applications ranging from seismology to astronomy. The FFT ultimately transformed entire industries—creating the foundation for digital signal processing, enabling technologies like MRI machines, digital audio, telecommunications, and countless other innovations that shape our modern digital world. Their story illustrates how elegant mathematical solutions to efficiency problems can have far greater impact than raw computing power alone.

Read the FFT Story

docs.title: The Information Revolutionary: Claude Shannon's Digital Gamble
docs.text:
At Bell Labs in the 1940s, a young engineer named Claude Shannon made a revolutionary observation that would transform the world: information could be measured, transmitted, and processed mathematically. Working in the premier think-tank of his era, Shannon developed information theory, introducing concepts like the "bit" and showing how any information could be encoded in binary digits. His groundbreaking 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" laid the foundation for the digital age, enabling everything from satellite communications to the internet. Shannon's work revealed the fundamental limits of data compression and transmission, providing the mathematical framework that makes modern digital communication possible. His insights into noise, entropy, and channel capacity became the bedrock of signal processing, proving that with clever mathematics, reliable communication was possible even through noisy channels. Shannon's story demonstrates how abstract mathematical thinking can solve practical problems and create entire industries.

Read the Shannon Story

docs.title: The Moog Revolution: Analog Synthesis Meets Electronic Innovation
docs.text:
Before Robert Moog revolutionized music in the 1960s, electronic instruments were complex, expensive machines relegated to research labs and experimental studios. Musicians were limited to traditional acoustic instruments or primitive electronic devices that required teams of technicians to operate. Moog approached the challenge differently, combining his engineering background with his passion for music to create modular synthesizers that musicians could actually use. His breakthrough innovations included voltage-controlled oscillators, filters, and amplifiers that could be patched together like an electronic puzzle. The Moog synthesizer democratized electronic music creation, putting the power of sound synthesis into the hands of individual artists. From the otherworldly sounds of "Switched-On Bach" to the iconic bass lines of funk and disco, Moog's instruments shaped the soundtrack of modern music while demonstrating how signal processing principles could create entirely new forms of artistic expression.

Read the Moog Story

docs.title: Echoes in the Sky: Robert Watson-Watt and the Radar Revolution
docs.text:
In 1934, with Nazi rearmament casting a shadow over Europe, British engineer Robert Watson-Watt faced an impossible challenge: how to defend Britain's skies against an increasingly powerful German air force. When asked to investigate the feasibility of a "death ray" weapon, Watson-Watt instead proposed something far more practical yet equally revolutionary—radar. Working against time and skepticism, he demonstrated that radio waves could detect aircraft at unprecedented distances. His team developed the Chain Home radar network, a string of coastal stations that would give Britain its first early warning system. During the Battle of Britain, these "echoes in the sky" provided crucial advance notice of incoming German bombers, allowing RAF fighters to intercept threats with devastating effectiveness. Watson-Watt's radar technology, built on principles of signal processing and electromagnetic wave propagation, not only helped save Britain but became fundamental to modern navigation, weather forecasting, and countless civilian applications.

Read the Radar Story

docs.title: The Wavelet Revolution: Ingrid Daubechies' Mathematical Journey
docs.text:
Ingrid Daubechies, a brilliant Belgian mathematician working in her garden in 1980, saw mathematical patterns where others saw only flowers and soil. Recognizing the limitations of traditional Fourier transforms in analyzing real-world signals that change over time, she worked tirelessly to develop a revolutionary alternative. In 1987, despite skepticism from her male-dominated field, Daubechies created the first orthogonal wavelets with compact support—mathematical building blocks that could capture both frequency and time information in signals. Her breakthrough transformed numerous fields, from digital image compression to medical imaging, ultimately becoming fundamental to modern technologies like JPEG2000 and MP3 files. Breaking glass ceilings, she received the MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship and became the first female president of the International Mathematical Union and the first female full professor in Princeton's Mathematics Department. Beyond her mathematical contributions, Daubechies demonstrated that the qualities of great engineers and scientists—persistence, creativity, courage, and connecting abstract ideas to practical needs—are not limited by gender, creating waves of change that continue to inspire diverse new generations of mathematicians and engineers.

Read the Wavelets Story

docs.title: Story Ideas
docs.text:
Prompt

Please consult the course-description.md file in the Project knowledge area.

I would like to create some short graphic novels to tell stories about how individuals contributed to the field of signal processing over the last 100 years starting with the work of Claude Shannon at Bell Labs. Each story should be understandable by high-school students and not require complex calculus to understand. However, the stories can highlight the role of mathematics in innovation.

I am interested in stories about how individuals were not willing to put up with the status que and were willing to be advocates for change and new ways of doing things.

Can you please suggest some ideas for these stories? Create a catchy title for each story and create a one paragraph description of the story.

Let me search for some key figures in signal processing history, starting with Claude Shannon, to ensure accuracy in my suggestions.

Let me also search for a more diverse set of signal processing pioneers to give you varied story ideas:

Let me also search for additional signal processing pioneers to give you a more diverse set of story ideas:

Let me search for one more pioneer to give you a diverse set of story ideas:

Based on my research and the information provided, here are some engaging story ideas for graphic novels about signal processing pioneers who challenged the status quo. Each story is designed to be accessible to high school students while highlighting the mathematical aspects of signal processing innovations.

docs.title: Response
docs.text: I'll create some engaging stories about signal processing innovators who challenged the status quo. These graphic novels should be accessible to high school students while highlighting the mathematical aspects of their innovations.

docs.title: "The Information Revolutionary: Claude Shannon's Digital Gamble"
docs.text: Claude Shannon, a young engineer at Bell Labs in the 1940s, defies conventional thinking by reimagining how information itself can be understood through mathematics. This story follows Shannon as he develops information theory while working on wartime cryptography projects, showing how his playful nature (riding unicycles through Bell Labs hallways while juggling) and mathematical brilliance led to creating the foundation for our digital world. The story highlights how Shannon's revolutionary 1948 paper that defined "bits" of information transformed communication theory and laid the groundwork for computers, smartphones, and the internet we use today.

docs.title: "Wavelets of Change: Ingrid Daubechies' Mathematical Revolution"
docs.text: This story follows Belgian mathematician Ingrid Daubechies as she develops wavelet theory in the 1980s and early 90s, revolutionizing signal processing with her "mathematical building blocks." Initially facing skepticism in a male-dominated field, Daubechies persevered to create compact wavelets that enabled everything from MP3 music files to medical imaging. The narrative follows her from her garden (which serves as a metaphor for her mathematical work) to her becoming the first woman to receive certain prestigious mathematics awards, showing students how abstract mathematics can solve real-world problems and break through gender barriers.

docs.title: "Algorithm of the Century: Cooley and Tukey's FFT Revolution"
docs.text: In the midst of the Cold War, James Cooley of IBM and John Tukey of Princeton tackled what seemed like an impossible mathematical challenge - making Fourier transforms fast enough for real-time processing. Their 1965 Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm, motivated by the need to detect Soviet nuclear tests, dramatically reduced calculation time and revolutionized signal processing. The story explores how their algorithm, which rediscovered work from Gauss 160 years earlier, became one of the most important computational tools of the modern era, enabling everything from MRI machines to digital music.

docs.title: "Hyperbolic Visions: Maryam Mirzakhani's Mathematical Journey"
docs.text: Growing up in Iran, Maryam Mirzakhani initially wanted to be a writer before discovering her passion for mathematics. This story traces her journey from being the first Iranian woman to win gold medals at the International Mathematical Olympiad to becoming the first woman to receive the Fields Medal, mathematics' highest honor. Though her work focused on hyperbolic surfaces and complex geometry rather than direct signal processing applications, her revolutionary approaches to mathematical problems represent the kind of breakthrough thinking that has advanced all scientific fields, including signal processing.

docs.title: "Echo Chamber Breaker: The Digital Filter Revolution"
docs.text: This story follows a composite character inspired by several pioneers who developed digital filtering techniques in the 1970s and 80s. Our protagonist challenges the analog signal processing establishment by creating new mathematical models for digital filters that would eventually become standard in everything from noise-canceling headphones to voice assistants. The story shows how mathematical persistence and computational thinking transformed signal processing from analog to digital realms against significant resistance from established experts.

docs.title: "The Missing Signal: Rediscovering Hidden Pioneers"
docs.text:
This multi-timeline story follows a modern-day student who discovers the overlooked contributions of women and minority scientists to signal processing history. As our protagonist researches the field for a school project, they uncover forgotten papers, uncredited innovations, and the social barriers that kept brilliant minds from receiving proper recognition. Through parallel storytelling, we see both the historical innovations and the modern-day quest for historical justice, showing students how mathematics has been a collaborative effort across diverse communities.

Each of these stories emphasizes how innovation comes from challenging conventional thinking, using mathematics to solve complex problems, and persisting through obstacles both technical and social. The narratives aim to inspire high school students by showing how mathematics connects to real-world applications and how individual passion can transform entire fields.
